# Google

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the **public domain**. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia<note>Handwritten notes, stamps, or sketches made by previous readers or librarians in the margins of a book.</note></term> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

### Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition<note>Commonly abbreviated as OCR, this is the mechanical or electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten, or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note></term> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. <term>Copyright infringement<note>The use of works protected by copyright law without permission, infringing certain exclusive rights granted to the copyright holder.</note></term> liability can be quite severe.

### About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at <insert>http://books.google.com/</insert>

## About this book

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books available online.

It has survived long enough to no longer be protected by copyright and has become part of the **public domain**. A public domain book is a book that was never protected by copyright or whose legal copyright terms have expired. The classification of a book as being in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are a link to the past; they represent a wealth of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.

Comments, notes, and other <term>marginalia<note>original: "annotazioni a margine"; these are handwritten notes, stamps, or marks made by previous readers or librarians in the margins of a book.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file as a testament to the long journey the book has taken from the original publisher to the library, and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them universally available. Public domain books belong to the public, and we are merely their custodians. However, this work is expensive; therefore, to continue offering this service, we have taken some steps to prevent illicit use by commercial entities, including the imposition of restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Do not use these files for commercial purposes* We designed Google Book Search for use by individual private users, and we ask that you use these files for personal, non-commercial use.

+ *Do not send automated queries* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google. If you are conducting research in the field of machine translation, <term>optical character recognition<note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the process of converting images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note>, or other fields where you need to use large amounts of text, we invite you to contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain the watermark* The Google "watermark" that appears in each file is essential for informing users about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Do not remove it.

+ *Ensure legal use* Regardless of how you use it, remember that it is your responsibility to ensure that your use is legal. Do not assume that because a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, it is also in the public domain for users in other countries. The criteria for determining whether a book is protected by copyright vary from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether a specific use of a book is permitted. Do not assume that because a book appears in Google Book Search, it means it can be used in any way and in any country in the world. Penalties for copyright violations can be very severe.

# ON THE TUSCAN POETRY

## BY MESSER ANGELO POLIZIANO.

---

### I.

## THE FIFTEENTH CENTURY IN ITALY.
## THE LITERATURE OF THE CONFEDERATION.
## FLORENCE, THE MEDICI, POLIZIANO.

---

> "Now all poetry has failed
> And empty are the houses of Parnassus....
> How can I hope that a Dante should arise,
> When already there is none found who knows how to read him?....
> The horns have sounded
> From every side to the retreat:
> The season is turned:
> If it shall return I know not; but I believe it will be late."

Thus <term>Franco Sacchetti</term> <note>A Florentine poet and novelist (c. 1332–1400) best known for his "Trecentonovelle."</note>, in a lament <note>original: "deploratoria"</note> for the death of <term>Boccaccio</term> <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the Decameron and one of the foundational figures of Italian literature.</note>, uttered these latest words on the great literature of the 14th century, and signified at the same time that grim foreboding—rarely in vain—which every vigorous generation holds regarding its successors. And in truth, just as a discus at the end of its course still marks a few turns in the sand through the force of its initial impulse, then wavers, then falls; so it was with Italian literature at the decline of the 1300s and the beginning of the century that followed. The allegorical vision of <term>Dante</term> <note>Dante Alighieri (c. 1265–1321), author of the Divine Comedy.</note>, already faded in the *<term>Quadriregio</term>* <note>original: "The Four Realms," an allegorical poem by Federico Frezzi written in imitation of Dante.</note>, finished darkening in certain poems barely mentioned by scholars: the elegiac psychologizing of <term>Petrarca</term> <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the humanist poet famous for his sonnets.</note>, already evaporated into the elegant...

<margin>
¹ <term>F. Sacchetti</term>, in *Rhymes of Cino da Pistoia and others of the 14th century*, Florence, Barbèra, 1863, page 528 (Diamond Edition).
</margin>

<summary>This page introduces the literary landscape of 15th-century Italy, using Franco Sacchetti's lament for Boccaccio to illustrate the perceived decline of Italian poetry after the era of Dante and Petrarch.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Italian literature, 14th century, 15th century, Franco Sacchetti, Boccaccio, Dante, Petrarch, Quadriregio, Florence, Medici</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of the literary transition from the late 14th century (the Trecento) into the 15th century (the Quattrocento). It explores the immediate aftermath of Boccaccio's death and the division of Italian literature into two distinct paths: a popular, vernacular tradition and a scholarly, humanist movement.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

the trite imaginings of <term>Montemagno</term> <note>Buonaccorso da Montemagno (c. 1391–1429), a jurist and poet whose work often imitated Petrarch.</note> turn sour among the strained phrases of <term>Cino Rinuccini</term> <note>A Florentine poet (c. 1350–1417) known for his polemical defense of the "Three Crowns" against early humanists.</note> and vanish in the slight imitations of <term>Giusto de' Conti</term> <note>A poet (died 1449) famous for his collection "The Beautiful Hand," which followed Petrarch’s style.</note>: regarding <term>Boccaccio</term>, who truly understood his hidden aims? Who continued his true and broad representation of the senses? What remained was the style—miserably stammered by a few, though nobly resumed by <term>Battista Alberti</term> <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), the quintessential "Renaissance Man," who sought to prove that the Italian vernacular could be as noble as Latin.</note>—which for most became a source of affectation and falsehood. Nor could it have happened otherwise. Those three miracles of the 1300s <note>Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio, often called the "Three Crowns."</note>, although they drew their intentions and methods from their own age, nevertheless advanced so far beyond their contemporaries in their conception of art and their use of learning: the latter neither wished to follow the medieval traditions alone after such a great example, nor did they know how to aid and continue the renewal those three had begun with adequate strength. They contented themselves with the outward forms, reproducing them in a counterfeit and impoverished way due to a lack of aptitude and practice. In short, the <term>triumvirate</term> <note>The "Three Crowns" of Italian literature: Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.</note> received loving admiration, even adoration, from the Italians, but left behind no school of followers.

Immediately after the death of Boccaccio [1375], two general tendencies and two facts began to reveal themselves, which, developing over the following hundred years, constitute the literary character of the 1400s <note>The Quattrocento.</note>.

<margin>An ink bracket marks the following section in the original manuscript.</margin>

On one hand, the popular and middle-class tradition—mixed with religious and romantic sentiments and drawing more than once from pure reality—having already been overwhelmed in the 1300s by the splendor of the triumvirate, now reawakens, regains its strength, and launches itself freely and restfully into the field. From this come the sacred and chivalric legends and, in their new dress, the poems in **eight-line stanzas** <note>original: "ottava rima," the classic meter of Italian epic poetry.</note> and the **stage representations** <note>original: "rappresentanze," referring to the *Sacre Rappresentazioni* or religious mystery plays.</note>. From this comes the satire of <term>Burchiello</term> <note>Domenico di Giovanni (1404–1449), known as Burchiello, a barber-poet famous for his nonsensical and satirical verse.</note> and his imitators; the **hymns of praise** <note>original: "laude."</note>, the **ballads**, the **carnival songs**, the **rhymed jokes** <note>original: "barzellette."</note>, and the **improvised verses** <note>original: "strambotti," a form of short, often satirical or amorous, folk poetry.</note>; all genres which, though wrongly despised by critics and seekers of elegance, are nonetheless the true poetic heritage of the 1400s and reflect its life and art, reuniting themselves at once with the pure 1300s through their ingenuity and the frankness of their forms. On the other hand, the men of letters—secretly aware of their own insufficiency in emulating the examples of their great predecessors—devoted themselves instead to treasuring knowledge and science, for which the three illustrious Florentines had come to be admired by their age even more than for the power of their inventions. They devoted themselves to resuming the work of restoration...

<summary>The author describes the decline of Italian literature following the "Three Crowns" and the subsequent split into two paths: a vibrant, popular vernacular tradition and a scholarly movement focused on classical learning.</summary>
<keywords>literary decline, Trecento, Quattrocento, popular poetry, Humanism, Florentine literature, poetic forms</keywords>

the Roman work begun by those men with devout ardor but left well short of the point of perfection to which they had led the Italian renewal. And behold; for every Petrarch who went searching the cities *of the barbarians*¹ <note>original: "dei barbari." Petrarch and later humanists used this term in the classical sense to refer to non-Italian regions, particularly Germany and France.</note> in search of some forgotten work of Cicero; for every Boccaccio who climbed with trembling joy into the library of <term>Montecassino</term> <note>The historic Benedictine abbey, which at the time had fallen into neglect, its precious library left exposed to the elements.</note>, and amidst the grass grown high on the floor—while the wind blew freely through the smashed windows and the doors left without locks, shaking the dust accumulated for many years on the immortal volumes—was indignant to find them missing the small parchment gatherings from which the stupid ignorance of the monks had made <term>amulets</term> <note>original: "brevi." These were small scraps of parchment containing prayers or charms sold to the superstitious.</note> to sell to women;² for every one such man, I say, behold dozens of them rising up, braving the dangers of long journeys, crossing mountains and seas, wandering poor and alone through inhospitable lands, among peoples either hostile or suspicious and whose language they did not know—among Germans, among Turks. They went, they said, to liberate the "glorious fathers" from the *prisons* <note>original: "ergastoli." A term used by Poggio Bracciolini to describe the neglected monastic libraries where ancient manuscripts were "imprisoned."</note> of the *Germans* and the *Gauls*.³ And the barons from the towers of the castle and the serfs from the soil perhaps laughed to see those thin Italians passing by, with their fixed gaze and dreamy air, laboriously climbing the ruined stairs of some Gothic abbey and descending radiant with a <term>codex</term> <note>A manuscript book of ancient text.</note> under their arm: they laughed, and did not know that from that codex was about to emerge the word and the freedom that was to level those towers to the ground and break those chains; they did not know that those poor strangers were the prophets of a god still unknown but the imminent successor of the medieval god—that deity with whose sanction you serfs were given as food to the baron's hounds, and your women burned as witches by the monks. Even today, the learned fanaticism of the 1400s is laughed at in Italy with injustice and ingratitude by those who enjoy its fruits; it is laughed at most zestfully by the most ignorant. But one is forced to admire the faith and the religion that the 15th century held for science and discovery, when one reads how <term>Guarino of Verona</term> <note>A pioneering humanist (1374–1460) who spent years in Constantinople learning Greek and collecting manuscripts.</note>, having lost in a shipwreck two chests of books he had brought from Constantinople, turned grey from grief...

...sorrow;¹ how <term>Panormita</term> <note>The nickname of Antonio Beccadelli (1394–1471), a renowned Italian poet and diplomat from Palermo.</note> sold a farm, perhaps that of his ancestors, in order to buy a manuscript of **Titus Livy**;² how ancient manuscripts were stolen with the same sense of devotion that some centuries earlier was reserved for the relics of saints;³ and, in the same way that a few centuries before one king would send another a most precious gift of a fragment of the wood of the cross, so, in this age, the Republic of Lucca testified its gratitude to Duke Filippo Maria of Milan with the present of two manuscripts;⁴ and **Cosimo de' Medici**, as a token of peace, sent to Alfonso of Naples a volume of Titus Livy, which was immediately opened with great greed by the king, against the advice of his courtiers and physicians. Influenced by the suspicions of those times, they begged him to be careful, fearing that in that book—a gift from an enemy—there might be hidden a poison that could kill a man just by being inhaled.⁵ Truly, that was a crusade of civilization; just as that brotherhood in human studies by means of the Latin language was almost a literary Catholicism against barbarism and spiritual tyranny. And **Poggio Bracciolini** gives proud testimony of this when, in the midst of the clerics of the <term>Council of Constance</term> <note>An ecumenical council (1414–1418) that ended the Western Schism but also condemned reformers like Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague.</note> and the bandits of Emperor Sigismund, he dared—perhaps alone in Europe—to venerate the great figure of **Jerome of Prague** before the pyre and to take into his heart the final notes of the hymn that the martyr of free inquiry raised to the throne of God amidst the vortex of flames fueled by the scepter and the <term>crosier</term> <note>original: "pastorale." The hooked staff of a bishop, here symbolizing the Church's role in the execution.</note>.⁶

But it is argued: this fervor of the Italian <term>men of the fifteenth century</term> <note>original: "quattrocentisti."</note> for antiquity was untimely; it came to interrupt the thread of national traditions in the art of the Middle Ages and prevented its development. As an Italian, I cannot even admit the doubt as to whether it would have been expedient for the originality of European literatures if nothing remained and nothing were rediscovered of Greek and Roman antiquity: I further deny that the scholarly movement of the 15th century was untimely or outside the national tradition. restoration was felt and acted upon by our people. Dante believed in the Roman Empire returning with Caesar, whenever that might be, to the Capitol, and he wrote in Latin—just as Petrarch wrote in Latin, waiting for it to return as the civil language of a renewed Italy and hastening with his prayers the republic of the <term>Scipios</term> <note>A famous family of Roman generals and statesmen, most notably Scipio Africanus, who defeated Hannibal.</note>. The chroniclers of the 13th century called Florence the daughter of Rome, saying she was built in the image of Rome by Caesar; in the feudal lords of Fiesole who harassed the commune, they could see only the descendants of <term>Catiline</term> <note>A Roman senator who led a famous conspiracy to overthrow the Republic; he was defeated in battle near Pistoia, near Florence.</note>, hereditary enemies of the senate; the nobles of the first circle of the city boasted of their pure Roman blood. Thus, **Poliziano** could also rightly call the city *Meonian*,¹ and could well say—as Catullus might have said of the Rome of his own time—that in her, *Athens had been transported with all its soil and every piece of its furniture*.² And if the people of Pavia, until the last century, celebrated the church office of a saint for **Boethius**,³ if Mantua held its **Virgil** as a saint and stamped his image on their coins and adorned their free banners with it, and in the feast of St. Paul sang a hymn where the Apostle of the Gentiles was introduced weeping over the mausoleum of the poet,⁴ if Dante, in agreement with his time, placed **Trajan** in paradise,⁵ what wonder is it that **Ficino** attempted to intersperse some maxims of **Plato** into the church liturgy?⁶ And if **Pomponio Leto**, out of love for Roman antiquity to which he had consecrated his free and proud soul and his impoverished life, changed the Christian names of the members of his academy into pagan ones; if he divided time by <term>calends</term> <note>The first day of the month in the ancient Roman calendar.</note>; if on the anniversary of the founding of Rome he prostrated himself with his followers before the statue of **Romulus Quirinus**; was this not a consequence—a fantastical one if you will, but still a consequence—of the Italian Renaissance having been inaugurated in the name of ancient Rome? This had been true since the day that the <term>monk of Brescia</term> <note>Arnold of Brescia (c. 1090–1155), a scholar and reformer who called for the church to renounce political power and helped establish a revolutionary Roman Republic.</note>, in the presence of the city of the apostles and martyrs, cried out to the people: "Let us rebuild the

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Italian Renaissance was a continuation of a political movement to reclaim Roman identity. It connects the cultural rebirth of the 15th century to the communal revolutions of the 12th century, while explaining why a "national" Italian literature was slow to form during the early 1400s.</meta>

<page-num>XII</page-num>

-> # ANGELO POLIZIANO <-

[...at the] Capitoline Hill, should the senate, the equestrian order, the consulate, and the tribunes be restored? The classical movement of the 15th century, therefore, proceeds directly from the political movement of the 12th century—that is, from the rebirth of the indigenous Roman principle against the Germanic feudal principle and against the papacy. How much glory resides in this final consequence of the <term>revolution of the communes</term> <note>The period starting in the 11th-12th centuries when Italian cities overthrew feudal lords to form self-governing republics.</note> will be easily seen by anyone who reflects on how Italy, at the same time it was opening a new world to industry and trade with **Columbus**, was also revealing and restoring the ancient world to reason, to imagination, to art, and to science; and it gave both of these worlds to Europe.

Thus, it happened that in the first fifty or sixty years of the 15th century, no properly national literature in the Italian language existed. This occurred partly because bourgeois and popular poetry attracted the masses—matching their understanding without requiring effort—and partly because the learned scholars did not care to address the people, believing that erudition alone was worthy of pursuit. In those days, remembering was admired more than inventing, and scholarship was seen as a form of creation. By "national literature," I mean that which rises above the divisions of schools and classes to become a mirror for the nation’s thought, following its movements and representing its ideals. The reason for this absence must also be sought in the political conditions of the time.

The literature of the 13th and 14th centuries—like a spark from the friction of two stones, or like lightning from the collision of two clouds—erupted from the conflicts of the Church with the Empire, then of the people with the Church and the Empire, and finally of the commoners against the established citizens. The indigenous element against the Germanic, the **bourgeoisie** <term>The middle class of merchants and professionals.</term> against **feudalism** <term>The medieval social system based on land ownership and military service.</term>, secularism against the **clergy** <term>The body of all people ordained for religious duties, especially in the Christian Church.</term>, reason against authority, the real against the ideal, sentiment against convention and mysticism—these were the true drivers of that literature. But the papacy, divided for seventy whole years between two or three contenders, was slapped by every prince and by the priests themselves in the councils of Constance and Basel. Meanwhile, a <term>soldier of fortune</term> <note>Specifically Francesco Sforza, who defied the Pope while ruling the city of Fermo.</note> established himself in the Marches—a region so often fatal to the emperors of the 13th century—signing his letters *“From our Girifalco in Fermo, despite Peter and Paul”*;¹ the papacy,

<page-num>XIII</page-num>

-> # ANGELO POLIZIANO. XIII <-

...not only the rages of Dante and Petrarch, but it had even become unworthy of the mockery of Boccaccio and Sacchetti. *Pope Martin isn't worth a penny* <note>original: "Papa Martino Non vale un quattrino"</note>—this couplet, sung behind the successor of Gregory VII, Innocent III, and Boniface VIII <note>These were the great "political" popes of the Middle Ages who asserted supreme authority over kings.</note> by the children of <term>Guelph Florence</term> <note>The Guelphs were the political faction that traditionally supported the Pope; the fact that even their children mocked him shows how far papal prestige had fallen.</note>, was the only sequel to Saint Peter’s tirade in Canto XXVII of the *Paradiso* <note>In Dante's *Divine Comedy*, Saint Peter delivers a famous, fiery speech against the corruption of the Church.</note>; it was the only poetry the papacy deserved in the 15th century. 

And what of the Empire? Who in Italy cared for the Empire anymore? Let the last of the House of Luxembourg—Sigismund, of that house which had stirred such hatred and love in the previous century—trade his alliances as he pleased, enlarge his hereditary lands, or act as the policeman for the priests at the **Council of Constance** <note>A church council (1414–1418) that ended the Great Western Schism but failed to reform the Church's core issues.</note>; Italy hardly knew he existed. Already, democracy had everywhere given way to tyrants—who inevitably emerge from democracy when it is poorly organized—transforming themselves into princes; or else the envious and fearful middle class had raised up lords to oppose the common people.

<margin>•</margin> Do you remember how Michele di Lando ended? He was the **Cavaignac** <note>Louis-Eugène Cavaignac was a 19th-century French general who suppressed a workers' uprising; the author compares him to Michele di Lando, who led the <term>Ciompi Revolt</term> (the 1378 rebellion of wool-carders) only to eventually side with the middle class against his own followers.</note> of the **Ciompi**, whose reward for saving the middle class from the vengeance of the commoners was to be driven into exile by those very people, as is always the case. The same obscurity that surrounds the end of that popular hero also enshrouds the slow fading of Florentine democracy. Intimidated by executions, scattered by exiles, flattered, or perhaps broken by poverty, the common people fell silent, withdrew, and vanished. They no longer appeared except to curse the losers or applaud the winning masters. Oligarchies took their place, followed by the dominance of a single man or a single family. 

Nor did these princes possess or even feel those great ambitions for which—according to politicians and, unfortunately, even poets—tyranny is sometimes forgiven. Since Giovan Galeazzo Visconti, none of them had ordered a "Crown of Italy" from their jeweler. Instead, there were the inglorious battles between the Angevins in the south and center, followed by the Angevins and Aragonese; skirmishes between the Venetian Senate (whose greed cannot be called ambition because it is too selfish), the weakness of Filippo Maria Visconti, and the cunning of Cosimo de' Medici; and the roaming of the mer... <meta>catchword: mer- (likely "mercenaries")</meta>

<page-num>XIV</page-num>

-> # ANGELO POLIZIANO. <-

...paths of fortune <note>The transcription reads "snade," likely an error for "strade" (roads/paths).</note> from one side to another, and a brave or lucky or shrewd man rising to the throne: these are the facts of the first half of the century, providing the stimuli, occasions, and subjects for a national literature. In truth, the only literature possible in those years was that of the **antiquarians** <note>Scholars and collectors obsessed with recovering the physical and literary remains of Ancient Rome and Greece.</note>, who—in the fervor of their discoveries and their adoration of the past—had no leisure to look at the present. They either did not notice it, or they only caught its fleeting and false appearances. Yet deep accents of indignation and love, like an echo of another time, were heard from time to time; though it is not given to us to gather them. Furthermore, those very antiquarians were preparing the future through the tools of criticism.

But the necessary progression of events caused a most notable change toward the middle of the century—one perhaps not sufficiently noticed—in the civil and literary conditions of Italy. First of all, due to the **Fall of Constantinople [1453]** <note>The capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman Turks, which sent a wave of Greek scholars and manuscripts fleeing into Italy.</note>, our homeland became the sole heir and preserver of ancient civilization, just as it was already the organizer of the new. This provided the stimulus for a more active and vital literature, an effect made even greater by the **invention of printing [1440... 1450]**, which very soon passed from Germany to us [1465]. 

Add to this that the end of the **Western Schism [1438]** <note>The period where multiple claimants to the papacy divided the Church; its end stabilized Rome as the center of the Catholic world.</note> made the papacy stable in Rome under a succession of more capable popes. Furthermore, the establishment of the **Aragonese** in Naples [1441] and the **Sforza** in Lombardy [1447], the new dignity of the **Este** family [1450] in Ferrara, and the rise of the **Medici** in Florence, better defined the boundaries and relations of the major Italian states. This led the peninsula to a more peaceful and ordered way of life. Under the shadow of this confederation <note>Refers to the Peace of Lodi (1454), which established a balance of power between the five major Italian states.</note>, forty years of flourishing, if not most glorious, independence began—years so often remembered and lamented later by the historians **Machiavelli** and **Guicciardini**. 

In this quiet, comforted by material prosperity and cheered by pastimes, festivals, and civil and princely magnificences, Italian poetry climbed back from the streets and squares into the palaces and royal courts. There it struck or reaffirmed an alliance—a bit servile, to tell the truth, as often happens with newly established powers—with classical literature. And as the confederation had especially three centers around which the minor forces gathered: Naples for the south, Mi- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely referring to "Milano" (Milan) for the north.</note>

# XV

-> # ANGELO POLIZIANO. <-

...Milan for the North, Florence for the center: thus the literature of the confederation <note>Refers to the loose alliance of Italian city-states during the Renaissance.</note> had three schools or three capitals; Naples, with a display of erudition and a luxury of forms proceeding strictly through imitation, which later produced **Sannazzaro** <note>Jacopo Sannazzaro (1458–1530), famous for his pastoral work *Arcadia*.</note>; not Milan, which had too little in **Bellincioni** and **Visconti** and was reserved as a capital for a later renewal, but Ferrara with its dukes, already hosts to the troubadours, with its chivalric traditions and its noble and magnificent air, which opened the age of **Lombard poetry** splendidly with **Boiardo** <note>Matteo Maria Boiardo, author of the epic *Orlando Innamorato*.</note>; and lastly Florence, always democratic on one hand, and on the other, the harmonizer of diverse elements in art, in the same way that in the political order, under the **Medici**, it was the preserver of the balance. And this harmonization was necessary and was, as we shall see in its place, more profitable than that famous political balance.

For it was necessary above all to start from the beginning, and to root out the prejudice that only Latin was a worthy instrument of art and that Italian should be abandoned to the common people or used at most for trifles. This prejudice was born from the idea, constant in Italy, of the Restoration <note>The "Rinascimento" or rebirth of classical antiquity.</note>, for the love of which our vernacular was the last thing written by the **Neolatins** <note>The humanists who revived the use of classical Latin as a living literary language.</note>; nor did **Dante** himself at first consider it fit for anything other than writing love verses to women; it grew through the disdain that **Petrarch** and **Boccaccio** affected toward their own Italian works; it gained more ground the more the glory of writing in Latin extended, as Latin books were published to illustrate nearly the entire scope of knowledge, and that dead tongue bent itself admirably to the uses, needs, and even the pleasures of the day through the work of true and strong geniuses like **Poggio** <note>Poggio Bracciolini, a famous humanist and papal secretary.</note> and **Pontano** <note>Giovanni Pontano, a leading humanist in Naples.</note>. Thus it is less surprising that in Florence itself, scholars and collectors of manuscripts, like **Nicolò Niccoli**, were indignant that others found anything admirable and rare in Petrarch and Boccaccio, and especially in Dante. How? This "ignorant of all things" <note>original: *rerum omnium.... ignarum*</note>, this "erring" man <note>original: *errantem*</note>, this crude fellow who is not ashamed to write so ineptly in Latin, preferred over **Virgil**? One who showed he had "not even touched what remained of the pagan books in his time" <note>original: *non aver pur toccato quel che al suo tempo rimaneva dei libri pagani*</note>, **FROM WHICH HIS ART CHIEFLY DEPENDED** <note>original: *UNDE MAXIME ARS SUA DEPENDEBAT*</note>? One who had only read "the quiddities of friars and such annoyances" <note>original: *quolibeta fratrum atque huiusmodi molestias?* – referring to the dense scholastic theology of the Middle Ages.</note> Out with the...

# XVI

-> ## ANGELO POLIZIANO. <-

"A barbarian from the council of the learned! Let him be left to the shoemakers, the bakers, and that sort of common folk, since he has spoken in a way that seems to show he wanted to be familiar with this race of men."¹ (Poor and learned Master Niccolò <note>Niccolò Niccoli (1364–1437), a famous Florentine humanist known for his rigorous devotion to classical Latin.</note>, certainly bakers and shoemakers did not read his Latin). Add to this the generation of grammarians who taught Latin in the schools, who, out of the love a man takes for his profession or trade, did not cease from discrediting the vernacular <term>volgare: the common Italian language as opposed to Latin</term>. Consequently, until a few years into the 15th century, Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a historian and linguist who defended the Florentine language.</note> attests that "the Florentine tongue, though it was not much esteemed elsewhere, was for the most part held in contempt within Florence itself: and I remember, when I was a youth, that the first and most severe command that fathers generally gave to their sons and masters to their disciples was that they should not, for better or worse, read things in the vernacular, to say it barbarously as they did; and Master Guasparri Mariscotti of Marradi, who was my preceptor in grammar... having heard once, I know not how, that Schiatta di Bernardo Bagnesi and I were reading Petrarch in secret, gave us a good scolding and very nearly expelled us from school."²

And yet it was still Florence that, by tempering the ancient elements with the new, could restore dignity to the vernacular language; Florence which—pure and flourishing even with new elegances, and beautiful and powerful through new perspectives and attitudes—preserved on the lips of its people the speech of Boccaccio <note>Author of the *Decameron*.</note> and Sacchetti <note>Franco Sacchetti (c. 1332–1400), a poet and novelist.</note>. She wrote it with a freshness that did not envy the preceding century and its popular authors, among whom the most candid in both prose and verse was Belcari <note>Feo Belcari (1410–1484), known for his religious plays and poems.</note>. Florence, for whom the great writers of the 14th century were a source of civic glory; and even from the chair where Homer was interpreted, in one of those introductory lectures <note>Poliziano’s *Sylvae*, or poetic introductions to his university courses.</note> composed in exquisite Latin verses that allow us to judge the education and taste of these "New Athenians," she loved to hear their names repeated alongside the demigods and ancient bards by the colorful eloquence of Poliziano:

> Nor yet would I deprive wing-bearing Dante of this gift,
> [Who traveled] through the Styx, through the stars, and through the heights of the middle mountain.

> Flying beneath the beautiful face of the virgin Beatrice; <note>original: "Pulchra Beatricis sub virginis ora volantem." This refers to Dante Alighieri.</note>
> And he who repeats the Cupid-like triumph of Petrarch,
> And he who paints a hundred themes in twice five days, <note>A reference to Giovanni Boccaccio and the hundred stories of the *Decameron*, written over ten days.</note>
> And he who shows the seeds of hidden love:
> From these come the proclamations of your immense praise,
> O Mother Florence, powerful in both genius and wealth.¹

Some grammarian, therefore, or some pure antiquarian in Florence might have despised these new glories, but no one else. Thus, from the very beginning of the century, the learned and cautious Cino Rinuccini composed *an invective against certain detractors of Dante, Master Francesco Petrarch, and Master Giovanni Boccaccio, whose names are decently omitted.*² And Francesco Filelfo—the most energetic and quarrelsome Filelfo, who provided commentary on Dante in the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore—delivered an oration on December 21, 1450, in defense of Alighieri, who had been "called a poet for shoemakers and bakers by my most ignorant rivals."³ This same Filelfo later adorned Petrarch's *Triumphs* with rather strange commentaries and composed forty-eight cantos in <term>ottava rima: an Italian rhyming stanza form</term> about Saint John the Baptist. Both Alighieri and Petrarch were publicly explained in the Florentine University by Cristoforo Landini alongside Virgil and Horace; and Leonardo Bruni wrote the lives of both with great affection and sufficient Italian elegance. And Benivieni, greeting the great ghost of the <term>White exile: a reference to Dante, who belonged to the "White" faction of the Guelph party and was exiled from Florence</term>, was able to praise the Florentine people because

> . . . . . . . . . . from your worth,
> From your glory they grow ever more beautiful:
> Therefore, not only the hearts of their assembly,
> But the doors, the walls, the floors
> Have made a decoration of your image.⁴

Finally, Lorenzo de' Medici—long before Castiglione and Bembo <note>Baldassare Castiglione and Pietro Bembo, 16th-century authors who later standardized Italian courtly manners and language.</note>—defended the use of the Tuscan language against the accusations of the scholars. He celebrated its praises, discussed its poetic meters, and dared to place Petrarch above all the Latin erotic poets. He glorified the poetry of Dante as being without comparison, and the invention and abundance of Boccaccio as unique in the world; and he collected the rhymes of the minor and more ancient poets.

XVIII

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...and [Lorenzo de' Medici] illustrated them with a prose that stands as the first example of our literary criticism.<gloss>¹</gloss> But already Cristoforo Landini, beginning to lecture at the <term>Studio: The University of Florence</term> on the sonnets of Petrarch, had demonstrated that the Tuscan language—in its origins and its growth as well as in its merits—did not differ from Latin. He argued, however, that it was necessary to subject it to the rules of grammar and rhetoric, just as had been done for Latin, and to continually nourish and strengthen it through the study of the latter. He suggested that the past glories gave sufficient sign of the future glories one might expect from such efforts. Here he examines the most illustrious works of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; it will not be out of place to report some of his judgments:

> "And in our times you have had Leonardo Aretino <note>Leonardo Bruni (c. 1370–1444), a leading humanist, historian, and chancellor of Florence</note> and several others..... But a man who has put more industry into expanding this language than Battista Alberti <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), the famous 'universal man' of the Renaissance, architect, and philosopher</note>, I certainly believe none can be found. Read, I pray you, his many books composed on various subjects; notice with what industry he has strived to transfer to us every <term>eloquence: refined, artistic, and persuasive speech</term>, composition, and dignity found among the Latins. And Matteo Palmieri in his dialogues can hold his listeners' attention, not only by the weight of his thoughts but by his orderly arrangement and his ornate and flowery elocution. Nor should one hold Bonaccorso da Montemagno in low esteem for those <term>orations: formal public speeches, often delivered to government bodies</term> which, by ancient custom, are made in praise of justice to all the magistracies of the city. And this in prose.... The aforementioned Leonardo wrote verses; although he perhaps did not achieve every grace, yet because he shows himself full of learning and art, he will be most helpful to whoever wishes to be elegant... Battista Alberti has written <term>eclogues: short poems in a rural or pastoral setting</term> and <term>elegies: poems of reflection, typically lamenting the dead or exploring the sorrows of love</term> of such a kind that in the former he observes pastoral customs very well, and in the latter, he is marvelous in expressing—or rather almost painting—the emotions and disturbances of love. The aforementioned Leonardo wrote not only in our usual eleven-syllable lines <note>The hendecasyllable, the standard meter of Italian poetry used by Dante and Petrarch</note>, but in Sapphic and heroic verses; being a most sharp-witted man full of grace, he was ably and conveniently able to place and transfer into our language all the ornaments and colors found in the Latin verses in which he is so excellent. They have written, and perhaps even today they write..."

XIX

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...some others; who, because they do not lack learning, can easily bring the vein <note>referring to a "vein" of natural talent or poetic inspiration</note>, which they have in abundance from nature, to perfection. But these are few and rarer than the gates of Florence. All the other crowd, because they sail without a compass and without a rudder, can perhaps out of seven attempts <note>original: "delle sette una sola volta", an idiom suggesting a rare or lucky occurrence</note> only once, by good sight and natural prudence, glimpse the port and reach safety.<gloss>¹</gloss>» From all this, it can be inferred that in Florence there existed the traditions, the intentions, and the faculties to restore the Italian language to its dignity and to elevate it even further to the rank of a learned language, equal to Greek and Latin.

In the second place, classical studies had been too ardent and exclusive, so much so that they could not help but have a powerful influence on the little Italian that continued to be written by the men of letters. Consequently, not only the memories—even the most distant ones—of Greek and Latin authors, but the ancient coloring, the phrases, the formulas, the words, the turn and attitude of the sentence, and the meters were transported so raw and dry into Italian, blindly, without a shadow of reasoning or taste; entire Latin sentences were mixed with the vernacular, even in personal letters. How great this confusion was, and what this "learned barbarism" looked like, will be shown better by examples than by words. And the poems of the century provide far too many: even Feo Belcari <note>Feo Belcari (1410–1484), known for his simple, pious prose</note>, who is clarity itself when he writes lives of saints and <term>representations: sacre rappresentazioni, or religious mystery plays</term>, becomes clumsy and contorted like the others if he sets his hand to writing sonnets—that is, to poeticizing "learnedly."

I will report two such examples, among the most significant for the nature of the compositions from which I take them. In 1441, at the encouragement of Leon Battista Alberti and Piero de' Medici, in order to lift the spirits of the people occupied by the war with the Duke of Milan and to honor the presence of Pope Eugene IV, a competition of vernacular poetry was announced by the officials of the <term>Studio of Florence: the city's university</term>. The subject was *True Friendship*; the location of the recitation was Santa Maria del Fiore <note>The Cathedral of Florence, also known as the Duomo</note>; the prize was a silver crown fashioned in the likeness of laurel; the judges were the secretaries of the Pope. The recitation took place on the 22nd of October: there were...

XX

# ANGELO POLIZIANO

With the City Council <note>original: *la signoria*, the governing body of the Republic of Florence</note> and the Archbishop of the city present, along with the ambassador of Venice, a great number of prelates, and the Florentine people. Now then: in that very church <note>Santa Maria del Fiore, the Cathedral of Florence</note> where Dante was explained to the people, and before that same crowd that attended the plays of Belcari <note>Feo Belcari was a popular 15th-century writer of religious "Sacre Rappresentazioni"</note> and sang his praises, Messer Lionardo Dati, a Florentine, read a scene of his own in hexameter and Sapphic verses <note>These are classical Latin poetic meters, here awkwardly forced into the Italian language</note>, in which Mercury is introduced, saying, among other fine things:

> "Among the heavenly ones, daughter of the Nile and Pallas <note>Pallas Athena</note>,
> One goddess excels, who conquers with her great beauty,
> With a form no less decorous than that of Venus.
> She walks the heavens, now above where the steep
> Eridanus <note>a river constellation</note> cleaves, now where the Pleiades
> Girdled the sky below, now where all the gods watch her,
> Clothed and bright, distinguished in a thousand colors,
> Girded by the rainbow <note>original: *iris*</note>, which re-weaves her hem
> With gems and shining gold no less than Orion:
> And she is surrounded by every miraculous deed.
> This goddess, performing her office, reveals the golden gate
> Of the ocean to those wing-footed steeds that the proud boy
> Phaethon reined, he who was his own harmful, poor guide:
> She points with her finger the path they should cautiously travel
> Through the middle of the Zodiac, fleeing sleep and night:
> And later, when, thirsty, they long for rest,
> She loosens their manes, and feeds them with sweet poppy
> Or with the hanging clusters of the vine.
> The celestial choir calls her chaste Cronissa;
> Though Charon <note>While usually the ferryman of the dead, here the poet likely confuses the name with Chronos, or Time</note> is her only spouse,
> Both old and gray and not always exorable,
> Yet, though often requested by a thousand miserable lovers,
> She gratifies none—deaf, uncorrupted, and severe:
> And more than the other goddesses, Fortune <note>original: *Faturina*</note> billows like the sea.¹"

XXI

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

"...when writing and speaking to women, they always use the words of Poliphilo <note>Poliphilo is the protagonist of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, a famous 1499 book known for its extremely dense, invented language mixing Italian and Latin</note>,¹" and so he began, describing the dawn: 

> "At that hour when Phoebus <note>the sun god</note> was issuing forth, and the brow of Matuta Leucothea <note>the Roman goddess of the morning</note> was already whitening outside the ocean waves, he did not show his whirling wheels suspended, but diligently with his winged horses, Pyrois first and Eous <note>original: *Pyrois* and *Eous*, the names of the sun's chariot horses in Greek mythology</note>, appearing somewhat, he did not delay in very swiftly following the daughter of blushing roses <note>referring to the Dawn</note> to paint her twilight chariots.²"

Now, to do away with this strange mixture of two forms—this overgrowth of the dead language upon the living, this horrible **Mezentian** <term>Mezentian: a reference to the mythical King Mezentius, who cruelly executed people by binding a living person face-to-face with a corpse until they rotted; here it describes the forced joining of "dead" Latin and "living" Italian</term> conjunction in art, from which a monster threatened to emerge that, with its inert heaviness, would have suffocated all vitality of Italian thought—it was not enough to merely return to the written tradition of the 1300s. Unfortunately, Boccaccio, not so much in his *Decameron* as in his minor prose novels, had already led men of letters down that slippery slope. Rather, it was necessary to draw from the living source of common usage—to ask the people for that native strength and elegance which, by luck, they still preserved. 

And this could be done nowhere else but in Florence. But with this, a new danger had to be avoided, and another inconvenience remedied. On one hand, the Tuscan people, left to themselves without a literary standard coming from above, had run wild and bold in the field of language. Certain external forms had been vigorously disconnected; a forest of word-endings that appeared less graceful in literary works, of **ellipses** <term>ellipsis: the omission of words that are understood from context, common in speech but potentially confusing in writing</term> and **hyperbatons** <term>hyperbaton: the inversion of normal word order for emphasis</term> that brought life to the spoken word but clouded the written page, of **catachreses** <term>catachresis: the strained or figurative use of a word or metaphor</term> and truncations barely noticed in song but harsh and strange in text—all this was passing from popular poets to the learned writers. And on the other hand, since no writer had arisen in Tuscany for nearly a century to draw the attention of all Italy as a living standard of modern usage, the men of letters from other provinces, as if taking advantage of the rights of a confederation, were importing into their writings whatever words, phrases, and idi-

XXII

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO<-

idioms of their own dialect: it is enough to remember one among many, the most learned and ingenious **Boiardo** <note>Matteo Maria Boiardo (1441–1494), author of *Orlando Innamorato*, who wrote in a Northern Italian-inflected literary style</note>. Thus, that unity impressed upon the forms of the language by the powerful writers of the 1300s <note>the *Trecento*</note> was broken; that Tuscan supremacy was ignored—a supremacy which, without anyone thinking to impose it and no one even noticing it, had been voluntarily and concordantly accepted by all writers in the previous century. That admirable suitability of imitation with novelty, of usage with doctrine, of speaking from a spontaneous vein with writing in meditated reflection, of the freedom of the individual with the ideal norm of the nation, was—or seemed—miserably lost. To reconstitute it, merely returning to the usage of the common people was not enough, and might perhaps have been harmful; it was necessary for a genius so privileged to arise that, in him, the most diverse and unequal faculties might be tempered into a marvelous harmony: an imitator and an inventor, an improviser and an exquisite handler of style, a popular writer and a learned writer, a poet and a critic.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And even this was not enough. For the disuse of writing in Italian had brought about a sense of struggle; and the search for rare expressions in the imitation of the classics had brought effort: these two vices masked themselves, as always, behind a pretension that sought to be greatness but was merely pomposity <note>original: *tumidità*, meaning a "swollen" or turgid style</note>. If we add to this the inheritance that Italian poetry derived from the already academic conventions of the **Provençals** <note>the troubadour poets of Southern France</note>, from the mysticism of Dante’s contemporaries, and from the psychologism of **Petrarch**, we find the reason for the cleverness, the exaggerations, and the subtleties that flourished all the more in the poetry of the 1400s <note>the *Quattrocento*</note> as the inner fervor with which it was cultivated diminished. If, finally, we consider what a passion for composing and recomposing, for compiling, translating, and reading romances invaded those Italians who were not entirely literary men in those years, we might find in that taste the origin of the extravagances and surprises with which the common crowd of lyric poets, neglecting style, sought to capture the minds of readers toward the end of the century. This is why someone, setting their eyes on the songbooks of **Cei, Notturno, Aquilano, Sasso, Cornazzano,** and **Tebaldeo**, is amazed to find in many places the forerunners of the 1600s <note>the *Seicento*, an era known for the ornate and "conceited" Baroque style</note>. And the *perversion of style and sentiment followed*, as often...

XXIII

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO<-

...gion, the perversion of judgment. Thus, a contemporary of Cornazzano <note>Antonio Cornazzano (c. 1430–1484), a court poet and diplomat</note> celebrated him as *another Dante or Petrarch in vernacular verses*¹ and even in the time of Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a Florentine humanist and historian</note> there remained *those who held the style of Ceo or Serafino <note>Benedetto Gareth, known as "Il Chariteo" (the Cean), and Serafino Aquilano; both were known for a highly decorative, artificial poetic style</note> to be more beautiful than that of Petrarch or Dante.*² Furthermore, Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher</note> (and he had no need to beg for favors, nor can it be supposed that he wished to flatter his peer) frankly places the rhymes of de' Medici ahead of everything written by Dante and Petrarch "because Petrarch," he says, "lacks substance, that is, concepts; and Dante lacks words, that is, eloquence." And while it is curious to note the sharpness of certain criticisms he makes against Petrarch, it is equally useful to observe that, in this comparison, he allowed himself to be caught more by the appearances than by the true virtues of Lorenzo’s writing.³ At this point, to recall these straying minds, there was a greater need than ever for a man of admirable temperament who, knowing how to distinguish in ancient and modern writers the true and the beautiful from the false and the deformed, could provide cultured literature with an example and a universally acceptable norm.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And that man was Angelo Poliziano. To one more powerful than he—one who, being placed in the highest dignity of his homeland and magnificently exercising protection and generosity toward every kind of scholar and letter, was able to have his advice accepted as dictates and his example as law—to Lorenzo de' Medici, in short, was reserved the boast of restoring the Italian language to honor among the learned. And he, a citizen of Florence, born of a popular house, grandson to Cosimo <note>Cosimo "the Elder" de' Medici (1389–1464)</note> who even amidst the severe cares of his new power found time to compose verses in his mother tongue,⁴ and son to Lucrezia Tornabuoni, a pious and simple poetess, fulfilled this as a noble duty toward his country and his family. But that exquisite flower of sentiment called **good taste**, that harmony of talent called **judgment**, is not granted by power or wealth; and so, a poor youth who came to the city in search of fortune from a municipality of the dominion <note>Poliziano was born in Montepulciano, a territory under Florentine control</note> was destined to be the happy dictator of good taste.

XXIV

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO<-

...and of the judgment expected from Italy: he, by reconnecting the new literature to the final tradition of Boccaccio and refreshing the beauties of the classics within the living language of common use, was destined to open the beautiful age of refinement and form. This was understood by the sixteenth century <note>Italian: *cinquecento*</note>, when it almost unanimously recognized the Medici <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence and a poet himself</note> and Poliziano as its precursors, and through the mouth of Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a Florentine humanist and historian</note> declared:

> « He [the Medici] along with Master Agnolo Poliziano were the first who began in their compositions to withdraw and distance themselves from the common crowd, and, if not to imitate, then to desire or appear to desire to imitate Petrarch and Dante, leaving aside in part that completely vile and plebeian manner.¹ »

With what instruments and by what means Poliziano brought about this happy reaction in Italian art, I shall attempt to demonstrate in the remainder of this discourse. I shall report from the history of the Latin writer and from the life of the man only so much as serves to place the Italian poet in a clearer light; for a long discussion of the former would be too far removed from my subject; and of the latter, Menckenius,² Serassi,³ and Bonafous⁴ have treated sufficiently. Furthermore, my friend Isidoro Del Lungo will speak of him more fully, I hope, in a short while, based on documents and information now collected for the first time and compared with rigorous judgment.

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO<-

...yet at the heart of all the fantasies of the Middle Ages, **Boccaccio** was the first to attempt this with the intention of an artist; when in the *Teseide* and *Filostrato* he dressed the heroes from the time of the **Epigoni** <note>In Greek mythology, the sons of the Seven against Thebes</note> and the Trojan War in the fashions of the Round Table and the Paladins; and conversely, in the *Filocopo*, he draped the Moorish Florio in classical style. He did so even more when, in the *Ameto*, he led the nymphs of Theocritus and Virgil to dance in the shade of the poplars through the small valleys of Fiesole, blending the pure hexameters of Virgil and the more varied ones of Ovid into Dante’s *terza rima* and the *ottava rima* stanza. In the same way, **Poliziano** elevated a local, bourgeois event to the tone of an epic trumpet; upon the stages of performance, amidst decorations still sourced from church vestries, he introduced Syracusan shepherds and the virgin of the Thracian mysteries. To the terrible and grotesque hell of the friars, of Dante, and of **Orcagna** <note>Andrea di Cione (c. 1310–1368), a Florentine painter and architect known for his vivid depictions of death and judgment</note>, he substituted the classical hell of the *Metamorphoses*. This mixture of fantasies necessarily led to a new temperament of feelings, images, and style—somewhere between the art of perception and that of reflection, between pure naturalism and the fourteenth-century ideal, between **Homer** and **Dante**, between **Virgil** and **Petrarch**, and between **Ovid** and **Boccaccio**. The mixture was transitory; but the temperament of the style remained and marked the new age of perfection.

<margin>1 *Poliziano, Book of Epigrams: Works, cited edition, vol. II. And from this point forward*</margin>
A joust in Florence toward the end of the 15th century: a meager subject for ornamental poetry. True: but what other subject could such a man choose in such times? **Angelo Ambrogini**, born in **Montepulciano** to an honest but poor family [July 14, 1454] and brought to **Florence** while still a tender youth in search of studies and fortune, certainly did not possess that mysterious and profound poetic necessity that besieged the young soul of **Dante** with visions, or that stayed the young **Petrarch** among the cliffs of **Vaucluse** with a prophetic desire for contemplation and solitude. He did not have it; it is a confession far too candid that he makes at fourteen years old in his first Latin epigram.<sup>1</sup> Once, he says, study was dear to me: "but envious Poverty, smeared with filth, terrified my tattered breast <note>original Latin: *invida sed me Paupertas laceros terruit uncta sinus*</note>;" therefore, since the poet is but a fable to the common people, "I think it better to yield to the times <note>original Latin: *Esse reor satius cedere temporibus*</note>." That charm which, from Platonic lessons...

...from Ficino and from the <term>Peripatetic teachings</term> <note>The philosophy of Aristotle, taught by scholars who famously "walked about" while lecturing</note> of Argyropoulos, he was drawn back to the *blandishments of Homer*,$^1$ that beginning as a boy with the translation of the *Iliad* into Latin verses of most splendid profusion, which announced more than anything else a feeling for form, color, and harmony. A most noble feeling; but one that requires, in order to expand into work, quiet and leisure: *secure rest*,$^2$ <note>original: "secura quies"</note> as Virgil used to say; *the precious rest of poets*,$^3$ <note>original: "vatum pretiosa quies"</note> as our poet would also say later in his small villa at Fiesole. To acquire that rest, to possess that villa, it was necessary to make room for himself, to put himself in view, and to approach the powerful, because *to please the powerful is not the least of praises*.$^4$ <note>original: "piacere ai potenti è non ultima lode"</note> 

Thus, like Statius <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD known for his polished, occasional poetry for the imperial court</note> in Rome, so did Poliziano in Florence seek out images and sounds for every occasion and for every minor affair of the magnates: for the death of an Albizzi girl betrothed to a Della Stufa; for the Benivieni house, which was full of doctors and poets; for Pietro Riario, the nephew of Sixtus IV and Cardinal of San Sisto. Upon Riario's arrival [in 1473] to take possession of the archbishopric of Florence, the weather happened to be between cloudy and clear; and the poet sings that the sun wants both to see Sixtus and yet not to offend him—the great Sixtus,

> "The first hope of men..., and the first care of the gods:" <note>original: "Spes hominum prima..., primaque cura deûm:"</note>

Having entered the city, a downpour falls that puts an end to the drought; and here the poet cries out "miracle," and asks:

> "Can anyone deny that you are a god, Sixtus, holding dominion over the lands and dominion over the heavens?" <note>original: "An quisquam neget esse deum te Xyste tenentem Imperium terris imperiumque polo?"</note>

But to the Medici above all, to the two young heirs of that munificent family, did the "new Statius" dedicate himself—he was six years younger than Lorenzo and only one year older than Giuliano. And he was not only a <term>panegyrist</term> <note>A writer who composes formal speeches or poems of high praise</note> of public actions, whether good or not (such as the sack of Volterra), but he composed verses on everything: on the portrait of the girl *who is his darling* <note>original: "quae est in deliciis"</note>, on the fountain of Ambra, and on a poplar tree that turned green again in front of the palace on Via Larga. Does he see Lorenzo at the villa shielding his head from the sun with certain oak branches? And he, right then and there, on the spot, improvises:

> "How well you encircle your temples with the acorn-bearing oak, you who preserve the citizen not only..." <note>A reference to the Roman "civic crown" of oak leaves awarded to those who saved a citizen's life</note>

...but the people." A Spanish dog arrives for Lorenzo—one that strangles wild beasts but does not touch man? Very well: this dog is the perfect image for you, magnificent master: "Thus, O Lorenzo, does your punishment restrain the guilty; thus do the pious receive from you worthy rewards." <note>original: "Sic tua nam sontes, Laurenti, pœna coërcet; Sic referunt abs te præmia digna pii." Poliziano uses the dog's behavior as an allegory for Lorenzo’s justice: fierce toward criminals but gentle to the good.</note> Once the Magnificent, having provided as best he could for the provisions of the city which was suffering from high prices, departed for Pisa; alas, for the universal good, let him not remain there too long: there is the risk, if he does not return soon, that all of Florence might wish to be dead of hunger instead: "Alas, what are you doing? O Lorenzo, return yourself to your mourning homeland: it has not been made more joyful by your gifts. Sad it grieves, and the homeland would rather endure its previous hunger than endure the longing for you." <note>original: "Heu quid agis? patriæ, Laurens, te redde gementi...". Poliziano flatteringly suggests that the city's emotional "hunger" for Lorenzo is worse than the actual famine he just helped solve.</note> For Giuliano, with whom he had more easily forgotten the equality of their age, he did even more. In his name and in the persona of Giuliano as a lover, he wrote elegant songs, which ultimately came to this: "Do not be stingy with me then / Of that true pleasure which alone is everything, / And let me, after the flowers, gather the fruit: <gloss>1</gloss>" but the hand of the flattering poet revealed itself in the excessive praise of the lord-in-love placed into his own mouth. Then, when the beautiful lady died in the flower of her youth, the poet not only put into Latin verses a thought suggested to him by Giuliano for the epitaph, but accompanied her funeral with an epigram worthy of the *Greek Anthology*; which the reader will see gladly, since it concerns the Simonetta <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the legendary beauty of the Renaissance and presumed model for Botticelli's paintings, who died young in 1476.</note> celebrated in the poem of the joust:

> While the beautiful Simonetta is carried on her black bier
> and a charming grace breathes upon her lifeless face;
> Love, finding a time when the crowd would not guard against him,
> threw a thousand torches from those closed eyes;
> He captured a thousand souls with the image of a living smile;
> and mocking death, he said: "She is still mine";
> "She is still mine," he said; "you do not yet snatch her away entirely:
> behold, even lifeless, she serves as my soldier." 
> He spoke and groaned: for the boy <note>The "boy" refers to Cupid, the god of Love.</note> saw that those times
> were not suited for triumphs, but for tears.

It is a pity that the author of such elegant verses then wished to emulate not only the scurrility and filth but the impudence of Martial <note>A Roman poet (1st century AD) famous for his sharp wit but also for his habit of shamelessly asking his patrons for money.</note> stretching out his hand for pay! To you, he wrote one day to the Medici, to you my verse, to you everything serves the—

...my talent. But the common folk laugh, because my clothing shows its threads and my toes peek out from my patched shoes to enjoy the open air: they laugh and take me for an ignorant poet who did not know how to please you. You, on the contrary, pour praise upon praise on me from a full heart. Now, if you want to be believed and for the gossip to stop, **"Lorenzo, send me your clothes now."** <note>original: "Laurenti, vestes iam mihi mitte tuas." A cheeky request from Poliziano to his patron for a wardrobe upgrade.</note> Even Luther wrote to some Elector or other that his gown was tattered, and that he should send him some black cloth to make another:¹ but the German friar would not have asked for money with the specific and material word, *coins*, <note>original: "æra"</note> as the Florentine canon did. The latter joked in this way about Cardinal Sixtus <note>Likely referring to a member of the Riario or della Rovere family associated with Pope Sixtus IV.</note> who, for the two epigrams reported above, had only thanked him: **"I gave words to Sixtus; it befits a poet to give these gifts: It befits Sixtus to return coins; he returns words;"** <note>original: "Verba dedi Xisto, decet hæc dare dona poetam: Æra decet Xistum reddere; verba refert;" Poliziano plays on the phrase "verba dare," which in Latin can mean "to give words" or "to deceive."</note> and he brought Francesco Salviati into it—the very same one from the Pazzi conspiracy—so that he might remind the cardinal that **"no poet here, however, is heavy with coins;"** <note>original: "nullo hic vates est tamen ære gravis;"</note> and finally with cynical impudence he concluded: **"To one calling you a god, Sixtus, if you had given the gifts he seeks, he would say now you were Jove."** <note>original: "Dicenti te Xiste deum si dona dedisses Quæ petit, iam te diceret esse Jovem." Jupiter (Jove) was the king of the gods, implying Sixtus would be the greatest of patrons if he actually paid.</note> These are shames excused in part by the literary customs of the century. <note>Humanist poets often adopted a "persona" of the starving artist to solicit patronage, a practice rooted in Roman traditions.</note> But how much Poliziano is pleased and honored by the sincere and profound affection that grew ever more for Lorenzo, who sustained his studies and soon welcomed him into his home! It was an affection mixed with gratitude, admiration, and friendship, in which one feels both the veneration of the inferior and the tenderness of an equal; an affection of which the good poet gave such bold proof during the Pazzi affair <note>The Pazzi Conspiracy (1478) was a plot to displace the Medici; Poliziano was present and helped usher Lorenzo to safety in the sacristy of the Duomo.</note> and which shines entirely in that most beautiful epigram written spontaneously on the occasion when he could not greet Medici upon his return to Florence from the dangerous congress with Ferdinand of Naples. <note>In 1479, Lorenzo famously traveled to Naples to negotiate peace with King Ferdinand I, a risky move that saved Florence from war.</note>

> O how I desire to touch the hand of the returning
>   Lorenzo and, joyful, to say a joyful welcome.
> But the great halls can scarcely hold the thick crowd,
>   The whole court rings with the voices of those greeting him.
> Everywhere the pious crowd of the purple senate <note>The "purple senate" refers to the high-ranking Florentine officials and perhaps clergy surrounding Lorenzo.</note>
>   Stands around: he himself stands taller than all.
> What shall I do? Shall I approach? I cannot; the envious crowd forbids it.
>   Shall I speak? But the sound lies frozen in my fearful mouth.

From all this, it is possible to observe how at that time and for such a man, a <term>tournament</term> <note>original: "giostra"; a public jousting match. But when exactly did Giuliano fight in the celebrated tournament, and when was the poem written? The chronological question is more important to the critique of the work than it might first appear; it has been resolved, I believe, in every part by my friend Del Lungo <note>Isidoro Del Lungo (1841–1927), a renowned Italian literary critic and expert on Poliziano.</note> in the following illustration which he has kindly allowed me to use.

...foundation in facts and in the text. Indeed, they did not even care if the facts and the text contradicted it. In considering the causes of this universal error, I believe I have found them in this: 1st, the joust of Giuliano sung by Poliziano was confused with that of Lorenzo sung by Luca Pulci, which took place in 1469 when Poliziano was exactly fifteen years old; 2nd, the verses of stanzas 4 and 5 of Book I were misunderstood and even distorted <note>See page 5 of this edition, in the notes.</note>; where people were eager to find an explanation for the poet's initial fortune with the Medici, for which no positive documents remain; 3rd, people relied on the old editors contemporary to the author, who attribute the poem to his early adolescence; words which, in the face of the authority of documents, must be declared either inaccurate or false. Some doubted this <note>Among whom it is only fair to remember Ginguené, *Literary History of Italy*, part one, chapter XX; and Giudici, *History of Italian Literature*, chapter X.</note>, to whom that did not seem like the poetry of a fifteen-year-old; and they conjectured, each in their own way. Of all of them (even the recent ones, like the agile Frenchman Mr. Bonafous), Menke was the most conscientious: "I truly know of no writer who can loosen this knot." <note>original Latin: *scriptorem qui hunc exsolvat nodum, ego quidem scio nullum.* From the *History of the Life of Angelo Poliziano*, page 44.</note> Nor could he truly loosen them, even by rectifying the errors, without the help of original and authentic documents. These I have found; and they are good, I believe, for "loosening the knot." <note>original Latin: *exsolvere nodum*.</note>

» The beautiful Simonetta, the graceful nymph of the poem, died on the night of April 26 to 27, 1476, of consumption <term>etisia | A common historical term for tuberculosis or a wasting disease.</term>. Lorenzo was in Pisa and was receiving news of her day by day, and from more than one person. <note>Medici Archive before the Principate, bundle XXXIII. In fact, if Master Angelo had written the *Stanzas* at fifteen in 1469—the year of Lorenzo's joust—why would he have returned seven years later to graft verses into a short poem that had remained unfinished? And what reason would there be to leave it unfinished—he, a young man who they say hoped for protection and bread from those verses? Furthermore: Poliziano [Book I, stanza 6] calls Giuliano's trophy *the second*; that is, as the editors well explain...

...mentators, coming after that of Lorenzo: indeed, in Book II, stanza 6, he speaks of the joust of 1469 <note>The "joust of 69" refers to a famous tournament won by Lorenzo the Magnificent, which was separate from the one Poliziano is actually celebrating here.</note> as something that happened long ago; and the commentators also recognize this. These same commentators then find in the verses: *And having placed my nest in your happy wood, from a hoarse bird I become a white swan* <note>original: "E posto il nido in tuo felice ligno Di roco augel diventi un bianco cigno" [I, 5]</note> a desire and a prayer from the poet (somewhat like a beggar) to enter the Medici household. This interpretation would indeed relegate the *Stanze* to Angelo’s earliest youth, or rather to his childhood. But those verses say nothing more than that he desires to sing of the deeds of Lorenzo, just as he now sings those of Giuliano; this agrees with the other lines: *But while I tremble and long for the high undertaking, and my wings are clipped by the beautiful desire, let us sing of your glorious brother* <note>original: "Ma mentre all' alta impresa tremo e bramo E son tarpati i vanni al bel desio, Lo glorioso tuo fratel cantiamo" [I, 6]</note>. Regarding these lines, if one understands them as "entering the household" and not as "singing of Lorenzo," I do not know what possible sense can be made of them; because a poem is indeed a <term>high undertaking</term> <note>Poliziano uses "alta impresa" to refer to the lofty artistic challenge of writing an epic, rather than a social promotion.</note>, but being admitted to a court is not. And in the stanza before, *From a hoarse bird etc.*, how much better is it understood that the subject should inspire him rather than the household! And *ligno* <note>The word "ligno" literally means wood or timber, but here it is a pun on the "Lauro" (Laurel), the poetic name for Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> is the laurel tree itself, that is, Lorenzo; not the house, which the poet would have more properly called the field or the garden where the tree had grown.

It should also be observed that the poet addresses Lorenzo as the principal citizen of the republic [I, 4]; he would not have done this in 1469, while Lorenzo's father, Piero, was still alive. Furthermore, there are those who say the *Stanze* must have been written before Lorenzo's marriage to Clarice Orsini, which took place in June 1469, the year of his joust; they argue this because Poliziano freely mentions [II, 4] the <term>Magnifico's</term> <note>The "Magnifico" is the traditional title for Lorenzo de' Medici, "Lorenzo the Magnificent."</note> love for Lucrezia Donati. But for those who know how simple and innocent a thing the "love of poets" was among our ancestors—much like that of the Provençal troubadours—arousing neither jealousy in wives or husbands nor scandal in the modest public; for those who remember that neither Dante took his wife Lady Gemma as his muse, nor did Petrarch ever complain that Laura was the wife of Count Hugo; to us, I say, who remember this, what value can such an objection have? The purely poetic character of this love is so true that Lorenzo does not even care to speak of it with factual accuracy. Indeed, in the *Commentary on some of his sonnets*¹ he says that Lu-
