<page-num>XXXII</page-num>

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...[Lu]crezia <note>Lucrezia Donati, the noblewoman who was the object of Lorenzo the Magnificent's courtly love.</note> pleased him for the first time after the death of Simonetta [on p. 129]; for Simonetta <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the celebrated beauty of the Medici court, who died young in April 1476.</note> is certainly the girl who died in April [on p. 124]. And he says this because it suits him all too well to weave this polite history, which allows love to be born from the pity for a deceased woman: not that it is true; because, if it were, he would not have turned his thoughts and verses to Donati except after [14]76, whereas the fact that he courted her even before [14]67 is drawn from the *Joust* by Luca Pulci [stanza VII]. Pulci also recounts that before that year of '67, during the celebration of the wedding of Braccio Martelli, Lucrezia was present [*New light reborn from Piccarda*] <note>original: "Nuova luce rinata di Piccarda"</note> with a sister of hers who seems to have been named Costanza; and there Lorenzo promised her, like the ancient knights, to hold a joust, which was then delayed for two years by Florentine wars [stanza VIII, following; and CLVII].

» But let us return to the *Stanze*; which, since because of Simonetta they cannot, according to the documents, be written except after [14]76; and the difficulties that would oppose this new chronology—I mean the difficulties created by the fault of the commentators—fall away before a more accurate study of the text; let us see then, with the guidance of the documents, to which year after '76 we should assign them.

» However, before proceeding with this research, it is necessary to point out that, if the argument drawn from the death of Simonetta did not necessarily push the *Stanze* to a date after '76, we would have evidence from both chroniclers ¹—completely overlooked by the learned disputants—and from documents ² that the joust which took its name from Giuliano <note>Giuliano de' Medici, the younger brother of Lorenzo, whose 1475 tournament is the subject of Poliziano's poem.</note>, because he took the first prize and wore a rich suit of armor (and I even have the name of the horse, *The Bear* <note>original: "l’Orso"</note>), took place on January 28, 1475. Thus, we should conclude with Palermo,³ that this is the joust sung of by Poliziano. But the date of Simonetta's death, I repeat, prevents us from doing so; unless we wish to say, like Emiliani-Giudici,⁴ that Poliziano wrote the *Stanze* some time after the joust was held, because it seems to us that they have many characteristics of <term>occasional poetry</term> <note>Poetry written specifically to celebrate a particular event, such as a festival, wedding, or tournament.</note>. At the very most, we could concede that the...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly debate over when Angelo Poliziano wrote his "Stanze per la giostra." The author argues against the traditional view that it was a work of early adolescence, suggesting instead that the poem was composed between 1476 and 1478.</meta>

<page-num>XXXIII</page-num>

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

Poliziano began his *Stanze* <note>The "Stanze per la giostra" is a famous unfinished poem celebrating a jousting tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> in [14]75 for that specific joust; could he have been only at the second book when Simonetta died? Would it not seem excessive that he spent fifteen months on the first book alone—he who improvised the play *Orfeo*? <note>Poliziano famously claimed to have written his play "Orfeo" in just two days.</note> And that from '76 to '78 he did not carry the short poem beyond that second book? Instead, by placing the *Stanze* after '76, in addition to matching the date of that death, the reason for their being interrupted is found in the famous Pazzi conspiracy, <note>The Pazzi conspiracy was a plot by the Pazzi family and others to displace the Medici as rulers of Florence; it resulted in the death of Giuliano de' Medici on April 26, 1478.</note> as I was about to demonstrate. But I wanted to interject this observation both for the sake of justice and so that it may be seen how, from another angle, the opinion of those who have Poliziano writing the *Stanze* in his fifteenth year <note>Poliziano was born in 1454; his fifteenth year would be 1469.</note> might be clarified as false. Now let us seek the true year.

» The good old editors—those who relegated the *Stanze* to his *early adolescence*—at stanza 35 of Book II [*Under such riddles to the youth / Was shown the light course of his fates, etc.*] <note>original: "Sotto cotali ambagi al giovinetto Fu mostro de' suoi fati il leggier corso, ec."</note> provide the heading: *A very true prophecy of the death of Iulio*: <note>"Iulio" is the Latinate form of Giuliano de' Medici.</note> and modern editors did not notice that in doing so, unless one makes a prophet of the poet, the *Stanze* are moved to a date after the Pazzi conspiracy, which was in '78. But a poem of love and jousts written after the death of the hero would have been an indecency, and in Poliziano a vice that he did not possess: ingratitude. Those verses, misunderstood by the old interpretation and not corrected by the modern ones, speak—to whoever looks closely—not of the death of Giuliano, but always of that of Simonetta: *Too happy* [Giulio], *if into his delight / Bitter death did not put its cruel bite*; <note>original: "Troppo felice... se nel suo diletto Non mettea morte acerba il crudel morso"</note> where "his delight" bitten by death cannot be understood as his own life, but rather his love cut short by the *bitter* end of Simonetta. It will be said that beginning the poem after Simonetta's death was as unseemly as writing it after Giuliano's death. No: for just as love does not end with death but endures and inspires even beyond the grave, so too can it be sung; and this concept is clearly expressed in the vision of Book II, especially at stanza 34, where Simonetta is seen emerging from the cloud of death, rising in the form of a joyful and happy goddess: *And she taking the governance of his life, / And making him eternal with her through fame.* <note>original: "E prender lei di sua vita governo, E lui con seco far per fama eterno."</note> Therefore, the date of the short poem lies between April 26, 1476, when Simonetta died, and (by a strange coincidence) April 26, 1478, when Giuliano was killed. Now from two

<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the timing of Angelo Poliziano’s composition of the "Stanze per la giostra." The author provides evidence from archival documents to prove the joust in question took place in early 1478, just before the Pazzi Conspiracy.</meta>

<page-num>XXXIV</page-num>

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

documents¹ show that in the early months of the fatal year [14]78, a joust was held in Florence. For this event, many lords and military leaders of Italy sent horses and jousters to the Magnificent <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the effective ruler of the Florentine Republic and a great patron of the arts.</note>; and in this joust, Giuliano <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478), Lorenzo’s younger brother, whose athletic prowess was a frequent subject of praise.</note> rode a brave horse which, after his death, was requested from Lorenzo for another joust held in June in Ferrara.

» Who can doubt, given they are squeezed into the brief span of two years, that this was precisely the joust of Giuliano celebrated by Master Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note>? According to custom, it must have been held between January and February of [14]78. Poliziano likely began the poem immediately: the two cantos were the work of the three months leading up to April, when the daggers of the Pazzi <note>The Pazzi conspiracy was a plot by the Pazzi family to assassinate Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici; it occurred on April 26, 1478.</note> cut short both the life of the young man and the song of his friend and client. This explanation for why the work remains unfinished satisfies us curious researchers of the past; it seems as just and honorable to us as it must have to his contemporaries. In contrast, those who believe Poliziano wrote the *Stanze* as a mere boy will never find a reason why such elegant poetry was never continued. After April 26, 1478, Poliziano set aside his lyre and laurels; dressed in mourning, he used the historian’s pen to record the bloody conspiracy. The faithful courtier was continuing his work: his heroes remained the same, only the form had changed. We are wrong to say the poem is incomplete; it was continued and finished within that very year. Its continuation is the *Commentary on the Pazzi Conspiracy* <note>original: "Coniurationis Pactianæ Commentarium," a Latin history written by Poliziano shortly after the assassination.</note>. »

Thus, when Ambrogini <note>Poliziano’s birth name was Angelo Ambrogini; he took the name "Poliziano" from his birthplace, Montepulciano.</note> set his hand to the *Stanze*, he had already made significant progress on his Latin translation of the *Iliad*:² a fact he mentions himself at the very beginning of the poem, where he speaks of the interruption he must make of his old work for the sake of the new.³ If we compare this statement with the mention the poet makes of his Homeric work in the elegy on the death of Albiera [1473] <note>Albiera degli Albizzi, a young Florentine noblewoman whose early death was mourned by many poets.</note>, as well as the reference—

it will emerge that the version of the *Iliad* was the perennial and loving work of those seven years of Angelo’s youth that passed between 1470 and 1478. But [Marsilio] Ficino, <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the leading philosopher of the Italian Renaissance and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> seized with admiration, wrote to the Medici: "You nourish in your home that Homeric youth, Angelo Poliziano, who expresses the Greek character of Homer in Latin colors. And he expresses it—and what is marvelous, at such a tender age—in such a way that it makes one who does not know Homer was Greek doubt which is the original and which is the Homeric portrait.²"

Certainly, such a wealth of harmony and Latin eloquence is astonishing, as is such boldness of touch and the ability to color and adorn: but the version is perhaps too Latin, such that it cannot fully render the image of the fated bard <note>Homer.</note>. Could it have been done otherwise? I doubt it. Yet, with greater care for the Greek forms, even if with less vividness, he translated at the same time [*while almost still a boy*] the *Fugitive Love* of Moschus, <note>Moschus was a Greek bucolic poet of the 2nd century BCE; Poliziano's translation of this poem was highly regarded for its technical precision.</note> preserving *not only the sentences but the rhythms as well and almost all the features*,³ so much so that the Latin version exceeds the Greek text by only three hexameters. And from his seventeenth year, he wrote Greek epigrams: among which experts praise the prayer to God composed in his eighteenth year [1472] and, from his twentieth [1475], the elegiac verses on the death of Theodorus Gaza <note>A Greek humanist and translator who was instrumental in bringing Greek learning to Italy.</note>: and that on the emerging Venus,⁴ done...

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...testing his skills against the ancients of the [Greek] Anthology, and chosen by the author himself as one of the few pieces he sent to Codro Urceo <note>Antonio Urceo, known as Codrus (1446–1500), was a prominent Italian humanist and professor.</note> to read, [this work] was boasted of by Urceo as superior to its models.¹ Scaliger² judged that even as a grown man, Poliziano never wrote Latin as well [as these Greek works]; according to Scioppius,³ they yield no ground to any of the Greeks.

He also composed much in Latin poetry at that age: but the elegy on the death of Albiera ⁴ <note>Albiera degli Albizzi, a young Florentine noblewoman whose death in 1473 at age fifteen moved many poets of the Medici circle.</note> deserves our particular attention. Written in 1473, in the poet's eighteenth year, it is *full, rhythmic, pure, witty, effective, and entirely worthy of such a man—in short, such that Scaliger, from whom these praises come, would have wished to have written it instead of the one said to have been sent by Ovid to Livia on the death of Drusus* ⁵ (and the comparison with Ovid is more fitting than the one with Callimachus rhetorically invented by Fabbroni); ⁶ the elegy in question is essentially an early blueprint of his poem for the Joust <note>Referencing Poliziano's famous "Stanze per la giostra," celebrating a tournament held by Giuliano de' Medici.</note>. The same mythological machinery [is present]: here it is the goddess Ramnusia <note>Another name for Nemesis, the goddess of retribution, who here punishes the world for Albiera's excessive beauty.</note> who, out of hatred for the excessive favor mortals show the Florentine maiden, calls upon Fever and Disease against her; just as there [in the *Stanze*] it is Cupid who sends the beautiful deer and then Simonetta <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the legendary beauty of the Renaissance and rumored beloved of Giuliano de' Medici.</note> to call the proud Giulio away from the studies of Diana to those of Venus. The same elegant anachronism is used to represent ancestral and modern customs, facts, and places with the colors of another time and other lands: Eleonora, daughter of Ferdinand of Naples, while traveling to marry Ercole, Duke of Ferrara, stayed in Florence on Saint John's Day: this is recounted in the following three distichs:

<page-num>XXXVII</page-num>

# ->ANGELO POLIZIANO. XXXVII<-

And if anyone were curious to know how one might or might not describe, in the language of the classics, the Borgo Ognissanti <note>A historic street in Florence named after the Church of All Saints (Ognissanti).</note> and the Prato <note>A large public square in Florence; the name literally means "meadow."</note>, listen to this:

> • There is a road; they call it Panthagia <note>original: "Panthagiam." Poliziano coins this from the Greek "pas/pan" (all) and "hagios" (holy/saint) to translate "All Saints" into a classical-sounding name.</note> by the name of Sulla; <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general traditionally considered the founder of the colony of Florence.</note>
> Here, temples dedicated to all the gods above shine.....
> Nearby, the meadows [Prato] offer up smiling colors,
> And the painted earth blooms with flowery buds. •

Likewise, in his Italian poem <gloss>¹</gloss> <note>Referring to the "Stanze per la giostra," Poliziano's famous poem celebrating a tournament held by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> he calls the pious Lucrezia Tornabuoni <note>The mother of Lorenzo the Magnificent and Giuliano de' Medici.</note> the "Etruscan Leda"; <note>In mythology, Leda was the mother of the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux); Poliziano uses this as a lofty way to describe the mother of the two Medici brothers.</note> this was a title of honor <note>The original uses "antonomasia," a rhetorical term for substituting a title for a proper name.</note> that the magnificent Piero <note>Piero "the Gouty" de' Medici, Lucrezia's husband.</note> might not have been too pleased with. So too, when Giuliano awakens from his sleep and his vision: "Already Mount Oeta seemed all of gold;" <gloss>²</gloss> here the poet would have done well to explain to us what Mount Oeta, a mountain in Thessaly <note>A region in Greece; Oeta was famous as the site of Hercules's funeral pyre.</note>, had to do with Giuliano de' Medici sleeping in the palace on Via Larga <note>The primary residence of the Medici family in Florence.</note>, from whose windows he certainly did not see the peaks made famous by the pyre of Hercules. Better, and with that solemn Latin gravity which is fitting for such occasions—and which is perhaps missed too often in the *Stanze* due to the subject matter—is the description of a Christian funeral:

> • Now the crowded procession leads the way; now the priest
> Chants mournful words; the bronze bells ring from the sacred towers....
> Every altar shines with waxed torches,
> Every altar glows with fragrant fires:
> And the venerable priests sing of eternal rest and light,
> And sprinkle the lifeless body with holy waters. •

In the end, in both the one poem and the other, there is the same luxury of description and allegorical personifications, the same bright hues and bold, broad brushwork, and the warmth, abundance, and truth of natural emotions. The reader surely remembers the portrait of Simonetta <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the celebrated beauty of the Medici court and the beloved of Giuliano.</note> in the first book of the *Joust*: here now is also that of Albiera, who is the "older sister" of Simonetta in poetry:

> • Albiera shines forth, most beautiful of face among the other nymphs,
> And a trembling radiance spreads from her countenance.
> The breeze stirs the hair flowing over her white back:
> Her dark eyes shine with a sweet torch.
> And she surpasses her companions as much as the morning star, <note>original: "lucifer." In Latin, Lucifer is the name for the planet Venus appearing before sunrise.</note>
> Glowing with a crimson face, outshines the smaller stars.
> Young and old alike look at Albiera in amazement:
> He is made of iron whom neither her beauty nor her modesty moves.

# ->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

"With joyful minds they approve of Albiera, and with a favorable 
nod, with their eyes and their voices, they praise her....
Her whiteness was suffused with sweet blood, like 
white lilies mixed with red roses. 
How her happy little eyes radiated like a bright star: 
often Love <note>original: "Amor," referring to Cupid.</note> caught his flaming torches from them. 
Whenever she let her loose hair flow freely without law, 
she seemed like Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, often depicted with flowing hair while running through the woods.</note> to the trembling wild beasts: 
Or if she gathered it back again into a knot of yellow gold, 
she seemed like Venus <note>The goddess of love and beauty.</note> combed with a Cytherean comb. 
The little Loves <note>original: "parvi Amores"; the "putti" or winged babies that accompany Venus.</note> were forever secretly tidying her, 
as was the charming Grace <note>One of the Three Graces, symbols of beauty and charm.</note> with her easy hand, 
as well as honor, and the mature modesty of her young face, 
and beauty, and probity, and a rosy blush, 
chaste faith, a cheerful laugh, and modest manners, 
a graceful gait, and naked simplicity."

But in all of the *Stanze* <note>Poliziano’s most famous Italian poem, the *Stanze per la giostra*.</note> there is never as much emotion as in the couplets <note>original: "distici"; two-line units of verse.</note> in which the final moments and the farewells of Albiera are told: yet even from a single half-line, one who looks closely will see the image of the *nymph* <note>In the Renaissance, beautiful young women were often poetically described as nymphs.</note> wrapped in a sad cloud and will hear the words of Eurydice <note>In mythology, Eurydice was the wife of Orpheus who died and was briefly pulled back from the underworld before being lost forever.</note> sounding as she is pulled back from the breezes to the underworld:

"Now for the tenth time the Sun <note>original: "Cynthius," an epithet for Apollo, the sun god.</note> brought back the unlucky light 
and had covered his face with a pitch-black torch: 
When a final horror had already pressed upon the wretched girl's eyes; 
Alas, her face had fled, the color had fled from her mouth. 
She, about to die, nevertheless looks at her sweet husband, <note>Sismondo della Stufa, Albiera's betrothed.</note> 
she notices him alone with her failing sight. 
She feeds her dying eyes upon the sight of him: 
Her mind, returning from the midst of death, sees him. 
What grief is yours now, Sismondo, when you beheld the limbs 
of the young girl die as her soul was already fleeing? 
Yet she was not forgetful of you, nor of her parents; 
She calls to you; and pours such sounds from her mouth. 
—'Spare my soul, Sismondo, if the final words 
of your wife have any right or power over you, 
Spare your tears, I pray. I have lived, and I have finished my course: 
Now my fates call me far away from you. 
I die untimely indeed: but I shall depart to the shadows 
pure, and stained by no marks of sin..... 
Spare your tears, I pray, my husband: thus my spirit 
will escape happily from here into the thin breezes. 
But comfort the too, ah too sad faces of both our parents. 
Alas, the sound grows numb in my mouth;'"

And because it seems to me that these citations should complete the image of Poliziano the poet in the reader's mind—which might not be entirely whole from the Italian verses alone—I will also relate the famous description of the funeral procession:

> *Now the maiden is carried out, laid upon the black bier,
> Her shorn hair bound back by a lowly deceit.* <note>original: "humili fraude." This likely refers to the artifice used to arrange the hair of the deceased to maintain a semblance of her former beauty.</note>
> *Alas, where now are the charming smiles, where the sweet words
> Which were able to break the hardness of iron?
> Where now are the eyes that cast forth starry flames?
> Alas, where are the lips that rivaled crimson roses?
> O gods above, what does a short hour not snatch away from man!
> Ah, wretched ones, we are but sleep and a fleeting shadow.
> Yet neither had paleness changed her snowy limbs,
> Nor had a heavy wasting settled upon her cold face:
> But beautiful death imitated a light sleep;
> That brightness holds her face and her mouth in a faintness.
> Just as white lilies, plucked by a maiden's hand, grow faint,
> And a crown woven with snowy roses.*
<note>original Latin: "Iam virgo effertur... niveis texta corona rosis."</note>

In these last verses, the reader has certainly noticed more than one reminiscence of the death of Laura <note>The muse of the poet Petrarch.</note>, as it is described in the *Triumphs* <note>original: "Trionfi"; Petrarch's allegorical poem.</note>: and other Petrarchan concepts are found further above, such as: "Do not groan: as it is sweet to live, it is sweet to die" <note>original: "Ne geme: cum dulce est vivere, dulce mori est."</note> and "I believe now that even the divine powers can die." <note>original: "Credo ego iam divûm numina posse mori."</note> Such a conjunction of the two languages and the two poetries—which he learned to admire equally at the school of Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a prominent humanist scholar and teacher of Poliziano.</note>—announces the composer of the *Joust* <note>original: "Giostra," referring to Poliziano’s masterpiece, the *Stanze per la giostra*.</note>; who already appears with all his virtues and his vices in this Latin funeral elegy <term>epicedio <gloss>a poem or song performed over a body before burial</gloss></term>. And in the skillful mixture of the different manners of Lucretius, Virgil, and Ovid—which is already admirable in the funeral elegy and will be even more admirably so in larger proportions in the *Joust*—lies that happiness of appropriating, without any effort in the world, the most beautiful images and dictions of the most different authors as if they were the natural garment of his own concept; that wisdom of imitating while remaining original...

<summary>The author presents Poliziano's Latin elegies for Albiera degli Albizzi, noting how he blends classical Roman styles (Virgil, Ovid) with the Italian tradition of Petrarch to create a unique humanist voice.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Poliziano’s Latin elegies to his development as a vernacular Italian poet, specifically discussing his early training, his relationship with the Medici circle, and the debate surrounding the composition date of his masterpiece, the "Stanzas for the Joust."</meta>

<page-num>XL</page-num>

->## ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

Before he was an original poet, the young man from Montepulciano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) took his name from his birthplace, Mons Politianus (Montepulciano).</note> had long practiced his craft in the gymnasium of translating the *Iliad*. By writing in the two classical languages, he had made the indescribable beauties of antiquity his very marrow and blood; he held them so ready and organized in his mind that they came to his tongue and pen at the first moment, like household tools appearing before the eye of a diligent housewife. He was then made fluent in the use of the most vivid and domestic elegances through Florentine conversation and through the study—quite predictable in a student of Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a humanist and teacher of Poliziano, famous for his commentary on Dante.</note> protected by the Medici—of the three great authors of the fourteenth century <note>The "Tre Corone" (Three Crowns): Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.</note>, and finally by composing and improvising ballads and *rispetti* <note>A traditional Italian folk-poetic form consisting of eight lines.</note> among his joyful companions. Thus, around the age of twenty-four, the composition of the *Stanzas for the Joust* <note>Poliziano's most famous Italian poem, celebrating a tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> is understood and explained. But whoever has believed in the precocity of the *Stanzas* over any other proof of the young writer's genius has believed in one of those miracles that criticism must flatly reject. That wealth of the most hidden literary erudition is admissible, if you will, at fourteen years of age; but not such a wealth of exquisitely delineated images, nor such vividness and wisdom of imitation, of recasting, and of renewal in the first essay of a student. At fourteen, one may write with easy elegance in a dead language, having committed its most refined writers to memory with the fervor of adolescence; however, one does not create a style in a living language to which two authors like Dante and Petrarch have given their own stamp. A poem that, by changing the forms of national poetry, marks a new literary age, is not made at fourteen.

Educated in such elegance of letters, it is natural that Poliziano should also succeed in invention and arrangement in a way entirely different from those who had preceded him in treating similar subjects. Leaving aside a *Description of the Game of Football*,¹ composed at the beginning of the 15th century—which was entirely middle-class in subject and style, though not without a certain natural and effective elegance—we have two descriptions of noble jousts dating back only a few years before that of Poliziano; and both, like the *Game of Football*, are in octaves.

---

**¹** Published in the *Borghini*, a philological journal, Year I, No. 1, Florence, January 1863.

->## ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...and so it was; for the *ottava rima* <note>A rhyming stanza form consisting of eight iambic lines, which became the standard for Italian epic and narrative poetry.</note> was by then the established meter for narration and description, especially for subjects intended for wide circulation. Luca Pulci celebrated the joust held in the Piazza di Santa Croce on February 7, 1468 (Florentine style <note>The Florentine calendar began the year on March 25th; thus, February 1468 corresponds to 1469 in the modern calendar.</note>), in which Lorenzo de' Medici won the prize.<gloss>1</gloss> The author of the *Ciriffo Calvaneo* <note>An epic poem by Luca Pulci concerning chivalric adventures.</note> attempted to give the short poem a knightly tone; he attributed the cause of the joust to a garland of violets, requested as a gift by the young Lorenzo at a festival for the wedding of Braccio Martelli from "She who loves his youthful laurel, crowned by heaven alone with every grace, born of the noble blood of Piccarda" <note>This refers to Lucrezia Donati. The "laurel" (lauro) is a pun on Lorenzo's name. "Piccarda" refers to the noble Donati family, famously represented by Piccarda Donati in Dante's *Divine Comedy*.</note>—that is, Lucrezia Donati, the poetic lady of the man who would eventually marry Clarice Orsini. She, continues Pulci,

> ...She replied with skillful words,
> And begged him (though her plea was a command)
> That he promise her, if he wished to obtain it [the garland],
> That he would soon come to the field armed in the saddle
> And for her love would carry it.
> And she placed it on his head with a smile,
> With words so modest and so sweet,
> That one could see paradise
> And hear Gabriel when he said "Hail" <note>original: "Ave"—referring to the Angelic Salutation (the Annunciation).</note>.
> He, who shall never be parted from her
> And to whom she has given the key to her heart,
> Accepted the gift so gracious and worthy,
> A sign of prosperous fates and victory.

But he does not maintain this tone: the poet of the *Driadeo* and the *Eroidi* <note>Other works by Luca Pulci: the *Driadeo* is a mythological poem about wood nymphs, and the *Eroidi* is an imitation of Ovid's *Heroides*.</note> frequently recalls his mythology after the invocation to Apollo, and always does so clumsily. As proof, compare stanza XXV of Poliziano, which we all know by heart [*Zephyr already...*], with this one by Pulci:

> ...Progne had returned all cheerful,
> Although she wept for her Philomela <note>original: "Filomena." In Greek myth, Progne (the swallow) and Philomela (the nightingale) are sisters transformed into birds after a tragedy.</note>:
> Love was preparing his shackles and pillories,
> His yokes, his snares, and every chain of his;
> And Pan felt a thousand pipes sounding:
> Every field was full of flowers:
> Satyrs were seen sweetly following
> The Dryad and Napaeae <note>Nymphs of the woods and valleys.</note> goddesses through the woods.

-># ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

More graceful and more true to character is <note>The author is likely comparing Angelo Poliziano to Luca Pulci, who was mentioned on the previous page.</note> the brother of the author of the *Morgante* <note>Luigi Pulci (1432–1484) was the author of the *Morgante*; his brother was Luca Pulci. The text suggests that when Poliziano writes in his native Florentine spirit, he captures a specific charm.</note>, when, despite the grand air he has adopted, he is drawn by his Florentine nature to joke about his own subject. In anticipation of the tournament, the talkative curiosity of the Florentines—merchants who never stopped talking about arms and lance-thrusts—is finely turned into a joke.

> "At every corner the rumors grew:
> Who is it, who is the jouster at Santa Croce? <note>The Piazza di Santa Croce in Florence, a major civic space used for festivals and jousting tournaments.</note>
> And all the people ran to see...
> And a thousand charming tales were heard,
> And they lied by the pound <note>A metaphor meaning to tell exaggerated lies in great volume.</note> at Rigoletto’s shop,¹ <margin>1. That is: in the shop of Rigoletto and the armorer, etc.</margin>
> At the armorer’s, at the saddler’s:
> Not a word of truth would be told for anything.
> There were great disputes about bucklers <note>Small round shields.</note>,
> About lance-rests, arm-guards, and blunt spear-tips;
> And much was spoken of Anton Boscoli:
> And so the happy time passed by.
> And they spoke of Marin Giovanni,
> Of his works already so famous:
> Of Ciarpellone <note>Anton Boscoli, Giovanni Marino, and Ciarpellone were likely well-known men-at-arms or famous figures in Florence at the time.</note> and his long struggles,
> How he did marvelous things upon the field;
> And of many others from years gone by,
> Their ancient, worthy, and warlike trials:
> But above all others, in my opinion,
> The Buriassi ² <margin>2. "Buriassi" was the name given to those who brought the jousters onto the field and stood around them, giving them advice and training them, just as "godfathers" or seconds do today for those who must fight in a duel. —Varchi, *Ercolano*.</margin> proved their worth.
> The Buriassi were the fifth element ³: <margin>3. *Alimento*; a Florentine dialect version of the word *elemento* (element).</margin>
> They no longer replied except with affectation..."

### A few moments before the joust,

> "All the ladies were directly opposite:
> Therefore, before they [the jousters] enter the prison <note>A poetic way of referring to the enclosed tournament lists or perhaps the restrictive suits of armor.</note>,
> I believe every jouster, poor soul!,
> Would have wanted a kiss in the French style <note>A "kiss in the French style" typically refers to a kiss on the cheeks.</note>
> That would leave a rose upon each cheek."

<page-num>XLIII</page-num>

->## ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

And one of the jousters brings to mind the *Beoni* <note>original: *Beoni* ("The Drunkards"), a satirical poem by Lorenzo de' Medici</note> more than the legends of the Round Table:

> "Now let us return to that loafer,¹ to Cino;
> Who, seeing that Lorenzo does not rise,
> Put a large flask of wine to his mouth
> And drank the whole thing out of spite.....
> At every game Cino wanted to drink....."

Furthermore, the list of jousters is long (among whom the reader’s mind pauses on Francesco and Guglielmo dei Pazzi, who here in a game of arms—as later in politics—unhappily held the field against Lorenzo; on Iacopo di Poggio Bracciolini, also a future victim of the conspiracy; on Bernardo Rucellai, the "Sallust of Florence" <note>A reference to the Roman historian Sallust, known for his brief, punchy style; Rucellai was a scholar and diplomat</note> who was visited by Erasmus, but to whom he refused to speak Latin for fear of committing barbarisms <note>Erasmus was the greatest Latinist of the age; Rucellai was so fastidious about linguistic purity that he feared making a mistake in front of him</note>; and on Pagol Antonio Soderini, the solemn orator of the democracy in 1495);² the descriptions of all the horses, the harnesses, the equipment, and the liveries—magnificent and precious beyond belief—are prolix and minute, and not even a few clever turns of the native tongue can lessen the tedium of them. There are many strange emblems (some of which seem to anticipate the parodies of Tassoni <note>Alessandro Tassoni (1565–1635), author of the mock-heroic poem *The Stolen Bucket*</note>: Pier Vespucci, for example, "Had depicted on his shield / An anvil at sea that went by sail.") The poetry rises a little at the appearance of Lorenzo de' Medici on the field. Oh, Sacchetti and Pucci <note>Franco Sacchetti and Antonio Pucci, popular Florentine poets of the 1300s known for their more modest, communal spirit</note> and the popular poets of the fourteenth century would not have taken much pleasure in this twenty-year-old youth who spent ten thousand gold florins for a festival, who came to the joust adorned with the fleur-de-lis insignia granted to him as a privilege by Louis XI, the "Tiberius of France," and dressed in armor sent to him for the purpose by Duke Galeazzo, the "Caligula of Milan," <note>The author compares the French King and the Milanese Duke to tyrannical Roman emperors to highlight their ruthless characters</note> and who changed between two horses, one a gift from King Ferdinand of Naples and the other from Duke Borso d'Este. But the descendant of a house of greats, the gentleman fallen and become a courtier to merchants, sang:

> "After so much splendor came the sun;
> After gracefulness came nobility;
> The rose after the lily and the violets;
> Lorenzo, armed with great pride"

A more long-winded versifier, and infinitely more tedious than Pulci, is one Francesco of Florence, a poor blind man who lived in Cento; who in a full 204 stanzas wrote a description of the tournament fought in Bologna in 1470 by order of Giovanni II Bentivoglio. <insert>2</insert> The short poem is of a popular style, but crude: this is the opening of the account:

> "In the said city of such great fame
> A gentleman of the House of Bentivoglio
> (Sir Giovanni the world calls him:
> He was the excellent fruit of every virtue),
> To make the branch of his house green again,
> He ordained—and I shall tell you how—
> Another triumphant and great festival
> With armor on the back and helmet on the head."

# ANGELO POLIZIANO

-> The Bolognese had a captain <-
-> Who was a vigorous man in arms. <-
-> Messer Giovanni <note>Giovanni II Bentivoglio (1443–1508), the ruler of Bologna who commissioned the tournament.</note> took him by the hand <-
-> With a speech both splendid and joyful, <-
-> And thus he said to him: “O supreme gentleman, <-
-> I want our fame to fly throughout the world <-
-> To honor the feast of such a saint, <-
-> Our Petronius <note>Saint Petronius is the patron saint of Bologna; his basilica remains one of the city's most famous landmarks.</note> . . . . . . . . . . . ” <-

But the blind man of Bologna <note>Francesco of Florence, the poet introduced on the previous page.</note> also shares the same craze as Pulci for mythological erudition. It is true that, following the custom of popular poets, he invokes the Virgin Mary at the beginning and in the middle of his story; and he has Bentivoglio address a prayer to God at the start of the tournament. However, in that same stanza, he does not fail to have him beseech the almighty Mars to come to his aid: “As you were to the great Trojan Aeneas, who for Lavinia dealt a wicked death to Turnus, a king so powerful and brave.” Of a knight named Theseus, it is said: “He renewed the fame upon the field of that one <note>The mythological Theseus, Duke of Athens, who slew the Minotaur.</note> who fought for Ariadne in Crete, for the beautiful Cretan lady, and dealt death within the labyrinth to the cursed monster.” In comparison to the armor of another knight: “Certainly Minerva would have lost out, and I know not if Proserpina with all her grace could have produced such a work.” Elsewhere, the combat is described—anticipating a famous comparison by Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of the epic *Orlando Furioso*.</note>—as follows: “The forge seemed like that of Mongibello <note>original: "Mongibello"; a local Sicilian name for Mount Etna, where the god Vulcan was said to have his volcanic forge.</note>, where that smith Vulcan works.”

Yet the popular singer is even more fond of mythological and historical erudition if it is mixed with chivalric elements or presented under the guise of masked knighthood; this is the tradition of the romances from the previous century. Listen: “In his coming, he resembled a new Arcite <note>A tragic hero from Boccaccio’s *Teseida*.</note> in the city of Thebes, who wished to die for Emilia, for never was a Greek woman seen so supreme.” In another place, regarding the Bolognese knights: “Emperor Caesar within Thessaly did not do as much against his enemies, as Lucan, a historian of great worth, wrote;” but then, immediately after, he also cites King Mambrino <note>A legendary pagan king from chivalric literature whose golden helmet was a sought-after prize.</note>. One jouster “seemed like Hector upon Galatea <note>The name of Hector’s horse in medieval chivalric accounts of the Trojan War.</note>,” and another like “Alexander, Emperor of Macedonia, upon his horse Bucephalus.” And so he continues entirely in descriptions and enumerations just like Pulci; except that he has this advantage over him: he makes his combatants give speeches of twenty-two stanzas <note>original: "ottave"; the eight-line poetic form standard in Italian epic poetry.</note> at a time. And he resembles Pulci—

Thus the lords, who would have liked to but did not yet dare to openly declare themselves princes, held those festivals and displays, as Machiavelli noted, to "give men something to think about, to take their thoughts away from matters of state."¹ Later, in 1495, Savonarola, depicting for the Florentines the moral portrait of the tyrant—that is, Lorenzo de' Medici—assigned these among other characteristics to him: "And many times, especially in times of abundance and peace, he occupies <insert>the people</insert> with spectacles and festivals, so that they might think of themselves and not of him...;" and again: "The tyrant wants to be superior in everything, even <term>even</term> <note>original Latin: "etiam," meaning "even" or "also."</note> in the smallest things, such as in games, in jousting, in racing horses;... and in all other things... in which competition occurs, he always seeks to be first."² And the intentions of the tyrants were, for their part, aided by the poets, whose too-frequent fault is to allow themselves to be dazzled by outward appearances and, in the service of power and fortune, to ignore truth and virtue. If this accusation seems too general, the citations from the two poems will show at least that it would be unjust to weigh too heavily upon Poliziano alone. <page-num>XLVIII</page-num>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

While the habit of classical reminiscences and mythology was common at that time, there is a vast distance between mere fashion and true art. The poem of Poliziano, although written almost at the same time as that of Pulci—setting aside the "blind man of Cento" <note>A reference to Francesco of Florence, mentioned on the previous page, who was from the town of Cento.</note>—seems, as Roscoe¹ well said, to be a century later in matters of taste.

In its type of invention and its method of treatment, it is cast in the mold of encomiastic poems <note>Poems written to praise a specific person or event.</note>, mixed with fable and lyricism, which abound in Latin literature from Statius until the final decline of the 5th century. In this Tuscan poem, as in our author's Latin *Silvae* <term>Silvae: A title used for collections of occasional or "extemporaneous" poems, famously used by the Roman poet Statius</term>, Statius and Claudian appear to be those among the ancients who had the greatest hand in shaping his imagination into a peculiar way of conceiving ideas. It would be both curious and useful to investigate why, during the Middle Ages and the early Renaissance, the authors of the "decadent" period were felt and imitated—with their striking defects—more so than the exquisite modesty of style found in the Golden Age; Seneca more than Cicero, Ovid and Lucan more than Virgil and Tibullus, and Claudian more than Horace. Our author perhaps could not, due to the nature of his subject, turn to other examples. But what liveliness, warmth, and movement we find here compared to the rigidity and rhetorical tone of his masters! What variety in the wealth of his imitations! What readiness and happiness in the way he assimilates and recreates the work of others! 

Giuliano, the scorner of Love and his followers [Book I, stanzas 8-16], is indeed the Hippolytus of Euripides <note>A character from Greek tragedy who rejects romantic love in favor of the hunt.</note> and in part the Narcissus of Ovid:² but certain tints borrowed from the "painter of the beautiful, shy lady of Avignon" <note>A reference to the poet Petrarch and his descriptions of his muse, Laura.</note> make the researcher lose the trail of the first original. In the praises of country life placed in the mouth of the graceful hunter [Book I, 17-21], you will first hear the echo of Horace’s epode³ and Virgil's *Georgics*;⁴ but right in the middle, a Tuscan landscape painted from life—with a brush that foreshadows that of the Flemish masters—erases that first sensation. And Cupid’s soliloquy as he meditates on revenge [Book I, 23-24] and the description of the hunt [Book I, 25-33] will remind you, if you like, a bit too much, the former of Venus’s prologue to the Hip— <note>The text cuts off mid-word as it refers to the prologue of the play *Hippolytus*.</note>

...refined and crowned; the speech where Juno opens the story of the *Aeneid*¹; and collectively, the hunt of Dido,² that of the Calydonian boar,³ and the more ancient hunt of Ulysses.⁴ What does it matter? This does not prevent the invention in the subsequent *Stanzas*—where a deer is placed by Love before Giuliano to lead him away from the hunt and conduct him to the place where he sees the beautiful Simonetta [I, 34-37]—from transporting the reader’s mind <margin>☛</margin> into the world of romances of adventure and the snares set for a beloved knight by some beautiful fairy. This is so even though the image of the deer is composed of that same light air from which Apollo and Venus, in the works of Homer and Virgil,⁵ compose the false images of heroes they protect to save the real ones from the fury of their enemies. In the portrait of the nymph and in Giuliano’s falling in love, it seems the poet has gathered from Sappho and Tibullus, from Virgil and Ovid, the purest flower of the sensory world. Nor was it enough for him; he also wished to make use of those sensations of external nature which, in harmony with inner feeling, inspired the Provençal poets, as well as the abstractions of Cavalcanti, the mysticism of Dante, and the psychology of Petrarch; his mind was always choosing that which, in them, marks the ultimate limit of natural perfection. Because the image of Simonetta <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the legendary beauty of the Medici court and presumed model for Botticelli's Venus.</note>, one of the most beautiful in our poetry, is as softly colored as Alcina or Armida <note>Alcina and Armida are famous, seductive enchantresses from the epic poems of Ariosto and Tasso, respectively.</note>, but not sensual like them; she is at once pure and serenely thoughtful, yet not too transparent and ethereal like Portinari <note>Beatrice Portinari, Dante’s spiritualized beloved.</note> almost always is, or as the lady from Avignon <note>Laura, the beloved of Petrarch.</note> is at times. She stands at the summit of the natural; she is a Greek statue, a statue by Canova; a Hebe or a Psyche, moving with the step of a goddess through a flowering spring landscape. In the painting of this fifteenth-century poet, nature feels the presence of the goddess, or rather feels the deified part of itself: "The whole forest laughs around her, and eases its bitterness as much as it can⁶"; "Every breeze falls silent at her divine speech, and every little bird sings⁷"; "She moved her slow steps over the grass with an act adorned with loving grace; the [woods] made..."

<page-num>L</page-num>

...then sweet laments were born, and the little birds began to weep; but the green grass under those sweet footsteps turns white, yellow, vermilion, and blue.¹» Let us look with love upon this figure, for she is perhaps the complete archetype of Poliziano's poetry; she bears witness to the young and pure Renaissance, to the dignity restored to matter, to the flesh, and to form against the mortifying asceticism <note>The practice of self-denial and spiritual discipline, often involving the "mortification of the flesh" in medieval religious life.</note> and the exhausting idealism of the Middle Ages. In contemplating her, you feel that the age of Giotto and Fra Angelico—for whom the entire life of a figure is confined to the radiance of the brow and the contemplating eyes—is over. You feel and recognize Masaccio, Rosselli, Perugino, and Raphael; Titian, Giulio Romano, and Guido Reni will come later, and with them, or shortly before, Ariosto; then the Carracci and Tasso will arrive.

But we have seen nothing more than the prologue of the action thus far: with the flight of Love to the realm of his mother [I, 68], it would seem that we should enter into the main subject. This is not the case: an episode presents itself to us—that is, a description that would have seemed interminable even to Ovid, as it takes up 52 octaves <note>A poetic stanza form consisting of eight lines (ottava rima).</note>; it is the greatest defect and, at the same time, the greatest merit of this Tuscan poem. It is the description of the kingdom and the palace of Venus [I, 69-120] which our poet has transplanted wholesale from the *Epithalamium <term>Epithalamium</term> <note>A song or poem specifically written for a bride on her way to the marital chamber.</note> for Honorius and Maria* by Claudian,² except for some precious material he took from Sidonius Apollinaris,³ the pagan Bishop of Clermont who, unable to achieve elegance, flaunted luxury in his wedding songs, as is common among barbarians. But how have the 47 verses of Claudian—already many—been expanded to 52 octaves? For the topography of the sweet kingdom, as for the description of its allegorical inhabitants, some color has been added from Petrarch’s *Triumphs*.⁴ The garden of the Phaeacians⁵ "which in Homer’s verses still grows green,⁶" and the Latin *Georgics* where he describes plants, and the poet of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Ovid.</note> where he narrates the origins of plants and flowers, have admirably enriched Poliziano’s flora and fauna. ...between them by nature and instinct live in miraculous harmony in the kingdom of Venus, certainly had its first concept from the mythical descriptions of the Golden Age <note>A primordial era of peace, harmony, stability, and prosperity in Greek and Roman mythology.</note>. And there is a very singular one in the second *Grove of Love* <note>Original: *Selva d’amore*</note> by Lorenzo de’ Medici; between which and the *Stanzas* <note>Poliziano's *Stanze per la giostra*.</note> there is a surprising similarity in certain descriptions and similes: as an example, the comparison of the tiger whose cubs are taken away—famous in many Latin poets and which Messer <note>A respectful title for a gentleman or scholar.</note> Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano.</note> imitated most specifically from Claudian¹ and Ariosto² from Messer Angelo—is also found with the same rhymes in the *Grove* by Medici. Which of the two poems was written first is not certain; but it is certain that Lorenzo preceded Poliziano by a few years, and it is probable that the client <note>Poliziano, who lived under the protection of the Medici family.</note> wished to flatter the patron by imitating his poetry, as Pulci did in the *Beca da Dicomano*. In any case, as another argument regarding the innovations brought by Poliziano to the poetry of his time, let these octaves <note>Eight-line poetic stanzas.</note> by Medici³ be compared to their sisters in the *Joust* <note>Original: *Giostra*.</note>.

> “And one could see in a stubble field
> The little sheep stay joyful with the wolf,
> In a pair, without suspicion of each other;
> The wolf was not fierce then, nor she timid.
> Nor was the fox malicious and deceitful:
> And there is no need for the peasant girl
> To keep the cur <note>Original: *botol* (a small, aggressive dog).</note> to chase it away from the chickens;
> But it seems, if it even comes there, it makes them a feast.
> The hare and the hound lie in one bush;⁴
> One does not bark, and the other does not yet moan.
> Between the greyhound and the roe deer and the stag there is peace,
> Nor does any hope or fear in swift feet:
> They play among themselves, and they like to provoke
> Each other at times; and, if they run together,
> They do not run to escape the fierce bite
> But only to surpass each other in the race ...
> Not yet was there in the breast of mortals
> The fierce desire to satiate themselves on flesh.
> Through nourishment we become bestial,
> Which strips human blood of its nature:
> Hence there is war between man and animals.”

But whoever delights in these comparisons and studies the similarities of sentiment and literary style of a century <note>Reconstructed from the cut-off text "u / colo".</note> should also look in the *Morgante* <note>An epic poem by Luigi Pulci (1432–1484).</note> for the 42 stanzas of the canto where the classes and individuals of the animal kingdom <note>Reconstructed from "an / come".</note> are described, just as they are woven into the precious pavilion given by Luciana <note>A character in Pulci's *Morgante*.</note> to Rinaldo. Now: is this love for description—almost scientific, almost like a catalog—of the various productions of nature <note>Reconstructed from "na / animali".</note> (animals, plants, flowers, precious stones) a recurrence or a lingering trace of medieval tradition? The Middle Ages <note>The text likely said "Il medio evo" here, though the word is cut off.</note>, while it considered nature with the wonder of a child and the terror of a savage, led by the hand by magic and alchemy <note>Reconstructed from "al / mia".</note>, was transported from the threshold of natural curiosity (where science prepares <note>Reconstructed from "pre / la scienza".</note> itself) into the inner sanctums of poetry, where imperfect perceptions are recomposed into phantasms. From this came the many *bestiaries* <note>Medieval books providing descriptions and moralizing interpretations of real or imaginary animals.</note> of French poetry of the 12th and 13th centuries,² the first elements of the *Romance of Reynard* <note>Original: *Roman de Renart*, a medieval cycle of animal fables.</note> and of La Fontaine <note>Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695), famous for his fables.</note>, and the treatises on the virtues of precious stones, translated then into the allegorical poetry of the author of *The Intelligence* <note>Original: *L'Intelligenza*, a 13th-century Italian didactic poem.</note>,³ and which played such a large <note>Reconstructed from "sì [gran]".</note> part in the enchanted palaces of the romance poems of the 16th century. Or truly, was that passion for putting on display <note>Reconstructed from "mo / stra".</note> almost every moment an inventory of natural productions—made by fantasy more than by science—a presentiment <note>Reconstructed from "pr / timento".</note> of the ancient world in the presence of the discovery of the new <note>Likely referring to the Americas or "New World" discovery.</note>? This new world, with its portentous fertility, was destined to far surpass all the beauty, richness, and horror <note>Reconstructed from "or / immaginato".</note> imagined by the philosophers, poets, and mages of Greece and the Middle Ages <note>Original: *mezzi tempi*.</note>?

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between poetry and the visual arts, moving from the descriptive nature of Lorenzo de’ Medici and Luigi Pulci to the refined classicism of Angelo Poliziano. <meta>catchword: POLIZIANO.</meta>

...of Venus, and especially of the engravings that adorn the doors. This recurrence of poetry to its sister arts—which begins with the shields of Achilles¹ and Hercules² and was later imitated in that of Aeneas³ by Virgil (who also knew how to draw tears over the painting of the death of Troilus in the temple of Carthage⁴)—was natural for a people with such a spontaneous understanding of art as the Italians. Thus, since the end of the thirteenth century <term>duecento: the 1200s</term>, the author of the poem in *nona rima* <note>A nine-line stanza form; the author refers to the anonymous poem "L'Intelligenza."</note> used the paintings and engravings of the Palace of Intelligence to summarize the romantic deeds of all the great cycles of stories.⁵ And who does not recall the verses where Dante gathers moral allegories from throughout history to carve them with his pen—as fierce as Michelangelo’s chisel—into the terraces of Purgatory?⁶ If, therefore, this beautiful artifice had been utilized by the contemporaries of Niccolò and Andrea Pisano, and of Giotto, it certainly must have appealed to the imagination of a poet in the century that opened with Ghiberti and Donatello. Indeed, in those engravings more than anywhere else, Poliziano proved himself an artist of admirable style. It is true that Hesiod and Ovid, the Homeric hymns and the epigrams of the *Anthology*, Theocritus and Moschus, provide him with the basic outlines; but how he fills them in! In one place, he creates a Bacchic scene where the eleven-syllable line <term>endecasillabo: the standard line of Italian poetry</term> riots, leaps, and staggers like drunken satyrs; in another, a "Rape of Europa" where the verse moans like the companions of the Phoenician maiden left upon the shore. Everywhere, the fifteenth-century <term>quattrocento: the 1400s</term> rhyme breathes truth and life, much like the most miraculous works of design in the following century! Elsewhere, the poet’s pen seems transformed into a Greek stylus. It is as if he—the future diviner of the power of Michelangelo (to whom, at age sixteen, he suggested the "Battle of Hercules with the Centauri"⁷, that stupendous proof of the "child titan")—wished from his small room to almost contend with Phidias and Praxiteles <note>Famous sculptors of ancient Greece.</note> to carve the pure image of Venus Anadyomene <term>Venus Anadyomene: "Venus rising from the sea"</term>, just as Virgil had once contended with the three Rhodian sculptors to represent in writing the...

...strenuous and terrible group of the Laocoön <note>A famous ancient Greek sculpture depicting a Trojan priest and his sons attacked by sea serpents.</note>. Departing from this long episode and returning to the epic material, the return of Love <note>Cupid</note> to the realm of Venus, his boasts, and the praise and advice of his mother, as well as the dispatching of the little Loves to awaken the passion for jousts in youthful hearts [I, 121-II, 21], are all devices imitated from the wedding poems <term>epitalamici: poems written for a bride and groom</term> of the Latins. In those works, these cares, travels, and consultations of Venus, Cupid, and Hymen to arrange love and marriage were formal conventions; so much so that after Statius, who first brought them into play,² everything is full of them, from Claudian³ down to the three holy bishops: Sidonius Apollinaris,⁴ Felix Ennodius,⁵ and Venantius Fortunatus.⁶ And perhaps from this resemblance of the *Giostra* <note>Poliziano’s poem "Stanzas Begun for the Joust of the Magnificent Giuliano de’ Medici."</note> to ancient wedding poems, and from the mention of Lorenzo's loves in Book II, it happened that Varillas—confusing his memories and inventing where he did not remember, with the boldness with which many of his nation mask their ignorance of foreign matters—names a wedding poem composed by Poliziano in verses worthy of the age of Augustus for the marriage of Lo-

...[Lorenzo] de' Medici with Clarice Orsini,¹ and Mencken,² with the <insert>pedantry</insert> of a learned German, wastes his time searching for traces of that wedding poem <term>epithalamium: a poem written for a bride and groom</term>. Furthermore, in the meeting of Cupid with Venus, our author kept close to the style of Statius and Claudian, except for the superior elegance he brought to it. Just as with the sending of Iris to the House of Sleep ordered by Juno in the *Metamorphoses*,³ or rather drawing from the most solemn epic fantasies,⁴ he imitated the movement of Pasithea—at the command of Venus—to lead the dreams that, with their images, might awaken in Giuliano the desire to appear armed on the field [II, 22-26]. More original, though lacking in charm—except where Virgil, with the serene melody of his Eurydice,⁵ and Dante, with the apocalyptic omens of the *Vita Nuova*,⁶ contribute to representing the premature death of Simonetta—is Giuliano's vision [II, 27-38]. With the armor and the prayer to Pallas <note>The goddess Athena</note> by the hero who, having awakened, prepares for battle, the poem ends [II, 38-46]—or, more accurately, it is interrupted. Perhaps the poet himself lost hope or grew weary of a subject that was entirely laudatory and descriptive; or perhaps the blame should be placed on the dagger of Bandini <note>Bernardo Bandini dei Baroncelli, one of the Pazzi conspirators who assassinated Giuliano de' Medici in 1478</note>, which gleamed with a terrible light between the praise and the praiser. Angelo then turned his hand to the historical pen, as Del Lungo says, and thus also a little to the lyre of Horace. And because the ode to Gentile, Bishop of Arezzo, is a worthy completion of the *Giostra*; and because, in the judgment of the Latinist Fabbroni, it "can stand comparison with the most beautiful songs of the poet of Venosa <note>The Roman poet Horace, born in Venosa</note>;"⁷ and so that those who have read Poliziano's biography (written in elegant Latin by Bonafous) need not mourn with that worthy Frenchman the loss of the *Poem on the Murder of Giuliano*;⁸ I place before your eyes, kind reader, that ode or poem, whatever you wish to call it:

> Gentile, you who are the greatest part of my soul,
> Why are you so distressed by our common fate?
> Why do you wear away your spirit with mournful cares,
> And torture me as well?

The reader will certainly have noticed that phrase *France happy in her kings*, <note>Poliziano is likely referring to the diplomatic support offered to Lorenzo by King Louis XI of France</note> expressing at once a desire and a regret. The silences of despotism <note>Italian: *dispotismo*</note> are better suited to the leisure of the Muses, according to a common <note>Italian: *comune*</note> sentiment of courtly writers.

...the most beautiful parts of the first book are enjoyed so willingly, I do not know what would have happened to his fame [had he finished it]: a display of arms, moreover, described by the classic Master Angelo—even assuming that he never descended to the vulgar enumerations of Luca Pulci <note>Luca Pulci (1431–1470) wrote a more literal and technical poetic account of Lorenzo de' Medici's joust, which the author here finds less artistic than Poliziano's work</note>—it can be taken almost for certain that he would not have stood up to the comparison with the battles described by Ariosto and Tasso, who were quite different masters of arms and had other traditional heroes at their disposal. A panegyric <note>a speech or poem of high praise</note> spanning multiple cantos would have been just one more boring poem, read only by scholars; and already in the second book, the poetry declines in comparison to the first. Whereas, as it is, that fragment enjoys almost popular fame, and as a work of style, it truly stands among the rarest treasures of our literature. It does not possess the supreme perfection of the *Georgics* <note>Virgil's poem on agriculture</note> nor even that of the *Aminta* <note>Tasso's famous pastoral play</note>; both poems that mark the height of good taste in the two most refined ages of the double literature of Italy <note>A reference to Italy's dual heritage of Latin and Italian letters</note>.

Beyond the more significant improprieties in the general imitation and the structure of the poem which should be clear enough from what has been discussed so far, some small defects of versification and style are also noted in the *Stanze*. Others reproach the frequent use of *sdruccioli* <term>sdruccioli: rhymes where the accent falls on the third-to-last syllable, like "tavola" or "nuvola"</term>, calling it a *low sound for a serious subject*; but for those who seek variety in sounds above all, and who enjoy *sdruccioli* rhymes in their proper places in Dante and Ariosto, they will also please in Poliziano. Others turn up their noses at certain verb endings in *-orono* for the third-person plural of the perfect tense, and criticize Master Angelo for imitating the ancients more than was fitting for an elegant poet: one should rather have accused him of writing the spoken language of his time, because back then Italy had not yet, thank God, fallen so low that there was this curse of having to imitate even the language <note>The author is defending Poliziano's natural 15th-century Florentine usage against later critics who demanded a more rigid, artificial style</note>. With more reason he is criticized for several Latinisms; though not even the best are permitted to entirely shake off the yoke of their own century; and for some redundancy at the expense of effectiveness and propriety; and for a few unpleasant pairings of sounds; and for the impropriety of certain images, such as where he compared the little Cupids to so many galley slaves <note>In Book II, stanza 2, Poliziano describes the "little Loves" rowing a boat, using the term "galeotti," which the critic finds too unrefined for the subject</note> [II, 2].¹ But

<meta>This page continues the stylistic analysis of Poliziano’s "Stanze per la Giostra," transitioning from a comparison with later masterpieces like the "Aminta" to a specific examination of how Poliziano revolutionized Italian poetic meter.</meta>

<page-num>LVIII</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...the special character of the style of the *Giostra* <note>The "Stanze per la Giostra," Poliziano's unfinished masterpiece celebrating a Medici tournament</note> lies in this: the author is positioned between the end of a primitive, original literary age—both in invention and expression—and the beginning of an age of imitation and formal propriety. He retains the ruggedness and vigor of the first, while adopting the grace and softness of the second. The last traces of that first [primitive] age will gradually disappear in the *Bees* of Rucellai, the *Thyrsis* of Castiglione, and the *Cultivation* of Alamanni; the second [more refined] age would then shine in its purest form in Molza’s *Tiberine Nymph* and the most stupendous *Aminta*. The *Giostra* opens this series. Furthermore, that mixture of grace and strength, of refinement and ingenuity, contributes significantly to that "originality within imitation" that no one can deny to Poliziano.

I believe this was also aided by the meter the poet chose. To bring such a wealth of classical memories and imitations into the *ottava rima* <note>An eight-line stanza (ABABABCC), the standard meter for Italian epic poetry</note>—which until then had not truly been ennobled—was a way of disguising that imitation. Moreover, through the various fluctuations and movements of harmony that Poliziano was the first to introduce to that meter, he succeeded in echoing the diverse sounds of the ancient hexameter, the *terzina* <note>Dante’s three-line "tercet" meter</note>, and the *canzone* <note>A complex lyric song-form</note>, all of which necessarily emerged from his multifaceted imitations.

This perfection of the *ottava* is Poliziano’s most singular boast. Consider the state of the *ottava* as he found it: it was loose and rambling as Boccaccio <note>The 14th-century author of the *Decameron*, who first adapted the *ottava* for narrative poetry</note> had left it, who, being a natural master of prose and narration, left too heavy a mark of prose upon it; it was diluted, as the popular poets from Pucci <note>Antonio Pucci, a 14th-century Florentine town crier and popular poet</note> onward had reduced it; it was broken, as it had to be when emerging from the dialogue of stage plays; and finally, it was harsh and unequal, as it had become under the "rude grip" of [Lorenzo de'] Medici—a tyrant even of rhymes—in his attempt to turn it into a lyric form. 

To take it, I say, in such a condition, and through a unity of harmony give it its own specific metrical character which it has ever since retained; to instill within it such a harmonious variety; to make it vibrate, to broaden it, to round it out, and extend it; to impose upon it both the concentrated focus of the tercet and the swaying movement of the stanza, the decisiveness of a finished meter and the fluidity of a perennial one; to make it an echo for all the sounds of nature and imagination—from the whispering of plants, the moaning of the breezes, and the song of the nightingale, to Bacchic revelry, the rush of a galley, and the [terrifying] trumpet of Megaera <note>One of the Furies from Greek mythology, representing the sounds of war or vengeance</note>—and to do this as a young man, alone and without predecessors; while to bring the...

<meta>This page continues the metrical and historical analysis of Poliziano’s poetry, comparing his development of Italian verse forms to the long evolution of the sonnet and the achievements of later epic poets like Ariosto and Tasso.</meta>

<page-num>LIX</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...for the <term>canzone</term> <note>A structured lyric poem, often set to music</note> and the sonnet to reach their perfection from the initial attempts of Frederick II <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1194–1250) whose court in Sicily was the birthplace of Italian literary poetry</note> and Pier delle Vigne <note>A diplomat and poet (c. 1190–1249) credited with inventing the sonnet form</note>, it required a century and two different schools—those of Guittone <note>Guittone d'Arezzo (c. 1230–1294), a transitional figure between the Sicilian and Tuscan styles</note> and Guinicelli <note>Guido Guinicelli (c. 1230–1276), founder of the "Sweet New Style" (Dolce Stil Novo)</note>—and finally two men like Alighieri and Petrarch. To me, this historical process is a greater miracle than Poliziano having written the *stanzas* at fourteen years old; it is a feat such that, even if every other argument were lacking, it would attest to the great poetic faculty—at least in its external form—of my author. To Giordani <note>Pietro Giordani (1774–1848), an influential Italian scholar and friend of Giacomo Leopardi</note>, Poliziano's verse sometimes seemed harsh;$^1$ nor will I deny it, though I attribute the cause to the century in which he lived. But certainly, his <term>ottava</term> <note>The eight-line stanza (ABABABCC) used in Italian epic poetry</note> is never harsh. It seems to me that it gathers the two distinct virtues of Ariosto’s and Tasso’s: grave and sonorous, but not as overly-finished and booming as the latter; free and varied, but not excessively loose like the former. Poliziano's *ottava*, where it is truly beautiful, surpasses in my opinion those of the two great epic poets; it is the archetype of the Italian *ottava*.

After all this, the reader should not expect me to recount the various judgments of critics on the <term>Stanzas for the Joust</term> <note>original: "Stanze per la giostra," Poliziano's unfinished masterpiece celebrating Giuliano de' Medici</note>: most are nothing more than repetitions of the same formulas, and they are perhaps all encompassed by that of Giraldi: 

> "They were the first that appeared worthy of praise and that carried with them spirit and poetic grandeur. For these, Poliziano deserves more praise, perhaps, than for the other verses he wrote in the Latin language, where he had equals and superiors in his own time. But he did not have a single person who could come close to him in the *stanzas* by a long shot; he advanced so far beyond everyone who had written until his time, accompanying art with nature and meaning with the choice of words as much as the age in which he wrote allowed, that—even though he spreads himself more than is just in descriptions and episodes, a thing he perhaps would have corrected if he had finished the work—he succeeded marvelously.$^2$"

Regarding the <term>*Orpheus*</term> <note>Poliziano's "Fabula di Orfeo," one of the first secular plays in the Italian vernacular</note>, the discussion will be shorter, as it shares the same elementary composition and the same process of imitation as the *Stanzas*. The author, who intended his work to be condemned by the death of the protagonist—to be torn apart—says

...having composed it at the *request of the most reverend Mantuan cardinal, within the space of two days, amid constant turmoil.*¹ This, according to the research of Bettinelli,² must have occurred in 1472; that was when Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga <note>A powerful prelate and patron of the arts from the ruling family of Mantua</note> came from Bologna, where he served as apostolic legate, to Mantua. He entered the city in all the pomp of his new dignity on August 22, "with triumphs and magnificence performed in that year and the following, with great feasts and dinners." So says the contemporary chronicler Schivenoglia, as cited by Bettinelli. Because the chronicler does not record such magnificent displays during the Cardinal’s subsequent visits to Mantua, Bettinelli deduces that the *Orfeo* <note>Poliziano's "Fabula di Orfeo," one of the first secular dramas in the Italian vernacular</note> was one of those festivities of 1472; somewhat hastily, to be truthful. However, the objections raised by Tiraboschi³ are not very serious. The Mantuan chronicler, Tiraboschi observes, states that Cardinal Gonzaga made his solemn entry of 1472 in the company of the Pichi family; now, Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous philosopher and "prodigy of the age"</note> was nine years old in 1472; it is unlikely that a child was part of the official retinue. But first of all, the Mantuan chronicler names "the Pichi" and not specifically Giovanni Pico; furthermore, even if the Pichi were not there, it does not follow that Poliziano was not present or could not have written the *Orfeo*. Yet Poliziano was then, Tiraboschi continues, only eighteen years old: how could he have been chosen to compose a theatrical work? How could he have succeeded so happily? But what of it? This "Homeric youth" who was already translating the *Iliad*, who the following year was to write the elegy <note>A poem of mourning</note> for Albiera <note>Albiera degli Albizzi, a young Florentine noblewoman whose early death Poliziano memorialized</note>, who would soon improvise in Greek and Latin amidst the crowds while walking,⁴ who while walking would dictate his version of Herodian <note>A Greek historian of the Roman Empire</note> in just a few days⁵—would he not have succeeded in composing in his mother tongue, by assembling the classical memories that most suited his purpose, a fable as simple as the *Orfeo*, especially in its first draft? <meta>This page continues the discussion of Poliziano's biography and the dating of his play *Orfeo*, arguing that it was written during his time as a protege of the Medici family and represents a pivotal shift from religious to secular drama in Italy.</meta>

<page-num>LXI</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...a client of the Medici, with a fine reputation as a poet in the two learned languages <note>Latin and Greek</note> and in the vernacular? In any case, it is certain that the composition cannot be dated later than 1483, the year in which Cardinal Gonzaga died: so that, since the *Stanze* <note>Poliziano's *Stanze de messer Angelo Poliziano cominciate per la giostra del magnifico Giuliano de’ Medici*, a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance poetry</note> were composed in '78 or at least after '76, it follows that *Orfeo*, which so faithfully reproduces their manner and style, shortly preceded or followed them; and it remains always the first true Italian dramatic attempt on a non-religious subject.

For the *Rappresentazioni* <note>Religious mystery plays or "Representations" that dominated the medieval stage</note>—that is to say, the dramas of the time—even though they did not lack comic and profane parts and indeed abounded in satire, still struggled to detach themselves from the Church, which was the cradle of drama in every nation. Not that the traditions of secular theater were dead in Italy; but the experiments were never anything more than literary exercises, and they were conducted in Latin. Thus they were lost to the nation <note>Meaning they did not enter the popular Italian consciousness because they remained in scholarly Latin</note>, leaving aside the *Achilleide* <note>The Story of Achilles</note>, the *Ezzellinide* by Albertino Mussato <note>A 14th-century work about the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano, modeled on ancient tragedy</note>—a national subject shaped externally on the model of Seneca; and, whatever its merit, the prose dialogue on the ruin of the city of Cesena [1351], which in manuscripts is attributed to the laureate Francesco Petrarch but which scholars would prefer to attribute to Coluccio Salutati;¹ and the tragedy that Giovanni Mangini della Motta claims to have composed on the downfall of Antonio della Scala, when the lordship of Verona was taken from him;² and another in five acts and in iambic verse by Lodovico da Vezzano on the imprisonment and execution of Iacopo Piccinino ordered by Ferdinand I of Aragon [1464],³ in which, even more than the scene changes, it would be curious to see the dialogue between the king and the executioner, placed on equal footing much as De Maistre <note>Joseph de Maistre, a philosopher who famously mused on the social necessity and terrifying status of the executioner</note> would later have desired; and finally the *History of the Baetic War* <note>original: "Historia boetica," referring to the conquest of Granada</note>, that is, the capture of Granada narrated as a dialogue in Latin prose by Carlo Verardi and performed in Rome at the house of Cardinal Raffaello Riario in 1492, where in the same year was also performed *Ferdinand Saved* <note>original: "Fernandus servatus"</note>, also devised by Verardi and written in hexameters by his nephew Marcellino.⁴ Representations tha-

...of historical and, more importantly, contemporary events, in a way that later Italian dramatists either could not achieve or performed poorly. corrigendos*</note>² and the *Philogenia* by Ugolino Pisani of Parma, written around 1430,³ down to a near-contemporary of Poliziano, Battista Alberti <note>Leon Battista Alberti, the famous polymath
