believed it to be the work of Lepidus, an ancient comic poet.⁴ Appearing less distant in subject matter from true comedy were the *Polyxena* <note>original: *Polissena*</note> by Leonardo Bruni,⁵ the *Fraudiphila* <note>The Deceit-Lover</note> by Antonio Tridentone of Parma⁶ and the *Drunkards’ Diversions* <note>original: *Lusus ebriorum*</note> by Siccio Polentone, which were later translated into Italian prose and printed in Trent in 1482 under the title *Catinia*.⁷ I do not know the exact subject of *Armiranda* by Gian Michele Alberto of Carrara, which is divided into acts and scenes and, in a stage direction written in the classical style, is said to have been performed: "During the Megalensian Games <note>An ancient Roman festival honoring the goddess Cybele</note>, while Calixtus III was Supreme Pontiff, Frederick III was Emperor, Francesco Foscari was Doge of Venice, and Benedetto Vittorio and Leonardo Contarini were praetors of Padua <note>original: *Ludis Megalensibus, Calixto III sacerdote max., Friderico III cæsare, Francisco Foscareno Venet. duce, Benedicto Victorio et Leonardo Contareno Patavii prætoribus*</note>;"⁸ but certainly mythological in subject is the *Procne* <note>original: *Progne*</note> by Gregorio Corraro (who died in 1466), published in Venice in 1558 and shortly thereafter passed off as his own by Domenichi, the translator into the vernacular <note>original: *volgarizzatore*</note>.⁹ And in Mantua, where the eighteen-year-old Corraro wrote the Latin *Procne*,¹⁰ Angelo Poliziano—at roughly the same age and perhaps knowing few or none of these earlier experiments—cast *Orpheus* <note>original: *Orfeo*</note> into the Italian forms of the "sacred representation" <note>original: *sacra rappresentazione*; the traditional religious drama of the time</note>; this was the first step toward making drama secular. <page-num>LXIII</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...of public theater <note>original: *teatro civile*; theater for the general citizenry rather than a private courtly or religious audience</note>, the festivities of princes were necessary, or at least useful.

Let it be so then—since of the *Loves of Venus and Mars* <note>original: *Amori di Venere e Marte*</note> by [Lorenzo de'] Medici¹ only a fragment remains, nor could its chronological priority be otherwise confirmed; and since we do not know the nature of the *Iemsale*, composed in the vernacular <note>original: *volgare*; the Italian language as opposed to Latin</note> by the tragic writer Leonardo Dati for the second *Poetic Contest* <note>original: *certame coronario*; a public poetry competition held in Florence in 1441</note> of Florence²—let it be therefore among the other praises of Angelo Poliziano that he also secularized the theater. But, if one wishes to exaggerate this to the point of recognizing in *Orfeo* the first example of drama properly so called, one runs the risk of falling into error. You could—both for the moving subject matter and for the catastrophe <note>the final resolution or "unraveling" of the plot in a classical tragedy</note> and for the division into acts in the edition by Affò—call it a tragedy. You could, because of the roles played by the shepherds and the dryads, call it a *pastoral fable* <note>original: *favola pastorale*</note> and consider it the precursor to [Tasso's] *Aminta* and [Guarini's] *The Faithful Shepherd* <note>original: *Pastor fido*</note>. You could, for the song of Aristaeus and for the choruses of nymphs and bacchants, boast of it as the first musical drama <note>original: *melodramma*</note>:³ and a master of music, Mr. Germi, could dress it in harmonies, perhaps opening a new field for his art, or reopening a forgotten one. And Mr. Giovan Battista Mameli, to whom I owe this last piece of information,⁴ will be quite right to admire the creation of certain characters and the wisdom of the plot; in the third act, the satyr *Mnesillo*—a sketch of those figures who waited for full life from Shakespeare, being neither man nor beast—who, after admiring genius at first and then renouncing it because he cannot follow it, represents the common masses of men; in the fourth act, spectacular and at the same time moving, Orpheus is in the presence of death—like human art before the forces of nature—with the illusion of victory, until Tisiphone <note>one of the Furies in Greek mythology</note>, representing reality, rises to strike him down with the truth:

> "Come no further; rather, stay your foot;
> The law of the abyss is fixed and firm;"

in the fifth act, the man...

--- Page 69 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of Angelo Poliziano's Orfeo, transitioning from its categorization as a "secularized" play to a deeper critique of its structure as a traditional medieval-style "representation" rather than a modern drama.</meta>

<page-num>LXIV</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...who, great in talent and misfortune, separates himself from human society—which appears to him like a bacchanal <note>original: *baccanale*; a wild, drunken feast in honor of Bacchus</note>—and breaks its laws; and society—which draws its life and pleasure from that which is the source of pain to certain fated men—does not understand their pain and takes its revenge for their contempt. This revenge, though atrocious and horrific in its method, is nonetheless just and legitimate. All this may be true and beautiful; and in *Orpheus* <note>original: *Orfeo*</note> a sharp eye will discern the basic elements of various dramatic genres. However, *Orpheus* does not cease to be, in substance, a "representation" <note>original: *rappresentazione*; the traditional medieval form of religious or allegorical theater, often known as mystery or miracle plays</note>. As such, instead of the progressive development of characters and their conflict, it offers nothing more than a narration in dialogue, which rises to the level of a lyric poem where passion grows. It does not capture the supreme moment of the event to gather secondary circumstances around it, but rather exposes the story chronologically in all its parts. The scene is static, and in the moment where Orpheus prays before the locked gates of Hell while Pluto and Proserpina consult within, the stage is dual and parallel; there is no sense in even speaking of the unities of place and time <note>the classical Aristotelian rules that a play should take place in one location and within a single day</note>. The difference between *Orpheus* and other "representations" lies in this: Poliziano has replaced the stories of the Old and New Testaments and the legends of saints with the eclogue <note>original: *egloga*; a poem in a classical style on a pastoral subject, usually involving shepherds</note>. He brought to it a greater poetic quality of form and style, though not necessarily greater truth or passion (the dialogues between father and son in the *Sacrifice of Abraham* <note>original: *Sacrificio d' Abramo*</note> and certain passages of *Stella* <note>popular religious plays of the 15th century</note> are easily worth the elegant laments of the Thracian poet <note>Orpheus</note>); he also used a greater variety of meters to mark the transition from one social condition to another, or from one emotion to another, giving a large role to lyrical forms, which were handled, after all, by a great master.

While not rejecting one or the other, how do you explain this duality of the same composition, these two different versions? Both versions are substantially the same thing—a "representation"—except that in the second, I recognize some variations and some purely secondary novelties. I do not believe, as Father Affò¹ does, that the *Orpheus* found in the ancient...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Poliziano's play *Orpheus*, shifting from its structural analysis to a defense of its stylistic inconsistencies—such as the mixing of Latin and Italian—by placing them in the context of 15th-century courtly performance and traditional "representations."</meta>

<page-num>LXV</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

...prints and in the Chigi manuscript <note>a famous Vatican library manuscript containing works by Poliziano</note> is a patchwork by someone who, having taken part in or attended the performance, transcribed various pieces and threw them together at random, substituting their own work where memory failed. For anyone who considers *Orpheus* <note>original: *Orfeo*</note> as a "representation" <note>the traditional medieval form of Italian theater, usually religious in nature</note>, they will not make much of those great inconsistencies and improprieties that Father Affò <note>Ireneo Affò (1741–1797), a scholar and historian who critiqued Poliziano's work</note> notes so subtly in the older version. It does not even bother me that Orpheus comes out with his lyre in hand to sing the praises of the Cardinal of Mantua <note>Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga</note> through the mouth of the actor Baccio Ugolini <note>a renowned singer and lutenist who played the lead role</note> in a Sapphic ode <note>a four-line stanza form modeled after the ancient Greek poet Sappho</note>. When a drama is created for the festivals of the powerful and the theater becomes nothing more than an extension of the court, it was always the custom that one of the characters—whether mythological, historical, or from any era—would make some allusion or openly address some boastful flattery to the monarch, especially at the end during the "license" <note>original: *licenza*; a concluding section where the poet directly addresses the patron</note>. Such anachronisms and improprieties do not offend the good taste even of the most modest poets of more regulated eras, whether their names be Molière, Racine, Metastasio, or Monti; provided the only listener in whom everything converges is Louis XIV, Maria Theresa, or Napoleon. In those days, Poliziano had written a Latin ode for the Cardinal of Mantua; the festival was held for the Cardinal of Mantua: to excuse himself to the learned elite for having composed a fable "in the vulgar style" <note>original: *in stilo vulgare*; meaning written in Italian rather than the more prestigious Latin</note> and to allow the ode to be admired by a larger audience, what better occasion than to entrust its recitation to the poetic character of Orpheus? Dante himself, beyond the Latin verses scattered here and there throughout his *Comedy*, had placed an entire Latin triplet in the 7th [Canto] of *Paradise* <note>original: *Paradiso*</note>. And did the angels and saints of the popular plays not spout off, from time to time, verses of the Bible in the Latin of the Vulgate <note>the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> in the middle of Italian stanzas <note>original: *ottave volgari*</note>? And in these same plays, were the doctors not introduced to speak a "barbarous" Latin, and moreover, rhymed in eleven-syllable verses in the style of the *ottava*?¹ And in personal letters, was it not customary to mix the domestic vernacular with the more or less elegant Latin of the schools? It is one thing for a thing to displease us in the 19th century; it is another that it could not exist in the 15th. I imagine the furious applause and the murmur of admi—

# LXVI ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...ration in which the learned audience erupted, when Baccio Ugolini, dressed in the Greek style with a white priestly stole, with laurel around his youthful head and the learned lyre in hand, descended from the mountain intoning with a full and excited voice those most elegant Sapphic stanzas:

> "Run now with your whole violent stream,
> O Mincio <note>original: *Minci*; the river flowing through Mantua, the site of the premiere</note> celebrated by the sacred Muses!
> Behold, a Maecenas <note>A famous Roman patron; here referring to Cardinal Gonzaga</note> and a Virgil <note>original: *Maro*; the great Roman poet was born near Mantua</note> now
> belong to you alone!
> And now let the neighboring waves of the Po,
> resounding with many a swan, submit to you,
> however spiritedly it tosses the weeping alders
> and the stars." <note>This Latin ode celebrates Mantua as a new center of the arts, rivaling the great river Po</note>

With all due respect, then, to the most learned Father Affò, I for my part maintain that the *Orpheus*, as it appears in the Chigi manuscript and in all the old prints—always preceded by the letter to Canale <note>Carlo Canale, a court official and Poliziano's friend</note> where the author expresses his wish that the play be **immediately torn apart, just like Orpheus himself** <note>original: *di subito non altrimenti che esso Orfeo lacerata*</note>—is properly the one that Poliziano **composed in the space of two days amidst continuous turmoil**. And with such haste, one might, if they wished, excuse those flaws that so offended Affò. 

But, despite the severe disapproval of its author, *Orpheus* circulated, and its fame spread: and the time came when it was requested from Poliziano to be performed magnificently on the occasion of festivals in some Italian court. And then the author returned to his youthful work; he polished it, varied it, and expanded it: certain improprieties that were too glaring were removed; the ode for the Cardinal, which no longer had a place there, disappeared and the most elegant chorus of the Dryads <note>nymphs of the trees</note> was put in its stead. But note that the Latin verses from Ovid placed in the mouth of Orpheus as he leaves the underworld did not disappear at all—in fact, others from Claudian <note>a late Roman poet whose style Poliziano admired</note> were added: so true is it that Latin caused no annoyance. 

I suppose that the second version, the *tragedy of Orpheus*, so highly praised by the worthy Affò, resulted from this. This must have been after 1480, when Pomponio Leto <note>a famous humanist who revived ancient theater in Rome</note> in Rome had his academicians perform the comedies of Plautus in Latin, and Ercole I, Duke of Ferrara, took pleasure in seeing performed in the courtyard of his palace the *Menaechmi* <note>a comedy by Plautus involving mistaken identity between twins</note>—translated by himself into the vernacular [1486]—and the *Amphitruo* translated into *terza rima* <note>a rhyming verse form consisting of stanzas of three lines, famously used by Dante</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Poliziano's play Orpheus, moving from the author's initial hasty draft to the play's dissemination and potential revision for the theatrical court of Ferrara. It places Orpheus in the context of other early Renaissance adaptations of classical and secular themes.</meta>

# LXVII ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...by Pandolfo Collenuccio, as well as the *Cusina* <note>original: *Cusina*; a translation of Plautus's *Casina*</note> and the *Mostellaria* <note>original: *Mostellaria*; 'The Haunted House' by the Roman playwright Plautus</note> likewise in *terza rima* <note>A poetic form of three-line stanzas with interlocking rhymes, famously used by Dante</note> by Girolamo Berardo, and other tales by the comic poet of Sarsina <note>Referring to Plautus, who was born in Sarsina</note> translated by Battista Guarino.&#185; And who knows whether Poliziano might have revised the *Orpheus* specifically for the service of the court of Ferrara, which was all ablaze with classical performances from 1486 onwards? Evidence for this suspicion lies in the fact that both manuscripts containing the second version are from Reggio—that is, from the dominion of the House of Este <note>The ruling family of Ferrara and Reggio, major patrons of Renaissance theater</note>. And thus, *Orpheus* would appear more and more linked with some of the plays that so resemble it in external form, also composed around that time at the request of Duke Ercole and performed at his court;&#178; the *Cephalus*, for example, by Niccolò da Correggio, divided into five acts of *ottava rima* <note>An eight-line stanza form common in Italian epic poetry</note> not without some choruses [1486]; the *Timon*, taken from a dialogue by Lucian and adapted into five acts of *terza rima* by Boiardo; the *Philostratus and Pamfila*—which, once the modern names are changed to ancient ones, is nothing other than the *Prince of Salerno* <note>A tragic story from Boccaccio’s *Decameron*</note> adapted into five acts of *terza rima* with short songs in the style of choruses by Anton of Pistoia; and the *Demetrius, King of Thebes* versified by the same author in the same style. In any case—both in the plays mentioned and in the *Melandro* and the *Riso* written by Alessandro Caperano during the papacy of Alexander VI (and titled *Comedies*, one *sylvan*, the other *pastoral*), as well as in the *Philolaurus*, a tragic act by Bernardo Philostrato, and in the *Amaranta* by Casalio, a mixture of *ottava* and *terza rima*—in short, in all that ephemeral theater of eclogues <note>Short pastoral poems, often in dialogue</note> that occupied the last two decades of the 15th century and served as the transition from sacred representations (which were becoming a bit less ecclesiastical, such as the *Saint John and Paul* by Lorenzo de' Medici) to the *Sophonisba* of Trissino and the *Rosmunda* of Rucellai; Poliziano's *Orpheus*, which is certainly the first such play composed, must have played a major part in determining the genre, the style, and the versification.

But as of yet unnoticed by bibliographers and scholars is a third version of *Orpheus* in the Riccardian Codex 2723, where the ode and the couplets from Claudian and Ovid are missing.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Poliziano’s Orpheus, specifically examining the textual variations between versions and what they reveal about the play’s intended audience and widespread popularity among the Italian people.</meta>

# LXVIII ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...three octaves are missing (one in Orpheus’s prayer, “Furies, there is no need for you to roar,” <note>original: “Non bisogna per me, Furie, mugghiare”</note> and the others in a dialogue between Pluto and Minos) which, in performance, likely required a dual-level stage. This simplification was perhaps attempted for the sake of the common people, who could neither understand classical Latin nor afford lavish theatrical apparatus. For the *Orpheus*—listen here, you inlayers of ballads and popular poems condemned to die of asphyxiation in the studies of literary ladies after thirty years, and you counterfeiters of <term>rispetti<gloss>a traditional Italian folk song form, usually consisting of eight hendecasyllabic lines</gloss></term> and <term>stornelli<gloss>a short, often improvised folk poem or song, common in central Italy</gloss></term> destined to bore people with the accompaniment of the inevitable piano—the *Orpheus* pleased the people. And so it should have been: that descent into hell must have touched their imagination, because it was part of their traditions. That richness and volatility of harmony, that easy flow of versification, that colorful and simple elegance, is exactly what the Italian people seek above all else in poetry. 

Nor do I rely solely on the version in the Florentine manuscript to prove the popularity that *Orpheus* once enjoyed, though I would not know how to explain it otherwise; for an arbitrary corruption does not seem admissible in a manuscript from Florence, the author’s home, and from the author’s own time—a manuscript so beautiful, complete, and authoritative. Rather, I recall the various editions of *Orpheus* that were published separately from the *Stanzas* <note>Poliziano’s famous poem *Stanze per la giostra*</note> during the sixteenth century, produced by printing houses known in bibliographic annals for producing only those works that had a market among the common people. I recall that the fame of *Orpheus* had even passed into the convents of nuns—which can no longer be explained by court performances. Indeed, a sixteenth-century sister found a way to couple the recitation of the Office of the Virgin Mary with the somewhat profane memories of the chorus of the Bacchantes, writing this imitation or varied copy in the style of a drinking song:

-> Bacchus, Bacchus, euhoe! <note>original: *evoè*; a ritual cry of the followers of Bacchus</note> <-
-> He who wishes to drink, come to me. <-
-> I have already emptied my horn: <-
-> Turn the wine-cask a bit this way: <-
-> This world turns round and round, <-
-> And the brain goes for a stroll. <-
-> Let everyone cry out here and there, <-
-> Just as they see me doing. <-

Finally, I recall the popular version of *Orpheus* produced in the style of a "Story" <note>original: "Storia"</note> in simple but not inelegant <term>octaves<gloss>specifically *ottava rima*, a stanza form of eight eleven-syllable lines, traditional for Italian epic and folk poetry</gloss></term>, in which Poliziano's most splendid stanzas are mixed in without causing any awkwardness. I would not dare to claim that the *History and Fable of Orpheus* <note>original: "Historia e favola d’ Orfeo"</note>—printed in Florence near the Bishopric in 1558, which begins "O good people, there once was a shepherd"—is the oldest example of such a popular version; I have never happened to see it except cited by Libri in one of his catalogues.¹ But the *Story of Orpheus of the Sweet Lyre* is still reprinted today in those usual small notebooks of scrap paper <note>these "quadernetti" were cheap chapbooks sold by wandering peddlers at fairs and markets</note> through which the poems and legends of the 15th century are preserved among the rural generations: the most recent edition is from Prato in 1860. The fact that the composition is old and certainly possesses a spirit of poetry and elegance, even in those parts not imitated from the original, is proven by the octaves which serve as an introduction to the events—taken entirely from Poliziano's play—detailing how Orpheus fell in love with Eurydice.

> He played so very sweetly
> Upon his viola, that he made the flowing water
> Of the river stop to listen;
> He calmed the winds and the storm at sea:
> Birds, trees, stones, and every person
> Came to hear Orpheus play,
> And whoever stayed to hear such sweet sound
> Left everything else abandoned...
> And he began to play sweetly,
> And singing, he spoke these words.

— O nymph of singular beauty

That I love you above every other beautiful thing,
Consent to be my dear wife.

Know that I am the son of fair Apollo

You are the one who has robbed and taken

Turn towards me that shining face,
Which is a mirror of true grace:

Jove will lose his high monarchy:
In life I will be your visible servant,
And after death, if it shall be possible.

I bless Cupid’s bow

Where the flame has made an eternal nest,

That you may accept me as your servant;
For I am the son of the Sun, as I have told you,
And for this I love you still with pure affection.

Who has troubled me eternally!

Eyes, weep; and in sighing moans
Weep, my heart, for you have a lawful cause;
Weep and sigh, for she is dead
Who was your peace and your consolation.

Ah, let me pass out of courtesy.

One shows snakes, and another is moved by wrath.

So many serpents, Orpheus said to them.
If you knew my bitter sorrows,
You would keep company with my laments.
Therefore let the wretched man pass,
Who has heaven and all the elements as enemies.

And in these octaves, it seems to me also curious and important to notice the distortions of the pagan underworld <note>original: "inferno dei gentili"</note> operated by popular sentiment in the Middle Ages. > “Had a stone lifted from a cave,

For the rest, the "popular story" of the anonymous author proceeds hand in hand with the "fable" of the court poet.

Thus, with both poems—the descriptive and the dramatic—Poliziano, to use the happy metaphor of Giovio, *brought among the people the most stupendous flowers chosen from the Greeks and the Latins.<sup>1</sup>* This is because the fable of *Orpheus*, like his *Stanzas*, is a work of the highest learning in its verse, derived almost literally in many parts from Virgil and Ovid, and filled with imitations of Theocritus and Moschus <note>Ancient Greek pastoral poets whose style Poliziano emulated to create a refined, rural atmosphere.</note>; the chorus of the Dryads <note>Tree nymphs.</note> and that of the Bacchants <note>Female followers of Dionysus known for their ecstatic and wild rituals.</note> are the oldest and most elegant examples of strictly classical lyric poetry in Italian literature. In the latter, critics of the past century recognize the origin of dithyrambic poetry <note>A form of wild, rhythmic Greek hymn; later revived as a sophisticated literary style.</note>, cultivated then with more or less successful but always highly erudite industry in the two ages that preceded us. Finally, even to the fable of *Orpheus* one can apply what Ugo Foscolo judged of the *Stanzas*: “The spirit and the modes of the Latin language of the classics had already been transfused into prose by Boccaccio and others. But Poliziano was the first to transfuse them into poetry; and he transfused into it at the same time as much elegance as could be derived from the Greek. In fact, there is no language that, like Italian, can soak up all that is simple, lovely, and energetic in the forms and qualities of the Greek, especially in poetry; and if it could obtain the same prosody <note>The patterns of rhythm and sound in poetry.</note> and the same genre of verse and could at the same time free itself from the necessity of articles, perhaps it would have nothing to envy in the Greek.<sup>2</sup>” And here lies the—

<page-num>LXXVII</page-num>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

It is a wonder how, despite the deeply classical studies of which he so proudly boasted, Poliziano managed to be a popular poet in his day; indeed, his *Stanzas* <note>Referring to his famous unfinished poem, *Stanze per la giostra*, written to celebrate a tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> still maintain a nearly popular fame today. Like many of his ballads, their native grace and beauty are clear to all readers without the need for scholarly dissertations to teach one how to enjoy them. Why is this? And how did it happen? 

One should note well that in one of his letters, Poliziano explicitly declares himself opposed to the exclusive imitation of a single author;$^1$ and that the writers of the sixteenth century preferred the Latin poems of Pontano and Sannazaro <note>Giovanni Pontano and Jacopo Sannazaro were renowned Neo-Latin poets of the Renaissance.</note> far more than his own.$^2$ This was because in their works, they could taste the distinct flavors of Horace, Tibullus, and Virgil, whereas in Poliziano’s work, their erudition was insulted by not finding the specific footprints of any one model. Because Poliziano—knowing all the ancient writers as a great philologist <term>philologist: a scholar who studies the history of language and the nuances of literary texts</term> and having turned them all into his own lifeblood through the assimilation of good taste—did not particularly imitate any of them. Strong as he was in learning and talent, he dared to stamp even that dead language <note>Referring to Latin.</note> with his own mark; he dared to give it his own movements and spread a fresh color over the ancient verse. 

It is easy to imagine, then, by what process the man who so mastered Latin became an imitator in Italian. There were beauties a thousand years old that, in his verse, appeared to be born today: there were images slightly dimmed or worn down by the heavy hands of the scholiasts <term>scholiasts: ancient or medieval commentators who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) in the margins of classical manuscripts</term> and the imitators, and in his rhymes they bloomed again, splendid and fragrant, like roses and violets after a spring rain. Homer took on the likeness of Dante, Virgil that of Petrarch; and in everything there was Angelo, the "Homeric youth," <note>Poliziano was famously nicknamed the "Homeric youth" because he began a masterful Latin translation of the Iliad at the age of sixteen.</note> who was renewing the poetic language of Italy.

> "We attempted.... not to stain Latin chastity with inept foreignisms nor with Greek-style figures, unless they are such that they have by now been accepted; we attempted to have the two languages <note>original: "le due lingue" (referring here to the source Greek and the target Latin)</note> preserve the same clarity, the same elegance, and their own sense and character: no tediousness of vocabulary, no laborious anxiety.$^3$"

Here, the critic truly explains the poet: and these words, with which Master Angelo declared the method he maintained in translating the historian Herodian <note>A third-century Greek historian whose works Poliziano translated into Latin for Pope Innocent VIII.</note> into Latin, mark the dif—

# III.

## BIBLIOGRAPHY OF THE *STANZAS* AND THE *ORPHEUS*.
### NEW ATTENTION GIVEN TO THEM IN THIS EDITION.

---

Those readers—if indeed a preface deserves readers—who care little for bibliography may leap over this chapter and the fifth. In these, I describe all the manuscripts and printed editions known to me; for now, those of the *Stanzas* and the *Orpheus*, and later those of the *Rhymes*. I do this to justify the method I have used in bringing Poliziano’s poems to light once again, and for the satisfaction of those who believe bibliography is to literary history what statistics are to civil history.

### MANUSCRIPTS.

First to be noted is the paper manuscript in folio format preserved in the Riccardiana Library in Florence, marked with the number 2723 and titled *Rhymes of Poliziano, of Lorenzo de' Medici, of Dante, and others*. In addition to the *Stanzas* with their rubrics <term>rubrics: headings or instructions traditionally written in red ink</term> and the *Orpheus* (which follows them in a much simpler form, as we previously noted, than what is found in the Chigi manuscript and the printed editions), it contains many *rispetti* <term>rispetti: a traditional form of Italian folk poetry, usually consisting of eight lines</term> and *canzoni a ballo* <term>canzoni a ballo: dance songs or ballads intended for musical performance</term> by the author. It also includes the Latin ode *Now heavy with its horn* <note>Original Latin: "Iam cornu gravidus."</note> written in 1482, which is found among Poliziano’s printed Latin works; and the epistle *to the most illustrious Lord Federico, together with the vernacular collection sent to him by Lorenzo the Magnificent* <note>This refers to the *Raccolta Aragonese*, a famous anthology of Tuscan poetry.</note>, which is wrongly attributed to Poliziano and which I have already reprinted according to the text of this manuscript in the *Poetry of Lorenzo de' Medici* [Barbèra, 1859]. Finally, it contains a short Latin prose piece said to be composed *for a certain youth in the Pisan university concerning the praise of the liberal arts* <note>Original Latin: "pro quodam adolescente in gymnasio pisano de laudibus artium liberalium."</note> which begins *If I had undertaken so much of my own accord* <note>Original Latin: "Si mea sponte tantum hoc suscepissem."</note>, which...

...with such a beginning is not found, as far as I have noticed, among the author's Latin works. At the end, after various poems by our author and others, is the letter to Filippo Beroaldo <note>A prominent humanist scholar (1453–1505) and contemporary of Poliziano.</note> that begins *Inform me* <note>original Latin: *Certiorem me*</note>, placed before Book VI among the printed letters. This is certainly an autograph <term>autograph: a manuscript written in the author's own hand</term>, as can be gathered by comparing it with other writings by Poliziano’s hand and from the frequent crossings-out and corrections above the lines of words and entire phrases, which could only be made by the author. Lami, in the *Riccardian Catalog* <margin>1 Lami, *Catalog of manuscript books kept in the Riccardian library of Florence*; Livorno, 1756.</margin> seems to consider the entire codex <term>codex: an ancient manuscript in book form</term> to be an autograph, citing it under the heading *Angelo Poliziano* in this manner: *Rhymes and Letter to Filippo Beroaldo, autographs* <note>original Latin: *Rime et Epistola ad Ph. Beroaldum, autographos*</note>. In this opinion, I believe he stands alone. On the back of leaf 97, one finds written: *1487. This book belongs to Francesco, son of Lorenzo, son of Bernardo dei Medici, and his friends*; but especially in the final leaves, the codex is a miscellany <term>miscellany: a manuscript containing a variety of different works or documents bound together</term>. Furthermore, this date and other notes placed at the top of certain anonymous poems by different hands toward the end show the manuscript was compiled in the last two decades of the century. There are entries from 1488: the most recent, "On the 8th day of February 1496," stands at the top of a tailed sonnet <term>tailed sonnet: a "sonetto caudato," or a sonnet with extra lines added to the end, often used for satirical or humorous purposes</term> alluding to the disturbances stirred up by Brother Girolamo <note>Refers to Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar who took control of Florence after the Medici were expelled.</note>. However, the handwriting of the *Stanzas*, the *Orpheus*, and some of the rhymes resembles, if one wishes, that of Poliziano (which is not surprising to anyone who has noted how, in the second half of the 15th century, various hands of writing appear almost identical); and it is certainly from the same period. 

Furthermore, observing that in Book II of the *Tournament* <note>Poliziano’s poem *Stanze per la giostra*.</note> only the first three verses of stanza XII are transcribed, and no more than the first verse of stanza XIV, with the remaining space left blank, leads one to suspect that the manuscript might be a copy made directly from the autograph writing. The cause of these gaps may be either that the author had not yet completed those two stanzas at that time, or that the original writing was not clear to the scribe <term>scribe: a person whose job was to copy out manuscripts</term>. I am inclined toward the first opinion, as I remember noticing those same two gaps in a small fragment of the *Stanzas* that I saw briefly among some old papers in the Palatina Library in Florence. For all these reasons, I believe I am not far from the truth in considering the codex...

## PRINTS. — THE FIRST ERA.

By dividing the printed editions of the *Stanzas* and *Orpheus* into three main eras, I hope to save words for myself and make research easier for scholars; in the first era, I include those produced from 1494 to 1541. Of these, without exception—or with very few—the following features are common. The *Stanzas* always have marginal rubrics <term>rubrics: headings or directions traditionally written in red ink</term> that identify descriptions, comparisons, transitions, etc., just as they are read in manuscript Riccardiano 2723 and as Poliziano was accustomed to attach to every work of his. The *Orpheus* appears there without division into acts, under the title of *Fable* or *Feast* <note>original: *Favola* or *Festa*</note>, shorter and simpler than the version usually read after Affò’s edition. Furthermore, they contain the stanza of Echo [*What do you do, Echo...*] and the ballad that begins *Love can never say*. Most of these prints follow the first Bolognese edition by Benedetti; some others derived from the Bolognese edition of Bazaleri [1503] also contain the song *I am constrained*. One might say the reading <term>reading: the specific wording of a text in a particular edition</term> is the same in all of them; the very few variations, when they are not typographical errors, are hardly noticeable. For the descriptions, I will make use of the catalog by Volpi,$^1$ as well as those by Gamba,$^2$ Brunet,$^3$ Libri,$^4$ and Batines.$^5$

1494. VERNACULAR WORKS | OF POLIZIANO. <note>original: *COSE VOLGARE DEL POLITIANO*. "Vernacular" refers to works written in Italian rather than Latin.</note> At the end: *Here end the stanzas composed by Master Angelo Poliziano made for the joust of Giuliano, brother of the Magnificent Lorenzo de’ Medici of Florence, together with the feast of Orpheus and other refined pieces carefully printed in Bologna by Platone delli Benedicti, most accurate printer, in the Year 1494 on the ninth day of August.* It is a large octavo <term>octavo: a book size where sheets are folded three times to create eight leaves</term> in the shape of a quarto <term>quarto: a book size where sheets are folded twice to create four leaves</term>; in Roman type; with three octaves <term>octave: an eight-line poetic stanza</term> per page; without page numbers or re—

It is designated; of 42 leaves marked **A-F**. [*Register <term>register: a list of the quires or gatherings that make up a book, usually found at the end</term>. ABCDEF. All are quaternions <term>quaternion: a gathering of four folded sheets, making eight leaves</term>, except D which is a ternion <term>ternion: a gathering of three folded sheets, making six leaves</term> and F which is a binion <term>binion: a gathering of two folded sheets, making four leaves</term>*]. Some variations are to be noted between the copy owned and described by Commander Bertoloni ¹ and the one preserved in the Palatine Library in Florence. Bertoloni's copy carries the title on the first leaf as we have reported it; the Palatine copy has instead *The Vernacular Things | of Master Angelo Poliziano*: the Bertoloni copy has the dedicatory letter on the second leaf as seen by Gamba; the Palatine copy does not. *Here they end* <note>original: "Qui finischono"</note> is read at the end of the Bertoloni copy, as well as the one seen by Gamba; *Here they end* <note>original: "Qua finischono"</note> is read in the Palatine copy and the one seen by Brunet. Let bibliophiles judge these differences. The letter from Sarzio deserves to be reproduced here as a historical document. Regarding Sarzio, Poliziano—while publishing the work of Herodian through the same printer Benedetti the previous year—wrote to Andrea Magnanimo that for the work of correction: “you could have no one more suitable nor more for your use than Alessandro Sarzio, your fellow citizen, a man of letters and devoted to us, so... by no means sleeping on a friend's business,”²

<page-num>LXXXIV</page-num>
<header>ANGELO POLIZIANO.</header>

->*Alessandro Sarzio to the illustrious and most reverend Antonio Galeazzo Bentivoglio,*<-
->*Apostolic Protonotary and Archdeacon of Bologna, Greetings.*<-

*In these past days, Most Reverend Monsignor, there came into my hands certain stanzas by my and your most refined Poliziano—who is no small glory to the truly magnificent and noble Medici family, a house always most happily joined with the illustrious Bentivoglio family. He composed these stanzas long ago for the joust <term>joust: a tournament or sporting contest between knights on horseback</term> of the Magnificent Giuliano de' Medici during his early youth; however, due to certain considerations or impediments, he did not bring them to completion. Nevertheless, even though they were imperfect and uncorrected, they seemed to me very elegant and beautiful, full of invention, full of learning and grace; so much so that I judged it a great shame if they were to be lost or never brought to light. For this reason, I have given them to Plato de' Benedicti <note>original: "Plato de' Benedicti" — referring to the printer Francesco "Platone" de' Benedetti</note> to be printed, and I have dedicated them to your Most Reverend Lordship under these crude but brief words of mine. I have done this to satisfy those who delight in such refinements and to honor you, my most respected patron, at least in small matters, since I cannot yet do so in great ones. I believe also that, if Poliziano is somewhat displeased that these stanzas of his—which he long ago disregarded—are being printed, he will on the other hand be pleased that, since they had to be published eventually, they are being released under the title and name of your Lordship; to whom he is most devoted, as I can well testify. The Play of Orpheus <note>original: "La festa ancora di Orpheo"</note>, which he once composed in Mantua almost extemporaneously, will be printed along with them, because it too is a thing of great charm in the judgment of the learned. I am certain that both will be most welcome to your aforementioned Lordship, if for no other reason than the quality of the author; for even the first rough drafts <note>original: "primi disgrosamenti"</note> of talented men are usually pleasing. For my part, I pray that you, my Most Reverend patron, will accept this very small token of my great loyalty willingly and with a serene brow; measuring not the ability of Alessandro Sarzio, your servant, but his will: he who always commends himself to you. Farewell.*

Printed separately from the poem are stanzas 69-120 of Book I of the *Joust* <note>The "Giostra," Poliziano's famous poem celebrating a tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici</note>, which contain the description of the kingdom of Venus.

## SECOND ERA.

To this era, which may be termed "Aldine" <note>named after the press of Aldus Manutius and his successors, famous for their high-quality scholarly editions and the invention of italic type</note>, belong the printings of the *Joust* issued from 1541 through 1612. They have this in common: they contain only the *Stanzas* without the marginal <term>rubrics</term> <note>brief explanatory headings or summaries usually printed in the margins</note>, without the accompaniment of the letter from Sarzio, the Latin epitaph, or the sonnet, and without the stanza on the echo and the <term>canzonetta</term> <note>a short, light vocal song or poem</note>. The reading of the text is notably modified or altered in all of them, though not entirely in the same way; the printings of the *Orpheus* <note>Poliziano's "Fabula di Orfeo," one of the first secular dramas in Italian</note> are few and little known during these 62 years.

We stated that the second era may be called "Aldine": and indeed, the edition of the *Stanzas* produced by the sons of Aldus in 1541 was and is—for this and the following era—accepted as the standard for reprints, cited by the <term>Academicians of the Crusca</term> <note>the official institution for the oversight of the Italian language, founded in 1583</note>, and sought after, praised, and glorified by bibliophiles and bibliographers. Yet the Aldines had done nothing more than copy an obscure and lowly earlier edition. Although that earlier edition does not strictly fall within the dates I have assigned to the second era, it was unobserved and unimitated in the preceding period. However, because it was copied exactly as it was by the Aldines—who, I repeat, set the standard for all subsequent editions up to our own day—it can and must be considered the work that opens the two modern eras of the printings of the *Joust*. It is as follows:

**1526. THE MOST | beautiful STANZAS | of Master An | gelo Poliziano | by Master TIZZO | NE GAIETANO of Po | fi diligently revised.** <note>original: "LE STAN | ZE bellissime | di messere An | gelo Politiano | da messer TIZZO | NE GAIETANO di Po | fi diligentemente reviste."</note> At the end: *Printed in Venice in the workshop of me, Giacopo da Lecco, in the year 1527, and finished today, which is the first of February.* <note>Venetian printers often used a calendar where the new year began in March, meaning "1526" on a title page might correspond to early 1527 in modern reckoning</note> In octavo: 24 leaves, <term>signatures</term> <note>letters at the bottom of pages used by binders to order the sheets</note> A-F ii, unnumbered; 5 stanzas per page: some lines of the title page are in red ink: after the subscription, there is a woodcut figure.

<header>ANGELO POLIZIANO.</header>

the emblem of Pegasus: it contains only the *Stanzas*. And, since the esteem held for the Aldine press—of which this edition is a predecessor—is so great, it will not be useless to report here some examples of the great and clumsy liberties taken by Master Tizzone <note>Tizzone Gaetano, a 16th-century editor known for his heavy-handed "corrections" of classic Italian texts to make them fit contemporary grammatical rules</note> in correcting Poliziano’s stanzas, even though we have noted the variations of the different editions in the commentary placed below the *Stanzas*.

In the dedication, then, to the excellent Lord *Mario Savorgnano*, Master Tizzone informs us that, having come into his hands **much torn, the stanzas of Master Angelo, he—having learned in his early years to be pitying—as soon as he saw them, knowing how to use pity, became most pitying in healing their wounds so unjustly made.** <note>original: "molto lacerate, le stanze di messere Angelo, egli, avendo apparato ne' primi anni ad esser pietoso, subito vedutele, sapendo usar la pietà, divenne pietosissimo in sanar lor piaghe ingiustamente fatte."</note> And of this "pity," the slaughter he carried out through the *Stanzas* remains an indelible proof, just as the elegance and syntax of the dedication serve as proof of his ability to act as a corrector. 

But, beyond the presumption of this Gaetano <note>referring to Tizzone Gaetano</note>, the revision had another cause. Especially after the influence of Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), an influential scholar who proposed that the Italian language should be modeled strictly on the 14th-century works of Petrarch and Boccaccio</note>, the Tuscan tongue became the national language: except that, to reduce it to the condition of a common language at least in writing, it was necessary to subject it to laws or rules that were derived not from the Tuscan people, but exclusively from two writers: Boccaccio and Petrarch; and not always well. 

The consequence was that from then on, the written language lost much of its primitive agility and ingenuity and had to proceed in a measured and cautious manner. And the worst part was that the new regulators, who arose from every side and in every fashion, gave these new rules a retroactive effect (as one would say today). Therefore, to strip away every trace of the ancient purity that by then smelled too much "of the villa" <note>meaning "too rustic" or "too provincial"</note>, the ancient writers were revised and corrected at the whim of these new Priscians <note>a term for pedantic grammarians, named after Priscian, a famous Latin grammarian of the 6th century</note>. 

And Poliziano’s *Stanzas* were subjected to exactly such a revision by the work of Master Tizzone. Everything he knew of the place and time in which they were composed—the Florentinisms, the local idioms, the irregularities—he wanted to sweep away. He wanted to impose the yoke of grammar on one who was born to provide the very examples for grammar. Where the meter of the verse seemed too harsh or languid, it was stretched and reinforced with new words. It is known that the Florentines used to end the third person plural of certain verbs in *-ono* and *-órono*, which in the common language end in *-ano* and *-àrono*: and Poliziano followed the Florentine usage in this as well. Now, these Florentinisms stank...

to the Romanesque philologist <note>A sarcastic reference to Tizzone Gaetano’s preference for the standardized Italian favored in Rome over Poliziano’s native Florentine dialect</note>; and he chased them away in a fury. But sometimes it happened that those endings occurred at the end of a verse, and the subsequent rhymes depended on them, or the preceding ones were linked to them: and the "worthy" grammarian would then remake the verses for Poliziano. And as for how he remade them, listen to this. In stanza LXI of Book I, at the end of the verses, there is an *erono* and a *schierono* and in the middle: "Having heard the signal, to the hunt *they made a stop*." <note>original: "Sentito il segno, al cacciar posa ferono." The ending "ferono" (they made) is a traditional Florentine form.</note> What does the corrector do? He amends the Florentine endings, and with "Fidenzian" elegance <note>Refers to Fidenzio Glottogrysio, a satirical character representing pedantic, overly Latinized speech</note> he remakes the Latin for Poliziano: "Having heard the signal, to the hunt *they command an end*." <note>original: "Sentito il segno, al cacciar fine imperano."</note> The last two verses of stanza LXII say: "The long voices struck back *resound*, And 'Julius, Julius' the valleys *respond*." <note>original: "Le lunghe voci ripercosse abondono, E Iulio Iulio le valli rispondono."</note> What is this? cries the bold corrector; and with a sudden stroke of the pen, "they *abound* And to 'Julius' it seems the valleys *respond*." <note>original: "abondano E Giulio par che le valli rispondano."</note> Well done, Master Tizzone! What ears you have! And this "it seems" often pleases the Pyrrhonist grammarian <note>A skeptic who doubts the reality of sensory perception</note>, who always seems to fear for the human race, lest it give itself over too much to the deceptions of the senses. Whence, when the poet in stanza CX of Book I affirms "Around him <insert>*Polyphemus*</insert> his sheep graze" <note>original: "D'intorno a lui Polifemo le sue pecore pascono." Polyphemus is the famous Cyclops from the Odyssey.</note> with a verse whose slow harmony allows the imagination to wander over the expanse of the Cyclopean flock, the "good" critic on the other hand—for the sake of a *cascono* [they fall] which appears two lines above—is inclined to doubt; and pursing his lips and shaking his head a little, he says: "Near him it seems his sheep *graze*:" <note>original: "Presso a sè par sue pecore che pascano."</note> which, as you can hear, is a verse most worthy of Poliziano. Finally, in stanza XXVI of Book II, there is an *allacciono* [they lace] and an *imbracciono* [they embrace], which rhyme with *giacciono* [they lie]. He wanted to remove them, and he did so with this elegant repair of verse 2 where *giacciono* was: "When without suspicion it seems they *lie*." <note>original: "Quando senza sospetto par che giacciano."</note> From the corrections cited so far, no one would ever suppose that the corrector was very fond of beautiful harmony. And yet this is one of the many times in which such suppositions prove less than true. The corrector exercises over the verses of poor Master Angelo a truly <term>proud judgment of the ears</term> <note>original: "superbum aurium iudicium"; a phrase from classical rhetoric describing the refined ability to judge poetic meter and sound.</note>: accustomed perhaps to the measured rhythm of Monsignor Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo, the primary architect of standardized 16th-century Italian</note>, that which does not suit him, he hates as harsh and collapsing. Listen: Master Angelo writes [II. 6] "His shining weapons *scatter a flash* That makes the air *tremble with splendor*." <note>original: "L'armi lucenti sue sparger un lampo Che faccia l'aer tremar di splendore."</note> Oh, no! He meant to say "That *makes the air tremble with splendor*." <note>original: "Che faccian tremar l'aere di splendore."</note> And yet in

that unexpected pause on the fourth syllable, and in the speed of the other sounds, one could feel and almost see the vibration and refraction of light rays. Elsewhere, to accompany the image of something slow, dark, and misty with sound, Poliziano says stupendously:
> “And already of dreams the black company:” <note>original: "E già de' sogni la compagnia negra."</note>

where the dragging harmony is a master’s artifice. But that disguised accent on the ninth syllable is instead a mortal sin to the corrector; and like a "good lad," he fixes everything with an archaism:
> “And already of dreams the black companion.” <note>original: "E già de' sogni la compagna negra." Here, the corrector changed "compagnia" (company/group) to "compagna" (companion) to force a more standard rhythm.</note>

And this, despite having a fresh example from Monsignor Bembo:¹
> “Sweet murmur of a living fountain” <note>original: "Dolce mormorio di fontana viva"</note>

and, what is more, from Ariosto:
> “Which the high tops of beeches and firs 
> Make tremble with joyful murmurs.”² <note>original: "Che l' alte cime con mormorii lieti / Fan tremolar dei faggi e degli abeti."</note>

Of other damages, one could not guess the cause, unless attributing it to ignorance. For example: Poliziano, describing the cypress tree—who was once a beautiful youth according to mythology—says, following Ovid:
> “Cypress still bathes his eyes for the stag
> With *hair now rough and formerly flowing and blond:*” <note>original: "Bagna Cipresso ancor pel cervio gli occhi / Con chiome or aspre e già distese e bionde." Poliziano describes the tree's needles as "rough hair" and the boy's original hair as "flowing and blond."</note>

and the corrector "mends" it:
> “*Hair now rough now formerly flowing and blond:*” <note>original: "Chiome or aspre or già distese e bionde."</note>

and goodbye to the delicate allusion to the youth that was required by the preceding verse, and goodbye to common sense. Elsewhere, concerning the emerging Venus, Poliziano—following the Homeric hymn—paints:
> “The *Hours treading the sand in white robes.*” <note>original: "L' Ore premer l' arena in bianca veste." The "Hours" (Horai) are Greek goddesses of the seasons and attendants of Venus.</note>

The corrector seems not to have known even by hearsay of these robed "Hours," and substitutes them with none other than "honor":
> “The *honor treading the sand etc.*” <note>original: "L' onor premer l' arena ec."</note>

Poliziano, referring to a constellation distinct from Bootes and the Wain <note>The Big Dipper</note>, says:
> “And *already the starry chariot Icarus bows:*” <note>original: "E già il carro stellato Icaro inchina."</note>

the corrector, making one and the same of Icarus and Bootes, writes:
> “And *already the starry chariot to the choir bows.*” <note>original: "E già il carro stellato al coro inchina."</note>

Another time, the corrector himself violates grammar, leaving the sense suspended. Venus prays to Pasithea to send Sleep to Julian:
> “Make *him show the fair Julius such an image
> That makes him eager to show himself on the field:*” <note>original: "Fa' che mostri al bel Iulio tale imago / Che 'l faccia di mostrarsi al campo vago."</note>

and the corrector changes it to:
> “*That makes showing himself on the field eager.*” <note>original: "Che faccia dimostrarsi al campo vago."</note>

These are a few among the many examples of the "integrity" and "legitimacy" of a reading that has passed into the honors of the *vulgata*. <note>term: vulgata (vulgate) — The commonly accepted or "standard" version of a text, which the author here argues is actually full of errors.</note>

² Ariosto, *Orlando Furioso*, VI, 24.

It certainly surpasses all previous printings in its regular spelling without comparison. Furthermore, it faithfully reproduces the edition revised by Gaetano, with the addition of some new "patch-ups." <note>The term "conciero" (patch-up) implies clumsy or artificial repairs to the text.</note> Nevertheless, it was cited by the Academicians of the Crusca <note>The Accademia della Crusca is the official guardian of the Italian language; they were notoriously strict about using only "pure" Florentine sources.</note> who, despite their squeamishness toward non-Tuscans, accepted the glass of Master Tizzone da Pofi as Florentine gems this time. <note>The author is mocking the Crusca for being fooled by Tizzone’s artificial edits, which they mistook for authentic old Florentine dialect.</note>

->XCV<-
->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

1560. *First part of the Stanzas by various illustrious poets, collected by Master Lodovico Dolce etc. Newly reprinted and diligently revised and corrected.* In Venice, by *Gabriel Giolito de Ferrari*; in 12º <note>Duodecimo: a small book size where each sheet is folded into twelve leaves.</note>; and in the same place and same format in 1563-65, 1569, 1570, 1575 and [by the *Gioliti*] 1581. These various reprints can be considered as a single edition regarding the text, in which *Dolce* collected all or nearly all the "patch-ups" <note>The original term "concieri" refers to artificial or clumsy editorial repairs to a text.</note> of *Master Tizzone* and *Aldus* and added some of his own. This was noted by *Volpi*, who nevertheless made use of the *Giolito* printings for the *Cominiana* editions:

> "We have noticed the excessive zeal of *Dolce*, or someone else, in having wanted to change many words at a whim—words that can be defended by the authority of *Dante* and other excellent Tuscan writers: such as *labbia* <note>An archaic term meaning face, countenance, or lips.</note> singular into *labbia* plural; *reddito* <note>Returned.</note> into *tornato*; *bobolce* <note>An archaic term for plowmen or ox-drivers.</note> into *bifolce*; as well as having given some verses a different turn."

This last point was not so much the daring of *Dolce* as it was of Master *Tizzone*. Beyond this, *Dolce* had certain whims for changes entirely his own, in which, however, he was followed by no one but *Sermartelli*: for example, at stanza xvi of Book I, he reads *obligate vostra alta natura* <note>original: "obligate your high nature"</note> instead of *obliate* <note>original: "forgotten"</note>; at stanza cxxv where *Venus* asks her son

> "Do you make Jove bellow once again in Tyre?" <note>original: "Fai tu di nuovo in Tiro mugghiar Giove?" This refers to the myth of Jupiter abducting Europa from Tyre.</note>

he puts *bellow as a bull* <note>original: "in toro mugghiar." Dolce likely thought this was a correction since Jupiter took the form of a bull, but he missed the geographical reference to Tyre.</note>. Even more notable is the correction to stanza vii of Book I, where *Poliziano*, following an ancient and poetic tradition that assigned the most beautiful of heroines to the strongest of heroes in the Isles of the Blessed, had written:

> "And if up here fame echoes the truth
> That the daughter of Leda, O sacred Achilles,
> After you left your body within the tomb,
> Still inflames you with sparks of love..." <note>The "daughter of Leda" is Helen of Troy. Poliziano is referencing the legend that Achilles and Helen were wed in the afterlife on the island of Leuce.</note>

When was it ever said that Achilles was in love with Helen? (thought *Dolce*, who had reduced *Homer* into poems of eight-line stanzas <note>An "octave" or "ottava rima."</note> as God willed): you should have said *Polyxena*, Master *Angelo*. and the tireless polygraph <note>A prolific writer who writes on many subjects.</note> reworked the Latin of the translator of Homer, the poet of *Ambra*, and the critic of the *Miscellanee* <note>Poliziano’s famous work of philological criticism.</note> in this way:

> "That the daughter of Hecuba, O sacred Achilles." <note>original: "Che d' Ecuba la figlia, o sacro Achille." Polyxena was the daughter of Hecuba and Priam; some medieval traditions claimed Achilles died for love of her.</note>

It is a marvel, however, that most learned men have approved and retained *Dolce’s* correction in their editions, such as the *Volpi*—inexhaustible commentators on Latin poets—as well as *Serassi*, and (though only in the first edition of the *Stanzas* annotated by him) *Nannucci*.

1568. STANZAS BY.... MADE FOR.... *Newly reprinted and corrected. In Florence by Bartolommeo Sermartelli.* In 8º.

->XCVI<-
->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

In this reading, as Gamba <note>Bartolommeo Gamba (1766–1841) was a famous Italian bibliographer known for his registry of Italian literary classics.</note> noted, it frequently aligns with the Aldine edition <note>Refers to the prestigious press of Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note> and even more so with the printings by Dolce; it possesses nothing of its own except for some insignificant variations. Preceding the *Stanzas* is a dedication from the printer which we include here as a historical document.

---

->*To the very magnificent Master Bernardino, son of Master Niccolò de' Medici, his most respected lord.*<-

> Just as there is no doubt that the first person who sang loftily in *stanze* <term>stanze: the plural of 'stanza,' the basic unit of Italian narrative poetry</term> or rather *ottava rima* <term>ottava rima: a rhyming stanza form consisting of eight lines of eleven syllables each, which became the standard for Italian epic and heroic poetry</term> (which manner of verse, as heroic Tuscan, is today held in the highest esteem) was the most learned Master Angelo of Montepulciano <note>Poliziano’s name is derived from his birthplace, Montepulciano (Mons Politianus in Latin).</note>, who lived in the most happy times of the magnificent and great Lorenzo de' Medici—the splendor not only of this our homeland but of all Italy—so it is true, in the judgment of the best critics, that his aforementioned *Stanzas*, composed for the Joust of the Magnificent Giuliano, are and always shall be numbered among the best that have ever been made. Indeed, I will dare to say, based on what I have many times heard, that aside from those by the most learned Lodovico Martelli and by Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), an influential poet and linguist who standardized the Italian language based on Petrarch and Boccaccio.</note> (let others say what they please), these are without contest the best. And if it seems that in some places they lack a certain "something" of greatness and strict observance that others have since used in similar poems, no one should marvel at it; for it is very true that it was precisely then that Tuscan poetry began to flourish and rise again in our most sweet and graceful tongue, largely through the work and study of Poliziano himself, having been until then in little account for many years due to the lack of care of our ancestors. It is not, I say, a great feat that others who came after Master Angelo have somewhat better enriched and adorned their rhymes of this sort; since, as the proverb says, it is quite easy to add to things already discovered. But ceasing now to make a longer discourse on this matter; having reprinted the said *Stanzas* to please many who wish to have them separate from the volumes of other works, I thought—since they discuss the eminent deeds of the ancient heroes of your most illustrious family—that they should go forth this time under your name. For although they are not a new thing, they are nevertheless such that they are always seen as both new and most learned...

->XCVIII<-

### THIRD ERA.

To the third era, which may be termed the Cominiana <note>Named after the Comino printing press in Padua, renowned for its scholarly precision and beautiful typography during the 1700s.</note>, belong the editions of the *Stanzas* and the *Orpheus* published from 1728 onwards. The specific characteristics of the editions from this era are that in the *Stanzas*, the reading of the Aldine text <note>original: "testo aldino" — the version printed by the famous Aldus Manutius in Venice, considered a standard of quality.</note> is more or less preserved; in the *Orpheus*, the ancient texts are followed until 1777, after which the new text by Affò <note>Ireneo Affò (1741–1797), an art historian and critic who discovered a different, more complete version of Poliziano's *Orpheus*.</note> prevails. Some rhymes begin to be added to the two major works, and from 1812 onwards, all or nearly all of them are collected. However, we must not occupy ourselves with the rhymes in this chapter.

**1728.** THE MOST ELEGANT | STANZAS . . . . . . . . . *now restored by comparison with various ancient editions to their true reading, and augmented by a song and various notes. In Padua, at Giuseppe Comino's.* In octavo. The edition is edited by the Volpi brothers <note>Gaetano and Giovanni Antonio Volpi, scholars who ran the Comino press.</note>; they followed the Aldine text and that of Dolce from 1570, and stated they had consulted a Florentine printing from 1513, though they rarely or almost never turned to it: and this edition was cited by the members of the Accademia della Crusca <note>The premier institution for the Italian language, which uses specific "cited" editions to establish linguistic authority.</note>.

**1747.** . . . . . . . . . *with the life of Poliziano written by the Abbot Pierantonio Serassi. In Bergamo, by Pietro Lancellotti.* A magnificent edition in large quarto, in a thick and clear typeface [Volpi]. The text is merely a reprint of the preceding one: to the *Stanzas* is added the *Tiberine Nymph* by Molza <note>Francesco Maria Molza (1489–1544), a poet whose pastoral work was often paired with Poliziano’s.</note>.

**1749.** ORPHEUS | A FABLE BY MASTER | A. P. | *diligently corrected | and restored to its true reading.* Included at the end of *The Cyclops of Euripides* newly translated and illustrated, published in Padua, by *Giuseppe Comino*; in octavo.

THE FABLE | OF | ORPHEUS COMPOSED BY M. | A. P. | *and now for the first time restored to its true and sincere reading. In Padua. By Giuseppe Comino.* In octavo, of 24 pages. This is the same version already published at the end of the *Cyclops*; except that here it is preceded by a notice from the printer and a testimony from Menckenius <note>original: "Menckenio" — likely referring to Friedrich Otto Mencken, a German scholar who wrote a history of Poliziano’s life.</note> regarding the *Orpheus*. In the notice, it is stated that the edition was taken from the Florentine one of 1513 commissioned by Ser Piero Pacini da Pescia <note>A famous early publisher in Florence known for woodcut-illustrated books.</note>, «... by virtue of which several verses were restored, many errors were amended..., and various ancient words and manners of speaking were adopted which then

> "But amidst so much study that our best scholars have applied to it, and amidst so many cares of even the most diligent printers, is it then true that Poliziano's *Stanzas* are entirely free of error? This doubt of the most illustrious Betti seems to me, through the examination of the various texts I have conducted, to be strengthened and raised to the level of certainty. For if Betti adds, "Who after the death of the poet might have frankly dared to lay a hand on the most elegant *Stanzas*, I do not know;¹" here too the answer is ready: the corrupter was Master Tizzone Gaietano da Pofi. <note>Tizzone Gaetano (c. 1480–1550) was a grammarian and editor known for his "corrections" to the works of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio, which later scholars often viewed as intrusive meddling.</note> Having thus clarified how Master Tizzone had, in 1526, corrupted the genuine reading of Poliziano, and how the most accredited editions from the Aldine <note>Books printed by the press founded by Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note> onwards are nothing but a shameful reproduction of Tizzone's clumsy alterations <term>concieri</term> <note>Literally "repairs" or "patches," used here pejoratively to describe poor editorial changes.</note> along with others added to them; and having clarified how the printings prior to 1526 agree admirably with the two Riccardian manuscripts, and with these almost always agrees—especially in the most significant passages—the Chigian manuscript 2333, reproduced in the Roman printing of 1804 and...

...the Oliverian manuscript <note>A manuscript held in the Biblioteca Oliveriana in Pesaro, crucial for correcting Poliziano's text.</note>, the principal variants of which were published by Betti in the *Saggiatore* and in the *Arcadico* <note>Refers to the *Saggiatore* and the *Giornale Arcadico*, influential 19th-century Italian scholarly journals.</note>; once all this was clarified, there was no longer any doubt regarding the method to be held in a new edition of the *Stanzas* <note>Poliziano’s *Stanze per la giostra*, a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance poetry.</note>. And so it was: to take as a foundation the Florentine <term>codices</term> <note>Manuscript books written by hand.</note> and the printings prior to 1526, the Roman edition of 1804, and the Oliverian readings; to report in the notes the few discrepancies between these texts, and the many arbitrary and shameful ones of the corrupt and commonly accepted version. 

Regarding the *Orpheus* <note>Poliziano's *Fabula di Orfeo*, one of the earliest secular plays in Italian.</note>, then; although the new version in which Father Affò <note>Ireneo Affò (1741–1797), a famous scholar who discovered a more "theatrical" version of the play.</note> gave it in 1776 pleased us and seemed quite authoritative due to the antiquity of the manuscripts, we still could not hold the opinion that his was the only legitimate *Orpheus* as composed by its author. Therefore, we reprinted both the first *Orpheus* (as Serassi republished it from the Chigi codex in the Cominiana edition of 1765, adding in notes the variants of the old printings and the Riccardiano codex 2723) and the second version (as given by Affò, with the variants of the two Reggian codices reported by him, omitting the others from the Cominiana edition and the old version we had already reproduced a few pages prior). 

But we also reprinted the preface and the observations of the learned scholar from Parma <note>Father Affò.</note>; inserting into the footnotes those that touch upon the style and internal structure of the play, while leaving the longer ones—of broader and more varied erudition—at the end on their own. And beneath both the *Orpheus* and the *Stanzas*, we placed the commentary with which Vincenzo Nannucci adorned the latter in 1812 and the former in 1814. We consulted both editions from those two years for the commentary on the *Stanzas*, making special use of the first, of which we possess a copy containing some marginal notes and additions in the commentator's own hand. We trimmed away a bit of the wording, more so than the comparisons and citations; the Greek passages we translated into very faithful prose <note>Originally translated into Italian by the editor; here rendered in English.</note>; we also corrected some things, not out of an assumption of greater learning, but where textual criticism or other similar reasons required it; and we added some material from Fornaciari¹, Betti², and others, as well as—always distinguishing it with an asterisk—some of our own. # ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...reason to laugh behind our backs: but we, while admiring and venerating the critics, the philologists, and the [academic] fashion as much as they deserve, will dare to humbly observe that, if Monsieur Sainte-Beuve <note>Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve (1804–1869), a preeminent French literary critic known for his "Literary Portraits."</note> desired for the modern André Chénier <note>André Chénier (1762–1794) was a French poet whose work was deeply influenced by Greek and Latin classics.</note> a commentary like those of Boissonade regarding the Greeks¹ and if Mr. Becq de Fouquières has recently fulfilled the wishes of that illustrious critic,² I should be forgiven for having reprinted and expanded a commentary on the *Stanzas* of Poliziano, the father of the Renaissance and of the "poetry of imitation." <note>This refers to the Renaissance practice of *imitatio*, where poets creatively wove fragments of classical authors into their own original works.</note> And here the name of Chénier brings to my mind those most elegant verses of his:

> Friend, thus Apollo <note>original: "Phoebus," the Greek god of music and poetry.</note> pours his bounties upon me.
> Often I invade the riches of ancient authors.
> More often their writings, those generous spurs,
> Set me ablaze with their flame, and I create alongside them.
> A stern judge, spying on my works,
> Suddenly with loud cries denounces twenty passages
> Translated from such-and-such an author whom he names; and finding them
> He admires himself and is pleased to see himself so learned.
> Why does he not come to me? I would make known to him
> A thousand of my thefts that he perhaps ignores.
> My finger on my cloak reveals to him in an instant
> The invisible seam that goes winding
> To join a foreign purple to my fabric.
> I will show him the art, unknown to the common man,
> Of separating before his eyes, by following their bond,
> All these united metals of which I have formed my own.³

What Chénier says toward his critic, Poliziano could apply toward his commentators: from whom, for this very reason, no one should expect or promise themselves a work that is entirely perfect and responsive to every whim. For the rest, the work of Nannucci <note>Vincenzio Nannucci (1787–1857), a philologist whose previous work on Poliziano is being expanded here.</note> recommends itself; for my part, I have done the best that was permitted to me.

³ A. Chénier, *Epistle IV, to Le Brun*: cited edition page 315.

->CVI<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

## IV.

### VARIOUS RHYMES. — CONTINUOUS AND SCATTERED *RISPETTI*. — BALLADS.
<note>*Rispetti* are a traditional Italian folk poetic form, usually consisting of eight hendecasyllabic lines, used primarily for love songs.</note>

---

That Poliziano took up and continued the tradition of Boccaccio in art seems true to us even with regard to his lyric poems. These are all concerned with love, as we must reject the few rhymes on various subjects published under his name and take little account of the *lauda* <note>original: "lauda," a song of praise or sacred folk song.</note> attributed to him. And it is a natural love and one of the senses that is sung and described, or turned into a joke, by the poet of the *Stanzas*, <note>Poliziano’s most famous work, *Stanze per la giostra* (Stanzas for the Joust).</note> sometimes with the fire of passion that reigns in Boccaccio's *Fiammetta*, and other times with the grace and ingenuity of the *Nymphs of Fiesole* and the *Decameron* where it is comic, and even with the fine irony and sarcasm of the *Corbaccio*. <note>The source text says "Laberinto," another name for Boccaccio's "Il Corbaccio," a biting satirical work.</note> And here, especially, the comparison already made by others between our poet and Valerius Catullus <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century BCE known for his emotional intensity and technical mastery.</note> becomes appropriate. He resembles Catullus not only "for the abundance of graceful images, for the elegance and purity of the forms of speech, and for the native sincerity of the style,"¹ but even more so for this reason: just as Valerius Catullus—while deriving Greek poetry into the Roman tongue through his *Thetis and Peleus*, *Berenice's Hair*, and the elegy to *Allius*—preserved for Latin its own inherent ingenuity and cast the hexameter <note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet, the standard for epic poetry.</note> in the great mold of Homer rather than in the Alexandrian patterns <note>Refers to the highly polished and complex style of the Greek poets from Alexandria.</note> that pleased the more refined poets of the following age, he remained at the same time entirely Roman in his hendecasyllables, his epigrams, and perhaps his wedding songs <note>original: "epitalamii," poems written specifically for the bride and groom.</note>, as much for his way of feeling and the quality of his jokes and wit as for his style and versification. Consequently, his rhythm later seemed broken and harsh to those who had grown accustomed to Propertius and Ovid, and his lyric poetry lost out when compared to the very fine but somewhat foreign elegance of Horace. Similarly, Poliziano, transplanting Greek and Latin beauties into the *Stanzas* and the *Orfeo* with a variety of rhythm that annoyed those born after Tasso, and using the language of his own time which seemed mixed and li- <note>The text breaks off here mid-word; likely "libera" (free) or "linguaggio" (language).</note>

---

¹ Bonanni, preface to two Songs by A. P., Florence, Barbèra, 1858.

<summary>This page analyzes Poliziano's lyric poetry as a continuation of Boccaccio's style and compares his technical approach to that of the Roman poet Catullus.</summary>

It specifically examines how his work shifted from a "licentious" or popular Florentine style toward a more refined classical elegance that rivaled Petrarch and the Latin elegists.</meta>

->CVII<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

<meta>The word "[li]centious" follows from the previous page's "Bere-" (likely "Berlicenziosa" or "licenziosa").</meta> [li]centious after the theories of Bembo, <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547) was an influential scholar who codified the Italian language, favoring a return to the strict styles of Petrarch and Boccaccio.</note> was later a writer entirely Florentine and of the people in his *rispetti* <note>original: "rispetti," a traditional Italian folk poetic form, usually eight lines long.</note> and in his dance songs, which were necessarily forgotten when popularity in literature was lost and mocked.

However, even in the lyrics there is some sample of the first classical manner of the ***Stanzas*** and the ***Orfeo***. Ginguené <note>Pierre-Louis Ginguené, a French literary historian.</note> and others with him wrote that the song "Mountains, valleys, caves, and hills" <note>original: "Monti, valli, antri e colli"</note> is, after Petrarch, the Italian poem that best captures his style.¹ And if this is to be understood regarding the versification and the external structure, it is well said. But in substance, that song is already an elegy, where the rapture of the senses is expressed with bolder colors and with less deep shading than Petrarch usually employs. And even more so, the other song "I am constrained..." <note>original: "Io son costretto..."</note> takes after the elegy, even in its meter; which, with the various pauses of the four-line stanzas <note>original: "strofe di quattro versi"</note> flowing one into another, and with the <term>settenario</term> <note>a verse line of seven syllables</note> following two <term>endecasillabi</term> <note>the classic Italian eleven-syllable line</note> one after the other, has almost the swaying gait of the <term>distico</term> <note>a distich or couplet, typically used in Latin elegiac verse</note>. If instead of the gentle sadness of Tibullus you find in these elegies the heat and ornaments of Propertius and a certain grace and ease between Catullus and Ovid, you will nonetheless judge them superior to the many written in <term>terzetti</term> <note>tercets, or three-line stanzas</note> that were produced afterward. And you will regret that the poet did not compose any others, and especially by means of interlocking <term>quartine</term> <note>quatrains, or four-line stanzas</note> did not make our vernacular learn something of the incomparable delicacy found in the Latin elegy on violets.
