# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...most harmonious <note>The text likely completes the word "armoniosissimo" from the previous page.</note> and worthy of Poliziano.<note>1</note> I am pleased for the readers to read it in the original Latin, as a completion and illustration of his vernacular lyrics:

> O beautiful violets, little gifts from our Venus,
> In whom lies the sweet pledge of such great love;
> What earth brought you forth? With what nectar
> Did the soft west winds and the breeze scatter your fragrant tresses?
> Did golden Venus nourish you in the Acidalian fields? <note>Acidalia is a spring in Boeotia where Venus and the Graces were said to bathe.</note>
> Did Love <note>original: "Amor," referring to Cupid.</note> tend to you beneath the Idalian grove?
> I would believe the Muses <note>original: "Pieridas," another name for the Muses, daughters of Pierus.</note> adorn their lyres with these garlands

> With this flower the Hour <note>original: "Hora," one of the goddesses of the seasons.</note> binds her ambrosial hair;
> With this the charming Grace covers her untamed breast;
> With this Aurora <note>The goddess of the dawn.</note> binds the ribbons to her brow,
> When she unfolds the rosy day from the spring sky.
> With such gems the violet-beds of the Hesperides <note>Nymphs who guarded a mythical garden of golden apples.</note> glow;
> With these flowers the breeze possesses the painted grove;
> Among these, the blessed spirits <note>original: "pii manes," the benevolent souls of the departed.</note> play through the distinct grasses;
> The herb of spring Chloris <note>The Greek goddess of flowers, equivalent to the Roman Flora.</note> produces these offspring.
> O violets, happy beyond measure, you whom that hand gathered—
> That right hand which stole wretched me from myself—
> You whom she moved with rosy fingers to that beautiful mouth,
> From where Love hurls his arrows at me.
> Perhaps this grace comes to you from there as well:
> Such great honor breathes from the mouth of my lady.
> See how that one charms with a milky color;
> See how this one blushes with purple petals.
> This is the color of my lady, when pleasing purple
> Paints her milky cheeks with a sweet, rosy blush.
> What a sweet scent she breathes from her lips, how far it spreads:
> Behold, violets, that scent remains in you.
> O fortunate violets, my life and my delight,
> O harbor and breeze of my soul.
> From you at least, violets, I shall pluck pleasing kisses;
> I shall touch you three and four times with a greedy hand.
> I will saturate you with my tears, which pour through my sorrowful face
> And over my breast like a living river.
> Drink up these tears, which cruel love squeezes from my eyes
> As fuel for a slow-burning flame.
> Live forever, violets; let neither the summer with its suns
> Nor the winter with its biting cold wither you.
> Live forever, consolation of my wretched love,
> O violets, O pleasing rest for my soul.

Such was the gallantry of the salons, where the elegy could be enjoyed and rewarded with smiles and praise by more than one woman, as well as by men. For these were the times in which the beautiful young girl Alessandra Scala <note>A famous Florentine woman scholar known for her command of Greek.</note> recited Sophocles's *Antigone* with such certainty of pronunciation and meter <term>prosody: the patterns of rhythm and sound used in poetry</term>, and with such truth, that the learned listeners were all captivated; and to Poliziano’s praises, delivered in Greek couplets, she responded—humbly rejecting them, however—in Greek couplets herself.² But it was not always so: more than once, the delicate Greek and Latin verses were set aside, and the "Magnificent" Lorenzo himself, in the character of Vallera, a peasant from Mugello, sang the *Nencia* <note>Referring to "La Nencia da Barberino," a poem by Lorenzo de' Medici written in a rustic, peasant dialect.</note>, and Pulci <note>Luigi Pulci, a poet in the Medici circle famous for his humorous and epic works.</note> matched him with the coarser praises of *Beca* <note>Referring to "La Beca da Dicomano," a parody of Lorenzo's poem written by Pulci.</note>. Then Poliziano, standing up, would reel off <term>rispetti: a traditional Italian poetic form, usually a single stanza of eight lines, often used for courting</term> regarding the beauties of Lady Ippolita Leoncina of Prato. Afterward, they would all go out together, accompanying themselves with craftsmen and improvisers of the common people—less cultured but more lively—and either entered into a contest of <term>strambotti: short, often satirical or witty poems, frequently improvised</term> among themselves, or, to the sound of the viola and the mandolin, they went out on summer evenings singing of the various fortunes and conditions of love through the streets of Florence. They would strike up serenades and songs of parting at the doorways of beauties who were less refined and haughty, but more striking than the noblewomen. Thus Florence, also by means of the Medici court, continued its traditional duty toward literature: which was to harmonize ancient examples with modern and popular sentiment.

Lorenzo de' Medici, moreover—the prince of this renewal and founder of a dynasty—had, besides his own taste as a poet, another reason for bringing the art of the palaces closer to that of the streets, the squares, and the fields. For the House of Medici, whose born adversaries were the Acciaioli, the Pazzi, the Frescobaldi, the Salviati, and the Soderini <note>These were powerful Florentine families who opposed the Medici's rise to power; the Pazzi are famous for their 1478 conspiracy to assassinate Lorenzo.</note>, drawing closer to the common people meant refreshing their own strength. But given the conditions of the time, this drawing closer could not, nor should it any longer, have a political appearance; co-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

This part had been represented by Silvestro da Vieri and by Giovanni, son of Cosimo. Now, what his ancestors did with the tools of democracy, Lorenzo accomplished through popular poetry. He did not cultivate or elevate it solely through the sentiment of an artist, but to find the means and reasons to mingle with the common people. Under the guise of civil equality, he sought to ~~win them over~~ and master them by corruption; by flattering them in their ~~weakness~~—their love of festivals—he distracted them more than ever from their ancient institutions. What Messer Giovanni began with the *catasto* <term>catasto: a detailed tax census of households and property used to distribute the tax burden in Florence</term>, his magnificent great-grandson completed with poetry. It was the first and last time, I believe, that a tax register and poetry found themselves in agreement; both conspired toward the ruin of liberty.

I hope those of my readers who are accustomed to viewing our literature only from a classical perspective (which is undoubtedly most useful to those seeking examples and lessons in style) do not suspect at this point that bringing up popular poetry and representing Poliziano as an imitator of the common folk is merely one of those posthumous and predetermined estimations of which critics make use more than once. Today, "popular literature" is the fashion; one might think: "to follow the trend, you represent Poliziano as an imitator of the people." No. When we have the fact of the appearance of a poetic form whose first literary practitioners clearly profess to imitate the popular manner (as do Medici and Pulci in *Nencia* and *Beca* <note>Referring to the poems "La Nencia da Barberino" and "La Beca da Dicomano," which used rustic, peasant dialects</note>); when in all the more or less literary *rispetti* <term>rispetti: a traditional form of short Italian folk poetry, typically consisting of eight lines with a specific rhyme scheme</term> of the fifteenth century we find a unique system of figurative language, formulas, and versification—a system that finds its only counterpart in the *rispetti* sung every day in the Tuscan countryside—we are forced to infer that a popular Tuscan poetry pre-existed Medici, Pulci, and Poliziano, and that they drew from it. Otherwise, one would have to suppose that the *rispetti* not only of Valdarno but of the mountains of Pistoia and Mount Amiata are an imitation of *Nencia* and *Beca*, and that our peasants had read Poliziano in the editions of Ciampolini and Silvestri, who were the first to publish most of Messer Angelo’s *rispetti*. That the people accepted performances from the religious festivals of the cities, that some story or legend or short poem...

->CXII<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

Varchi passes over both these popular compositions without further review.¹ But the ancient <term>strambotto: a light, often humorous or satirical poetic form, typically an eight-line stanza</term>, which was certainly not an *eight-line stanza* <note>original: "ottava"</note> in the beginning, must have been something heterogeneous and outside the standard metric forms. A memory of this confusion is perhaps found in the songbook of the Aquilan <note>Serafino de' Cimminelli (1466–1500), a famous poet known as "The Aquilan"</note> where the name *strambotto* is given to both *strambotti* properly so called and to <term>barzellette: playful, rhythmic songs or verses</term>. Another clue is the transfer of the word into the Spanish language as *estrambote* <note>original: "estrambote"</note> to signify that which is added outside the conventional rules to a piece of regular poetry, such as the "tail" added to a sonnet. Hence, the derivation assigned to it by Redi ² from the ancient word *motto* <note>meaning a song or poetic composition</note> is perhaps true; it would be like a *stran motto* <note>meaning "strange song"</note>. Indeed, *strammotto* continues to be used in some Italian dialects, and it is printed in the *Introduction to Vernacular Things* <note>original: "Tirocinio delle cose volgari"</note> by Diomede Guidalotto of Bologna [Bologna, 1504] and in the *New Work* <note>original: "Opera nuova"</note> by Bernardo Accolti [Venice, 1519]. However, the other etymology from *strambo* <note>meaning "odd," "twisted," or "crooked"</note> is not improbable, and it pleased Crescimbeni ³ more, because in *strambotti* one reads the most bizarre fantasies and witty conceits.

Regarding the <term>rispetto: a respectful, often courtly, short poem of eight lines, expressing devotion to a beloved</term>, I also believe, along with Salvini ⁴ and Crescimbeni, that the name derives from the reverence and veneration that the singers show toward the object of their love and from the honor they render her through singing. I could not bring myself to accept another etymology by the same Salvini, who suggests that they are called *rispetti* "as if they were reciprocal or mutual songs, because those who are drawn by lot to succeed the main officials in their absence or lack are also called *rispetti* <note>Salvini is comparing the poems to "stand-ins" or "alternates"</note>." From the etymology itself, it appears that the *strambotto* was the form of whim rather than passion, reserved for light love, irony, and mockery; while the *rispetto* was almost the elegiac and lyrical expression of pure, deep, and exalted passion. The *eight-line stanzas* inspired by the beautiful Leoncina are *rispetti*; but Poliziano titles his string of somewhat cynical advice to the modest *wife of another, who was dear to him*, as a *letter in strambotti* <note>original: "lettera in istrambotti"</note>. *Strambotti* are also those stanzas that begin: "The night is long for those who cannot sleep."

> And it seems to me that I am talking with you:
> Wherefore from this I take delight.
> Oh me, how I wish I would not wake!
> Lilies and violets <note>original: "vivuole," a Tuscan dialect variant of "viole"</note> seem to be in my bed.
> Oh me, for I had such great consolation,
> O noble lady, from your vision!
> Indeed, search within your heart and mind
> For what you find there, my sweet soul.
> And you will find there your dear servant
> Who stays there on his knees night and day,
> And always prays to Almighty Christ
> That he might do what would please you:
> You are cruel and are not moved to pity,
> And it seems you enjoy making me die."

The following poem draws closer and closer to the <term>rispetti: traditional Tuscan folk poems, usually eight lines long, expressing "respect" or devotion</term> that are still sung today; in it, the repetition of the concept of the words in the last lines is very noticeable—a feature that has become the characteristic of this genre:

> • I have lost my fresh garland,
> The one my beloved <note>original: "amanza," a term for a sweetheart or mistress</note> gave to me.
> What will I do if she asks me for it?
> I will say: I lost it on this road.
> If she asks me for it with good reason,
> I will say: I gave it to a young man <note>original: "garzone"</note>."

->CXVII<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO. CXVII

...from a Laurentian manuscript of the mid-fifteenth century¹ another poem appears that will perhaps seem even fresher and more voluptuous:

> • Tonight I dreamed of what it was,
> Tonight I dreamed of what it might be;
> That I was among the white and red roses,
> That I was in the arms of my beloved <note>original: "amanza," a sweetheart or lover</note>.
> O vain dream that deceives the people:
> I tightened my arms and found nothing. •

Such must have been the antecedents and the models that Poliziano was able to find in the amorous poetry of the *rispetti* <term>rispetti: a traditional Italian folk song or poem, usually consisting of an eight-line stanza</term>. From these, he chose the best part, leaving to [Lorenzo de'] Medici and [Luigi] Pulci the parody that allows one to glimpse the mocking laughter of the bourgeois over the country folk. Whether Poliziano gathered the *rispetti* he called "continuous" <note>original: "continuati," a series of stanzas linked together to form a longer narrative or thematic poem</note> into an ordered series—to represent now an epistle, now an elegy, now a serenade, a departure, or a dialogue—or whether, in a burst of improvisation, he struck an image, a concept, or a feeling with "scattered" verses <note>original: "spicciolati," individual, standalone stanzas</note>; he always treated this genre seriously. Not that he, being most learned, ever thought of raising them to the dignity of a classical composition, as the Aretine [Bernardo] Accolti did later, transforming them into epigrams in this manner:²

> • Love cried out—I am held in little esteem,
> I too would like a temple among mortals:—
> To which Cytherea <note>Citerea: another name for Venus, the goddess of love</note> said—Your temple is in a place
> That forces men and gods to adore you.—
> Then the god of the amorous fire
> Said—Mother, satisfy my thoughts;
> Tell me what place you have chosen for my temple:—
> Venus responded—The face of Giovanna. •

On the contrary, he allowed himself to yield to the ease of natural Tuscan; but he put so much genius and affection into those humble trials, and knew how to add so much elegance through culture to the grace of his native tongue, that he was perhaps the first in poetry to give the stamp of Atticism <term>Atticism: a refined, polished, and simple style of expression modeled after the ancient Greeks</term> to Florentine localisms and the finish of art to familiar expression. By virtue of these qualities, readers of Poliziano are usually happy to forgive some inequality or harshness and some irregularity and a...

->CXVIII<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...a bit of grammatical and rhythmic anarchy, especially when considering that a good portion of those *rispetti* <note>original: "rispetti," folk poems usually of eight lines</note>, passing from mouth to mouth, must have suffered more than one alteration, and others were truly composed on the fly. Of this—besides the nature of such poetry and the certainty that Poliziano improvised even in Greek and Latin ("<term>You who are able to produce sublime verses on the spot</term>," <note>original Latin: "Qui potes extemplo sublimes edere versus"</note> as Gioviano Crasso wrote to him),¹—we have a hint in this passage from one of his letters to [Lorenzo] the Magnificent dated June 20, 1490: "The night before last, I heard our Piero singing improvisations; he came to ambush me at home with all these improvisers. He satisfied me wonderfully, <term>especially</term> <note>original Latin: "presertim"</note> in his witticisms and in his retorts, and in his ease and pronunciation, such that I seemed to see and hear Your Magnificence at every turn."² In this "ambush" by Piero, it is easy to discern the pride of the young man who comes to choose a worthy judge in the old improviser, who was once a companion in the revelries of his magnificent father.

Furthermore, the practice of improvising, especially in <term>ottave</term> <note>eight-line stanzas with an ABABABCC rhyme scheme</note>, lasted for a long time in Florence. And at times it must have served as an outlet for loves, memories, and political rages; for [Giovan Battista] Busini has left us a memory of one Alessandro Pazzi—who, degenerate in his blood, was singing improvisations after 1512 with Pietro Paolo Boscoli in the chamber of Cosimo and Zanobi Buondelmonti—who began a stanza in praise of the Medici by saying *Palle Palle* <note>The rallying cry of the Medici supporters, referring to the "palle" or balls on the family coat of arms</note>, to which Pietro Paolo, who was a most rare and virtuous youth, added:

> ". . . : And balls, balls let them be,
> Since your ancestors to this sound
> Were killed, hanged, and dragged."³

Under the Medici principality, people continued to improvise popularly at the Marmi and elsewhere; challenges between poets followed one another in the taverns and the streets to the sound of the guitar and the violin, even under the Lorraine principality, and some names of improvisers remain in the folk tradition. But the last of the famous poets who in his youth gained fame from these songs—which were, however, diminished and possessing barely a shadow of the ancient spirit—

->CXIX<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...stylistic elegance, Sestini <note>Bartolomeo Sestini (1792–1822), a poet known for his work in the Tuscan tradition</note> was the classical author of the romantic *Pia* <note>referring to the poem *La Pia de' Tolomei*</note>. Today, the improvised Tuscan song—after languishing for a long time in the <term>ottava</term> <note>an eight-line stanza with a specific rhyme scheme</note> that the audiences of the Quarconia and Borgognissanti <note>popular theaters in Florence known for vernacular and folk-style performances</note> imposed upon Stenterello <note>the traditional Florentine "mask" or comic character representing the common man</note> at the end of every act—is now breathing its last. This is because the improvisations performed like a play upon the stage do not belong to our current subject. This topic could not be better concluded than with this most accurate judgment by Professor Alessandro D'Ancona:

> "Certainly, we do not pretend to assert that modern <term>rispetti</term>, <term>strambotti</term>, or <term>stornelli</term> <note>different forms of short, often improvised, Italian folk poems</note> are in every way what they were in the fifteenth century. However, except for a few modifications necessarily brought about by the passage of time and oral transmission, it could be asserted that—due to the tenacity of the common people in retaining ancient customs—in their entirety and their most general aspect, they are the very models to which the Medicean school <note>the literary circle of Lorenzo de' Medici and Poliziano</note> adhered for its imitations. Indeed, our people today do not sing but repeat; they do not invent but reproduce a treasure of verses to which they are attached by tradition. Even when they believe they are improvising, they are merely reshuffling and reuniting images and verses scattered across various compositions. This folk poetry, which is now being collected and which has seemed like a revelation, is but the last echo of the youth of a race; a youth revealed in the naive strength, the energetic sincerity, and the primitive purity of those songs. Our people today would no longer know how to compose in that manner, but by receiving them and transmitting them from generation to generation, they continue to modify them only slightly. We, by gathering these fragments from the living voices of the mountain women, are rediscovering the scattered limbs of the past. By lending an ear to the song of the farmer, we catch a sound that, though now almost lost in the plains and valleys of the Arno, continues to resonate among the rugged peaks of the Apennines, serving as a final refuge against the progress of an encroaching civilization.¹"

->CXX<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...kind was Poliziano. Anyone with even a passing knowledge of thirteenth-century poetry will easily believe that the Provençal-Sicilian lyric system—so complex and artificial in its apparent coarseness—may well have been in fashion in the imperial palaces of Sicily, in the tyrannical courts of Upper Italy, and in the towers of Ghibelline <note>A political faction in medieval Italy that supported the Holy Roman Emperor</note> feudal lords. However, in the squares of southern cities, under the Bolognese and Tuscan porticos, and in the dances and festivals of the people, that was not the poetry to be understood and enjoyed. And anyone who reads through the collections of rhymes from that first century <note>the 1200s, the dawn of Italian literature</note> will often be surprised to find several songs that are entirely dissonant from the general tone, in which a completely different order of ideas, feelings, and forms clearly appears. What do the dialogues of Ciullo d'Alcamo $^1$ <note>Cielo d'Alcamo, author of a famous humorous dialogue</note> and Ciacco dell'Anguillara $^2$ have to do, I ask you, with the songs of Pier delle Vigne <note>Chancellor to Frederick II and a leading poet of the Sicilian School</note> and Folcacchieri? And the lament of the <term>mal maritata</term> <note>the "badly married woman," a common folk theme about a woman unhappy with her husband</note> so awkwardly intruded into a song by Frederick II,$^3$ and the other lament of a woman whose lover has been led astray found among the rhymes of Odo delle Colonne,$^4$ and that of the crusader's beloved published under the name of Rinaldo d'Aquino,$^5$—even to those who look no further than the forms—must appear entirely distinct from the songs of the Provençal and courtly school. In the latter, there is such uniformity of concepts, formulas, and rhythm, such pretension and effort; conversely, in the former, there is an agile movement, a domestic and indigenous air, a true expression, a simple and melodic meter, and never a trace of imitation. But let us take another step and turn to the songbooks of Guido Cavalcanti and Dante. Here, the vigor and novelty of the imagery, the height and depth of feeling, the harmony of coloring, and the powerful, severe, virgin language announce the true art of the nation. This is well and good: but those scholastic treatments <note>references to medieval philosophical and theological academic methods</note> that more than once hinder the movement of the poetry, that mysticism that overshadows it, that allegorism that envelops it and a...

->CXXI<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...even to those whom such a small thing darkens, was he this way for everyone? For the noble ladies, for the young, for the craftsman, for the burgher? I doubt it. Let us turn some pages and read: "For a little garland / That I saw, every flower / Will make me sigh," "Fresh new rose, / Pleasant spring;"¹ and again "I was in thoughts of love, when I found / Two young country girls" and "In a little grove I found a shepherdess / Fairer than the star, in my opinion."² What a difference between the plainness, the gaiety, and the vivid sparkle of the senses and colors in these graceful stanzas, and the abstruse austerity of the song "A lady entreats me"³ <note>original: "Donna mi prega," a notoriously difficult philosophical poem by Guido Cavalcanti, though here discussed as part of the complex style of the era</note> and "You who, understanding, move the third heaven!"⁴ One would say they were by a completely different author: and certainly, one must admit that these latter rhymes belong to a different order of poetry than that of the songs and sonnets. And so it is in fact. 

Without being "popular poetry" in the strictest sense, those first Sicilian and Tuscan dialogues and laments point to an art that—free from every influence of imitation and system—developed within a circle of ideas and sentiments derived from or inspired by rural nature and real life; an art that approached the people and was perhaps understood and accepted by them. Yet, in the beginning, it had no fixed forms: but, once the poetic primacy passed from the Sicilians to the Tuscans—especially after the Battle of Benevento <note>Fought in 1266, this battle led to the collapse of the Sicilian School's influence and the rise of Tuscan culture</note> and the resulting prevalence of the Guelph <note>The political faction supporting the Pope and often associated with the rising merchant/popular classes</note> and popular party—it settled easily and durably into the character of the **ballad** <term>ballata</term> <note>A poem intended to be sung as an accompaniment to a dance</note>. It is not that this was an exclusively Tuscan discovery from the latter half of the thirteenth century: poetic forms are not invented by one people or generation alone. On the contrary, there is much truth in the opinion of Minturno,⁵ that the "song for dancing" <note>original: "canzone a ballo"</note> is perhaps the oldest composition of vernacular poetry. And, since the people everywhere and always show themselves tenacious of ancient institutions, perhaps it proceeds from those *dance-songs* <note>original: "ballistea"</note> and *little leaping dances* <note>original: "saltatiuncula"</note> recorded by Vopiscus <note>Flavius Vopiscus, a historian of the late Roman Empire</note> where he relates how the children sang in those, in the military fashion, the war deeds of Emperor Aurelian: ⁶ *dance-songs* and *little leaping dances* which...

->CXXII<-

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...they must have been the poetry of the people in <term>rustic or military language</term> <note>original: "lingua rustica o castrense," referring to the informal Latin spoken by peasants and soldiers, as opposed to the literary Latin of the elite</note>, and it would not be difficult to find more than one allusion to them in the Latin poets. Certainly, Calpurnius is very clear there where he has one of his shepherds say: “Whether it pleases you to sing, or to beat the earth with a joyful three-step rhythm to songs: it is also permitted to sing some dances.”¹ <note>original: "Seu cantare iuvat seu ter pede laeta ferire / Carmina: nonnullas licet et cantare choreas." Calpurnius Siculus was a 1st-century Roman pastoral poet.</note> Little remains of Latin popular poetry, yet enough to perceive how, among the peoples most uniformly subject to the dominion of Rome, it survived for a long season mixed with the various customs of the common people, only to then slowly transform into a new literature. And in this derivation of the <term>ballada</term> <note>the "ballata" or ballad, originally a song intended to accompany dancing</note> from ancient vulgar Latin poetry lies the reason why Varchi—who nearly dismisses it among the "plebeian" meters—did not know to what sort of ancient classical compositions it could be compared.² And for this very reason, the form of the ballad was common to all peoples of the Latin-speaking world. The Provençal people have them, because they too possessed, separate from courtly and feudal verse, a more naive and domestic poetry; and they have them in that same meter that pleased Lorenzo de' Medici for many of his <term>carnival songs</term> <note>original: "canti carnascialeschi," songs composed to be sung during the rowdy celebrations of Carnival in Florence</note> and Poliziano for his ballad *It happens to me....* <note>original: "E' m' interviene...."</note>; they have, what is more notable, ballads that are quite light and already freed from certain moral conventions, as our thirteenth-century citizens of the free communes did not dare to create: this too is a sign of the premature corruption in that people <note>referring to the people of Provence</note>, so sensitive and harmonious but so profoundly spoiled by feudalism. The following poem, which I translate from the collection by Raynouard <note>François-Juste-Marie Raynouard was a famous 19th-century scholar of the Troubadours</note>, could, by its meter, its sentiments, and its style, make a fine appearance among the most gallant and free-spirited in our own collections of the 1400s and 1500s.

> “I am a pretty young thing, so I carry a heavy grief
> Because of my husband, whom I neither want nor desire.
> For I will tell you plainly why I am such a lover,
> Because I am a tender young girl and a child,
> And I should have a husband who would make me joyful,
> With whom I could play and laugh at all times.
> But may God save me if I am ever in love with him;
> I have not the slightest desire to love him,
> Rather, when I see him, I feel such shame,
> That I pray for death to come soon and kill him.

->Since my friend has loved me for a long time,<-

->And the beautiful hope that I so love and desire.<gloss>1</gloss>” <note>This poem is a translation of an Old Occitan (Provençal) ballad. The author uses it to show that the "ballata" form was common across the Romance-speaking world before it was refined in Italy.</note><-

It is certain, however, that in Italy the <term>ballata</term> <note>a "dance-song" characterized by a refrain (ripresa) that is sung at the beginning and repeated after each stanza</note> received its final and typical form amidst the open-air festivals of the Tuscan people. Its quick and cheerful <term>epode</term> <note>a shorter verse following a longer one, often providing a rhythmic "snap" to the stanza</note>, the easy unfolding of the <term>stanzas</term> through two middle <term>mutations</term> <note>original: "mutazioni"; the two symmetrical parts of a stanza in a ballad</note> into the final <term>turn</term> <note>original: "volta"; the part of the stanza that links back to the rhyme and melody of the refrain</note> where the same harmony and rhyme always return, shows clearly that it must have been sung by the dancers themselves while dancing, or sung by another to set the pace for the dance's turns. 

Thus; while the <term>canzone</term> <note>a high-style lyric poem, usually philosophical or tragic in nature</note> was the garment of high philosophical and mystical poetry, and the <term>sonnet</term> was the artistic meter through which the rhymers recognized one another—using it for their skill-tests, <term>poetic contests</term> <note>original: "tenzoni"; a formal exchange of poems between two authors, often debating a point of love or philosophy</note>, and the imaginative representation of psychological states—the <term>ballata</term> became the form for poetry that was more sensory and colorful. It was common to the common folk and the middle class as well as to the poets proper when they wished to draw closer to the people. And if Dante’s songs were set to music by Casella <note>a reference to Purgatorio II, where Dante meets his friend, the musician Casella</note>, and Petrarch’s sonnets by other masters, there was even greater reason for the <term>dance-songs</term> <note>original: "canzoni a ballo"</note> to be, as they said then, set to melody. 

Even from the earliest times, Boccaccio recalls that Minuccio of Arezzo—who set a ballad by Mico da Siena to a "sweet and pitiful sound" on behalf of a girl named Lisa—went to sing it to King Peter of Aragon:<gloss>2</gloss> from this we also gather how ballads were composed about real events and private affairs. Many of those that survive today must have been of this sort, though their specific references are now lost to us. But Guido Cavalcanti, Dante, and Cino da Pistoia, those sweetly amorous souls, gave...

->CXXIV<-

to the <term>ballata</term> <note>ballad</note>, while remaining an expression of sensory and natural love, that note of delicate refinement which it then preserved throughout the <term>Trecento</term> <note>the 1300s, or the 14th century</note>. <term>Petrarch</term> <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), a foundational scholar and poet of the early Renaissance</note> composed few and not insignificant ones; he was a poet already more reflective than his times, who could not easily adapt to that form: yet even those few were set to music. And this is not the place to explain what celebrity this genre of poetry enjoyed in the 14th century, and how ballads, as soon as they were composed, were clothed in musical notes and ran from one end of Italy to the other, and even into England and France. But we have evidence of the role they played in domestic life and in conversations by the way ballads are introduced in the *Decameron* <note>Boccaccio’s famous collection of 100 tales</note> and in the *Pecorone* <note>A collection of novellas by Ser Giovanni Fiorentino</note>: indeed, in the first editions of the *Cento Novelle* <note>The "Hundred Tales," another name for the Decameron</note> certain dots can be seen above the verses which must have indicated the measure of the melody. However, with the decline of morals, the ballad lost that ideal quality which, in the time of <term>Dante</term> <note>Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), author of the Divine Comedy</note>, was reflected even in its sensory form; it became increasingly vulgar, without, however, losing its grace, gaiety, or pleasantness; until <term>Franco Sacchetti</term> <note>A late 14th-century poet and novelist</note> was the first, or among the first, as an author of short stories, to adapt it to the burlesque and the mocking style. In such a new dress it entered the <term>Quattrocento</term> <note>the 1400s, or the 15th century</note>; at which time, like many other types of composition, it finally freed itself from certain constraints of learned literature.

At this point <term>the Medici</term> <note>Referring here to Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and a prolific poet</note> took hold of it; he who, for his own ends, had occupied the poetry of the countryside, was not likely to forget that of the urban middle class, which was a more manageable and already proven instrument of corruption. He took it, and with that versatile, restless genius of his, never content merely to imitate, he gave it three different attitudes, three different forms; he made three distinct genres out of a single one. First, he sang of the pleasures of a sensual love, the annoyance of waiting, and the spite of not obtaining what one wants, using maxims of a joyful <term>Epicureanism</term> <note>a philosophy that, in this context, emphasizes the pursuit of earthly pleasure and the avoidance of pain</note>; then he turned to mocking the beloved and the love he had previously celebrated; finally, he lapsed openly and carelessly into obscenities. To this progression of subject matter corresponds a progression of form: first plainly lyrical, then elegantly comic, and finally maliciously narrative. And just as allegory, which was sacred to the <term>Duegento</term> <note>the 1200s</note> and <term>Trecento</term>, had been twisted—distorting with the times—into obscene double-entendres; so, the roles of certain...

->CXXV<-

meters, perhaps not without a silent intent of mockery, the four-line stanzas of <term>hendecasyllables</term> <note>lines consisting of eleven syllables</note> with consecutive rhymes for the first three and a matching rhyme for the last at the end of every stanza—a meter of grave and solemn pace already sanctified in the <term>laudes</term> <note>devotional songs of praise</note> of the blessed <term>Jacopone</term> <note>Jacopone da Todi (c. 1230–1306), a Franciscan friar and poet known for his intense religious lyrics</note>—were adapted for the parody of confession made by the magnificent author of <term>spiritual hymns</term> <note>refers to Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note>; they were adapted to the cynical licenses of <term>carnival songs</term> <note>songs composed for the rowdy street festivals of Florence</note>. And just as the delicacy and clean elegance of antiquity had yielded to a certain brazen nudity, so too, instead of the full harmony of stanzas of six <term>hendecasyllables</term> and the graceful mixture of <term>hendecasyllables</term> and <term>septenaries</term> <note>lines of seven syllables</note>, the agile and skipping little stanzas made entirely of <term>septenaries</term> and <term>ottonari</term> <note>lines of eight syllables</note> were used more frequently. The former styles remained, it is true, when the <term>ballata</term> <note>ballad</note> expressed—if not the ideal—at least the more courtly side of love; but the living sentiment, and all that was most lively and cheerful, as well as irony, sarcasm, and the malicious or coarse tale, preferred the <term>septenary</term> and <term>octosyllable</term> stanzas. And the use of that poetry spread so far that even <term>spiritual hymns</term> became nothing more than an imitation of songs worse than profane, and almost always took their tune and intonation from them: hence in the old collections of <term>laudes</term> one often happens to read <gloss>To be sung like....</gloss> <note>original: "Cantasi come...."</note> followed by the opening line of an obscene ballad. Thus the devout persisted in their custom of using the very weapons of the world and the flesh to overcome the one and tame the other: the system is dangerous, but it is always worth noting when a <term>Tartuffe</term> <note>a reference to the character of the religious hypocrite from Molière's play</note> risks experimenting with it.

Master <term>Angelo</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent scholar-poet of the Medicean circle</note> followed the <term>Magnificent</term> as a loyal client even in the three different directions he took with the <term>ballad</term>. However, adorned as he was with every elegance of classical literature, more than once he was able—without stripping it of its native character or easy gait—to raise the ballad to the movement and tone of the <term>ode</term> <note>a more formal, elevated lyric poem inspired by Greek and Roman models</note>. Here too he knew how to imitate like a master, renewing and often surpassing his models. To anyone reading that admirable model of elegance and spontaneous, smiling softness—of a truly rosy facility—which is the <term>ballad on the roses</term> <note>Poliziano's famous poem "I' mi trovai, fanciulle, un bel mattino," which celebrates youth and beauty</note> [III], it will seem as if they feel the same aura of melancholy and pleasure which, in the contrast between the thought of death and joy, breathes from the poetry of...

In any case, Poliziano imitated several epigrams regarding roses by an uncertain author from the late Latin decline. ² But let those epigrams be compared with the Tuscan <term>ballata</term> <note>a poem intended to be danced to, or a song in that style</note>: and one will see how, in the act of poetic imitation, what was the trickery or illusion of the alchemists can appear as truth—the miracle of changing even the most base metal into gold. And even those who, in small things, wish to find proof that the spirit of the Renaissance—brought to such a high degree in Italy in the 15th century—then permeated all the literatures of Latin Europe, should compare to Poliziano’s verses this ode by Ronsard <note>Pierre de Ronsard (1524–1585), a foundational figure in French Renaissance poetry</note>, who certainly never saw the ballad which remained in manuscript until 1813:

And another comparison could show the difference in spirit and elegance between the Renaissance and the Middle Ages; that between the <term>ballata</term> <note>a song-poem meant for dancing</note> *Welcome, May*—where the medieval tradition still continues—and the many songs of the troubadours and ancient rhymers on the return of spring, the last of which are the *rondeaux* <note>a form of French verse with a recurring refrain</note> of Charles of Orléans. Finally, for whoever compared the two ballads by our author [Poliziano] that most profoundly sing of beauty and love according to their sensible nature [poems VIII and XI] with the sonnets inspired by the religious contemplation of beauty by Cavalcanti, Alighieri <note>Dante Alighieri, author of the Divine Comedy</note>, and Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a prominent poet of the "Sweet New Style"</note>, all the various notes of the two ages and the two types of poetry would become clear. Furthermore, from a careful examination of Poliziano’s first ballads belonging to the middle style of lyric, it will appear that Angelo is the only poet who represents Anacreon to the Italians—the true Greek Anacreon, the intimate friend of Polycrates <note>the tyrant of Samos and patron of the arts</note>. The Anacreontic odes of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, though sometimes elegant and not infrequently witty in their inventions, are still merely schoolroom imitations. But in Poliziano, there is—if not the exact genius—the spirit, the soul, the passion, the color, and the effortless simplicity of Anacreon. And this was quite right. In Poliziano’s time, poetry was still addressed to the people: Poliziano wrote those songs to be truly sung. Like Anacreon, Poliziano would never have thought of locking himself in a room to compose an ode or a <term>skolion</term> <note>a short song sung by guests at ancient Greek banquets</note> in imitation of an ancient model.

...predecessor, just to succeed. The public’s interaction with the poet revitalized poetry, breathing warmth and truth into it. Anacreon <note>a Greek lyric poet known for themes of love, wine, and song</note> and Poliziano expressed in their verses not just their own feelings, but—whatever they might be—those of their time and the people among whom they lived: the former was the natural poet of the second age of Greek lyric poetry; the latter was exactly what was suited to that springtime of the Italian Renaissance that preceded the ill-fated [year 14]94 <note>the year 1494 marked the invasion of Italy by Charles VIII of France, which ended the peaceful "Golden Age" of the Medici</note>. This is true both in the ballads of this second manner and in the few that border on, or even enter, the third manner, which is characterized by obscene allegory. But what a difference there is between the crude cynicism of the stories and allusions of those earlier poets, and the candid ingenuity and good-natured mischief of the two ballads by our author, *It happens to me...* and *My ladies, you do not know* <note>original: "E' mi interviene..." and "Donne mie, vo' non sapete"</note> [XVI, XVII], which can only be compared to the most successful works of Berni <note>Francesco Berni, an Italian poet famous for his humorous and satirical verse</note> and La Fontaine <note>Jean de La Fontaine, the famous French fabulist</note>! And what a wonder it is to see the "poet of the roses" enter the field of proverbs and wordplay, and roam through it entirely at his ease as if in his own domain. Nor could such a comparison be made by following the traces of decline with ballads of a later age; for this genre vanished at the end of the fifteenth century <term>Quattrocento</term> <note>the 1400s, often considered the height of early Renaissance creativity</note>, coinciding with the end of the great original literature it had accompanied, modifying itself according to different periods. It is true, however, that throughout the sixteenth century <term>Cinquecento</term> <note>the 1500s</note>, the ballads written by the fifteenth-century authors remained in popular use. This is attested by the various popular editions of that century, all of which have become extremely rare today due to heavy use; it is also attested by comic playwrights who put into the mouths of their characters common folk maxims, entire verses, or wit and proverbs taken and derived from the ballads. In Salviati's *The Crab* <note>original: "Granchio"</note>, ³ the boy Fanticchio mocks an old woman by singing Poliziano's stanza "An old woman ogles me," <note>original: "Una vecchia mi vagheggia"</note> including the refrain. ->CXXX<-

[the popula]rity of the ballads in the centuries that followed: and Antonio Guadagnoli in a certain passage recalls "the village girls who come to Florence to sing May <note>referring to "Cantar Maggio," a traditional Tuscan May Day celebration involving folk songs</note> and begin one of their songs, *Welcome May,*¹" which is exactly the beginning of one of the most elegant [ballads] by our author <note>Poliziano</note>. It has never happened to me to hear that or anything similar: however, the meter of the eight-syllable stanzas, with the obligatory refrain <term>intercalare: a refrain or chorus repeated at the end of each stanza</term> at the end of every stanza—which is nothing more than the repetition of the first line—I myself have heard in the *Maggi*, a type of folk performance that was sung and is still sung today in the Pisan Maremma <note>a coastal region in Tuscany</note>. It is certain, however, that after the fifteenth century <note>the Italian *Quattrocento*</note> the ballad no longer had a life of its own: the madrigal which succeeded it in popularity, especially in the second half of the sixteenth century, and even more so the *ariettas* <note>short, light operatic or song airs</note> of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, signal the shrinking of art into decadence. Truly Chiabrera <note>Gabriello Chiabrera (1552–1638), a poet who sought to introduce Greek lyric forms into Italian</note>, who was a poet if in nothing else then in the lively and harmonious variety of his meters, attempted to restore the ballad:² something similar was also done in his *scherzi* <term>scherzi: literally "jokes," these were lighthearted, playful poetic compositions</term> by Redi, the last of the [great] Tuscans:³ but in the former there is too much artifice, and the excessive elegance betrays that "Greek foreignness" <note>an affectation of Greek style and vocabulary</note> that Poliziano disliked; as for the latter, it is clearly seen that he composed his ballads for music—and for the music of courts and palaces. The Romantics between [18]20 and [18]40, by reviving the name "ballad" and applying it to their imitations of imitations of Victor Hugo's early style, committed one of those many anachronisms for which they will remain famous—they who boasted of bringing truth back to art and reconnecting it with history. And may reason save the youth from Romantic ballads; which, representing a false Orient and a false North, a false Middle Ages and a false chivalry, a false religion and a false populace, along with false sentiments and the utterly false whims of little brains who believed themselves to be and wished to appear great and robust, achieved nothing in the end but the renewal of an "Arcadia" <note>The "Arcadia" movement was an 18th-century literary academy that sought to simplify poetry but often became artificial; the author here argues Romanticism was just as fake</note> that was all the more harmful for being more pretentious.

# ANGELO POLIZIANO

->CXXXI<-

One might expect a mention of the love affairs of Angelo Poliziano. But little is known of them; and they were certainly not of the kind that inform an entire life of poetry, such as those of the "Fathers of Italy," Dante and Petrarch. We know nothing more than the name and the homeland of Ippolita Leoncina of Prato, who was celebrated with great heat by our author in his Italian verses. Later, he loved *Alessandra*, the beautiful and learned daughter of Bartolommeo Scala, who gave her in marriage to Marullo; because of this, Poliziano fell out with both of them, persecuting them with the most bitter Latin verses, especially the second <note>Marullo</note> under the name of *Mabilio*. However, I do not believe he wrote Italian verses regarding his love for *Alessandra*; he did, however, touch upon it in Greek; and I am pleased that he himself confesses never to have had anything but words from the girl:

> (“To me who desires the fruit, you send only flowers and leaves: they signify that I labor in vain.”)¹

I, to tell the truth, am glad not to have to interfere in the private life of Poliziano:

> “A happy genius placed in an unhappy form; nor were his morals without stain: perfect only in his literary works:”

as a learned foreigner wrote of him with sharp brevity.² However, it is a duty to note that a large part of the *rispetti* and ballads were composed in his early youth, and perhaps before Poliziano was elected Prior of San Paolo through the favor of Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note>, who was in the habit of making the men of letters attached to him into canons: a better treatment, in any case, than that of the Dukes of Este, who wanted *Ariosto* as a stablemaster and called *Tasso* a servant. The Priory of San Paolo was nothing more than a secular benefit with some slight ecclesiastical obligation; and only in 1486 was Poliziano numbered among the canons of the Metropolitan <note>the Cathedral of Florence, Santa Maria del Fiore</note>, although he was never truly a priest. But, stepping out of the sacristy, it is also true that Poliziano composed many rhymes at the request of others: as is revealed in a letter from 1490 where the good Prior complains that people, still besieging him in his little house, do not even leave him time to say the Office <note>the daily cycle of prayers required of clergy</note>.

> “Here is one who asks me for <term>Fescennine jokes: ribald or scurrilous verses, often improvised at festivals</term> <gloss>carnival songs</gloss> for the days of Carnival, and another for sermons³ for the brother-

³ Some of Poliziano's sermons will be included in the volume of *Vernacular Prose*.

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...fraternities; others ask for pious songs to be played on the viola, others for licentious songs for serenades. This one, a fool!, comes to recount his loves to me—an even greater fool for staying to listen to him: that one asks me for a device <note>An "impresa" or heraldic emblem</note> whose meaning should be clear only to his lady, and which would vainly exhaust the conjectures of others.¹ » From this, it can be inferred that many of those rhymes must have been dashed off in a hurry without much thought, merely to rid himself of the annoyance of such requests, showing how little Poliziano valued them. And this occurred while his contemporaries held him in the highest regard, even as a poet in the vernacular <note>The "volgare" or everyday Italian language, as opposed to Latin</note>. Relying only on the eloquent testimony of other poets, Antonio da Pistoia began a sonnet on the rhymers of his time in this way:

> « Who writes well in verse, among the Tuscans?
> — Do you mean in the vernacular? — In the vernacular and in Latin —
> Lorenzo is good, and so is his son Pierino;
> But in both, Poliziano is worth more.² »

With a different tone, Cassio da Narni sang:

> « Among the most famous *poets* was Poliziano
> Who with a beautiful manner recited to the others
> Many of his stanzas; and his polished and supreme style
> Could be seen to delight everyone:
> He held Lorenzo de' Medici by the hand
> Who walked toward the same goal alongside him.
> Ah, Italy, flower of the world! From whence does it derive
> That you have such sons and yet are deprived of wit? ³ »

And the good and most ingenious Luigi Pulci spoke of him with the affection of a friend and the emphasis of a poet, both in that octave where he professes himself indebted to Poliziano for information regarding his subject matter (whence Teofilo Folengo⁴ and the restless, troublesome friar Ortensio Lando⁵ invented the story that the *Morgante* was actually the work of Poliziano, gifted by him to Pulci), and even more so toward the end where he says he wishes to place...

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

Petrarch, who returned to his Italian verses time and again with the perfecting patience of the file and sent them to this person and that, never mentioned them—or hardly once—in his own works,¹ nor did he ever care that they should be printed; he, who nevertheless had a high opinion of himself and published his Latin works with great ceremony. To give back to the immortal ancients some of that light which he had received from them, by explaining obscure passages, correcting errors, removing interpolations, and filling in defects; and to bring to these laborious industries the splendor of an imagination that beautified and colored everything, even philological questions; to translate from Greek into Latin those writers and writings that proved most resistant to the common crowd of translators; to enter with <term>The Universal Scholar</term> <note>original: *Panepistemon*; a work classifying all branches of knowledge</note> and with <term>Logic</term> <note>original: *Dialectica*</note> into the portico and the peripatetic walk; by collating the text of the <term>Pandects</term> <note>original: *pandette*; a compendium of Roman civil law</note>, to guide literature to invade even the field of law;² to ascend at twenty-nine years of age the chair of Greek eloquence in the <term>Florentine University</term> <note>original: *Studio fiorentino*</note>, and to see gathered around him a crowd of listeners who, for the sake of this young countryman, abandoned the elderly Greek Demetrius Chalcondyles; and among those listeners to see seated more than once the Medici, Lascaris, and Pico della Mirandola; and among those students to number Carteromachus, Volterrano, and Crinito, as well as William Grocyn—later professor of Greek at Oxford and friend of Thomas More—and Linacre, hailed as the restorer of humane studies in England, and Dionysius, brother of Johann Reuchlin, and the two young Texeiras, sons of the Great Chancellor of Portugal; and to receive letters from King John II of Portugal in which he was praised and encouraged to write, according to the records sent to him, the Latin history of the King's deeds;³ and papal briefs from Innocent VIII in which thanks were given and rewards assigned for his translation of <term>Herodian</term> <note>original: *Erodiano*; a 3rd-century Greek historian of the Roman Empire</note>;⁴ this, for Angelo Poliziano, was glory. <page-num>CXXXV</page-num>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

With an enormous nose and a slight squint in his left eye, he would stand up; and with a full, sonorous voice, varied and colored by the accent of passion, he recited his own verses—the verses he had composed in his small villa at Fiesole, near a hedge of roses, as the gentle breeze blew from the mountain in the mild light of your sunsets, O sweet Tuscany. Then, the deformed rhetorician suddenly became beautiful: some ray of the ancient deities shone upon his pale forehead, and the silence of the audience became more solemn, because these "new Athenians" <note>A reference to the Florentine intellectuals who viewed their city as a rebirth of ancient Greek culture.</note> believed they saw before them a resurrected priest of Apollo. And if the subject of his learned lessons was Homer—his great love—after singing of his portentous birth and even more portentous blindness, he would intone his praises thus:

> To him, venerable antiquity gave altars and temples;
> Him she worshipped in bronze, in stone, and in yellow gold:
> Him alone she placed as the authority over our tender years,
> The leader and guide of wandering youth:
> Even the laws of life acknowledged him as master:
> From this fountain, all wisdom waters the learned papyri:
> Once, the land of the Ganges <note>India</note> translated him into its own
> Voices: seven cities, in their fighting zeal,
> Claim his birthplace for themselves:
> And the avenger Ptolemy, from his ancestral river,
> Defended him from the laws of the Sithonian lash <note>original: *sithonii patientem iura flagelli*; Poliziano refers to the harsh critic Zoilus, known as the "Homer-scourge," who was said to have been punished by King Ptolemy.</note>:
> The King of the Macedons <note>Alexander the Great</note> also enclosed him in captive, jeweled gold,
> And consulted him in the midst of arms;
> With him, he invited sleep, and from him he was accustomed
> To conceive tomorrow’s wars, and to boast of triumphs won for him.
> And let us, therefore, with grateful piety, dedicate to him
> This crown woven from Pierian flowers <note>The Pierides were the Muses; thus, flowers of poetry.</note>,
> Which, among the nymphs of Caiano, the most beautiful,
> Ambra gave to me, gathered joyfully from the grass of her native bank:
> Ambra, the love of my Lorenzo, whom the horned Umbro,
> Old Umbro <note>The river Ombrone</note> begat—most pleasing to his master, the Arno—
> Umbro, who at last shall not break forth from his bed.<gloss>1</gloss>

Or perhaps Virgil had touched his mind and soul with the modest breadth of his style: and he, turning to the young men, [would say]:

> "And who, O youths, surveying the miracles of such
> Eloquio, would not think himself to be looking out
> Over the immense tracts of land and sea? Here, with fertile abundance..."

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

Crops grow lushly here, there the flock <note>original: *Armenium*; likely referring to Armenian sheep, prized in antiquity for their wool</note> shears the soft grass, here the elm is clothed with pliant vines; from that side, oaks rise with mossy trunks, from this, the vast seas lie open; this shore is rough with thirsty sands, from these mountains run cold rivers; here massive rocks lean over, there stony caves open their folds, and over there, secluded valleys lie low. And just as a discordant appearance tempers the beautiful world; so rich eloquence clothes itself in various forms, and is now carried along with a vast, rushing force in the manner of a river, now dries up in a parched bed, now relaxes itself, now restrains its wide wanderings, now is fitting in its unrefined state, now shines bright with charming flowers, and sometimes beautifully mixes all things at once. Oh, precious rest of the bards, oh joys known only to the pious, sweet madness, incorruptible pleasure, and the ambrosial tables of the gods! Who, seeing such things, would envy kings? Let them keep for themselves their soft clothing, gold, and gems: only let the malicious common folk stay far from here, and let no profane person break into these sacred mysteries.$^1$ <note>Poliziano uses the "profane" to refer to those who do not appreciate the divine nature of poetry.</note>

Or rather, Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet known for "Works and Days," which details rural life</note> and the *Bucolics* <note>Pastoral poems by Virgil</note> awakened in him that <unclear>se</unclear>cret love for country life, which so often burst<unclear>s forth</unclear> from his poetry and prose: and then, with verses that could not be distinguished from those of Virgil (in the judgment of Villemain) *and which possess their free rhythm, movement, and harmo<unclear>ny</unclear>*,$^2$ he would begin by invoking Pan <note>The Greek god of the wild, shepherds, and rustic music</note>:

• Pan, be present, and indulge me with verses beneath the arch of a curved rock; while Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> is in mid-heaven, while the turtle-dove, widowed by the loss of her mate, moans, and the collared wood-pigeons repeat their learned songs. Here your beloved pine tree resonates with a gentle whisper: here a wandering breeze whistles through the cone-bearing cypresses: here, driven by bubbling veins, the pure water leaps from its springs and splashes among the colored pebbles: here your playful Echo <note>The mountain nymph who could only repeat the words of others</note>, long a seeker of our song, sports beneath the nearby shadows. Happy is he in spirit, and most like the gods themselves, whom glory, shining with false paint, does not trouble, nor the evil joys of haughty luxury: but who allows his days to pass in silence and with a humble lifestyle...

<margin>² Poliziano, *Rusticus*.</margin>

> “Grant me this life, O great inhabitants of heaven: thus give me delights, thus the charms of my labors, thus give me always easy wealth. Let my ambitious prayers go only this far: never, certainly never, will I pray that my brow should shine with an enviable red hat <note>original: *rutilo... galero*; a reference to the red hat of a Cardinal, indicating Poliziano’s lack of interest in high ecclesiastical power</note> or that a heavy mitre with a triple crown <note>original: *tergemina... corona*; the papal tiara</note> should rise for me. Such things I meditated upon, at leisure, in a cave at Fiesole. In a suburban villa of the Medici, where the sacred mountain looks down upon the Maonian city <note>original: *Mæoniam*; a poetic name for Florence, alluding to its supposed Lydian or Etruscan roots</note> and the winding coils of the long Arno, where the good Lorenzo <note>original: *Laurens*; Lorenzo de' Medici, Poliziano's great patron</note> grants happy hospitality and peaceful rest—Lorenzo, not the least glory of Apollo, Lorenzo, a faithful anchor for the tossed Muses. If he permits me more certain leisure, I shall be inspired by a greater god: no longer will only the steep forest and mountain rocks echo my voice, but you—if there is any faith—you perhaps one day, O my sweet foster-mother, will not despise my song, even though you are the mother of great poets, Florence; and learned eloquence will sing of me in three languages.”² <note>The "three languages" refers to Poliziano's mastery of Latin, Greek, and the Italian vernacular.</note>

Fortunately <unclear>n</unclear> a secretary of Cardinal Alessandro Falconieri, the Abbot Niccolò <unclear>ò</unclear>, a great collector of ancient codices and prints, copied <unclear>o</unclear> some poems from it that were there under the name of Poliziano: the <unclear>la</unclear> copy is in the paper manuscript number 94 of the Casanatense <unclear>a</unclear> Library in Rome, and the poems were then published <unclear>ca</unclear> by Mr. Bonanni in 1858:<sup>2</sup> of which more will be said in the proper place.

# ANGELO POLIZIANO. CXXXIX

The <term>codex</term> <note>a manuscript book</note> belonging to Doctor Buonafede Vitali—which Affò utilized for the new edition of *Orfeo* [see Chapter III]—also contained four sonnets by Poliziano, in addition to *Orfeo* and many other verses by his contemporaries.<sup>1</sup> Evidence of such a poet working in that specific form of poetry, of which we know nothing regarding him, would have been a delectable find. However, our desire for them is tempered by Affò’s note that one of those sonnets [which begins *The sun already held the shadows and the fears* <note>original Italian: "Il sole avea già l’ ombre e le paure"</note>] is attributed by Crescimbeni<sup>2</sup> to Bernardo Bellincioni. Perhaps the others were not truly Poliziano's either; in any case, everyone would have liked to confirm this. I certainly would have liked to determine if that Vitali <term>codex</term>, of which I have been unable to learn anything else, might by chance be the same as DCCCXXXVI. B. 362 [Part IV, *Italian codices*] of the Estense Library in Modena. According to the description in the <term>manuscript</term> catalogue, this is a small <term>in folio</term> <note>a large book size made by folding a sheet of paper once</note> which contains, exactly like Vitali’s, poems by many of the late fifteenth-century poets; for example, the *Psyche* and various sonnets by Niccolò da Correggio, five sonnets by Toschi of Ferrara, five by Giovanni Pico, and six by Angelo Poliziano. I would have wished to verify this and see them: but the codices were and still are packed in crates; and so my desire vanished into smoke.

The <term>paper codex</term> in <term>oblong octavo</term> <note>a small, wide book format</note> of sixty leaves, numbered XLIV and preserved in <term>pluteus</term> <note>a combination reading desk and bookshelf used in the Laurentian Library</note> XL of the Mediceo-Laurenziana, would be most precious if we were to believe Bandini, who described it as: " *as far as Poliziano's poems are concerned, it seems to be an autograph* <note>original Latin: "quoad Politiani carmina, ut videtur, autographus"</note>.<sup>3</sup> " In any case, the reading is mostly excellent; and the handwriting is certainly from the time of Master Angelo, or rather from his youth. After many rhymes by Dante, it contains Poliziano’s stanza on the echo, five ballads, twelve scattered <term>rispetti</term> <note>a traditional Italian folk poem, usually eight lines long</note>, and the sequenced <term>rispetti</term> beginning *O triumphant over every other....* Another <term>paper codex</term> of 81 pages <term>in folio</term>, preserved in <term>pluteus</term> XLI of the same library under number XXXIII, dates from the 16th century and features beautiful handwriting with pen drawings. It contains various rhymes from the 15th century; by Poliziano, it has the song—

...clearly, *This showing of oneself...* <note>original Italian: "Questo mostrarsi...."</note>; and without reason it attributes to him the *song of the vendors, Good things we have...* <note>original Italian: "Buona roba abbiam...."</note>, which actually belongs to [Lorenzo de'] Medici.

Of no less authority than the first Laurentian <term>codex</term> <note>a manuscript book</note>, and dating from the same period or only slightly later, is a <term>paper codex</term> <note>a manuscript made of paper rather than parchment</note> from the Magliabechiana collection in an <term>oblong quarto</term> <note>a medium-sized book format wider than it is tall</note> format (number 1034, Class VII). It is found under the heading *Miscellaneous* <note>original Latin: "Variorum"</note> and titled *Tuscan Poetry by various ancient authors.* Poliziano's rhymes, consisting of ten <term>ballads</term> <note>a form of Italian verse intended for dancing or singing</note>, are gathered in a small notebook along with others by the Magnificent [Lorenzo de' Medici], by [Bernardo] Bellincioni, and by Giovanni Ridolfi; it is written in a fine hand and offers a superior reading of the text. By contrast, the readings are poor in another Magliabechiana manuscript (number 735, Class VII *Miscellaneous*), titled *Carnival Songs*. This is a small <term>quarto</term> from the end of the 15th or the beginning of the 16th century; here, in addition to the *Triumph for the promotion to the purple [cardinalate] of Giovanni de' Medici*—which is incorrectly attributed to Poliziano—are a short song set to music and some <term>rispetti</term> <note>short, folk-style poems, usually of eight lines</note>.

A copy of various poems by Poliziano, taken from the Florentine manuscripts described previously, is found in codex number 27 of the voluminous collection of ancient rhymes transcribed by [the scholars] Moucke and Biscioni. This collection was acquired by the Marquis Cesare Lucchesini and later passed into the library in Lucca. Even this copy was of some use to us, thanks to the kindness of our friend G. Pierotti, who was gracious enough to send us the variant readings and some marginal notes.

In the <term>miscellaneous paper codex</term> 771 of the Riccardiana library, there are two pages of neat and correct handwriting, probably from the early sixteenth century. These were once folded in the form of a letter and addressed: TO THE NOBLE AND ENER | getic soldier: my most revered | lord. Lord Andrea Magnano | [Magnanimous?] with the following written below: *Remember from time to time your Zenobio Masolini of Prato* <note>original Latin: "Mementote interdum vri Zenobii Masolini de Prato"</note>. These pages contain, along with a few Latin verses by our author—among which are the ode *A girl more delicate* <note>original Latin: "Puella delicatior"</note> and the <term>elegies</term> <note>poems of lament or serious reflection</note> *Happier as a stag...* <note>original Latin: "Laetior ut cervus..."</note>—four ballads and the *echo* <note>a poem where the last syllables of a line are repeated to create a new meaning</note>.

We should also mention the manuscript of Luigi Poirot, which served as the model for the first edition of the two very elegant ballads for Ippolita Leoncina [*Who does not know...*, and *Blessed be the day...*]. Poirot stated to Doctor Rigoli—who published those ballads in his *Essay on Rhymes from the 14th to the 17th Century*—that he "had obtained them in a modern copy from the library of the Florentine Seminary."¹

<page-num>CXLI</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

And the two last <term>ballads</term> <note>poems intended to be set to music and danced to</note> and twelve others from those already published—along with the <term>rispetti</term> <note>short, typically eight-line folk poems</note> arranged in the manner of a serenade [*O triumphant over...* <note>original Italian: "O trionfante sopra..."</note>] and fourteen scattered <term>rispetti</term> plus five unpublished ones—are also contained in a <term>codex</term> <note>a manuscript book</note>, though missing a few pages, belonging to the most distinguished professor Giuliano Vanzolini of Pesaro. When this excellent gentleman learned that I intended to produce a new edition of Poliziano’s vernacular works, he came forward—even though he himself had intended to reproduce the poems of his <term>codex</term> together with the *Tournament* <note>original: "Giostra," Poliziano's famous unfinished poem celebrating Giuliano de' Medici</note> according to the <term>Oliveriano</term> <note>referring to the Biblioteca Oliveriana in Pesaro</note> reading—and spontaneously, without even knowing me, offered me the various readings (most of which are highly valuable) and the five unpublished <term>rispetti</term> from his manuscript. Such kindness is certainly unknown to professional <term>philologists</term> <note>scholars who study the history and authenticity of texts</note>, but it is natural in those who love study and the humanities for their own sake, like Vanzolini, who is a man of most elegant scholarship. Poliziano’s readers, along with myself, will certainly be most grateful to him for such a beautiful gift. At the back of Professor Vanzolini’s <term>codex</term> is an *Epitaph for Lena from Prato, called "The Hundred," by Zanobi Masolini* <note>original: "Epitaphio della Lena da Prato chiamata Cento per Zanobi Masolini"</note>, the same man who sent the two Riccardian papers with Poliziano’s verses to Andrea.

Only for the sake of the catalog’s completeness do I mention, finally, the Riccardian paper <term>codex</term> in <term>quarto</term> <note>a book format where the paper is folded twice to create four leaves</note> number 2599, which contains various letters, memoirs, and poems pertaining or alluding to the House of Medici. These were collected and copied by Giovanni Mazzuoli, known as "The Little Street-Walker" <note>original: "lo Stradino"</note>, famous in the annals of 16th-century Florentine burlesque poetry. From this <term>codex</term>, the Florentine editors of 1814 extracted the chapters and the epitaph on the death of [Lorenzo] the Magnificent, which were incorrectly attributed to Poliziano.

### PRINTED EDITIONS. — FIRST PERIOD.

This period, which could also be titled "the age of collections," includes the printed editions of the *Tournament* from 1494 to 1537. All of these, except for the one revised by Gaietano, contain the short song *Love can never say* <note>original: "Non potrà mai dire Amore"</note> with the stanza of the echo, and some also include the song *I am constrained* <note>original: "Io son constretto"</note>, as we noted in the appropriate place. It also includes the following collections where ballads or songs by our author are found.

This is a small <term>quarto</term> <note>a book size created by folding a full sheet of paper twice to form four leaves</note> of 36 leaves, unnumbered, with <term>signatures</term> <note>letters printed at the bottom of pages to guide the binder in assembling the book</note> a–fiiii (c and e are <term>duerni</term> <note>gatherings of two sheets, forming four leaves</note>, d and f are <term>terni</term> <note>gatherings of three sheets, forming six leaves</note>, and the rest are <term>quaderni</term> <note>gatherings of four sheets, forming eight leaves</note>). And that sonnet follows on the back page—a wretched riddle; it begins:

> To give delight to you, my experienced readers, <note>original: "Per dar dilecto a uoi lector mie pratichi"</note>

It hints at the subjects of some ballads, and ends:

> Good Grisel with his sweet songs <note>original: "El buon grisel con suo soaui canti"</note>
> the lettuce-man with Ciullozo also harmonizes;
> they would draw saints out of paradise.
> And they all sing in a rough-and-ready style; <note>original: "alla carlona," meaning in a simple, unpolished, or informal manner</note>
> see Sbracia who is there before them;
> follow along with the song at a favorable hour.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Come now, you who give to us,
> let us begin here with the sweetened one,
> so that it may please the whole company.

At the beginning of the second leaf is the <term>rubric</term> <note>a heading or title, traditionally written in red ink</note>:

### § BALLADS OF THE
### Magnificent Lorenzo de' Medi-
### ci & of Master Angelo Polizi-
### ano & of Bernardo Giambur-
### lari & of many others.

At the end of the book are several <term>ottave</term> <note>eight-line stanzas</note> titled *Respect<unclear>s</unclear> of Love*, whose final words are *Therefore make your choice like a wise woman*. In this collection—both under their own title [leaves 22–2<unclear>6</unclear>] and mixed with others by Lorenzo de' Medici—are many of the ballads <unclear>of</unclear> Master Angelo; these almost always agree in their reading and spelling with the <term>codices</term> <note>manuscript books</note> I have examined.

## SECOND AGE.

Includes from 1698 onwards the various publications of unpublished poems or those "unearthed" from previous collections, which then came to form the two rich editions of 1814 and 1825 and this latest one of ours, which is the most complete of all.

1698. The Abbot Giovan Mario Crescimbeni published the song *Mountains, valleys, caves, hills* <note>original: "Monti valli antri colli"</note> in Book I of his *History of Vernacular Poetry* <note>original: "Istoria della volgar poesia"</note> printed in Rome in this year by Chracas and then again in 1714 and finally in Venice in 1731 by Basegio. The song was reproduced in the Cominian <note>referring to the press of Giuseppe Comino in Padua, known for high-quality scholarly editions</note> and other eighteenth-century editions of the *Joust* <note>original: "Giostra," Poliziano's famous poem celebrating a tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici</note> recorded in chapter III.

1747. To the *Stanzas* <note>original: "Stanze"</note> printed this year in Bergamo by Lancellotti [see chapter III], P. A. Serassi—who edited them—had intended to accompany the other poems of the Noble Author <term>N. A.</term> collected from ancient books and from the famous Chigian manuscript <note>a significant manuscript in the Chigi collection of the Vatican Library</note>; and in fact, he gave to the press a small volume, which he then, out of scruples, did not want published; rather, he destroyed it. A copy of 100 numbered leaves <term>cc. num.</term> existed, with only the frontispiece, seen by Gamba in the library of Marquis Trivulzio; and it contained ballads, serenades, *strambotti* <note>a traditional Italian verse form consisting of an eight-line stanza</note> and other things unpublished until then. From several indications, it seems that Monti and A. M. Maggi made use of it, both for the critical emendation they made of the 1814 Florentine edition in the *Proposta* <note>a famous linguistic work by Vincenzo Monti titled "Proposta di alcune correzioni ed aggiunte al Vocabolario della Crusca"</note> and for the new Silvestrian edition of 1825.

This illustrates a paleographic error where the editor misread the manuscript.</note>. Nevertheless, the Florentine edition of 1814 is cited in the fifth and final printing of the *Dictionary of the Accademia della Crusca*; certainly because it was more complete than those that came before.

1819. The editors <term>edd.</term> of the *Vernacular Works of Messer Angelo Poliziano* published in this year in Venice by Molinari, for the ballads <term>ballate</term> already printed before the preceding Florentine edition, followed the text of one or the other of the printings of the *Songs for Dancing* <note>original: "Canzone a ballo"</note> from 1562 and 1568, reproducing and even correcting the sequence numbers to serve the citations of the Dictionary. For the newly printed items, they asserted they had removed the most easily corrected oversights; in some cases where common sense was not sufficient for correction, they omitted the corrupted and missing passages; and they were pleased to also leave out indecent matters. Maggi, in the work cited above, asserts, and with reason, that every error he had recorded in his notes was faithfully transplanted from the Florence edition by Carli into the Venice edition by Molinari.

1822. Marchini also, in reprinting a *second edition* of Poliziano's Rhymes in Florence, assured that Dr. Ciampolini had been able to restore many items to their true reading...
