**1825.** And in this year there was released from the presses of Silvestri the edition entitled *First corrected and reduced to a good reading of the Italian Poetry of Master Angelo Poliziano*. Inspired by the criticism of the *Proposal*, overseen by Anton Maria Maggi and also by Vincenzo Monti, the Silvestrian edition is certainly worthy of much consideration. Having accepted—except for the chapters on the death of the Magnificent <note>Lorenzo de' Medici "The Magnificent," Poliziano's patron.</note> deemed unworthy and the song *I am constrained* <note>original: "Io son constretto"</note> attributed to Giuliano de' Medici—all the rhymes already printed in the Florentine editions of 1814 and 1822; a good number of corrupted verses and mistaken rhymes were healed, according to the standards already given in the *Proposal* and also on the authority of a Trivulzian codex <term>cod. trivulziano</term>. Many corruptions of sense, language, and syntax were repaired, providing accounts in some small notes at the foot of the page of the less immediate emendations and reporting the incorrect variant more than once. And those emendations—except for some boldness in favor of a grammar and prosody <term>prosodia</term> <note>The study of poetic meter and the patterns of sounds in poetry.</note> that did not belong to Poliziano or his times—are for the most part very successful: for although the opponents of Monti’s critical school may deny or diminish many things, they cannot deny the brilliance of intellects that were frankly and learnedly vivid and sharp. The Academicians of the Crusca <note>The Accademia della Crusca is the Italian linguistic academy that maintains the purity of the language.</note> also did this edition the honor of citing it in the fifth printing of the *Dictionary* <term>Vocabolario</term>.

**1825.** If Dr. Luigi Rigoli, in the *Essay of rhymes by various good authors who flourished from the 14th to the 18th century* <note>original: "Saggio di rime di diversi buoni autori..."</note> published in Florence by the Ronchi printing house, erred by presenting as unpublished 19 *strambotti* <note>A traditional Italian verse form, typically consisting of eight lines with an alternating rhyme scheme.</note> by Poliziano already published partly by Serassi in the Comino edition of 1765 and partly by the Florentine editors of 1814, he certainly gave a most precious gift to seekers of ancient elegances by being the first to bring to light the two marvelous ballads for Leoncina <note>Leoncina Pierzi de' Albizzi, a noblewoman and contemporary of Poliziano.</note> which begin *Who knows not how she is made...* <note>original: "Chi non sa com' è fatto..."</note> and *Blessed be the day...* <note>original: "Benedetto sie 'l giorno..."</note> Rigoli’s *Essay*, for those compositions by Poliziano which he produced first, was also cited by the Academicians in the fifth impression.

**1858.** *Two Dance Songs* <note>original: "Canzoni a ballo"</note> *of Angelo Poliziano taken from a manuscript of the Corsini Library* <note>The Corsiniana, a famous library in Rome.</note> *and now published for the first time by Domenico Bonanni, vice-librarian of said library. It is preceded by an elegant and complete letter from the editor, Mr. Bonanni.

**1859.** In this year, the compiler of the present edition published in the first number of *Poliziano, Literary Studies*, published in Florence by the Cellini press, *Ten Stanzas of Love* based on the Riccardian manuscript 2723 <term>cod. 2723 riccard.</term>; and republished in the sixth number certain *Love Respects* <note>original: "Rispetti d'amore"; "Rispetti" are a traditional form of Tuscan folk-poetry often adapted by Renaissance poets.</note> from the 15th-century edition of the *Little Ballads* <note>original: "Ballatette"</note>, which he believed could be restored or attributed to Angelo Poliziano, along with four stanzas already published, but then restored for the first time to a better reading.

And here at last is the present edition: for which we have not merely seen, but minutely considered, almost all the printed versions recorded in this and the third chapter. And just as for the *Stanzas* <note>Poliziano's most famous work, the "Stanze de messer Angelo Poliziano cominciate per la giostra del magnifico Giuliano de’ Medici."</note> we returned directly to the manuscripts <term>codici</term>, deducing the legitimate reading from a comparison of them with the old printed versions, we have done the same for the minor rhymes. As for the ballads; the manuscripts and the old printed versions—not the modernized ones of the sixteenth century, although these too were scrupulously compared by me, but the anonymous ones of the fifteenth century—have both assured me of the genuine reading and saved me from the need for the arbitrary emendations to which the Silvestrian editors <note>Editors of the 1825 edition mentioned on the previous page.</note> sometimes surrendered themselves. For I have accepted Poliziano's diction and prosody exactly as it was, without the pretense of making it grammatically regular and modern, but rather attempting to illustrate and explain it in truly obscure and rough passages. And where I could not help myself through the comparison between the manuscripts and the old prints, and what I had before my eyes was certainly erroneous, I believed I should make use of the most evident and simple emendations of Maggi <note>Anton Maria Maggi, a scholar known for his linguistic corrections.</note>, even daring to put forward some of my own. But I have given an account of everything in the notes; where I also collected the various readings, even the manifestly incorrect ones, from all the manuscripts and all the printed texts, perhaps with excessive detail. In this way, the newly made commentary on the minor rhymes contains spe-

<page-num>CLI</page-num>

-> # ANGELO POLIZIANO. <-

...cially textual criticism; I did not, however, neglect explanations and illustrations where they were most necessary, especially in the dance songs featuring slangy idioms <term>riboboli</term> <note>These are witty, often street-level Tuscan idioms or clever wordplays.</note> and proverbs <term>proverbi</term>. The distinction between the dance songs and other legitimate rhymes, and those that are uncertain or apocryphal <term>apocrife</term> <note>Works of doubtful authorship attributed to Poliziano.</note>, was adopted by me after an examination of the sources and the arguments put forward to assign them to Master Angelo. The classification of the "respects" <note>A traditional Tuscan folk-poetry form, typically an eight-line stanza.</note> into continuous <term>rispetti in continuati</term> and detached <term>spicciolati</term>—and the arrangement of the latter into series—was imposed upon me by the nature of such compositions, by a careful study of the manuscripts <term>codici</term>, and by logic. Readers of Poliziano's rhymes often complained that they could not find their way through the various tangles of the diverse stanzas <term>stanze</term>. The previous editors offered a rather witty excuse:

> "We will note here once and for all (as stated in the Silvestri edition on page 115) that these compositions in eight-line stanzas <term>ottava rima</term>, under the name of stanzas <term>stanze</term>, short love poems <term>strambotti</term>, serenades <term>serenate</term>, etc., are written at a whim, and with such leaps here and there, that often some stanzas have no connection to the others."

This is, quite simply, to label Master Angelo as a madman or a person without reason. The fact of the matter is that the first Florentine editors of 1494 did not always know how to distinguish well between detached respects <term>rispetti spicciolati</term> and continuous ones <term>continuati</term>. The former are eight-line stanzas standing alone, like the songs of our country folk, or pairs of stanzas; the latter are lyric stanzas <term>stanze liriche</term> of varying lengths. These editors mixed them all together as if they were continuous compositions, merely hacking them apart here and there as if with an axe <term>accétta</term>; and often, they joined what was separate and separated what was joined. 

Therefore, having observed that the manuscripts <term>codici</term> never agree on an ordered series for these various respects but instead mix them differently; having assured myself through both theory and example that the respect <term>rispetto</term> and the love poem <term>strambotto</term> are compositions consisting of a single independent eight-line stanza; having noted that even Poggiali <note>Gaetano Poggiali (1753–1814), a noted Italian bibliophile and editor.</note> had sensed this when, publishing twenty stanzas from the Riccardian manuscript <term>cod. riccard.</term> <note>A manuscript held in the Biblioteca Riccardiana in Florence.</note> in his *Series*, he did not transcribe them in sequence but selected them from here and there as detached compositions; and finally, having noted in the manuscripts the certain distinction between continuous <term>continuati</term> and detached <term>spicciolati</term> perhaps first introduced by Poliziano himself, I decided to divide such compositions into two series. I gathered under the title of "continuous" those that were so qualified in the manuscript and were transcribed in sequence with specific...

distinctions in their proper places, and also those which presented a certain order of thought and feeling; as for the others, to have forcibly presented them under the name of *stanzas* <term>stanze</term> as if they were a single composition would have given readers a very poor opinion of the discursive faculties of Master Angelo. Instead, I have distinguished these under the title of *Detached Respects* <term>rispetti spicciolati</term> <note>These are short, independent folk-style poems, usually eight lines long, that do not belong to a larger sequence.</note> into several series, according to the ideas and sentiments they expressed, so that the reader, through comparison and proximity, might better taste their original beauty.

I have nothing more to say regarding my studies on this edition of the vernacular poetry of Master Angelo Poliziano: these efforts may appear and indeed be lacking and defective due to the unhappiness of my own talent and strength, but not through any fault of a fickle, arbitrary, or presumptuous will; the scrupulous patience with which I have pursued them for five years assures me of this. And here the duty falls upon me to give public thanks to my friends Isidoro Del Lungo and Carlo Gargiolli <note>Prominent 19th-century Italian philologists and scholars.</note> who aided me with much effective help in this long and fatiguing labor, as well as to pray that those knowledgeable in ancient letters might admonish and correct me where I have erred and supplement my defects with their own learning.

## VI.

### Conclusion.

---

> When Death was leading a triumph for the deceased Lorenzo <note>original: "Duceret extincto cum Mors Laurente triumphum." This refers to Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent), Poliziano's great patron.</note>
> And was carried joyfully on horses draped in black,
> She looked back at a man striking the strings with a frantic thumb,
> While sobs shook his very core.
> She marveled and held her team; he raged, and with a pious mouth
> Demanded Lorenzo back from all the gods.
> He mixed tears with prayers, and grief with tears;
> Grief provided him with unrestrained words.
> She [Death] smiled; and not unmindful of that ancient complaint
> When the paths of the underworld opened for Orpheus,
> She said, "This man even tries to repeal the laws of hell,
> and lays his hands upon my rights!"

<page-num>CLIII</page-num>
<header>ANGELO POLIZIANO.</header>

-> Immediately hard Fate struck the weeping poet, <-
-> And broke his learned breast mid-song. <-
-> Alas! Thus you were snatched away; thus evil fates bore you off, <-
-> Poliziano, master of the Italian lyre! . ¹ <-
<note>original: "Protinus et flentem percussit dura poetam, / Rupit et in medio pectora docta sono. / Heu ! sic tu raptus ; sic te mala fata tulerunt, / Arbiter ausoniæ, Politiane, lyræ!" These lines are from a Latin elegy by Pietro Bembo mourning Poliziano’s death.</note>

With this imagery, at once splendid and sorrowful, Pietro Bembo—the Venetian who succeeded the Tuscan in the literary dictatorship of the second period of the Renaissance—reclaimed the memory of Angelo Poliziano for the sake of glory and affection. He sought to protect it from the malicious rumors spread by the Republicans and the *Piagnoni* <term>Piagnoni</term> <note>Literally "the Weepers," this was the nickname given to the followers of the austere friar Girolamo Savonarola, who opposed the perceived decadence of the Medici circle.</note> following Poliziano's death on September 25, 1494, just two years and five months after the passing of Lorenzo the Magnificent. It was a death that, if you consider the age of the learned humanist and the great expectations his century held for him, seems premature; yet, it may easily seem to you to have arrived at the right time if you reflect upon the poet’s fame and the man’s personal loyalties. Thus, he was not reserved to mourn the vast ruin—set in motion by such a small impulse—of the edifice raised with such painstaking industry by his "Magnificent" protector. 

Only one month more, and Angelo Poliziano would have seen the doors of that palace closed in the face of one of his pupils <note>Referring to Piero "the Unfortunate" de' Medici, Lorenzo's son and Poliziano's former student.</note>, the very palace where Lorenzo, returning from Naples in 1478, had been welcomed with applause and tears. He would have seen those common people—aroused by the incitements of another <note>Girolamo Savonarola</note>—turning silent or threatening and mocking; the same populace who, in a bloodbath, had brutally avenged the death of Giuliano de' Medici <note>Lorenzo's brother, murdered in the Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478.</note> and surrounded the surviving brother with such savage love. He would have seen the arrogant Piero, Cardinal Giovanni <note>The future Pope Leo X.</note>, and the noble Giuliano hurrying away, scattered, in disguise, and trembling on the path to exile—an exile certainly deserved by tyrants, but always sorrowful and bitter when those tyrants are still fellow citizens. 

Only one month more, and Angelo Poliziano would have seen the small and deformed Charles VIII of France enter the city with his lance resting on his thigh <note>A traditional gesture signifying a city taken by conquest rather than by invitation.</note>—a city that had once repelled the imperial pride of two Henrys—and race through all of Italy with no more trouble than needing a bit of chalk to mark the lodgings for his troops, for the barbarians, for the Gauls. He would have seen the library of San Marco dispersed by the fury of the mob; he would have seen those codices, collected with such gold and love by Cosimo, Piero, and Lorenzo, trampled and torn—the very same manuscripts that he, poor philologist!, had spent his life gathering...

<header>ANGELO POLIZIANO</header>

...through Lombardy and Venice; the splendors of the palace on Via Larga <note>The Medici Palace, the center of Florentine political and cultural life.</note> were plundered, and what remained after French greed was abandoned to the common people. The soldiers of the King of France stood amazed—much like the savages of Alaric <note>The Visigoth king who sacked Rome in 410 AD; the author compares the French soldiers to ancient barbarians.</note> once did—at the wealth and the craftsmanship of the vessels, utensils, and ornaments in the house of a Florentine citizen.<margin>1</margin> And after that, what a roar of wars; what a coming and going of foreigners of every generation through this garden of the Renaissance; how much blood and how much mud in this temple raised to the Muses and the Graces by the descendants of Dante and Arnolfo <note>Arnolfo di Cambio, the architect of the Florentine Cathedral and the Palazzo Vecchio.</note>. Rest in peace, O poet, in your humble tomb in San Marco. No longer in the villa of Careggi <note>The country estate where the Medici and their circle held philosophical discussions.</note> will there be the symposia of the Academy around the wreathed bust of old Plato; no longer through the splendid and noisy streets during the nights of Carnival will there be the floats and masquerades where the arts of design and the arts of the word competed in magnificence; no longer at the rosy sunsets of May will there be the dances of noble ladies in the Piazza of Santa Trinita. Even poetry—that charming Tuscan folk poetry that fled so gracefully from the churches of the austere thirteenth century and became so lively and mischievous in the school of Giovanni Boccaccio, Franco Sacchetti, and your Lorenzo—even she, in the fears of death, has become a *pinzochera* <term>pinzochera</term> <note>A term for a woman who makes an outward show of extreme piety, often associated with lay members of religious orders.</note>: just as they dressed your corpse in the Dominican habit by order of Friar Girolamo <note>Girolamo Savonarola, the firebrand preacher who took control of Florence’s moral life after the Medici were expelled.</note>, so they have dressed her. The *Welcome May* and the *Triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne* <note>Famous secular and festive poems by Poliziano and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> are forgotten: no, not forgotten, but abominated as anathema. Oh, if it were given to you to hear, a low, slow, sinister sound would strike your ear—the obscurely and menacingly allegorical song of monastic democracy:

-> To the sieve, to the sieve, to the sieve <-
-> Come down, every one of you; <-
-> And with bitter tears <-
-> You shall see in this sieve <-
-> Indignation, confusion, boredom, and toil. <-
-> We are all masters of sieving <-
-> And grinding the people: <-
-> If there is any unbeliever here, <-
-> Let him come to be tested; <-

## ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...the first steps: the friar of terror and death, Girolamo Savonarola, accompanies her <note>Refers to the personified "folk poetry" or the spirit of the Italian Renaissance mentioned on the previous page.</note> to her burial. It is true that she will rise again, but only for a moment and like a terrifying apparition, to announce the end of Great Italy—the Italy of the people. In the final year of Pier Soderini’s <term>Gonfalonier: The supreme magistrate and head of the Florentine Republic's government.</term> term as Gonfalonier, a great wagon will pass through the streets of Florence, pulled by buffaloes and painted with the bones of the dead and white crosses. Atop it sits Death in the frightening form given to her by the Christian art of the Middle Ages. Surrounding the wagon is a great number of knights dressed as dead men on emaciated and skeletal horses, covered in black cloths with white crosses. Each knight is accompanied by four grooms, also dressed as the dead, carrying black torches. A black banner featuring skulls and crossbones leads the horrible company, which drags ten black banners behind it, intoning the *Have Mercy* <note>original: "Miserere" — the opening word of Psalm 51, traditionally sung in funeral rites and times of penitence.</note> with trembling and unified voices. Wherever the wagon stops, certain tombs—constructed with wonderful art around the vehicle—will open, and from them will emerge people dressed in black with white skeletons painted on their chests and backs. Carrying black torches, they sit upon their graves, and with muffled trumpets and a hoarse, lifeless sound, they sing:¹

> “Sorrow, weeping, and penitence
> Torment us always:
> This dead company
> Goes about crying 'Penance!'
> We were once as you are now,
> You will be as we are:
> Dead we are, as you see,
> So dead we shall see you:
> And in the afterlife it is of no use,
> After the evil is done, to do penance.
> We too, during Carnival,
> Went about singing of our loves;
> And thus from evil to evil
> We went on multiplying:
> Now through the world we go crying:
> Penance, penance.
> Blind, foolish, and senseless,
> Time steals everything away:
> Pomps, glories, honors, and states...”

<page-num>CLVII</page-num>

<header>ANGELO POLIZIANO.</header>

->All pass away, and nothing stays:<-
->And in the end the tomb<-
->Makes us perform our penance.¹<-

Yes: penance for the many follies of the peoples, penance for the great corruption and cowardice of the lords, penance for the sins of everyone. Great Italy is about to die. In vain Niccolò Machiavelli <note>The famous political philosopher who sought to unite Italy and protect it from foreign "barbarians."</note> labors around her with the heroic remedies of despair; in vain Francesco Ferrucci <note>A celebrated Florentine commander who died defending the Republic against Imperial troops in 1530.</note> seeks to re-infuse her with the blood of his own purest veins. She is already dead, and her grave is the high Apennines: the Pope and the Emperor, newly shaking hands after so many long centuries, sit on guard over the buried woman; only Guicciardini <note>Francesco Guicciardini, a historian known for his detached and often cynical analysis of Italy's downfall.</note> remains standing by the tomb like an anatomist in a graveyard, cold and impassive, to study the causes of death in the corpse.

From then on, a folk art—or even an art that approached the common people—became increasingly impossible. And how, in fact, could the municipal poetry of the "fat people" <term>Popolo grasso: The wealthy merchant class and elite guilds of Florence.</term> and the artisan plebs survive? They were accustomed to the open air of the streets and squares, but now they stood before the halberds of foreign soldiers stationed under the Loggia of Orcagna <note>The Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence.</note> and beneath the balcony of the Palace of the Priors. They stood before the grim face of the servant of the Inquisition, while the municipality was crushed in the iron grip of the centralizing principality. Nothing remained of the trade guilds but a shadow, while the merchant bourgeoisie was dressed up like puppets in gold braid and fringes. Even here, bibliography—for those who know how to question it—marks the shifts in the nation's sentiments and literary spirit through the sum of its figures compared to the passing years, which are necessarily linked to the nation's civil history. It shows us the impact of the popular rhymes of Angelo Poliziano, appearing quite promptly and repeatedly at short intervals in two editions of the *Little Ballads* <note>original: "Ballatette"</note> that followed each other rapidly, probably at the start of the last decade of the 15th century. Then, until after 1540, there is nothing more. For this silence of the press, the reason must be sought not only in the proud disdain of the Renaissance—which had already been shaped into courtly and academic life by the [Venetian...]

# ANGELO POLIZIANO.

...[Poli]ziana and Lombard <note>The text likely refers to regional styles or influences on Poliziano's work.</note>, dislikes openly expressed by Doni where he says that Poliziano's vernacular works were not read much in his time;¹ but the blame must also be placed on the grim austerity of the Democracy of '94 <note>The 1494 Florentine Republic influenced by the radical friar Girolamo Savonarola.</note>, the hardships of Pier Soderini’s term as Gonfalonier <note>Soderini was the leader (Gonfaloniere) of Florence from 1502 to 1512.</note>, the suspicions of the restoration of '12, the sublime storm of the Republic of '27, and the terrors and armed vigils of the new Principality. Toward the middle of the sixteenth century, collections of Poliziano's *frottole* <term>Frottola: A common type of light, popular Italian secular song of the late 15th and early 16th centuries.</term> and ballads began again, and as many as thirteen are counted up to 1614; all are Florentine, and almost all in editions intended for the use of the common people. In this flowering, it is easy to see the work of the Principality <note>The Medici Duchy.</note>, which, through entertainment and idleness, wanted at least to show that it had restored to the people the joyful life of the times of Lorenzo the Elder <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent."</note>. And the by-now degenerate people abandoned themselves to it; but oh, with what lack of appetite and with what the look of a sick man! How sad was that merriment, which knew nothing but how to repeat the poetry of a century prior, the songs of the dead! For that matter, the men of letters no longer had anything to do with those collections: they gathered in academies, and displayed great periods of prose to their Most Serene Duke and Lord, and split hairs over grammar, and hailed Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo, the influential cardinal who defined the "correct" style of Italian literature based on 14th-century models.</note> as divine, and also tormented the melancholy Tasso <note>Torquato Tasso, the great epic poet who suffered from mental illness and was famously subjected to harsh, pedantic criticism of his work.</note> a little bit. From 1614 to the middle of the eighteenth century, there was not a single reprint of the ancient little songs and ballads: one is barely printed at the end of the most elegant *stanze*. And with good reason: to Spanish-influenced Italy <note>A period when much of Italy was under the direct or indirect control of the Spanish Habsburgs, characterized by formal etiquette and aristocratic culture.</note>, the poetry of the Florentine citizenry must have reeked strongly of the plebeian: she had her madrigals, her ariettas, and her Anacreontics <note>Light, lyrical poems typically about wine and love.</note>; then came Arcadia <note>The Academy of Arcadia, an 18th-century movement that sought to simplify Italian poetry through pastoral themes.</note> with its eclogues. If, from 1765 to our own day, as much as possible of Poliziano's minor rhymes has been gradually collected, it was due to that instinct of "Alexandrian criticism" <note>A reference to the scholarly, archival approach to literature typical of the Library of Alexandria, here meaning philological research.</note> awakened during the Italian renewal—an instinct to complete and organize the treasures of the past and to study the language therein with great specificity. But fundamentally, the substance and the craftsmanship of that art remained unknown to most: almost no one noticed that Poliziano's *rispetti* <term>Rispetti: A traditional Italian folk-poetic form, often used for serenades.</term> and ballads arose from the very vein of ancient Italian popular poetry.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thus, the minor poems of [Poliziano] achieved nothing, or very little...

Poliziano in the second period of the Renaissance and in the subsequent ages of Italian literature. The same can be affirmed regarding *Orfeo*: which, after serving as a model for the dramatic eclogues <note>A pastoral poem, often in the form of a dialogue.</note> of the Este court and being reprinted twenty-one times alongside the *Stanze* in the final years of the 15th century and the first thirty years of the 16th, lost its fame and value once classical theater was established in Italy through the works of Ariosto, Bibbiena, Machiavelli, Trissino, and Rucellai. The only four editions—all of them popular—recorded between 1527 and the middle of the seventeenth century attest that it remained somewhat dear to the common people, who long remembered those ancient performances.

The situation was different regarding the *Stanze* <note>Poliziano's "Stanze per la giostra," an unfinished poem celebrating a Medici tournament.</note>: twenty-one editions from 1494 to 1540 and thirteen from 1540 to 1617—not to mention the reasoned praise accompanying them in the dedication by Sermartelli [1568 and 1577] <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "Vedila nel cap. III di questo Discorso" (See it in chapter III of this Discourse).</note> which clearly reflects the opinion of the literati of the time—show well how the learned and classical poetry of the second and third periods of the Renaissance recognized its principles and its motif in Poliziano's *Giostra* <term>Giostra: Italian for "Joust" or "Tournament"; refers here to Poliziano’s masterpiece.</term>.

Indeed, the spirit of that second period [1494–1530], which is among the saddest and most splendid in Italian history, emanates entirely from the preceding age—the age that closed in 1494 with the descent of Charles VIII <note>The French king whose invasion triggered the Italian Wars and the fall of the Medici.</note> and with the deaths, occurring within a very short interval, of Boiardo, Poliziano, and Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous humanist philosopher.</note>. In that earlier age lie the reasons for all the glories of the fifty years that followed: the illustrious men of the early sixteenth century, the directors of the literary and artistic movement, were educated in those traditions, those customs, and those studies. In that age were born the three great Florentines who embodied the final spirits of Tuscan liberty: Machiavelli in 1469, Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo</note> in 1474, and Guicciardini in 1482. Also born in 1474, a contemporary of Michelangelo, was Ariosto—the Dante of the senses, the Homer of the classical Renaissance blossomed from the midst of the strong and crude Middle Ages. Men of the *Quattrocento* <term>Quattrocento: The 1400s, or the 15th century in Italian art and literature.</term> were also the two classics of refined poetry, Sannazaro [1458] and Bembo [1470].

And these two names lead us back to Poliziano: with whom Sannazaro engaged in poetic rivalries—one of many signs of the aversion between the courtly school of Naples and...

This youth, with a genius so much lesser than his own, would complete a literary transformation that, if not great, was solemn; he would achieve, in the happiness of a long life, such glory as Poliziano had never even dreamed of—a glory like none in Europe since Petrarch, honored in competition by popes, kings, emperors, and senates, hailed by the people, and bowed to unanimously by the tumultuous republic of men of letters. 

Except that for the future of Italian letters, it would have been desirable for the life of Lorenzo de' Medici to have lasted longer, and with it, the literary primacy of Tuscany. Outside of this land, far from this air, literature finally separated itself from the people, losing as much in power and life as it gained in regularity and dignity: the language became exhausted, it withered. <meta>This page continues the analysis of Poliziano's linguistic legacy, contrasting Pietro Bembo’s strict imitation of 14th-century models with a more inclusive Florentine tradition that valued Poliziano’s own contributions.</meta>

<page-num>CLXI</page-num>

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

for use <note>The author is referring to Pietro Bembo, mentioned on the previous page, who advocated for a standardized Italian based strictly on 14th-century models.</note> he believed he had to treat it as a dead language, restricting it to the examples and rules of two writers <note>Petrarch and Boccaccio.</note>. And the wisest and most refined of his Lombard contemporaries, Baldassar Castiglione <note>Author of "The Book of the Courtier" (1528), a foundational text on Renaissance manners and language.</note>, was forced shortly thereafter to write:

> “I do not know... how it can be good, instead of enriching this language and giving it spirit, grandeur, and light, to make it poor, thin, humble, and obscure, and to seek to put it in such straits that everyone is forced to imitate only Petrarch and Boccaccio; and that in matters of language one should not yet believe in Poliziano, Lorenzo de’ Medici... and several others who are indeed Tuscan, and perhaps of no less learning and judgment than Petrarch and Boccaccio were.¹”

Nevertheless, the spirit of Poliziano remained to inform, gracefully and vividly, the Florentine classicism of Giovanni Rucellai <note>A didactic poet and one of the first to adapt Greek tragedy into Italian.</note>; of Luigi Alamanni, the elegant author of mythological poems, eclogues, elegies, and Pindaric odes; of Lodovico Martelli, an exquisite Petrarchist and writer of praised stanzas; and of Della Casa <note>Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556), famous for his book on etiquette, "Il Galateo."</note>. It remained, notably in what is his most principal merit—the joining of ancient elegance with local vividness and vernacular idiom—with Firenzuola <note>Agnolo Firenzuola (1493–1543), a monk and writer known for his polished prose.</note>, who inherited the reputation of the author of the *Ballate* <note>Poliziano’s dance songs.</note>, was born a year before his death [September 28, 1493], and was entirely the Poliziano of prose. And already, through his mastery of the eight-line stanza <note>The "ottava rima," the standard meter for Italian epic poetry.</note>, Angelo Poliziano dominates the entire sixteenth century—that learned century which, as the Italy of the common people died, testified to the vitality of the Italian intellect before the amazed barbarians <note>A reference to the foreign powers (France, Spain, Holy Roman Empire) invading Italy during the Italian Wars.</note> who broke in from every side; whether it was with Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of "Orlando Furioso."</note> taking refuge from grim reality in an ideal world in vain contested, or with Tasso <note>Torquato Tasso, author of "Jerusalem Delivered."</note> releasing the elegy of individualism, splendidly closing the ancient age and opening the new one at the same time.

In the seventeenth century, Poliziano’s *Stanzas* <note>Referring to his famous "Stanze per la giostra."</note> met the same fate as the *Divine Comedy* and the *Canzoniere* <note>Petrarch’s songbook.</note>: only two reproductions of a sixteenth-century edition are counted, and those from the early years. Certainly, the *Giostra* had nothing to do with the *Adone* <note>The "Adone" (1623) by Giambattista Marino, characterized by the ornate, complex style of the Baroque era.</note>; yet the literary tradition of which that short poem is the first link continued in Chiabrera <note>Gabriello Chiabrera (1552–1638), a poet who sought to reform Italian verse by looking back to Greek models.</note> and his school. And it rose again,

->ANGELO POLIZIANO.<-

after the wretched transition of the Arcadia <note>The Academy of Arcadia, an 18th-century literary movement that sought to simplify the "bad taste" of the Baroque but was often criticized by later writers like Carducci for being superficial and overly sentimental.</note>. In the Italian renewal inaugurated around 1750 by Parini <note>Giuseppe Parini, a foundational poet of Italian Neoclassicism known for his social critique.</note> and concluded after 1830 by Giacomo Leopardi <note>Italy's most significant lyric poet of the 19th century, who deeply valued the classical tradition.</note>: a renewal which, despite some minor elements and certain deviations, was substantially and profoundly classical. From 1728 to 1826, one can count no fewer than 31 editions of Poliziano's Italian poems; and this was only right in an age that produced the *Day* and the *Odes* of Parini, the *Musogonia* and the *Feroniade* of Monti <note>Vincenzo Monti (1754–1828), a poet famous for his technical mastery and adaptation of classical themes.</note>, and the *Graces* of Foscolo <note>Ugo Foscolo, whose poem "Le Grazie" is a masterpiece of Neoclassical imagery.</note>.

Where the arts of the word <note>A reference to literature, poetry, and rhetoric.</note> are aiming, what path they are taking, and what they are to achieve today in Italy, I truly do not know: nor do I know if many will still have the time and the desire to read the Tuscan poems of Master Angelo Poliziano in this new printing. These poems, in any case, will remain held in honor as long as even a spark of the ancient Italian spirit lives, as long as a single accent of the Tuscan tongue sounds. Furthermore, unfortunate is that criticism which would ever dare to boast of not caring for form; unfortunate is that nation which, pretending to despise art—the holy art of the fathers who were great—speaks of regeneration and renewal.

Florence, October 15, 1863.

GIOSUÈ CARDUCCI.

# EMENDATIONS AND ADDITIONS

---

Once the printing of the Volume was completed, I found in the Magliabechiano manuscript 342, Class VII <note>The Magliabechiana is a foundational collection of the National Central Library of Florence, named after the bibliophile Antonio Magliabechi.</note>, the *Orpheus* as it was published by Affò <note>Ireneo Affò (1741–1797), an art historian and philologist who published an influential edition of Poliziano’s *Orfeo*.</note> and with only a few variant readings. The manuscript, written with great accuracy toward the end of the 15th century, includes many poems by authors of that century, mostly non-Tuscans, and very specifically from the provinces subject to the rule of the House of Este <note>The d’Este family governed the Duchy of Ferrara and Modena; their court was a major center for Renaissance art and drama.</note>. The *Orpheus*, however, is inserted among the poems of Tebaldeo <note>Antonio Tebaldeo (1463–1537), a Ferrarese poet and diplomat.</note>; and Follini <note>Marco Follini, a librarian and scholar of the early 19th century.</note> also attributes it to Tebaldeo in his description of the manuscript. But the authority of the Magliabechiano manuscript is of very little weight against the consensus of the other manuscripts that attribute the *Orpheus* to Poliziano in its first version, and against the two Reggian manuscripts seen by Affò that attribute it to him even in the second version. Nevertheless, the fact of finding the *Orpheus* in a manuscript containing almost exclusively poems by non-Tuscan authors—especially from Ferrara, Modena, and Lombardy—and the fact of finding it right among the poems of the Ferrarese Tebaldeo, does it not seem to add some further probability to my hypothesis that this play was recomposed in its second redaction to serve the dramatic festivals of the court of Ferrara?

# BOOK ONE.

---

<margin>Proposition.</margin> <note>In epic poetry, the "proposition" is the opening statement where the poet announces the subject and themes of the work.</note>
> The glorious spectacles and fierce games
> Of the city that loosens and pulls the reins
> Over the great-souled Tuscans, and the harsh domains
> Of that goddess who paints the third heaven,
> And the worthy prizes for honored pursuits,
> My bold mind drives me to celebrate;
> So that the great names and exceptional, singular deeds
> Fortune, or death, or time may not steal away.

---

**St. 1.** — **v. 1. GAMES.** From the Latin term *ludi*: *here, a festival of arms or a joust.* <note>original: "ludi"</note> **Properly, public spectacles held on the occasion of festivals:** Vettori, *Cultivation*, V: “they had won the principal *games* of Athens.” — **v. 2.** * “Both to restrain and to give... loose... reins,” Virgil, *Aeneid* I. <note>original: "Et premere et lassas... dare... habenas"</note> — **v. 3.** **DOMAINS.** Here meaning *commands* or *power*; used in the Latin sense: “And may your *domains* always stand over my head,” Propertius says to the girl: “The harsh commands and the proud *domains*, You did not hear...” Leopardi. <note>original: "regna"</note> — **v. 4. PAINTS:** *colors, adorns, beautifies.* Venus is placed in the third sphere of the heavens. <note>In the medieval and Renaissance view of the universe, Venus occupied the third planetary circle or "heaven."</note> — **v. 5. PURSUITS**, the act of attending to a thing and the thing itself to which a man attends; used in the Latin sense: “roughened by the *pursuits* of war,” *Aeneid* I: “the *pursuit* of the hunt,” *Flowers of Italy*; and Ariosto in Medoro’s prayer to Diana “... my king... Who while living imitated your holy *pursuits*.” <note>original: "studi," "studiis," or "studii"</note> — **v. 6.** “A **mind** full to bursting bids me bring forth in bold song,” Claudian, *The Abduction of Proserpine* I: * “My spirit moves me to speak,” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I. <note>original: "Mens" and "Fert animus dicere"</note> — **v. 8.** “No day shall ever erase you from the memory of time,” *Aeneid* VIII. <note>original: "Nulla dies umquam memori vos eximet ævo"</note>

<summary>This page introduces the opening stanza of Poliziano's poem, declaring his intent to immortalize the jousting feats of Florence and the power of Venus. The accompanying commentary provides extensive classical parallels, linking the poet's vocabulary to Virgil, Ovid, and other ancient authors.</summary>

# THE JOUST.

<margin>
Invocation
to Love.
The effects 
of love.
</margin>

<note>Stanza 2</note>
O handsome god, who through the eyes breathes into the heart
A sweet desire filled with bitter thought,
And feeds yourself on weeping and on sighs,
Nourishing souls with a sweet poison,
You make noble whatever you look upon,
Nor can a base thing remain within your breast;
Love, to whom I am forever subject,
Reach out your hand now to my lowly intellect.

<margin>
The Author’s 
Apology.
</margin>

<note>Stanza 3</note>
Support the burden that weighs so heavily on me;
Guide my tongue, Love, guide my hand:
You are the beginning, you the end of this lofty undertaking:
Yours shall be the honor, if I do not pray in vain.
Tell me, lord, with what snares the noble mind
Of the Tuscan baron was captured by you

---

**St. 2. — v. 1-2.** “Love, love, who from the eyes distills desire, bringing sweet pleasure to the souls of those against whom you wage war,” Euripides, *Hippolytus*. <note>original: « Amore, amore, che dagli occhi stilli desiderio, inducendo voluttà dolce alle anime di quelli contro cui militi »</note> * “...sweet desire that Love breathes into me,” Petrarch. <note>original: « .... dolce desio che Amor mi spira »</note> — **v. 3.** “...I feed on tears, and you know it,” says Love to Petrarch. <note>original: « .. io mi pasco di lagrime, e tu ’l sai »</note> — **v. 4.** Virgil, regarding the subject of Love: “And deceive with poison.” <note>original: « Fallasque veneno. »</note> * “Flattering, he nourished the sweet evil,” Seneca, *Hippolytus*. <note>original: « Blandiendo dulcem nutrivit malum »</note> “...I already feel in my heart among my veins / Sweet poison,” Petrarch. <note>original: « ..sento al cor già fra le vene Dolce veneno »</note> “....into the heart descended that sweetness mixed / With a secret poison,” Tasso, *Aminta*. <note>original: « .... al cor scendea quella dolcezza mista D’ un secreto veleno »</note> — **v. 5-6.** “Without whom (Love) nothing is perfect, nor virtuous, nor noble,” Divizio, *Calandria*. <note>original: « Senza il quale (Amore) non è cosa alcuna perfetta nè virtuosa nè gentile »</note> — **v. 6.** “Love is indeed the source of every nobility,” Luigi Pulci, *The Joust of Lorenzo*. <note>original: « Amor pur fonte è d’ ogni gentilezza »</note> “You are the one who ennobles hearts,” Boccaccio, *Amorosa Visione*. <note>original: « Tu se’ colui che ingentilisci i cori »</note> Love made Petrarch such, “That never by any means / Could a base thing please him.” <note>original: « Che mai per alcun patto A lui piacer non poteo cosa vile. »</note> * These are common concepts among the ancient lyric poets: but Lorenzo de’ Medici says of the eyes of his lady, “They make noble everything that looks at them.” <note>original: « Fan gentil ogni cosa che li miri. »</note> — **v. 8.** “Ah, lend a hand to my weary wit, Love...” Petrarch. <note>original: « Deh, porgi mano all’ affannato ingegno, Amore... »</note>

**St. 3. — v. 1.** <term>Burden</term> (fascio), metaphorically: a weight, grievance, or load of both soul and body. See the Dictionary of the Crusca. “I am so tired under the ancient burden / Of my sins,” Petrarch. <note>original: « Io son sì stanco sotto il fascio antico Delle mie colpe »</note> * Also in prose: “Considering that they could not support such a great burden by themselves... they sent themselves to Brabant,” Giovanni Villani. <note>original: « Considerando di non poter per loro medesimi sostenere sì gran fascio .. si mandarono in Brabante »</note> — **v. 3-4.** An imitation of the solemn invocations of ancient bards. “In you I shall end and from you I shall begin,” Homer: “From Jove let us begin, and in Jove end, O Muses,” Theocritus. “From you the beginning, for you the end,” Virgil, *Eclogue VIII*. <note>original: « A te principium, tibi desinet »</note> — **v. 5.** <term>Lord</term> (signor). Petrarch also in several places calls Love his lord. — <term>What</term> (che), a relative of quality and quantity, corresponding to the Latin *qualis* and *quantus*. — * <term>Snares</term> (lacci). “A snare that she wove of silk / Stretched among the grass... Then I was caught,” Petrarch. <note>original: « Un laccio che di seta ordiva Tese fra l’ erba... Allor fui preso »</note> — **v. 6.** <term>Baron</term> (barone), meaning Giuliano de' Medici. * Ancient writers used this term even for apostles and saints, and also for Romans and Greeks. — **v. 7.** He calls Giuliano the "younger son" because he was the younger brother of Lorenzo, both being the sons of Piero.

...of Cosimo the Elder, "Father of the Fatherland," and of Lucrezia de' Tornabuoni, called by excellence with the title of Leda. — verse 8. **NETS**. Regarding the metaphorical *nets of Love*, thus Lucretius, Book IV: "For to avoid the snares, so that we are not thrown into the traps of Love, is not as difficult as, once caught in the nets themselves, to escape and break the strong knots of Venus." <note>original: « Nam vitare plagas in Amoris ne iaciamur Non ita difficile est, quam captum retibus ipsis Exire et validos Veneris Perrumpere nodos. »</note> Also Petrarch: "Love among the grass a graceful net / Of gold and pearls stretched out..." <note>original: « Amor fra l' erbe una leggiadra rete D' oro e di perle tese... »</note>

Stanza 4. — He dedicates his work to Lorenzo, brother of Giuliano, and uses for the name of Lorenzo the allegory of the laurel (<term>lauro</term>), as Ariosto also did in Song 3, stanza 7, and Petrarch for the name of Laura. Also Horace, Book II, Ode 5, made use of a similar allegory: "And lay down your side, tired from long military service, beneath my laurel." <note>original: « Longoque fessum militia latus Depone sub lauro mea. »</note> — verse 1. * Variant: *Well-born Laurel, and you*: this is a correction by Dolce and Sermartelli which did not pass, like many others, into all subsequent reprints. — * **VEIL** "the cover of the beech tree" <note>original: « tegmine fagi »</note> Virgil, Eclogue I; and Ariosto, Eclogue: ".... Under the shadowy veil / Of an ancient elm." — verse 3-4. * Allegorically; and perhaps it should be understood as political enmities, as more clearly stated by Poliziano in the *Nutricia*: "Lorenzo... safe in whose shade the Arno looks upon the thunderbolts of wars, laughing from afar." <note>original: « Laurens... cuius securus ad umbram Fulmina bellorum ridens procul aspicit Ar-nus. »</note> — verse 5. **STEM** (<term>stelo</term>), from the Greek *stele* (column or pillar). We call the stalk of herbs and flowers a "stelo." * It pleased Giusti: "Of the tree of Christ the sacred stem." Some ancient printings and the Aldine edition, followed by the Cominian editions and by Molinari, read *ostelo* <gloss>lodging or hostel</gloss>; an error of the first Bolognese editor; and that praying to be received into the Medici palace would be a form of begging with unbecoming forwardness: by good fortune, the Riccardian manuscript 1576 clearly reads *stelo* as does the Chigian manuscript reproduced by Biondi in the Roman edition (1804). S. Betti noted in the *Arcadian Journal* vol. XXIX, 1026: "Rightly... Nannucci has restored... the true word *stelo*, taking away that most ugly *ostelo* which disfigures all the other editions; with the exception of the Florentine of 1577 by Sermartelli, the Bergamasque of 1747 by Lancellotti, and the rare and excellent Roman one of 1804." — verse 7. * *Beginning and end*, read Dolce and Sermartelli along with Aldus, and all subsequent printings that from here on I shall call the *Vulgate*. — verse 8. * Variant: *For I live only*: Oliverian Code, according to Betti, as cited above. Ariosto: "That Tuscan Laurel loved on earth and in heaven... whose medicinal..."

**Stanza 5.** — **verse 1.** "Behold, will that day ever come to me when I may tell of your deeds? Behold, will it be permitted to me to carry [your name] through the whole world?" <note>original: « En erit unquam Ille dies mihi cum liceat tua dicere facta? En erit ut liceat totum mihi ferre per orbem... »</note> From Virgil's *Eclogues* VIII. — **verse 3.** * **THE SPIRIT OF THE LIMBS**, understood as the governing spirit that guides the body: "While spirit guides these joints" <note>original: « Dum spiritus hos reget artus »</note> from the *Aeneid* IV. "Noble spirit who guides those limbs" from Petrarch. — **verse 4.** * **BY THE FATES**, by the disposition of the fates; in the Latin style: "driven by fate" <note>original: « fato profugus »</note> from the *Aeneid* I: "All things by fate rush toward the worse." <note>original: « Omnia fatis In peius ruere. »</note> from the *Georgics* I. — * **FROM THE CRADLE**; in the Latin style: "even from the cradle" <note>original: « usque a cunabulis »</note> from Plautus. "And I believe from the swaddling clothes and the cradle heaven provided this remedy" from Petrarch. — **verse 5.** * **RESOUND YOU**, make your name ring out. "The lyre... our songs will resound you." <note>original: « Te lyra... te carmina nostra sonabunt. »</note> from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* X: which Simintendi renders as "The lute... will sound you: our verses will sound you." "He who takes so little of the path before me, all Tuscany [resounds with his name]." from Dante's *Purgatory* XI. "I will make sonnets for you that will sound your evil life" from Bellincioni. — * **verse 6.** From east to west. The Atlantic Ocean is our ultimate western limit; for this reason, as it seems the sun sets there, the Poet calls it *the sea that darkens our sky*. — **verse 7.** **LIGNO** instead of *legno* (wood/tree), just as Petrarch said *digno* instead of *degno* (worthy), retaining the Latin form <term>lignum</term>. Here, it means "tree": "You shall see me come to your beloved tree." from Dante's *Paradise* I. The Poet indicates the desire he had to enter the House of Medici. * "...I placed the nest of chosen thoughts in that soul-plant" from Petrarch. — **verse 8.** From a rough and weak singer, he may become a noble poet.

**Stanza 6.** — **verse 1.** * Note the two verbs constructed with the dative. Sacchetti did the same with "to hope": "everyone hoped in [to] the paternal walls." — * **verse 2.** Dante also gave wings to desire, *Purgatory* IV, 29: Firenzuola "seeing the wings of such laudable desire clipped." — **verse 4.** **Giulio** for <term>giulivo</term> (joyful), through the suppression of the 'v' often used by the ancients. Likewise *loica* for *logica*. — **verse 5.** * **BLOOD**, the Medici family — **FROM A SECOND BRANCH** :

D. S. Volg. In Latin: <term>pulvis</term> (dust) is also taken for the field in which an exercise is completed; hence Ovid could say metaphorically, "And let our horse run in its own dust." <note>original: « *Inque suo noster pulvere currat equus.* »</note> *Fasti* II. — **verse 8.** Longus in his *Pastorals* also says that Love wings souls: "Love who wings the feet and hearts of his own" Petrarch: * and Michelangelo Buonarroti "Love awakens and moves and wings the wings for a high flight."

S... in truth: A. — <term>ECHOES</term> : "his voice still echoes down here" Petrarch. * And Tasso in his sonnets used "rimbombare" (to echo/resound) transitively: "...the name... that carries and resounds your honors." — **verse 2.** * The first to change this reading from *That the daughter of Leda* to the other *That the daughter of Hecuba* was Ludovico Dolce in his *First Part of the Stanzas of various illustrious poets* (Venice, 1570, by Giolito). But Dolce and all those who followed him, among whom were also the very learned Volpi, were mistaken. And the one who kindled the son of Peleus <note>Achilles</note> with amorous sparks after the tomb was not Polyxena daughter of Hecuba, but Helen daughter of Leda, with whom, according to the account of Ptolemy Hephaestion cited by Photius, he contracted marriage among the dead on an island in the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> consecrated to the rest of departed heroes (See Bayle's Dictionary, article <term>ACHILLEA</term>, and the observations of the celebrated Cavalier Luigi Lamberti upon this passage of Poliziano inserted in the <term>POLIGRAFO</term>). Note from the Silvestri edition, Milan, 1825. Our author also says in his *Ambra*: "Add that the beautiful daughter of Tyndareus <note>Helen</note> shall be given to a beautiful husband <note>Achilles</note>, burning with shining stars." <note>original: « *Adde quod et pulchro tradetur pulchra marito Tyndaris Aeacidae stellis fulgentibus ardens.* »</note>. It is useless to add that the Riccardiano, Chigiano, and Oliveriano Manuscripts read *That the daughter of Leda*. — **verses 5-6.** Poliziano excuses himself for the interruption of Homer, whom he was then translating into Latin verses; this translation was either lost or still lies buried in the hiding places of some library (* Angelo Mai rediscovered the first books). — **verse 5.** * Var. **Let it be silent a little** : D. S. — * <term>TRUMPET</term>, used for epic song; in the Latin style. Alexander at the tomb of Achilles: "O fortunate one who found such a clear trumpet" Petrarch. More similar to our author is the manner of Chiabrera: "He desired the illustrious trumpet of the invincible seed of the royal Peleus."

The life of Julio before he fell in love.

In the lovely time of his green youth,
While the first flower still bloomed upon his face,
And the fair Julio had not yet experienced
The sweet-bitter cares that Love bestows,

<margin>v. 6. **Italian**:</margin> Fazio degli Uberti also used the phrase "Italian lands" in his *Canzoni*. <note>original: *italice*</note>. Editors Didot and Silvestri, followed by the Common Edition, corrected this to the more modern *italiche*. At one time, certain linguistic purists refused to recognize the adjective "Italic"; others defended it because it was used by the scholar Cesari. — **Towns**, meaning cities: "Above the beautiful river Arno at the great town." <note>original: *gran villa*. In older Italian, *villa* often referred to a major city or commune.</note> Dante, *Inferno XXIII.* "The town of Nantes." *Villani XI:* "Populous towns of fragrant India." Ariosto.

— <margin>v. 7. **To tune the lyre**,</margin> to harmonize the voices of the instruments and coordinate them with the song. "O Muse of the Pierian spring, who regulates the sweet sound of the golden shell!" <note>original Latin: *O, testudinis aureæ Dulcem quæ strepitum, Pieri, temperas!*</note> Horace. "Tuning the strings to a sharp sound" from a translation of Boethius. — <margin>**Arms**,</margin> meaning battles or combat: "Did I not know how much, in his first arms, the desire for glory was burning and sweet in a generous heart?" <note>original: *armi prime*</note> Caro, *Aeneid, XI.*

<margin>**Stanza 8.** — v. 1.</margin> "In the sweet time of the first age." Petrarch. **Green**, meaning youthful: "green age" <note>original Latin: *ævum viride*</note> Ovid. "All my flowering and green age." "...in the most flowering and green age." Petrarch. — <margin>v. 2.</margin> "...youth was clothing his cheeks with the first flower." <note>original Latin: *prima genas vestibat flore iuventa*</note> Virgil's *Aeneid VIII.* "Before the youthful flower shadows your sweet cheeks." <note>original Latin: *Ante genas dulces quam flos iuvenilis inumbret*</note> Claudian. "The first flower of the first hair had not yet marked him." Tassoni. — <margin>v. 4.</margin> Catullus says of Love: "Holy boy, who mixes joys with the cares of men" <note>original Latin: *Sancte puer, curis hominum qui gaudia misces*</note> and of Venus: "She mixes sweet bitterness with cares." <note>original Latin: *Dulcem curis miscet amaritiem*</note> Anacreon: "And Venus dipped the tips, taking sweet honey; and Love mixed gall therein." Plato in the *Timaeus*: "Love is a mixture of pleasure and sadness." Who then does not remember Petrarch's "A little honey, much aloe with gall" and similar phrases? — <margin>v. 5.</margin> Variant... *in peace and liberty*, found in some old printings: *in peace, in liberty*: used by Didot and Silvestri and the Common Edition. — <margin>v. 6. **To rein**,</margin> to put on the bridle and hold back. Here it seems to mean to rule, to handle, or to guide with the bit. "One who reined a great winged steed." Ariosto. — <margin>v. 7. **Herds**.</margin> Servius, in his commentary on the third book of Virgil's *Georgics*, notes: "A herd <term>armentum</term> is properly called that kind of livestock which is suitable for the work of arms, such as horses and oxen"; hence Virgil: "Horses are armed for war: these herds threaten war." <note>original Latin: *Bello armantur equi: bellum hæc armenta minantur*</note> *Aeneid III.* — <margin>v. 8.</margin> "And to outstrip the winds with the speed of feet" <note>original Latin: *Cursuque pedum prævertere ventos*</note> Virgil: "to compete in the race" <note>original Latin: *contendere cursu*</note> *Aeneid V*; Ugo Foscolo in *The Graces*: "And they competed to run with the winds."

<margin>The noble deeds of Julio.</margin>
Now making him leap in the manner of a leopard          9
Now dexterously making him wheel in a tight circle:
Now making a slow dart whiz through the air,
Often inflicting sharp suffering on wild beasts.
Thus lived the vigorous youth:
Neither thinking of his bitter and dread fate,
Nor yet certain of his future laments,
He used to mock afflicted lovers.

<margin>Words of the author.</margin>
Ah, how many nymphs sighed for him!                              10
But the youth was always so haughty,
That the loving nymphs never bent him,
His cold breast could never be warmed.
<margin>Honorable exercises of Julio.</margin>
He often made his stay in the woods,
Always unrefined and rigid in appearance;
And he defended his face from the sun's rays
With a garland of pine or green beech.

**Stanza 9.** — **v. 2.** * He made him perform a pirouette, "to urge into a winding circle" <note>original Latin: *torto stringere gyro*</note> Manilius, Book V: "to drive in a shorter curved circle" <note>original Latin: *curvo brevius compellere gyro*</note> Tibullus, *Panegyric*: "with neck rotated he begins to take his outspread course in a circle" <note>original Latin: *cervice rotata Incipit effusos in gyrum carpere cursus*</note> Lucan, *Ad Pisonem*. — **v. 3.** "They hurl slow spears with their arms." <note>original Latin: *lenta lacertis Spiculo contorquent*</note> *Aeneid*, Book VI. <term>Whiz</term> <note>original: *ronzare*</note>, used metaphorically for the noise made by objects thrown or pulled through the air with violence. — **v. 4.** "We who are able to give certain wounds to the wild beast." <note>original Latin: *Qui dare certa feræ dare vulnera possumus*</note> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I. — **v. 6.** * <term>Dread</term> <note>original: *diro*</note>, cruel: "dread fortune." Firenzuola, *The Golden Ass*. — **v. 8.** * Variation: *only to mock*: found in an ancient edition. — <term>To mock</term> <note>original: *gabbarsi*</note>, in a neutral sense, means to make fun of or to jest.

**Stanza 10.** — **v. 1.** "Many boys and many girls sought him." <note>original Latin: *Multi illum pueri multæ petiere puellæ*</note> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book III: * "often sighing for the girl in her blonde guest." <note>original Latin: *puellam in flavo sæpe hospite suspirantem*</note> Catullus, LXIV. — **v. 2-3.** "But there was such hard pride in that tender form, that no boys and no girls touched him." <note>original Latin: *Sed fuit in tenera tum dura superbia forma, Nulli illum pueri nullæ tetigere puellæ*</note> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, as cited above. And Rinuccini in his *Daphne*: "Every nymph in sorrow and tears he had placed for his beauty, but the bitter hardness of his heart did not bend the afflicted lovers." — **v. 3.** * Variation: *bent him*: Common Edition and the Oliveriano manuscript. — **v. 4.** * Variation: *Nor could*: Didot and Silvestri editions. — <term>To be warmed</term> <note>original: *riscaldarsi*</note> meaning to conceive love, from the Latin *calesco* used especially by Horace with the same meaning: Terence, *The Eunuch*: "come near this fire: now you will grow warm more than enough." <note>original Latin: *accede ad ignem hunc: iam calesces plus satis*</note> * "...you warm my breast with love." <note>original: *d’amor mi scaldi il petto*</note> Dante, *Paradise*, Canto III. — **v. 5.** Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, on the same subject: "Many sought her; she rejected those seeking her, impatient and without experience of a man, she wanders through pathless woods, nor does she care what Hymen, what Love, or what marriage might be:" <note>original Latin: *Multi illam petiere: illa aversata petentes, Impatiens expersque viri, nemora avia lustrat, Nec quid Hymen quid Amor quid sint connubia curat*</note> and elsewhere "...The other flees the name of a lover, rejoicing in the hiding places of the woods and the skins of captured beasts, an emulator of the unwed Phoebe [Diana]." <note>original Latin: *Fugit altera nomen amantis, Sylvarum latebris captivarumque ferarum Exuviis gaudens innuptæque aemula Phœbes*</note> — **v. 8.** "And his head wreathed with sharp pine." <note>original Latin: *Pinuque caput præcinctus acuta*</note> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book VIII. * Variation: *or of green beech*: Riccardian manuscript 1576.

<margin>Julio’s virtuous exercises.</margin>

Then, when the stars already appeared in the sky,
He would return to his home all full of joy;
And in the company of the nine sisters <note>The Nine Muses, goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note>
He would sing celestial verses with great desire,
And he awakened a thousand flames of ancient virtue
In the hearts of men with his lofty songs:
Thus, calling human love a form of lasciviousness,
He took his pleasure with the Muses or with Diana. <note>Diana was the goddess of the hunt and a symbol of chastity.</note>

<margin>Julio’s true piety.</margin>

And if at times in that blind labyrinth
He saw a poor, wretched lover wandering,
Laden with grief, and with pity painted on his face,
Following the footsteps of his female enemy, <note>In courtly love poetry, the beloved lady is often described as a "foe" or "enemy" because her beauty "attacks" the lover or because she rejects his advances.</note>
And where Love had bound his heart,
Feeding his soul there on two holy lights— <note>The lady's eyes.</note>

**Stanza 11.** — v. 1. * Thus the two Riccardian Manuscripts. The old printed editions read *Then when they appeared in heaven*; hence the correction of the Aldine edition, which became the common reading, *And then when they appeared in heaven*. D. reads *glowed* instead of *appeared*. — **APPEARED** <note>original: *PAREAN*</note>: *Parere* here means to appear. The Latins also used the verb *parere* for *apparere* (to appear): Apuleius used *paruerit* for *apparuerit*; and Seneca: "...I surely appeared <note>original: *Parui*</note> everywhere worthy of Jove." * Boccaccio, *Amorous Vision*, V: "every star appeared in the sky." — v. 8. **WITH DIANA**. "She cherished Ortygia <note>An island associated with the birth of Diana.</note> for its pursuits and the goddess herself for her virginity." <note>original Latin: *Ortygiam studiis ipsaque colebat Virginitate deam.*</note> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book VIII.

**Stanza 12.** — v. 1. * **LABYRINTH**, the error of love: "At the first hour of the sixth day of April, I entered the labyrinth." <note>original: *Sull' ora prima il dì sesto d'aprile Nel laberinto entrai.*</note> Petrarch. — v. 2. **WRETCHED** <note>original: *MISERELLO*</note>: Catullus: "...the fires consume the inner marrow of the wretched <note>original Latin: *misellæ*</note> girl." — v. 3. "With wonder, I believe, I was painted." <note>original: *Di meraviglia, credo, mi dipinsi.*</note> Dante, *Purgatorio*, Canto IV. **PITY** <note>original: *PIETÀ*</note> here, as in the cited passage of

Petrarch, has the sense of distress or pain, which Dante calls *pietà*. — v. 4. **HIS ENEMY** <note>original: *NIMICA SUA*</note> Petrarch called Laura *my sweet warrior* and *my sweet and bitter enemy*. — v. 6. **TO FEED** <note>original: *PASCER*</note> meaning *to delight*, as was said by the Greeks: Euripides, *Phoenissae*: "hopes feed exiles." * Dante, regarding the usurers who look into their purses: "And from this it seems that their eye feeds itself." <note>original: *E quindi par che 'l lor occhio si pasca.*</note> See further below, *Stanza 122*. — **HOLY LIGHTS** <note>original: *LUCI SANTE*</note> and holy face, a phrase especially used by Petrarch. — v. 7. **CRUEL** <note>original: *CRUDEL*</note> for the plural *crueli*. Petrarch used *mirabil* for *mirabili* in the *Triumphs*, and Firenzuola used *parol* for *parole*: but these licenses, says Buonmattei, are excused in the great poets but I do not know if they are praised in anyone else. See the Dictionary of the Crusca. Here it means a snare: * Luca Pulci, *The Joust of Lorenzo*: "Love prepared his shackles and stocks." Or perhaps it means shame, error, or similar. # BOOK ONE.
<meta>catchword: quanto</meta>

->Trapped in the cruel pillories of love;<-
->He thus assailed them with bitter reproaches.<-

<margin>Julio’s words to young lovers.</margin>
<margin>Where love originates.</margin>
<margin>What love is.</margin>
— Shake off, poor wretch, the blind error from your breast, 13
Which steals you from yourself and gives you to another:
Do not nourish a vain fury with flattery,
Which rises from sluggish lasciviousness and idleness.
He whom the erring common folk call Love
Is a sweet insanity to those who see more clearly:
The world has given such a beautiful title as "Love"
To a blind plague, to a pleasant evil.

<margin>Against women and the way they lead their lives.</margin>
Ah, how wretched is the man who changes his will 14
For a woman, or ever rejoices or grieves for her!

<meta>This page continues Julio’s (Giuliano de' Medici) speech against the dangers of love. # BOOK ONE.

Ah, how much more sorrowful among the wretched is he
Who can suffer a woman's fierce pride!
For the more her face is filled with beauty,
The more she hides deceits within her deceptive breast.

<margin>That the eyes are the primary cause of love.</margin>
With these <note>the woman's eyes</note> Love ensnares youthful eyes,
Love, who steals away every manly thought;
And whoever once swallows the sweet bait
Never again cares for his own liberty;
But, as if Love had mixed Lethe <note>the mythical river of forgetfulness</note> there,
You soon forget your noble nature;
Nor does a manly thought then sprout within you,
So much does he strip you of your own worth.

<margin>Praise of the rustic life.</margin>
How much sweeter, how much safer it is
To follow the fleeing beasts in the hunt
Through ancient woods far from ditch or wall,
And to track their dens by a long trail!
To see the valley, the hill, and the pure air,
The grass and flowers, and the clear, icy spring water!

# THE JOUST.

> To hear the birds <gloss>often means</gloss> singing in spring, the waves resounding,
> And the leaves murmuring sweetly in the wind!

<margin>Pastoral pleasures.</margin>
> How pleasing it is to watch the goats hanging from a cliff, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 18.
> And grazing on this or that shrub;
> And the mountain-dweller in the thickest shade
> Waking his bagpipes and his uncultured verse!
> To see the earth covered with apples,
> Every tree almost hidden by its fruit;
> To see rams butting, cows lowing,
> And the crops waving just as the sea does!

<margin>Rural exercises.</margin>
> Now the rustic master of the little sheep &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 19
> Is seen opening the gate for his flock:
> Then, when he moves them with his shepherd’s crook,
> It is sweet to observe how he speaks to each one.

---

When speaking of birds, the word used here <note>original: "svernar"</note> means *to sing*, and it specifically refers to the singing they do in the spring after emerging from the winter. — **\*** A poet of the 13th century: "And the little birds for love / Sing so sweetly in spring."

**Stanza 18. — v. 1.** **\*** PLEASING <note>original: "GIOVA"</note>, it delights. "I am one of those whom weeping pleases" — Petrarch. "This life pleases me" — Tasso, *Aminta*. Derived from the Latin: Lucretius, Book V, "it is a joy to approach untouched fountains" <note>original: "iuvat integros accedere fontes"</note>. — HANGING. "Go on, my little goats... I shall not see you... hanging from the bushy cliff far off" — Virgil, *Eclogue* I. **\*** "The goats hang from an airy cliff" — Pindemonte. — **v. 2.** "The goats nibble the shrubs" — Virgil, *Eclogue* X. — **v. 3.** THICKEST <note>original: "CONSERTA"</note>: Latin *consertus*. **\*** It refers to shade produced by branches that are *conserti*, meaning woven or intertwined together (Fornaciari). — **v. 5.** UNCULTURED <note>original: "INCULTO"</note>: "Rustic words" — Tibullus; "unpolished [verses]" — Virgil. — **v. 7.** "He looks out upon the wandering herds of lowing cattle" — Horace. — **v. 8.** "And the waving crops in happy fields" — Sannazaro. — **\*** Variant *vacche mugghiare* [cows lowing]: found in old editions.

**Stanza 19. v. 1.** — **\*** Variant *To the rustic master* [Al rozo mastro]. Manuscript Riccardiano 1576. — MASTER <note>original: "MASTRO"</note>: "the masters of the sheep" — Virgil. — **v. 2.** FLOCK <note>original: "TORMA"</note>: when referring to animals, a herd or group. — **\*** GATE <note>original: "SBARRA"</note>: here it refers to those partitions placed to block a path, the door of the sheepfold (Fornaciari). — **v. 3.** **\*** Variant *With his crook* [Con suo vincastro]. Manuscript Riccardiano 2723. — **v. 4.** **\*** Variant *It is sweet to observe* [Dolce è notar]. Manuscript Riccardiano 1576. — *how he speaks to each one* <note>original: "come a ciascuna garra"</note>. — SPEAKS/CHIPS <note>original: "GARRA"</note>: from the verb *garrire*. When said of birds, it means to chirp or screech; of men, it means to scold or rebuke, almost threatening others with shouts. **\*** But here, could the words *how he speaks to each one* not be interpreted more generally, as in how he says his piece to each sheep? Even the Latins used the verb *garrire* to mean "to talk nonsense" (Fornaciari). And the poet Sacchetti, in one of his ballads, out of love for certain shepherdesses, wishes to become a shepherd and mountain-dweller to follow the sheep: "And now I would say Biondella and now Martino" (nicknames that country folk give to their sheep).

# BOOK ONE.

### BOOK ONE.

> Now the peasant is seen taming the hard clods &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 19. (cont.)
> With the rake, or handling the hoe;
> Now the young country girl, ungirt and barefoot,
> Stands spinning with the geese under a rocky ledge.

<margin>What the Golden Age was like.</margin>

> In such a way the ancient peoples of old &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 20.
> Are believed to have enjoyed the Golden Age:
> Mothers were not yet made sorrowful
> By sons dead in martial labor;
> Nor was life yet entrusted to the winds;
> Nor did the bull yet complain of the yoke:
> Their houses were great, leafy oaks,
> Which had honey in the trunk and acorns on the branches.

---

Is this the *chatter* <note>original: "garra"</note> of Poliziano? Note the verb *to chatter* <note>original: "garrire"</note> used with the dative case: **Barberino, Documents of Love.** "Chirp to him (to the baby) when he runs after a bird." — v. 5. "He tames the earth with rakes" <note>original: "rastris terram domat"</note>. **Virgil.** — v. 7-8. "The little old woman was up to spin, ungirt and barefoot" **Petrarch.** **Redi**, in a poetic jest: "A lovely little shepherdess, ... Simple, ungirt and barefoot, stood watching the geese under a ledge."

**Stanza 20.** — v. 1. * With a similar movement **Virgil** says: "Golden Saturn led this life on earth: nor had they yet heard the war-trumpets blown, nor yet the swords clatter on the hard anvils" <note>original: "Aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat: Nec dum etiam audierant inflari classica, nec dum Impositos duris crepitare incudibus enses"</note>. — v. 2. * **TO HAVE ENJOYED** <note>original: "ESSER GODUTE"</note>. **Boccaccio** also used "I am enjoyed" <note>original: "goduta sono"</note>, "being enjoyed," "they were enjoyed," instead of "I have enjoyed," etc., in three places in the **Decameron (Day IV, nov. 1 and 3)**, cited with a short note by **Cesari** in the **Verona Dictionary**. But he observes that when "to be" <note>original: "essere"</note> is used for "to have" <note>original: "avere"</note>, the participle agrees in gender and number with the agent (**Fornaciari**). — v. 3. * Variant: "They were" <note>original: "Eran"</note>: **A. D. S. Translation**: but "they were" <note>original: "eron"</note>, here and elsewhere always, is clearly read in the manuscripts and old prints: and it is an inflection of this third person plural, specific to the Florentine people especially in the 15th and 16th centuries, used also by **Machiavelli**, **Gelli**, and **Davanzati**, as well as by all the comic writers. See the *Essay on Anomalous and Defective Verbs* by **Nannucci**, who adds: "So our common people still use it." Provençal: *eron*. — v. 4. * **MARTIAL LABOR**, war. "Military service and the heavy work of Mars" <note>original: "Militiam et grave Martis opus"</note> **Virgil.** — v. 5. * **WAS ENTRUSTED** <note>original: "SI CREDEVA"</note>: it was confided, it was committed: this is a Latin usage (**Fornaciari**). "Now, even entrust your life to the winds" <note>original: "Nunc, et ventis animam committe"</note> **Virgil:** "He committed his life to the light breezes" <note>original: "animam levibus credidit auris"</note> **Seneca, Medea:** "those who entrust their life to the stormy sea" **Alamanni, Cultivation VI:** "...to the tempests the daring youth entrusts his life" **Tasso, Rhymes.** "The birds entrust their defenseless breasts to the wind" **Leopardi.** There are examples from the 14th century: this one by **Simintendi** in his translation of the **Metamorphoses** is very clear: "Ceyx was made into a new bird, and he did not entrust himself to the sky." — v. 6. * "And the pressed bullocks groaned under the yoke" <note>original: "Pressique iugo gemuere iuvenci"</note> **Metamorphoses I.** — v. 8. "And yellow honey dripped from the green oak" <note>original: "Flavaque de viridi stillabant ilice mella"</note> **Metamorphoses I.** "And hard oaks sweated dewy honey" <note>original: "Et duræ quercus sudabant roscida mella"</note> **Virgil, Eclogues.** — v. 7-8. * "Their homes were caves and dense thickets and branches bound with bark" <note>original: "Domus antra fuerunt Et densi frutices et vinctæ cortice virgæ"</note> **Metamorphoses I.**
