<note>This page contains a portion of Angelo Poliziano's "Stanze per la giostra," specifically the continuation of the description of the hunt.</note>

I am Megaera, the Tartarean <note>of the underworld</note> trumpet.
Like an animal that seems to gnaw itself with spite;
Like one who tucks a trembling tail between its legs.

<margin>Various duties of the hunters.</margin> <margin>29</margin>
The whole beautiful company scatters,
Some to the nets, some to the narrowest path.
One keeps the dogs in pairs, another uncouples them;
One already lets his loose, another calls and lures his back:
One spurs his good steed across the countryside:
One, well-armed, awaits the angry beast:
One sits upon a branch to keep a good watch:
One has the spear in hand and another readies his dart.

<margin>Various actions of the wild beasts.</margin> <margin>30</margin>
Already the boar within the ravine bristles his hair
And whets his teeth; already from a grotto
A wild goat leaps down; already the old herds
Of stags flee across the plain in a flock:
Fear has extinguished the fox's tricks:

***

The Furies, at Juno’s instigation, cause the killing of a doe to spark a brawl between the recently landed Teucrians <note>Trojans</note> and the Latins: "But the savage goddess, finding from her watchtower a time for doing harm, seeks the high roof of the stable, and from the topmost summit sounds the Tartarean note: at which immediately every grove trembled and the deep woods echoed." <note>original Latin: "At sæva e speculis tempus dea nacta nocendi... sylvæ insonuere profundæ." — Virgil, Aeneid VII, 511-515.</note>

**Stanza 29.** — **v. 1.** **COMPANY** <note>original: "COMPAGNA"</note> used instead of *compagnia*: a method used by the ancients of removing the 'i' from such words. **Inferno XXV** "Alone with one vessel and with that small company." <note>original: "Sol con un legno e con quella compagna Piccola." — Dante Alighieri.</note> *Compagna* was not only used in poetry, but also in prose: and the so-called "companies" <note>compagne</note> of mercenary soldiers are famous, or rather infamous, as we see recorded even by Muratori <note>Ludovico Antonio Muratori, a famous Italian historian.</note> in the years 1339 and 1342. (Fornaciari). — **v. 2.** * Variant in some old printings, *to the nets* <note>original: "alle rete"</note>. — **v. 3-4.** "Some remove the chains from the dogs, some follow the pressed footprints and desire to find their own danger" **Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII.** <note>original: "Vincula pars adimunt canibus, pars pressa sequuntur..."</note>

— **v. 7.** *To stay on watch* <note>original: "Stare a riguardo"</note> or *in regard*, to stay vigilant, to be on one's guard, with caution. — **v. 8.** * Thus the two Riccardian Manuscripts, namely: *he who readies the spear in his hand and he who readies the dart*. The printed editions say: *He who has in hand*.

**Stanza 30.** — **v. 1.** Homer, in the hunt of Ulysses, says of the boar: "As the attackers were near, and he from the woods, with bristling neck and eyes casting fire, stood near them." And Apollonius, Book I: "and he whets his teeth, horrific for his bristling hair." And Virgil: "and his hair stood on end" <note>original Latin: "comasque arrexit."</note>. — **v. 2.** **RAVINE** <note>original: "BURRON"</note>, an open place, steep and deep. — * **v. 2-4.** "Behold the wild goats, cast down from the summit of the rock, run down the ridges; from another part the stags cross the open fields in their course and gather their dusty ranks in flight and leave the mountains" **Aeneid IV.** <note>original Latin: "Ecce feræ, saxi deiectæ vertice..."</note> — *Spunta* <note>literally "sprouts"</note> means appears, or comes out. — **v. 5.** * Variant *of the fox* <note>original: "delle volpe"</note> in some old printings; of the...

# BOOK ONE.

The hares at the first assault go into a rout:
From its den every dazed beast emerges:
The cunning wolf retreats deeper into the woods,

And hidden there, the poor wretch still fears

The bolder the beast is, the more it takes to the woods:
The blood in all of them freezes within the heart:
The forest trembles; and every plant yields to him:
He knocks down trees, or uproots them, or shatters branches.

There, Love took counsel for his beautiful revenge,
As he who waits well for the right place and time;

<margin>The art used by Love to make him fall in love.</margin>
<meta>34</meta>
And with his hands, out of light air, he fashioned
The image of a proud and beautiful hind,
With a high forehead, with branching horns,
Completely white, graceful and slender.
And as she offered herself among the fearful beasts
To the young hunter,
Happily, he spurred his steed to follow her,
Thinking in a short time to give her bitter suffering.

He drew his faithful sword from its sheath,
And with such fury moved his steed...

That the thick wood seemed like a wide, open road.

"He girds himself with his sword" <note>original Latin: "accingitur ense"</note> Virgil. — v. 4. Iulio ran with his horse so headlong that it seemed he was on an open and free road, and not in a thick wood where running is difficult. — * v. 7. Variant: *How much it seems* <note>original Italian: "Quanto par"</note>: Riccardi Manuscripts. — v. 8. "To take or gain ground: to prepare oneself for combat by making room for battle, or to move back in order to attack with greater force." Dictionary of the Crusca.

**Stanza 36.** — v. 2. * HE IS INFLAMED <note>original Italian: "S' ACCENDE"</note>: this is used like the verb "to burn," meaning to desire ardently: "where you burn to return," as seen in Dante. And in Horace the verb "to rage" <note>original Latin: "furere"</note> is used similarly: "Behold, fierce Tydides rages to find you" <note>original Latin: "Ecce furit te reperire atrox Tydides"</note>; this specific use of the verb "to be inflamed" is missing from the Dictionary. — v. 3. "To press tracks" <note>original Latin: "Vestigia premere"</note> was a phrase also used by the Latin authors. — v. 5. * Variant: *at the lip* <note>original Italian: "a labro"</note>: Riccardi Manuscripts. — v. 7. * <term>FRUIT</term> <note>original Italian: "POME"</note>: "That sweet fruit which through so many branches" from Dante's *Purgatory* XXVII; "... that dear fruit comes" from Alamanni’s *Cultivation* III; and Vettori uses it in prose. The ancients sometimes used the ending *e* even for singular nominative nouns of the third declension to make them match those of the first and second. See Nannucci, *Theory of Nouns*. — Variant: *and the fruit* <note>original Italian: "e il pomo"</note>: D. S.

->## THE JOUST.<-

<margin>How Iulio was caught.</margin>

The beast vanished away from before his eyes;
But the youth no longer cares for the beast,
Instead, he pulls the reins tight on his steed,
And brings him to a halt upon the greenery.
There, filled entirely with wonder,
He stares fixedly at the form of the nymph:
It seems to him that from her lovely face and eyes
A new sweetness snows down upon his heart.

<margin>Comparison.</margin>

Like a tiger, from whose stony den
The hunter has stolen her dear cubs;
Furious, she follows him through the Hyrcanian forest,
Believing she will soon blood her claws;
Then she stops before the empty shadow of a mirror,
Before the shadow that seems to resemble her young;
And while the foolish beast falls in love with such a sight,
The predator devours the road.

---

*Stanza 38.* — *v. 1.* Variant: **vanished** <note>original Italian: "sparve"</note>: Common edition. — *v. 4.* **Greenery** <note>original Italian: "Verdura"</note>: the green grass of meadows or fields: Dante. "the spray / That spreads itself over the greenery." — *v. 6. Still/Fixedly* <note>original Italian: "Pur"</note>: nevertheless, from the Latin *iugiter* <note>meaning: continually or incessantly</note>. Boccaccio X, 10: "Still standing with a hard face, he said." Dante, Purgatory V: "to look out of wonder / Just at me, just at me." — Variant: **Him entirely** <note>original Italian: "Lui tutto"</note>: some old editions. — *v. 7-8.* Lucretius: "The drop of Venus's sweetness flowed into the heart" <note>original Latin: "Veneris dulcedinis in cor Manavit gutta"</note>: and Tasso in the Rimes: "And a happy ray seems / To burn in your beautiful eyes / Whence peace and sweetness and joy snow down." — Variant: **the heart it touches** <note>original Italian: "il cor gli tocchi"</note>: Riccardi Manuscript 1576.

*Stanza 39.* — This simile of the tiger whose children are taken away has been treated by various authors, both Latin and Tuscan; Silius Italicus, *Punica* XII; Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* I; Petrus Apollonius, *The Destruction of Jerusalem* III; Magnus Felicius Ennodius, *Poems* I, 9. But our author imitated it from Claudian's *The Rape of Proserpina* III: "Thus high Niphates <note>A mountain range in Armenia</note> is shaken by the Hyrcanian mother, whose cubs—a mockery for the Persian king—the trembling rider has carried away: she rages, swifter than her mate the West Wind, and scatters her wrath across her striped spots; just as she is about to swallow the man in her deep maw, she is slowed by the glass image of her own form." <note>original Latin: "Arduus hircana quatitur sic matre Niphates, Cuius, achæmenio regi ludibria, natos Avexit tremebundus eques: furit illa marito Mobilior zephyro, totamque virentibus iras Dispersit maculis; iam iamque haustura profundo Ore virum, vitrea tardatur imagine formæ."</note> Among the Tuscans, Ariosto used it in *Orlando Furioso* XVIII, 35, though without the idea of the mirror; and it had already been used by Lorenzo de' Medici, from whom Poliziano took even some of the rhymes: "Like the hunter who cunningly / Steals the dear cubs from the fierce tiger, / And although he takes a great lead ahead, / The beast, swiftest by nature, / Nearly reaches him and bloodies her claws; / But seeing her own image / In the mirror she finds on the sand, / She believes it is her son, and checks her course." — *v. 1.* Variant: **stony** <note>original Italian: "petrosa"</note>: D. S. Common edition. — *v. 2.* Variant: **hunter the dear** <note>original Italian: "cacciator i cari"</note>: D. S. **hunter his dear** <note>original Italian: "cacciator suoi cari"</note>: Common edition. — *v. 8. Devours the road*, a Latin phrase. Catullus: "He will devour the road." <note>original Latin: "Viam vorabit."</note>

"...she would seem like Pallas, if she carried the shield; if the spears, Phoebe <note>Diana</note>:" Ovid in the *Heroides*. <note>original: "videri Pallas, si clypeum ferret; si spicula, Phoebe"</note> "Take up the lyre and the quiver, you will become the manifest Apollo: Add horns to your head, you will be Bacchus." <note>original: "Sume fidem et pharetram, fies manifestus Apollo: Accedant capiti cornua, Bacchus eris."</note> — verses 5-6. * "Pride and Anger flee before her" Dante. <note>original: "Fuggon dinanzi a lei Superbia ed Ira"</note> "Anger and torment departed before you" Bembo. <note>original: "Dinanzi a te partiva Ira e tormento"</note> — *Basta* <note>stands/endures</note>, lasts, holds up. — verse 7. ## BOOK ONE.

She was seated upon the greenery <margin>47</margin>
Joyful, and she had woven a little garland
Of as many flowers as nature ever created,
With which her dress was painted.
And as soon as she took notice of the youth,
Somewhat fearful, she raised her head:
Then with her white hand she took up the hem,
And rose to her feet with a lap full of flowers.

Already she was setting off to depart from there <margin>48</margin>
The nymph, very slowly over the grass,
Leaving the young man in great torment
Since nothing else now pleases him except her.
But the wretched man, unable to endure this,
Attempts to stop her with some prayer;
Wherefore, all trembling and all burning,
He thus humbly began, saying:

"holy lights that make the air serene around them" and elsewhere "which brightened the sky around." * Guinicelli: "...if she appears... And one beautiful evening in Florence, when I was organizing these notes, I heard two country boys in the most remote parts of the city singing: "Where you pass, the grass is born; / It looks like a flowering spring;" which are more beautiful than the two lines by Poliziano.

<note>The following notes are scholarly commentary on the verses above, tracing Poliziano’s literary influences.</note>

v. 3-4. **Petrarch:** <note>Francesco Petrarca, the 14th-century poet who defined the Italian love sonnet.</note> « ...sweetly consumes and wastes me away. » * **The comparison of the frost** is a well-worn theme in Petrarch and the <term>Petrarchists</term> <note>Poets who imitated Petrarch’s style and themes.</note>: let us hear it in a folk song from Mount Amiata: « My heart wastes away like the frost. » — v. 6. **Theocritus:** <note>An ancient Greek pastoral poet.</note> « Alas, alas, cruel Love, why do you suck all the black blood from my body, clinging to me like a marsh leech? » * **And Casa:** <note>Giovanni della Casa, a 16th-century poet and diplomat.</note> « So burning a thought sits in my heart... That I fear it sucks the spirits from every vein. » — v. 8. « This one fear, that one shame prevents. » <note>original Latin: "Timor hoc, pudor impedit illud."</note> **Ovid’s Metamorphoses.**

**Stanza 58.** — v. 2. * **Variant: magnificent, the precepts:** D. S. <note>Refers to a specific manuscript or scholarly edition.</note> — v. 4. * **Variant: more [than] to hunt:** D. S. — v. 5-8. * Thus the Riccardian Manuscripts and the old editions: but the Author corrected or rather spoiled it, followed by D. and S. and the Vulgate <note>The standard printed version of the text.</note>, thus: *Now behold, a woman holds in her hand the keys / To all your desires, and all held tight in her / She keeps... See that now you are not who you were just a moment ago.* — * **WOMAN [WITH] THE KEYS IN HER HAND.** To have, keep, or carry the key or keys of a heart or something else; it is an image that our ancient poets had in common with the <term>Provençals</term> <note>Medieval poets from southern France who invented the tradition of courtly love.</note>, to signify mastery or the power of persuasion over that heart. See also stanza 46, verse 2. **Arnaldo di Marsiglia** « Love has taken the keys of me: » **Petrarch** « Of my heart, lady, you have one and the other key in hand » and « those beautiful sweet eyes which carried the keys of my thoughts: » also, he calls the woman « Sweet key of my heart. » Better than Petrarch and Poliziano, a folk song from Pistoia says of the beloved, the lady says: « I carry the keys of his heart in my breast. » v. 8. **Variant:** *who you are now* : see stanza.

**Stanza 59.** — v. 3. **YOU WERE YOUR OWN**, a Greek phrase, « I am yours » <note>original Greek: "sòs eimì"</note>: the Latins also have it; **Ovid:** « But I am yours, and with you... »

They see the sky covered in shadows;

These wretched folk no longer know what to do.

<meta>Commentary notes in two-column layout</meta>

...they flow together and then merge into one bed, or those in which they branch out as they discharge into the sea; perhaps named for the curvature. Serdonati: "The Indus discharges into the sea with two horns." <note>In classical geography, "horns" refers to the various branches of a river delta.</note> — **v. 3.** * That is: the point where the horizon first reddens in the morning; which is to say, the east. Variation: *At the first* <note>original: "Al primo"</note>: D. S. Volg. — **v. 4.** * Variation: *to the mortal* <note>original: "al mortal"</note>: Riccardian Manuscript 1576 and the old printings. — * **SITS** <note>original: "SIEDE"</note>, used to denote its position on a flat plain. "The land where I was born sits upon the coast" (Dante); "Paris sits in a great plain" (Ariosto). "The camp of Nola sits" <note>original Latin: "Campo Nola sedet"</note> (Silius Italicus, Book XII). — * **PLAYFUL** <note>original: "LASCIVE"</note>. In the Latin sense, *playful* describes a motion or a turn that is not rapid, but winding and almost teasing. — This stanza is taken almost entirely from Claudian, *Epithalamium of Honorius and Maria*: "A steep mountain on the eastern side of Cyprus casts a shadow, impassable to human step, and looks down upon the Pharian bed of Proteus and the seven horns of the Nile... Its summit spreads out into a plain." <note>original Latin: "Mons latus eoum Cypri præruptus obumbrat Invius humano gressu, Phariumque cubile Proteos et septem despectat cornua Nili... In campum se fundet apex."</note> (* Where Gesner notes that this mountain must be understood as located in the easternmost part of Cyprus, from which one more directly perceives the east on one side and the South or the mouths of the Nile on the other: this applies to our Author as well.) And Petrarch, in *The Triumph of Love IV*, thus described the island of Cyprus: "Beyond it lies, where the Aegean sighs and weeps, a delicate and soft little island, more so than any other warmed by the sun or bathed by the sea. In the middle is a shady and green hill, with such sweet scents and such sweet waters that it takes every masculine thought from the soul."

**Stanza 71.** — **v. 1.** * **CROWNS** <note>original: "CORONA"</note>: to surround or encircle: Lucretius, Book VI: "Myrtle groves crown the lake." <note>original Latin: "Lacum myrteta coronant."</note> *Inferno XXXI*: "Monteriggioni crowns itself with towers." — **v. 2. SLENDER SHRUBS** <note>original: "SCHIETTI ARBUSCELLI"</note>: Petrarch: "Slender shrubs and green, bitter foliage," where the critic Castelvetro notes: *slender* <note>original: "schietti"</note>, used as an epithet for the beauty of small trees that show they are destined to grow. * I would understand it as smooth, clean, without knots; according to that of Dante: "Not slender branches, but knotted and twisted," and Dante called the reed *slender* <note>original: "schietto"</note> (*Purgatory I*); and Petrarch: "a young and slender laurel." — **v. 3.** * **NEW** <note>original: "NOVELLE"</note>, fresh, recently sprouted: "new flowers" (Lorenzo de' Medici); "new grove" (Petrarch). — **v. 4.** "And upon the trees little birds speak sweetly" (Theocritus). — **v. 5.** "They resound with a sweet murmuring of—" <meta>The sentence is interrupted as the page ends.</meta>

---

"...strikes and marries the soil with fertile dew. Wherever he flies, spring color follows; all the earth swells into grass, and the arched sky lies open in mid-serenity: he clothes the roses in blood-red splendor, the blueberries in black, and paints the violets with a sweet dusky hue." <note>This Latin passage is likely a source text by Claudian, a 4th-century poet, whose descriptions of nature Poliziano is imitating here.</note>

**Stanza 78.** — **v. 5.** **GREEN BUD.** <note>original: "verde gemma"</note> Variant: *green buds*. The commentator Fornaciari explains these are "the buds or the buttons within which the roses stay wrapped before opening." — **IS CAPPED.** <note>original: "s'incappella"</note> **To cap**, to put on a hat, to cover. Dante uses this in *Paradise*, Canto XXXII: "it is fitting that she be capped." It is as if the rose makes a hat for itself out of that green, prominent skin that wraps it before it blooms. This phrasing also pleased the poet Caro, who, speaking of a mountain, said: "With snow it proudly caps itself." And the historian Botta described Mount Spluga as "a mountain eternally capped with snow." — **v. 6.** That is, it begins to open or bloom. We hear here the imitation of a Latin epigram: "The first was showing nipple-like buds... the second raised its crimson tips... the third had not yet opened the full circle of its cup... the fourth shone forth, its floral covering changed. While one raises its head, and another unfolds its knot..." <note>The Latin source is from the *Anthologia Latina*, describing the various stages of a rose's growth.</note>

**Stanza 79.** — **v. 1. LOVING CLOUD:** understand this to mean the dew. — **v. 2.** Variant: *blood-red and white*. — **v. 3. Ovid, Metamorphoses.** "He himself inscribes his groans upon the leaves, and the flower has <term>ai ai</term> <note>A Greek exclamation of grief, "alas, alas."</note> inscribed upon it, and the mournful letter is drawn." And in the works of Theocritus, the hyacinth is called "inscribed." Moschus, in his poem on the death of Bion, addressing this flower, says: "Now, o hyacinth, express your letters, and more fully welcome the <term>ahi ahi</term> <note>The Italian spelling of the Greek cry of woe.</note> into your petals." According to the poets, Hyacinth was a youth who, while playing at disc-throwing with the god Apollo, was accidentally killed; from his blood, the god caused a flower of this name to rise, which sometimes seems to have the word *ai* (an expression of pain) written on its leaves. — **v. 4.** **NARCISSUS** was an exceedingly handsome youth who, having once seen himself in a spring, became so captivated by his own beauty that he could no longer tear himself away.

...dear from gazing at himself, and there on the margin of that spring he died little by little of love for himself; and was changed into a flower that loves to grow along the streams (Fornaciari.) — **v. 6. * Clytie** was a nymph in love with the sun: she was changed into the flower called **heliotrope**, which is equivalent to the sunflower (Fornaciari.) <note>original: "Est in parte rubor, violæque simillimus ora Flos tegit: illa suum, quamvis radice tenetur, Vertitur ad solem" (In part it is red, and a flower very like a violet covers her face; she, though held by a root, turns toward her sun) — Ovid, Metamorphoses IV.</note> — **v. 7. * Adonis**, a young hunter, very dear to the goddess Venus, having been killed by a wild boar, from his blood was born a flower called the **anemone** or windflower. (Fornaciari.) — *v.* 5. \* Variant: *distills* <note>original: "destilla"</note>: *old editions A. D. S.* — *v.* 6. It returns the reward to the trees for their shade by fertilizing them as it flows around their roots, so that they grow more flourishing and beautiful.

Tasso, *Jerusalem Delivered* XVIII: "It [the river channel] bathes the woods, and the woods shade the river, with a beautiful exchange between them of moisture and shade." <note>original: "Bagna egli (il canale d'un fiume) il bosco, e il bosco il fiume adombra Con bel cambio tra lor d' umore e d' ombra."</note> \* Variant: *That reward* <note>original: "Che premio"</note>: *D.* — *v.* 7. \* **Each tree takes nourishment from the indicated streamlet.** (Fornaciari.)

**Stanza 82.** — *v.* 1. The fir is without knots from the middle down, whence also Ovid: "and the knotless fir" <note>original: "enodisque abies"</note>: toward the top it is knotty and hard. Monti says of the pine (*Feron.* III): "Born to defy on the watery waves the tempestuous assaults of the African and East Winds." — *v.* 3. "Holm-oak full of honeycombs" <note>original: "Ilex plena favis"</note> Claudian, *Rape of Proserpine*. \* Bees make their honeycombs in the cavities of the holm-oak (Fornaciari.) — *v.* 4. \* Alludes to the custom of crowning victors and poets with laurel (Fornaciari.) — *v.* 5. \* **Cypress** or...

Cyparissus was, according to the poets, a youth who, having accidentally killed his beautiful pet stag, fell into such grief that he would have died, had not Apollo taken pity on him and transformed him into the tree of that name (Fornaciari.) * ... 
> He groans nonetheless; and he seeks this final gift from the gods above, that he might mourn for all time... He groaned, and the sad god (Apollo) said: "You shall be mourned by us, and you shall mourn others, and you shall be present for those in pain." <note>original: "Gemit ille tamen; munusque supremum Hoc petit a superis ut tempore lugeat omni ... Ingemuit, tristisque deus (Apollo): Lugebere nobis, lugebisque alios, aderisque dolentibus; inquit."</note>

<note>Ovid, Metamorphoses X.</note> — verse 6. * So we read in the Florentine manuscripts; with the Chigi [Roman edition 1804]; with the Oliveriano by testimony of Betti in the place cited. Incorrectly, following Aldo, the Vulgate (excepting Dolce and Sermartelli, who were judicious this time) reads: **Now already outstretched and blond.** <note>original: "Or già distese e bionde."</note> Regarding which Fornaciari says: "It means that when Cyparissus was not a tree but a boy, he had outstretched and blond hair: now he has it rough. The common editions have *now already* instead of *and already*: an error I corrected based on the 1503 edition." Reading as our text and Fornaciari do, our verse corresponds to what Ovid says of Cyparissus: 
> "And the hair that just now hung from his snow-white forehead becomes a bristling forest." <note>original: "Et modo qui nivea pendebant fronte capilli Horrida caesaries fieri."</note> 

— verse 7. * **Tree** <note>original: "Arbor"</note> is read by D. and S. and the Vulgate along with A., and incorrectly. "Tree" <note>original: "Albero"</note> is specifically the poplar, as in Ariosto (III, 25): "With a great branch of a stripped poplar;" and Sannazaro: "the tree with which Hercules used to fall in love." Virgil: 
> "The poplar most pleasing to Hercules" <note>original: "Populus Alcidae gratissima"</note> 

and 
> "and the shady tree of the Herculean crown." <note>original: "Herculeaeque arbos umbrosa coronae."</note> 

— verse 8. * It is known that poplars and plane trees love damp places (Fornaciari.) 
> "The plane tree delights in the stream" <note>original: "Platanus rivo gaudet"</note> 

<note>Ovid.</note>

**Stanza 83.** — verse 2. * <term>Pliant</term> <note>original: "Lento"</note>. "It amazes me that all dictionaries lack the word <term>pliant</term> in the sense in which the Latins said 'pliant viburnum,' 'pliant broom'; in which meaning—that is, of bendable or flexible—it is used in Poliziano Stanza 83; it is in Alamanni's *Cultivation*: 'the pliant broom... the pliant willow;' it is in Rucellai: '...pliant willows;' it is in Ariosto XXIX: '...a soft and pliant thicket of brambles and greenery.' And Molza... 'a graceful and pliant branch.'" (Fornaciari, notes on the *Discourse on the excessive rigor of grammarians*.) Manuzzi inserted into his Vocabulary the examples brought by Fornaciari; to which one could add one from Caro who translates the Virgilian "pliant willow branch" <note>original: "lento vimine ramus"</note> as "a pliant branch." — verse 3. * Variant **wilder**: A. D. S. Vulgate. — verse 4. Rams, Ewes.</margin>

The rams arm their horns against one another;
One butts another and one hammers another
In front of the amorous ewe.

And the lowing bullocks at the foot of the hill <margin>86</margin>

With bloody and wet necks and chests,
Scattering the grassy earth to the sky with their feet.
<margin>Wild Boar.</margin>
Full of bloody foam, the wild boar seethes,
He whets his broad tusks and snaps his snout;
He roars and scrapes, and to arm his strength
He rubs his calloused hide against hard bark.

---

—always green according to the botanists (<note>original: "Perpetuoque virens buxus"</note> "And the boxwood, perpetually green" Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X), it has curly leaves and branches so thick and close together that they cannot be distinguished. — verse 3. **HIS GODDESS**, Venus, to whom it was sacred: <note>original: "Formosae myrtus Veneri"</note> "The myrtle is for beautiful Venus" Virgil. — verse 6. <note>original: "Inter se adversis luctantur cornibus"</note> "They struggle against each other with opposing horns" Virgil, *Georgics* III.

**Stanza 86.** — verse 1-4. <note>original: "Illi alternantes multa vi proelia miscent..."</note> "They join battle with great force, alternating blows: dark blood washes their bodies: and with horns turned against each other they press on with a massive groan" Virgil, *Georgics* III: and further down, regarding the defeated bullock preparing for new fights, <note>original: "Et temptat sese atque irasci in cornua discit..."</note> "And he tests himself and learns to throw his anger into his horns, leaning against the trunk of a tree, and lashes out at the winds with strikes, and rehearses for the fight by scattering sand." **Tasso**, *Jerusalem Delivered* VII, with little variation: "... the bull... bellows horribly, and with his bellows he awakens the spirits and burning rages within himself; and he whets his horn against the trunks, and seems to invite the winds to battle with vain blows; he scatters the sand with his foot, and challenges his rival from afar to a harsh and mortal war." And G. B. Lapini, imitating our author: "And the miserable bullock, never satisfied, sees his chest and neck become bloody." — verse 4-8. <note>original: "Spuinas agit ore cruentas"</note> "He drives bloody foam from his mouth" Virgil; and elsewhere: <note>original: "Ipse ruit dentesque sabellicus exacuit sus..."</note> "The Sabellian boar himself rushes forth and sharpens his teeth, and paws the ground with his foot, rubs his ribs against a tree, and hardens his shoulders on this side and that against wounds." Apollonius, Book I: <note>original: "rabidas excolligit iras..."</note> "He gathers his raging anger first in his mouth and whets his teeth, and bristling with stiff hair, he tests his strength against the hard trunks: white foam is spread through his crooked jaws." And Hesiod, in the *Shield of Hercules*, with more efficacy: "... Like a wild boar in the wooded valleys of a mountain, fierce to behold, with teeth protruding from his mouth, who turns in his mind to fight with the hunters, and crouching, whets his white tusk; and the foam drips around his mouth as he mashes it, and his eyes are like shining fire; horrific for the bristles standing straight on his back and around his neck." — 7. Variation: *rugge* [roars]: the stanzas.

**Vernacular Edition (Chigi)** (Roman edition, 1804) reads the same as our text. — **Rhymes**: songs. Dante, *Purgatory* XXVIII: "the little birds... with full joy the early hours / Singing, received among the leaves / Which held the bass-note to their rhymes." <note>original: "gli augelletti... con piena letizia l’ ore prime Cantando, riceveano intra le foglie Che tenevan bordone alle sue rime."</note> — verse 6. **Metaphorically** it means that human thought cannot reach the point of understanding all its high sweetness (*notes so blessed and so sublime*.) — verse 8. **THEY LEAP FROM BRANCH TO BRANCH**. Theocritus: "they fly from branch to branch." <note>original: "volano in ramo da ramo."</note> — **Variant** *at their pleasure*: old style.

**Stanza 91.** — verse 1. **SONG OF THE FOREST**: the song of the birds upon the trees of the forest is attributed to the forest itself: thus, even more boldly, Pindemonte writes: "The valley bellows, the hill bleats." <note>original: "La valle mugolar, belare il colle."</note> — verse 2. Horace, *Odes* II, 3: "They love to interlace a hospitable shade with their branches." <note>original: "Umbram hospitalem consociare amant Ramis."</note> — verse 3. **Hums**. *To hum* <note>term: Rombare—to make a noise, a buzzing, or a deep whistling sound</note>, by likeness to the noise made by wasps, bees, hornets, and also things thrown and pulled through the air with violence. Veronese additions. Even Caro says it of a bird: "... it came with wings humming as it brushed past." *The Shepherd's Love*. — verse 4. Phaedrus: "You unfold your jeweled tail." <note>original: "Genmeam caudam explicas."</note> Martial: "He unfolds his jeweled wings." <note>original: "Gemmatas explicat alas."</note> — verse 5. Ovid, *The Loves* II, 7: "The alluring dove gives kisses to her eager mate;" <note>original: "Oscula dat cupido blanda columba mari;"</note> and Tasso, *Aminta*: "Look there at that dove / With what sweet whispering and coaxing / He kisses his companion." — verse 6. **SHORE** <note>term: Proda—the edge of the land, particularly the bank of a river.</note>. — **Variant** *The white*: Comin. and Vernacular editions. — verse 7-8. That the parrot joins with the turtle-dove is asserted by Pliny: hence Ovid in the letter from Sappho to Phaon: "And the black turtle-dove is loved by the green bird." <note>original: "Et niger a viridi turtur amatur ave."</note> — **SQUAWKS**: *To squawk* <note>term: Squittire—to shriek intermittently with a thin, sharp voice</note>; it is specific to hounds when they flush out or follow wild beasts... and by metaphor it is transferred to humans and other animals. V. C.

**Stanza 92.** — verse 1. **WINGED BROTHERS**: "Winged boys everywhere" <note>original: "Pinnati passim pueri"</note> Claudian. —

You would see the goddess flashing from her eyes,

* So read the Riccardian Manuscripts, all the old editions, and also by the testimony of Betti, the Oliverian and Chigian manuscripts (Roman edition, 1804). But A. D. S. and the Vulgate read: *He who has his head of cypress... and only girdled with little grass.* <note>original Italian: "Lo quale ha di cipresso il capo... e sol d'erbetta cinto."</note>
Betti observes: "'Little grass' means nothing; but the name *ivy* <note>original: "edera"</note> has in itself a very clear sense of mythological erudition. Certainly Poliziano intended here to denote the status of a forest-dweller and the eternal youth of that Ganymede, whose name was said to come from *ganos*, which in Greek means *joy* <note>original Greek: "γάνος"</note>. And he meant to signify the first quality with the crown of cypress, a plant sacred to Silvanus <note>a Roman tutelary deity of woods and fields</note>;... the second he indicated by the belt of ivy, which is a plant always young and alive. Therefore the ancients crowned Bacchus with it, whom they also depicted as always young; and they made garlands of it for the Muses; indeed... those who in Sparta sanctified the Hyacinthian festivals in honor of Apollo adorned themselves with it likewise. — *v.* 1-8.
Jupiter violated Leda under the form of a swan: he changed himself into a rain of gold for Danae; into a serpent for Proserpina; under the guise of a shepherd he violated Mnemosyne. * In the *Metamorphoses*, Arachne embroiders these thefts of Jupiter into her tapestries: "She depicted Leda reclining beneath swan's wings..., how as a golden fire he deceived the daughter of Asopus <note>Danae</note>, as a shepherd Mnemosyne, as a variegated serpent the daughter of Deo <note>Proserpina</note>." <note>original Latin: "Fecit olorinis Ledam recubare sub alis..., Aureus ut Danaen Asopida luserit ignis, Mnemosynem pastor, varius Deoida serpens."</note>

Virgil: <note>original Latin: "Et molli circum est ansas amplexus acantho."</note> "*And the soft acanthus has embraced the handles all around.*" "It is a plant which shoots from its root several wide, beautiful, deeply-cut leaves, the ends of which curl naturally; and which, due to the height, thickness, and flexibility of its stem, is suited to be woven into garlands, ornaments, and the like. Hence the custom of sculpting its form in the capitals of columns of the so-called Corinthian order, on vases, etc.; and of weaving it into garments, veils, and the like. The shape of this plant therefore surrounded the sculptures described above, with interlacings of myrtles, roses, and other flowers." (Fornaciari)

Above and all around, the little Loves
Played naked, flying here and there:
And one, with wings of a thousand colors,
Went about fanning the scattered roses:
Another filled his quiver with fresh flowers,

<margin>124</margin>

Thus the drifting roses were caught again:
No one was tired of this playful frolicking.
When Cupid appeared with wings outstretched,
All out of breath, and around his mother’s neck
He threw himself, and with his wings he fanned the fire in her heart;
Joyful in appearance, and so weary that he barely
Could catch his breath enough to speak.

<note>The following notes provide historical context and literary parallels for the stanzas above, originally presented in a two-column layout.</note>

This scene was imitated by Berni at the beginning of the second book of *Orlando Innamorato*: "When you have him in your lap to lie down, to feed his greedy eyes upon your beautiful face." — verse 5. **CLOUD** (NEMBO), used here to mean a multitude or great number, a style frequently used by Latin authors. <note>original Latin: "... Nec blandus Amor nec Gratia cessat Amplexum virides optatæ coniugis artus Floribus innumeris et olenti spargere nymbo."</note> "Neither charming Love nor Grace ceases to scatter the green limbs of the desired wife with countless flowers and a fragrant cloud." (Statius, *Silvae*). Claudian, writing of Stilicho: <note>original Latin: "... nec signifer ullus Nec miles pluviæ flores dispergere ritu Cessat purpureoque ducem perfundere nimbo."</note> "...neither any standard-bearer nor soldier ceases to scatter flowers in the manner of rain and to drench the leader with a purple cloud."

**Stanza 123.** — verse 1. Statius, in the place cited above: <note>original Latin: "Fulcra torosque deæ tenerum premit agmen amorum."</note> "A tender crowd of loves presses upon the bedposts and couches of the goddess." — verse 2. # THE JOUST.

<margin>Words of Venus to Cupid.</margin>
— Whence do you come, son? Or what news do you bring? — 125
Venus said to him, and kissed his face:
Whence comes this sweat of yours? What trials have you performed?
What god, what man have you entangled in your snares?
Are you making Jove bellow again in Tyre?
Or Saturn growl on thick-wooded Pelion?
Whatever this may be, it seems no humble thing to me,
O son, O my only power and weapons.

**Stanza 2.** — v. 1-2. Corresponds to that passage by Claudian: « Rejoice, parent: we have brought back a huge trophy. » <note>original Latin: "Lætare, parens: immane trophæum Retulimus."</note> — v. 3. To take someone from the **choir of Diana** means to bring them under the power of Love; to be in Diana’s choir is to remain in a state of virginity. Thus Catullus: « We are in the protection of Diana, pure girls and boys. » <note>original Latin: "Dianæ sumus in fide Puellæ et pueri integri."</note> Callimachus has Diana say to Jove: « Grant me, father, to keep my perpetual virginity; » <note>original Greek: "Dos moi parthenien aioonion, appa, phylassein;"</note> translated by Ovid: « Grant me, my dearest father, he said, to enjoy perpetual virginity. » <note>original Latin: "Da mihi perpetua, genitor charissime, dixit, Virginitate frui."</note> — v. 6. *THE FAME CRIES OUT*: « Fame, which honors your house, cries out (celebrates) the lords, and cries out the district. » Dante, *Purgatorio*. — v. 7. *INDIANS*; used mostly by poets to signify the peoples of the East in general. — *OLD ATLAS*; Atlas, brother of Prometheus and king of Mauritania, whom myths say held up the heavens on his shoulders; he was changed into a mountain in the interior of Libya. Virgil: « ... there lies a land beyond the stars, beyond the paths of the year and the sun, where heaven-bearing Atlas turns the axis on his shoulder, fitted with burning stars. » <note>original Latin: "... iacet extra sidera tellus, Extra anni solisque vias, ubi cælifer Atlas Axem humero torquet stellis ardentibus aptum."</note>

Cosimo, nicknamed the <term>Father of the Fatherland (Pater Patriae)</term>, who, according to Leandro Alberti, was held in such high regard in this city (Florence) that he could dispose of it as he saw fit. He died in 1464; and was buried with this inscription: <term>BY PUBLIC DECREE, TO THE FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND</term> <note>original Latin: "DECRETO PUBLICO PATRI PATRIÆ"</note>. — v. 6. <gloss>* Variant: Added to it: Riccardian Codex 2723.</gloss>

* **THE WICKED HANDS** of the citizens intended to bring him harm, or rather to do away with Piero de’ Medici. These were the Pitti, the Acciaiuoli, the Neroni, and the Soderini; who in 1466, having brought the army of Borso, Marquis of Ferrara, onto the territory of the republic, sought to kill Piero and seize the government from the Medici. Discovered through the efforts of Lorenzo, they were banished—with the exception of Luca Pitti, who abandoned the faction.

*Stanza 4.* — *v. 1.* **LUCREZIA** Tornabuoni. — *v. 3.* We know from Valori (biographer of Lorenzo) that this Lucrezia was of the noble Donati family, equally distinguished for her beauty as for her virtues, and a descendant of Corso Donati... The circumstances of Lorenzo's love for this Lucrezia are described in detail in the *Commentary* on the first sonnet he wrote in her honor. (*See Poems of Lorenzo de’ Medici*, Barbèra, 1859, pages 35-63; and the preface to that work.) — *v. 4.* <gloss>Variant: "she is harsh": A. D. S. Vulgate.</gloss> — *v. 5.* <gloss>Variant: "than in Rome": A. D. S. Vulgate.</gloss> — **LUCREZIA**, the wife of Collatinus. — *v. 6. Daphne.* — *v. 8.* The poet repeats the same rhymes throughout the entire octave; <note>A poetic challenge where the words at the end of the lines remain the same (Lucrezia, Lauro, occhi)</note> just as Dante does out of reverence in the tercets of the *Paradiso* where he names Christ, Ariosto by necessity in stanza 45 of Canto XXVII, and Anguillara for the sake of eccentricity in Book I of the *Metamorphoses*.

*Stanza 5.* — *v. 1.* Ugolino Verini in his *Fiammetta* addresses an elegy to the aforementioned Lucrezia <note>Donati</note>, in which he seeks to make her feel pity for Lorenzo. — *v. 2.* Virgil: « The iron tower stands toward the breezes. » <note>original Latin: "Stat ferrea turris ad auras."</note> — *Purgatorio*, Canto V: « Stand, like a firm tower, that never shakes its top for the blowing of the winds. » <note>original Italian: "Sta, come torre ferma, che non crolla Giammai sua cima per soffiar di venti."</note> — *v. 3-4.* The golden arrow is the one that causes one to fall in love, and the leaden shafts cause one to flee from love. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I: « From his arrow-bearing quiver he drew two darts of different effects: this one puts love to flight, that one creates it. The one that creates it is golden and shines with a sharp point; the one that puts it to flight is blunt and has lead beneath... » <note>original Latin: "Deque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra, Diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem: Quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta... Quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub [plumbeo]..."</note>

<margin>Comparison.</margin>
Enough to make a stone become a lover,
Not just you, Mars; and such fire glows in her eyes,
As usually does in the beautiful, flaming Aurora <note>The Roman goddess of the dawn</note>:
Then she gathers her son close to her breast,
And stroking his blonde hair with her hand,

<margin>Venus’s second reply.</margin>
— Greatly, fair son, does your desire please me, 14
So that our glory might spread its wings ever further,
And he who wanders might return to the true path.
It is an obligation to serve one who commands well.
Yet it is necessary that Lauro <note>A poetic name for Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici</note> should take the field once more
And crown himself with a new garland;
For virtue shines more brightly in hardships,
Just as gold glows more brilliantly in the fire.

<margin>Note that the author, at the time he composed this, was reading Homer.</margin>
But first it is necessary that Iulio <note>Giuliano de' Medici</note> arms himself, 15
So that he may fulfill the world’s expectations of our fame.
And one who now sings of the arms of the brave Achilles <note>A reference to Poliziano himself, who was translating Homer's Iliad into Latin at the time</note>
And renews the ancient times with his style,
Shall become the weaver of our songs,
Singing of these examples of love;
Whereby, O fair son, we shall see our glory
Fly high above the stars.

<note>The following notes are presented in two columns in the original text.</note>

**[Left Column]**

Line 3. **Focili.** <note>The steel used to strike flint.</note> Dante, *Inferno* XIV: "the sand caught fire, like tinder under the steel [focile]." Petrarch, metaphorically: "and the silent steel of love draws from there a thin liquid fire." Boccaccio’s Commentary on Dante: "The *fucile* is a steel instrument used to make sparks fly from stones, which we call flints [focaie], by striking them." — **Apprendere.** To attach oneself, to take hold. * Perhaps better: to ignite, to catch fire. It is used in this sense in the ancient classics; Guido Guinizzelli: "Fire of love in a gentle heart catches [s'apprende]." Italian translation of Ovid's *Heroides*: "I am caught [appresa] by love." However, the dictionaries have no examples of *apprendere* used intransitively in this absolute way; yet the people of Tuscany say "the fire has taken [ha preso]." — Line 4. * **Game of Mars,** meaning battle. Horace says to Mars in Ode 2 of Book I: "Alas! sated by too long a game" <note>original Latin: "Heu! nimis longo satiate ludo"</note>.

Stanza 19. — Line 2. * Thus in the old editions,

**[Right Column]**

the Riccardiano Manuscript 2723 and the Oliveriano edition cited by Betti: but A. [Anfossi], followed by D. S. and the Vulgate, corrected it to: *Of its power the earth is all pregnant.* Petrarch says the same thing in a different way: "When the planet that distinguishes the hours returns to dwell with the Bull [Taurus], power falls from the inflamed horns that clothes the world in new color... The terrestrial humor was pregnant with itself." — Line 3. Variant: "later Spring": A. D. S. Vulgate. — **Si stende,** unfolds. — Line 4. * **Insegna:** standard, banner; metaphorically alluding to the luxury of the greenery: or also, a sign or token. — Line 5. * Variant: "the fire," S; "breaks/cleaves," D. — Line 6. **S' abbarbica.** To take root; properly the clinging that plants do with their roots inside the earth. Here, it attaches itself. * Dino Compagni, III: "rooting [abbarbicare] the peace."

Stanza 20. — Line 2. Variant: "be dry": D.

<margin>It appeared to Julio.</margin>

->Notes on the Text<-

...of the night ("And our air and my mind grow dark" <note>original: "E l'aer nostro e la mia mente imbruna"</note> **Petrarch**), it is dark in the twilight. *Variant from the Bazal.* and some old editions: **or truly brown**. — **Starry chariot**. "Night leads the starry chariot in a circle" <note>original: "Notte il carro stellato in giro mena"</note> **Petrarch**. — **Icarus**, a star of the constellation Bootes: A. D. S. <note>Abbreviations for specific manuscript or editor names</note> read **bows to the West** <note>original: al Coro inchina</note>, meaning the chariot of Bootes that turns toward the sunset, as the *Coro* or *Cauro* is the western wind. — *verse 5.* *Variant: in heaven* <note>original: in ciel</note>: A. D. — *verse 6.* *Variant: revealing* <note>original: mostrando</note>: A. D. S. — *verse 7.* *Sweet at the entrance, too bitter at the exit* <note>original: Dolce all'entrar, all'uscir troppo amara</note> reads the Riccardiano Code 2723; the old editions: ***Sweet at the start, then too bitter at the end***.

**Stanza 28**. — *verse 2.* **Arrogant** <note>original: Proterva</note>, here, differently from the 1st stanza, has the Italian sense of **proud** or at most **obstinate**. **Dante**: "Regally in her gesture still arrogant;" and **Machiavelli**: "You nonetheless remain arrogant and hard." — *verse 3.* **Column**, a metaphor for the stem or trunk of a tree: there are no examples of this in the Vocabularies. — *verse 4.* The olive tree, sacred to that goddess. — *verse 6.* **Protects** <note>original: Conserva</note>, defends, guards. Understand it as: the dress (**gown**) which, together with the aegis of Minerva, covers and defends the chaste breast of the woman. But some old editions read **to the chaste** <note>original: al casto</note>: and then the meaning is obvious. — **Gorgon**, the shield of Minerva. **Virgil, Aeneid II**: "Pallas... shining from a cloud and fierce with the Gorgon:" and, **Book VIII**, "the entwined snakes and the Gorgon herself on the goddess's breast, turning her eyes with her neck severed." It was the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose hair Minerva changed into snakes because she had violated her temple; and according to **Ovid**: "Even now, to strike her enemies with terror and dread, she carries upon her breast the snakes she created." — 7-8. **Petrarch, Triumph of Chastity**: "... these (the companions of Laura) had broken the arrows and the quiver and the bow of that arrogant one, and plucked his wings." *Variant: plucks* <note>original: spennecchi</note>: old editions.

**Stanza 29**. — *verse 1-2.* **Aeneid II**: "Alas... [how much he was changed from that Hector...]"

Swallows in a Greek epigram are called "morning-chatterers" <note>original Greek: ὀρθολάλοις</note>; and **Anacreon** in an ode complains that his sweet sleep is stolen from him by their "pre-dawn voices" <note>original Greek: ὑπορθρίαισι φωναῖς</note>. **Stanza 46.** — **v. 4.** **LAMP**, splendor. <term>Lampas</term>, in Latin, refers to the splendor of the sun or the day: <note>original: "prima lustrabat lampade terras Orta dies"</note> “The rising day was illuminating the lands with its first lamp,” **Virgil**; and also, simply splendor: <note>original: "... ipse autem (somnus) nec lampade clara Nec sonitu nec voce Deæ perculsus, eodem More iacet."</note> “But Sleep himself, struck neither by the bright lamp nor by the sound or voice of the Goddess, lies in the same manner.” **Statius, Thebaid X.** The examples of *lamp* in this sense found in Italian vocabularies are perhaps not entirely fitting: here they are. **Dante, Paradiso XVII, 5:** “was heard by Beatrice and by the holy lamp;” here lamp is metaphorically the blessed soul. **Petrarch:** “One of the beautiful number of the wise blessed virgins, indeed the first and with a clearer lamp;” here *lamp* is a <term>lampada</term>, a vessel in which an oil light is kept burning. — **v. 5-6.** Understand: let every memory eternally preserve the image of my works. It is an imitation (though not perfectly exact) of Dante’s “Well marked by the internal stamp” and “Marked by the stamp, in his appearance, of that righteous zeal.” <note>Variant: "disdains us"</note> found in some old editions.

<meta>Following the blank physical transition in the manuscript, this page contains the formal introductory letter for the play "Orpheus" (Fabula di Orfeo). It establishes the circumstances under which the work was written.</meta>

# ANGELO POLIZIANO

## TO MESSER CARLO CANALE

### HIS GREETINGS <note>original: "SVO S." This is an abbreviation for the Latin *Suo Salutem*, a traditional greeting meaning "Sends his greetings."</note>

---

The Lacedemonians <note>The ancient Spartans, famous for their harsh discipline</note>, my most refined Messer Carlo, used to immediately expose any of their children born with a physical disability or weak constitution, rather than allowing them to be <gloss>1</gloss> kept alive, judging such a lineage unworthy of Sparta. Similarly, I also wished that the play of *Orpheus*—which I composed at the request of our most reverend Cardinal of Mantua <note>Francesco Gonzaga (1444–1483), a prominent patron of the arts</note> in the span of two <gloss>2</gloss> days, amidst constant turmoil, and in the vulgar tongue <term>vulgar tongue: Italian, the language of the common people, as opposed to the Latin typically used for serious scholarly work</term> so it might be <gloss>3</gloss> better understood by the spectators—should have been immediately torn apart, not unlike Orpheus himself. I recognized this daughter of mine <note>Poliziano metaphorically refers to the play as his child</note> to be of a quality more likely to bring shame than honor to her father, and more suited to cause him melancholy than joy. But seeing that <gloss>4</gloss> both you and several others who love me too much are keeping her alive against my will, it is necessary for me to have more respect for paternal love and for your wishes <gloss>5</gloss> than for my own reasonable purpose. You have, however, a just excuse for your desire; for, having been born under the protection of so merciful a lord, she deserves to be exempt from the common law. Let her live then, since it pleases you so: but I truly protest to you that such mercy is an outright cruelty, and I wish this letter to be witness to my judgment. And you, who know the necessity of my obedience and the brevity of the time, I pray that you use your authority to resist anyone <gloss>6</gloss> who would attribute the imperfection of such a daughter to her father. Farewell <note>original: "Vale"</note>.

---

| | |
|:---|:---|
| <gloss>1</gloss> *be/was*, according to the Comino edition. | <gloss>2</gloss> *two*, Riccardian Manuscript; *two*, Comino edition. |
| <gloss>3</gloss> *be better*, in the printed editions. | <gloss>4</gloss> *that you*, in the printed editions. |
| <gloss>5</gloss> In the Riccardian Manuscript, this section is missing from this point until "because being thus," etc. | |
| <gloss>6</gloss> *anyone*, in the printed editions; except for the first edition by Benedetti. | |

<summary>In this dedication letter, the scholar Angelo Poliziano expresses his reluctance to publish his play "Orpheus," which he wrote in just two days for the Cardinal of Mantua. He characterizes the work as a flawed "child" that he would have preferred to destroy, but he yields to the pressure of his friends and the prestige of his patron.</summary>

POLIZIANO.

# THE FABLE OF ORPHEUS.
---

### *Mercury announces the festival.*¹ <note>The "festival" or "show" refers to the theatrical performance; this play is considered one of the earliest secular dramas in Italian.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Silence. Listen. There was once a shepherd,
Son of Apollo, named Aristeus:
He loved with such unbridled passion
Eurydice, who was the wife of Orpheus,
That, following her one day for love,
He was the cause of her bitter and cruel fate:
Because, as she fled him near the waters,
A snake bit her; and she lay dead.
<margin>9</margin> Orpheus, by singing, took her from hell;
But he could not keep the law that was given:
For the poor man turned around on the path;
So that she was stolen from him once more:
Therefore, he never wished to love a woman again;
And by women, death was given to him.

### *A* Shepherd *follows; and says*²

Pay attention, company. A good omen:
Since Mercury comes from heaven to earth.

— bitter event <note>original: "caso acerbo"</note>, Riccardiano Codex.
. — Thus the Riccardiano and the Chigiano.
² <unclear>o</unclear>ld prints: *That the poor man turned back.*
<unclear>T</unclear>he Riccardiano and the Chigiano read: *A Schiavone shepherd follows.* <note>Schiavone refers to someone from the Slavic/Dalmatian coast, often used in Renaissance theater to denote a character speaking in a specific dialect.</note> Why the "Schiavone" is involved, I cannot find, nor did Father Affò know. As if one were not to understand that the word <term>zavolo</term> <note>A dialect variant of "cielo" (heaven) or sometimes "diavolo" (devil), depending on context</note>—which is used in place of "heaven" in the last verse of this octave as read in the Riccardiano—was from some Schiavone dialect: *That from heaven [zavolo] to earth comes Mercury.*

<margin>44</margin> Mopsus, you speak these things to the dead:
So do not spend such words with me;
Lest the wind carry them away.
<margin>47</margin> Aristeus loves and does not wish to stop loving,
Nor does he seek to be cured of such sweet pain:
He praises Love who suffers well because of him.
<margin>50</margin> But if you care at all for my desires,
Pray, draw the pipe <term>zampogna: a traditional Italian bagpipe or folk flute used by shepherds</term> from your pocket;
And we shall sing beneath the shady leaves:
<margin>53</margin> For I know that my nymph longs for song.

### SONG.

Listen, woods, to my sweet words,
Since my nymph does not wish to hear.
<margin>56</margin> The beautiful nymph is deaf to my lament
And cares nothing for the sound of our pipe:
For this my horned herd complains,
Nor will they dip their snouts in pure water,
Nor will they touch the tender greenery;
So much does their shepherd’s plight grieve and hurt them.
Listen, woods, to my sweet words.
<margin>63</margin> The herd cares well for the shepherd:
The nymph cares nothing for the lover;
The beautiful nymph who has a heart of stone,
Nay, of iron, nay, of diamond:
She always flees from before me,
As a lamb is wont to flee from the wolf.

Who is this man who with such sweet notes

I see Ixion’s wheel stand still, <note>Ixion was punished by being chained to a perpetually revolving fiery wheel; the music is so beautiful that even his eternal torture pauses.</note>
Sisyphus sitting upon his stone, <note>Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down; here, he rests to listen.</note>

This man comes against the law of the Fates,

The others who similarly entered

-># PREFACE<-
->## BY<-
->### FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.<-

***

It is not necessary for me to dwell at length on demonstrating how great in every branch of literature was Angiolo Ambrogini of Montepulciano, commonly called <term>Angiolo Poliziano</term> <note>Poliziano (1454–1494) was a prominent Italian humanist and poet under the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, an ornament and splendor of the most flourishing 15th century; since very many ancient and modern writings are full of the praises so justly due to him. It is well enough known how much he excelled in Greek,¹ how much power he had in Latin, and how, finally, in the <term>vernacular</term> <note>Italian, as opposed to the "learned" languages of Latin and Greek.</note> he was greater than his contemporaries, and indeed even than the ancients.² Therefore, leaving aside the enumeration...

***

¹ One may see how much he was esteemed for this by Emmanuele Adramiteno and by Aldus Manutius. (*Poliziano's Letters, book 7, pages 194, 195.*) He held the chair of the Greek language in Florence in competition with Demetrio Calcondila. (*Jovius, Elogies of Learned Men, no. XXXVIII.*) And Antonio Codro Urceo, writing to our author, said thus: <note>original: "Angele mi observande, non tibi blandior, sed ex animo loquor: in aliis quidem non es Græcis inferior; in hoc vero etiam, ut sentio, superior. Quare non te tantum hortor ut edas quæ scripsisti, sed rogo et obtestor. Ede ede quam celerrime; ut et tu gloria, et literarum studiosi tua doctrina frui possint."</note> "My respected Angelo, I do not flatter you, but I speak from the heart: in other matters you are indeed not inferior to the Greeks; in this one, truly, you are in my opinion even superior. Therefore, I not only exhort you to publish what you have written, but I beg and implore you. Publish it, publish it as quickly as possible; so that you may enjoy the glory, and students of literature may enjoy your learning." (*Poliziano's Letters, book 5, page 149.*) He spoke thus regarding Poliziano’s book of Greek epigrams.

² The famous Giovanni Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a renowned Renaissance philosopher and friend of Poliziano.</note> justifies all this: <note>original: "Rhythmis præterea hetruscis Franciscum Petrarcam et Dantem elegantia et vi poetica, nec scriptura tantum, sed pictura earum rerum quas exprimit, facile æquavit."</note> "Furthermore, in Tuscan rhythms <note>Referring to the Italian language.</note> he easily equaled Francesco Petrarch and Dante in elegance and poetic force, not only in his writing but in the very 'picture' of those things he expresses."

<summary>This page introduces a preface by Ireneo Affò praising the humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano for his mastery of Greek, Latin, and Italian. It includes scholarly citations and testimonials from Poliziano's contemporaries, such as Pico della Mirandola.</summary>

--- Page 285 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by Father Ireneo Affò, building on the introduction of Poliziano's linguistic mastery. It specifically focuses on the precocious nature of his genius and introduces the "Orfeo" as the primary subject of this edition.</meta>

# PREFACE

...and his works and his merits, I shall for now direct my admiring thoughts to nothing other than that tender age in which he managed, by a rare example, to become so excellent, whereas others barely manage to perfect themselves in advanced manhood. Indeed, the fact that, while almost a boy, he translated from Greek into elegant Latin verse the *Runaway Cupid* of Moschus¹ <note>Moschus was a 2nd-century BC Greek bucolic poet; the poem "Amor Fugitivus" describes Venus searching for her runaway son, Cupid.</note> with such strictness, that he wove his beautiful *Stanzas* for the Joust of Giuliano de’ Medici in his greenest years,² <note>The *Stanze per la giostra* is one of the most famous poems of the Italian Renaissance, celebrating a tournament won by the brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> and that he composed so many other poems which are still the rarity of few libraries rich in the most prized manuscripts,³ makes him an object of wonder to us; knowing that all these things, so perfect and graceful, were the first fruits of his most rare genius.

It pleases me greatly to consider him so advanced in the sciences from his earliest years, since I must speak of a work that was precisely one of those productions that commend his youth. I speak of the *Orfeo*; which, although it has been printed many times, has nevertheless never obtained that integrity and perfection given to it by its author; the fault of that fate in—

***

(*Poliziano's Works, vol. 2, letter book 3, page 1335.*) Antonio Camelli, called "the Pistoia," sang in a sonnet:

> “Who writes verse well, who is a Tuscan? —
> Do you mean in the vernacular? — In the vernacular and in Latin. —
> Lorenzo is good, and so is his son Piero;
> But in both, Poliziano is worth more.”
->*Rhymes of the Ferrarese*, page 17.<-

¹ When Poliziano sent this translation of his to Antonio Zeno, he wrote: "I finally send to you, who have long desired and demanded it, the *Runaway Cupid*, which I translated from Greek into Latin while still almost a boy, preserving not only the sentiments but even the meters and almost all the features." <note>original: "Amorem fugitivum, quem pene puer adhuc e græco in latinum converti, non sententiis modo sed numeris etiam servatis ac lineamentis pene omnibus, cupienti flagitantique diu tibi mitto tandem."</note> (Letters, book 7, page 199.)

² Friedrich Otto Mencke, who wrote extensively the *History of the Life and Literary Merits of Angelo Poliziano* <note>original: "Historia Vitæ et in literas meritorum Angeli Politiani"</note> printed in Leipzig in 1736, says that this joust was held in 1468 (section 2, § 1, note (a), page 492). At that time, Poliziano was fourteen years old. Father Serassi, in his *Life of Poliziano*, observes that when he wrote the *Stanzas*, he had not yet entered into the favor and the court of the Medici; therefore he was still young. Thus it is perhaps not an exaggeration if Monsieur de Varillas (*Secret History of Florence, book 4*) says that at twelve years of age, Poliziano was writing poetry marvelously.

³ In the Chigi Library, Crescimbeni and Serassi saw many of Poliziano's rhymes. I have seen others, unpublished, in a manuscript of the Laurentian Library in Florence. Others are also found in the Riccardian Library and elsewhere.

Affò introduces his goal: to restore the integrity of Poliziano's play "Orfeo," which he argues has been corrupted in previous printings.</summary>

--- Page 286 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography and critical preface by Father Ireneo Affò, transitioning from a general praise of Poliziano’s early genius to the specific historical circumstances surrounding the composition of his play, Orfeo, in Mantua.</meta>

->BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.<-

...fate that often attends the works of others when they are published without the knowledge of the person who wrote them.

In Mantua, he composed it at the request of Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga <note>A member of the ruling family of Mantua and a significant patron of Renaissance humanists.</note> in the space of just two days and amidst constant distractions, as he himself made known: <gloss>1</gloss> and if one asks for the precise year, the Abbot Saverio Bettinelli has already quite probably concluded that it was in 1472. <gloss>2</gloss> This is because that most worthy prelate, who the year before had established his residence in Bologna with great pomp after being sent there by the Pope as a legate, <gloss>3</gloss> <note>A "legate" is a high-ranking ecclesiastical representative of the Pope.</note> desired at that time to come to his homeland where he was still Bishop, in order to be recognized for his high standing. He brought with him a large retinue of courtiers, among whom it is claimed were Galeotto and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—though they were then quite young <gloss>4</gloss>—and among whom it is not at all unlikely that one might find Baccio Ugolino (who we shall show in due time to have been an associate of his) and Carlo Canale, his chamberlain; <gloss>5</gloss> these men were, as will be seen, destined to be either actors in or witnesses to the *Orfeo* composed there. Poliziano was eighteen years old at the time: and it was during this period that the bond of friendship was forged between him and Ugolino, which kept them close until death; and having conceived such esteem and respect for Canale, he later felt disposed to entrust the *Orfeo* to him, as will soon be seen. The Cardinal entered Mantua on the 22nd of August and remained there until the 9th of October, as has been gathered from authentic documents: <gloss>6</gloss> therefore, it is held that during that stretch of time, the *Orfeo* was composed there and performed in a theater.

***

# PREFACE

It is merely an oversight by Father Giovanni A. Bianchi to say that the *Orfeo* was composed for the wedding or the tournament of Giuliano de' Medici: <gloss>1</gloss> <note>Giuliano de' Medici was the brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent; the "tournament" refers to a famous event in 1475 celebrated in Poliziano’s other famous poem, the Stanze.</note> and it is likewise an error of Mencke <note>Friedrich Otto Mencke (1708–1754), a German scholar who wrote a biography of Poliziano.</note> to suppose it was sent to the press by the author shortly after it was written. <gloss>2</gloss> Poliziano was too reserved in the matter of putting forth his works; indeed, he was utterly dismissive of his vernacular <note>original: "volgari" — referring here to works written in Italian rather than the more "prestigious" Latin.</note> pieces in particular. His friends, however, preserved them; and Carlo Canale, among others, was careful to keep *Orfeo* with him, as he had admired more than anyone the speed with which it was produced by the young poet.

Now, some time after this drama had been born, and having been informed of the care with which Carlo Canale and a few others guarded it, Poliziano took the opportunity to write to the said Canale, expressing to him how unworthy of others' attention he considered that composition, which he would have rather preferred to be covered in eternal oblivion, as it seemed to him imperfect and misshapen. Nevertheless, seeing that he loved it so much and that others did the same, he gladly declared himself willing to yield to his wish; and he recommended it to him, so that, as a work born under the Cardinal's auspices, he might be pleased to protect it.

This is the true spirit of the letter that follows; nor should we believe that this was a dedication ever placed at the front of *Orfeo* by its author. I wish to point this out so it is not believed that all copies containing this letter at the front should be considered as derived from the original: on the contrary, those that do not have it may be more genuine; for the pairing of this letter with *Orfeo* was merely an arbitrary choice by copyists, who mistook a letter of recommendation for a dedication. It is quite clear that Canale already possessed *Orfeo*, so it need not be supposed that it was sent to him by Poliziano with this letter. After the Cardinal died in 1483—as will be seen more clearly in one of the *Observations on Orfeo*—Carlo Canale went to Rome into the service of the Cardinal of Parma: and the following year Lodovico Gonzaga, brother of the deceased prelate, having been elected to the Church of Mantua and aspiring to the cardinalate, also went there: and we find that he recommended himself very warmly to Canale for these dealings of his, as I have been able to gather from the original letters—

# BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.

<margin>originals of this prelate preserved in various volumes in the secret archive of the city of Guastalla.^1</margin>

The *Orfeo*, then, remained in Canale’s hands in this handwritten form, and it also spread into the hands of others. There is no doubt that Canale's copy must have been perfect and exactly as the author dictated it; but we cannot be certain that the copies transcribed by others were of the same quality. It is probable that some who had heard the *Orfeo* recited, or had taken part in its performance, transcribed parts of it, later cobbling them together as they saw fit, and substituting other verses and turns of phrase where they found themselves betrayed by their memory. This would not be the only example of such an occurrence. This thought of ours is supported by three significant reflections: first, the eagerness that must have arisen in men to have this drama in their hands; second, the difficulty Poliziano had in letting it circulate under the eyes of others; third, the notable defects that we shall point out in our *Observations* regarding the *Orfeo* as it has been printed up to this day. The first leads us to conjecture that someone, by hook or by crook, took a fancy to wanting the *Orfeo*; the second persuades us that Poliziano did not want to release it; the third assures us that the transcriber, relying on their own or another’s memory while piecing it together, reduced it to such a state as to bring shame upon its author.

Thus, with the copies of *Orfeo* so varied, it was quite easy for a corrupted copy to fall into the hands of someone wishing to print it, resulting in the work being spoiled forever—until a correct manuscript was discovered, similar to the one that Canale and a few other friends of Poliziano already possessed, in order to restore it to its original dignity and repair the damage that would otherwise come to its author. Indeed, this is how the matter unfolded: for— <note>original: "imper-" — this is a catchword, the beginning of the word "imperciocchè" (because/for) which continues on the next page.</note>

...which resulted in Alessandro Sarzio, a most diligent collector of Poliziano’s <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant Renaissance humanist and poet under the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> works, receiving the very sweet *Stanze* <note>The *Stanze per la giostra*, written to celebrate a tournament won by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> of our Poet quite late, as well as the *Orfeo*. Unfortunately, the latter was in a corrupted state, yet he could not refrain from sending it immediately to the press, dedicating these works with his own letter to Monsignor Antonio Galeazzo Bentivoglio, the Archdeacon of Bologna.

This did not occur before 1494, as is suspected in the catalog of some of the principal editions of Poliziano’s <term>vernacular works</term> <note>Works written in Italian rather than Latin.</note> collected by Apostolo Zeno and expanded by Volpi,¹ but specifically in that very year of 1494. We are indebted for this certain news to the Abbot Don Petronio Belvederi of Bologna, who with great diligence and effort has compiled an index of all the books from the first century of printing <note>Known as <term>incunabula</term>, these are books printed before the year 1501.</note> found in the various libraries of learned Bologna. In the library of the Cassinese monks of San Procolo, he saw this first edition, produced in royal paper <term>quarto</term> <note>A book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note> through the work of Platone de' Benedetti, precisely in 1494 and completed on August 9th.²

The reason why Sarzio gave these works to Benedetti to print, rather than to another printer, is quite clear. This man, who was most accurate in his craft and who employed the most beautiful and clear <term>Roman typeface</term> <note>A clean, upright style of type, as opposed to the denser Gothic or "Blackletter" styles.</note> ever seen in those days, had been chosen the year before by Poliziano himself to print his Latin translation of Herodian <note>A Greek historian whose work Poliziano translated into Latin.</note>. This work was sent by the author with a Latin letter to Andrea Magnanimo of Bologna, recommending that he have it printed specifically by Benedetti and that he should ensure Alessandro Sarzio assisted with the proofreading. This was done; therefore, that work was seen emerging from those presses in the month of August 1493.³ Consequently, because of this previous labor, Sarzio believed he could not provide a more diligent printer for Poliziano’s vernacular works—nor one more acceptable to the poet—than Benedetti. ...[knew] <note>The Italian text begins with the fragment "peva," the end of "sapeva" (knew).</note> how little these youthful productions of his were cared for by their author, even though they were most worthy of the esteem of others, he took care not to reveal his intention to Poliziano, and gave them secretly to be printed, so that the poet’s modesty would not hinder the success of the undertaking.¹

Just then, as this work had barely come to light and perhaps had not even come before Poliziano's eyes, death—implacably armed—took the most learned author from the world in the flower of his age at forty years. He ceased to live in Florence on the 24th of September of that same year; that is to say, forty-six days after the last sheet of those poems had been pulled.² Everyone can clearly see that if they were published in an incorrect and incomplete state at that time, the author's death removed any hope that he, moved to compassion for these works of his, might later provide a perfect reprint.

Therefore, they were accepted by the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The long-distance community of intellectuals in Europe and the Americas in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> just as they were: and greedy printers always reproduced them according to the first edition. I will not remain silent about the second edition made in Bologna by Caligola Bazalieri in 1503; since this one, no less rare than the first, has served me as some light to illustrate the *Orfeo* and to weave this work of mine. This reprint was certainly not seen by whoever organized the aforementioned catalog, and therefore it was poorly cited. Mr. Floriano Cabassi of Carpi possesses a copy: and I, through Mr. Girolamo Colleoni of Correggio, my most singular patron and friend, was able to see and examine it. What is notable about it is that this printer, while leaving Sarzio's dedication exactly as it was, then dared to change those words, *I have given them to be printed by Plato de' Benedetti*, into these, *I have given them to be printed by Caligula di Bazaleri*; not realizing that, since Poliziano was spoken of as a living person in that letter,

his imposture would have been easily discovered. Niccolò Zoppino committed a similar blunder in the Venice reprint of 1513, produced for Giorgio Rusconi and organized by him; pretending, that is, that Sarzio <note>The original publisher of the first edition.</note> had given him those works to print:<gloss>2</gloss> and he repeated this again in the new production he made himself in 1524, as the aforementioned Mr. Colleoni, who owns it, assures me.

Let what has been said so far suffice to clarify how Poliziano’s *Orfeo* was born, how copies of it were spread, and how it finally came to light. Now I must show how the copy produced by Sarzio was imperfect and corrupted. Certainly every learned man has perhaps suspected it until now; but, unable to be sure of it, has spoken of it in terms that seem more insulting to the author than the editor. Doni, in his first *Library* <note>The *Libreria* by Anton Francesco Doni was one of the first bibliographical works in Italian.</note>, wrote that these vernacular works of Poliziano in his time—which were indeed the times of true good taste—were not read much.<gloss>3</gloss> In saying this, he could not have been referring to the *Stanze*, which, being highly esteemed, were included in almost all collections, especially those printed by Giolito and others; so they must certainly have been read with pleasure and greed: but he must have intended to speak of the *Orfeo* and some other youthful composition of our author, which were certainly seen as neglected in those days. If the *Orfeo* was not read much, it is a sign that it was seen as quite defective by men of letters. And indeed, the learned Quadrio <note>Francesco Saverio Quadrio, an 18th-century literary historian.</note> recognized it as such in our own century,<gloss>4</gloss> to say nothing of others who agree with him in confessing it to be lacking in every good dramatic law.

But how could such imperfection in this drama be reconciled with Poliziano’s profound erudition? I must confess that the *Orfeo* printed until now is full of inconsistencies, improbabilities, and errors, which I reserve for myself to demonstrate in my *Observations* that will follow the work:
