# BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.

But I cannot understand how Poliziano—who even at a young age was so learned—could have strayed so far from the proper poetic path. That Poliziano, who from childhood was so well-versed in the Greek poets that he not only translated, as we have mentioned, the brief *Amor Fuggitivo* <note>original: *Amor Fuggitivo* [Fugitive Love]</note> by Moschus, but even dared to set his hand to a translation of the prince of epic poets, Homer,<gloss>1. Poliziano himself assures us of this in the *Century of Miscellanies* near the end: "I was indeed applying myself to both branches of philosophy, but not very diligently, as I was naturally and by age more inclined to the charms of the poet Homer, whom I then also translated into Latin verse with wondrous ardor and wondrous study, as a youth." <note>original Latin: *Dabam quidem philosophiæ utrique operam...*</note></gloss> should he not perhaps have already tasted the *Poetics* of Aristotle and Horace? And did he not, without a doubt, already admire the models of tragic composition by Euripides and Sophocles? If we are not to deny him the fruit of such studies, could he ever—even when weaving a drama in great haste—lose sight of the most fundamental rules of the art?

These significant reflections, while they inspire admiration and respect for the immortal name of our Poet, must also persuade us that the *Orfeo* as it has been seen until now is not the genuine offspring of Poliziano. Thanks, however, to the diligence of those men of old who, by collecting the finest pieces from the pens of good writers into specific codices <note>A "codex" is a handwritten manuscript in book form, as opposed to a scroll.</note>, knew how to preserve this intact piece for us, which has lain unobserved until now among the dusty remains of antiquity. I cannot help but claim for myself a glory that is entirely my own: that of having discovered the whole and perfect *Orfeo* in an old miscellaneous codex that once belonged to Father Giambatista Cataneo, a Friar Minor Observant. It is now preserved in the choice library of our convent of Santo Spirito in Reggio—a library furnished with very rare books, founded and enriched by that learned religious man.<gloss>2. This religious man is praised by Muratori in Book I of *On Perfect Poetry*, chapter 3, page 26, of the first edition. But the manuscript of the *Rhymes* of Simon of Siena, which he saw in his possession, is no longer to be found in Santo Spirito. The codex of which we now speak is the same one cited by Giovanni Guasco in the *Literary History of Reggio*, book I, page 43; from which he drew those *Rhymes* of Correggio published there.</gloss> 

In this manuscript, among various rhymes by Niccolò da Correggio, Antonio Tebaldeo, and Timoteo Bendedei (both from Ferrara, and all contemporaries of Poliziano), one reads the *Orfeo* with the title of *tragedy*; it is seen to be perfectly and diligently divided into five short acts. Poliziano’s name is not attached to it, but this likely happened for no other reason than that whoever foolishly rebound that codex removed certain <term>quinternetti</term> <note>A term for small gatherings of paper or parchment, usually consisting of five folded sheets (ten leaves).</note> from the front, in which the same handwriting had written the...

...the whole first part of Poliziano’s *Stanze* <note>original: *Stanze*—The "Stanzas for the Joust," Poliziano's famous poem celebrating Giuliano de' Medici.</note>, at the front of which was written in cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral pigment used for titles and decorative initials in high-quality manuscripts.</note>: *Of Angelo Poliziano for Giuliano de' Medici* <note>original Latin: *Angeli Policiani in Julium Medicem*</note>. The *Orfeo* was intended to follow these *Stanze*: this is proven by the quality of the paper itself, the quarto format <note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves (eight pages).</note>, the handwriting itself, and the same care taken in writing the titles and subjects in vibrant cinnabar. However, the *Stanze* were removed and, by very poor judgment, rebound into another miscellaneous volume of various writings and prints, which is kept in the same library.

I immediately transcribed this tragedy as soon as I realized the differences between it and the printed *Orfeo*. I then set out to conduct diligent research to see if, by chance, another similar copy could be found that would support and authorize my new reading. It happened that at almost the same time, Dr. Buonafede Vitali of Busseto—my great teacher and close friend—acquired another ancient codex <note>A hand-written book.</note>. In this volume were rhymes by Iacopo Corso, Antonio Tebaldeo, Serafino dall’Aquila, Cariteo, Iacopo Cieco of Parma, Iacopo dell’Abazia, Bernardo Accolti, Niccolò da Correggio, Girolamo del Vescovo, our own Poliziano,<margin>1</margin> Baccio Fiorentino (that is, Ugolini), Bernardo Bellincione, Agostino Staccoli, Giambatista Corbani, Ciriaco Fiorentino, the Prothonotary <note>An official title in the Catholic Church; here likely referring to a specific poet-official.</note> (perhaps Niccolò Quercente, commonly called the Prothonotary), Panfilo Sasso, Paolo Antonio Fiesco, Gaspar Visconte, Ambrogio da Sanvito, Bernardo Pulci, and others unknown. Amidst so many rhymes, he found the tragedy of *Orfeo* transcribed without an author’s name, almost entirely identical to the one I discovered, lacking only the division of acts. Knowing my urgent interest, he took the trouble to transcribe it and send it to me with some of his observations regarding the variant readings.

Shortly after, I had the opportunity to see the codex with my own eyes to judge the age and value of both, in order to decide which might be more authoritative. I saw, however, that the Reggian codex <note>Referring to the manuscript held in the library at Reggio Emilia.</note> was by far the older and also the more accurate. Its characters <note>The style of handwriting.</note> are such that they show it was copied during Poliziano’s most flourishing period. The comparison with only the first part of the *Stanze* mentioned above can, in a way, prove its antiquity, as the second part—which remained unfinished—is missing. The paper, based on that practical knowledge...

<meta>This page continues Father Ireneo Affò’s detailed bibliographical analysis of the manuscripts of Poliziano's Orfeo, specifically focusing on dating the "Reggian codex" and comparing it to another manuscript owned by Dr. Vitali.</meta>

<page-num>125</page-num>

-> ### BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ ### <-

...which I performed while examining numerous writings in various archives, there can be no doubt that it dates from those days.<note>Affò is using his expertise in paleography (the study of old handwriting) and paper types to date the manuscript to the late 15th century.</note> In short, everything conspires to make the Reggian copy very venerable to us: and in truth, whoever transcribed it must have held it in very high esteem; for not only did they cleanly use <term>cinnabar|A bright red mineral pigment used for emphasis and decoration in manuscripts</term> in the titles and arguments, but they also tinted all the initial letters of the verses with a charming little yellow that is pleasing to the eye; a decoration not used for the other poems contained in that codex.

But the manuscript belonging to Mr. Vitali is certainly more recent than the other. Here is the undeniable proof. To determine the era of a codex, nothing can be more helpful than the historical details that can be found within it. If a book begins by giving us news of an event that has already occurred, the book certainly cannot be older than that event. This being the case, I observed that the first sonnet written in order in the codex is by Iacopo Corso and is composed upon the tomb of the Magnificent Lorenzo de' Medici, who died in the year 1492 <note>Affò writes 1493, though modern historians date Lorenzo's death to April 1492; the discrepancy often arises from different calendar systems used in Italian city-states.</note>, shortly before Poliziano himself passed away. Therefore, that book was not begun to be written until after that year. Furthermore, the subsequent compositions are seen to be written at times by different hands; and the Tragedy <note>The "Tragedy" refers here to the Orfeo itself.</note> is only encountered toward the end: so that it may be supposed it was not transcribed until after 1500.

These reflections induced me not to deviate from the Reggian codex in my planned correction of the *Orfeo*, while not neglecting the other copy in those parts where it seemed more accurate to me. I did not interrupt the course of my research to find, if possible, some other text; and having gone to Florence in the year 1771, I did not fail to visit the famous Laurentian <note>The Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, a historic library in Florence famous for its collection of manuscripts.</note> and other of those wealthy libraries: but all was in vain. Believing therefore that the two mentioned codices could suffice, I set about forming a perfect edition from them; one that would demonstrate how many beauties have been missing from the *Orfeo* until now, and that would provide a lover of such things with everything that could be desired in this regard through the variants of both the manuscripts and the printed editions. And because my primary aim was to persuade the reader that this is the true offspring of Poliziano, I wished to accompany this tragedy with various Observations at the end: which will serve for a continuous comparison between the *Orfeo*...

...printed so far and our own; and by showing how much more judicious, probable, complete, and perfect this work now appears for the first time, these pages will justify, as I hope, this opinion of mine before connoisseurs.

Regarding what some critics might quibble about the title of *tragedy* and the division of acts, I reserve my response for the *Observations* themselves; where I will clearly demonstrate that the title truly belongs to *Orpheus*, and that the necessary division into five acts, which every play must have, was well known in Poliziano's day. For now, I will frankly state that this is the first regular dramatic composition written in our language. <note>Affò is making a bold historical claim: that Poliziano's Orfeo (c. 1480) is the first "modern" play in Italian that follows the structural rules of classical Greek and Roman drama.</note> And indeed, if we look back through all literary history, and especially that of vernacular poetry <note>By "vernacular poetry" (volgar poesia), the author means poetry written in the local Italian/Tuscan dialect rather than in Latin.</note>; we will either find no Tuscan drama before 1472; or, if we find something that has the appearance of theatrical poetry, we see it is nothing more than an unrefined farce, an irregular dialogue, a jumble of nonsense. In Poliziano's day, theatrical spectacles were indeed in use: but those who wished to enjoy "perfect" ones were forced to stage some comedy by Terence or Plautus, or have one translated for theater use—which, however, did not begin very early.<sup>1</sup> Certain sacred representations <note>These were "Mystery Plays," medieval religious dramas that were popular but lacked the formal structure of classical theater.</note> that we have from those days, and other fables, are all trifles that have, as they say, neither head nor tail; without citing examples or pointing out the many that remain, I will let the most learned Quadrio <note>Francesco Saverio Quadrio (1695–1756) was a prominent Jesuit historian of literature.</note>, who handled so many of them, testify to this truth.

> "*No observation,*" he says, "*nor rule was followed in these compositions, neither regarding the unity of action, nor the duration of time, nor the identity of place, nor anything else required of good tragedy.<sup>2</sup>*"

There were men of talent in those times: but either di—

## BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.

Whether they hoped to be able to reach the perfection of Greek and Latin models, or wished, as is still common today, to follow the taste of the age, they continued to weave fables without method. Among these I include Niccolò da Correggio, certainly a person of great knowledge in his day and a poet of good reputation; who, having composed the *Fable of Cephalus* in the year 1486, declared in the prologue that it was neither a comedy nor a tragedy:

> “I do not give you this as a comedy,
> For their method is not fully observed:
> Nor do I want you to believe it a tragedy,
> Although you will see the chorus of nymphs.
> Fable or history, whatever it may be,
> I give it to you, and not for a price of gold.”

And truly he spoke well, because one does not know what it is. Vernacular tragedies <note>The "vernacular" refers to the Italian language as spoken by the people, as opposed to formal Latin.</note> before Poliziano are not to be found: Latin ones, however, there are, such as the *Ezzelino* by Albertino Mussato, which is perhaps the only one from the late Middle Ages. Vernacular comedies, none either: we have, however, the *Catinia* by Sicco Polentone in Latin. But in the vernacular, I say again, no trace is found of either tragedy or comedy before our author. I know that Bumaldi has written that Fabrizio da Bologna, who flourished around 1250, was a composer of tragedies in our idiom: <gloss>1</gloss> but, besides it being already known how many blunders Bumaldi committed, we see here his ignorance in not having understood Dante where he speaks of Fabrizio in the book *On Vernacular Eloquence*. Dante says that Fabrizio was a poet of tragic style: but what Dante meant by tragic style is known to men of letters; since he was accustomed to calling the sublime style by that name. <note>In medieval literary theory, "tragic," "comic," and "elegiac" referred to levels of style—high, middle, and low—rather than the modern definition of a play's ending.</note> Luigi Riccoboni likewise says that the comedy entitled *Floriana*, woven in *terza rima* <note>A rhyming verse scheme famously used by Dante in the Divine Comedy.</note> and mixed with other meters, dates from after the time of Dante or around 1400: <gloss>2</gloss> but it would take much effort to prove it. The most illustrious Scipione Maffei, speaking of it, said only these words: “*The Floriana, although in tercets with other types of verse, is called an ancient comedy in the second edition of 1526; and it was composed in the preceding century.*” <gloss>3</gloss> It is well and good that in 1526 it could be called ancient; but the enormous antiquity that Riccoboni attributes to it is not established.

Those other vernacular dramas then, which from that century are re—

are encountered divided into acts and which therefore seem, at least in their outward form, to approach either tragedy or comedy; and all those few works which likewise go by such titles, whether justly or unjustly adorned with them; such as the comedy that treats of the *Conversion of Saint Mary Magdalene* <note>original: "Conversione di sancta Maria Magdalena"</note> written by Antonio di Iacopo Alamanni and divided into five acts; the *Filostrato and Panfila* <note>original: "Filostrato e Panfila"</note>, two lovers, a tragedy by Antonio Camelli, called "the Pistoia"; the *Calandra*, a comedy by Bernardo Divizio da Bibbiena, which is the first perfect thing of that genre born in our language but written in prose; these, I say, and all such other things were born after the *Orpheus* <note>original: "Orfeo"</note> of Poliziano. So that one must conclude that our tragedy, as far as can be known from ancient memories, is the oldest of the best and well-defined Italian dramatic works that can be pointed out.

I am not usually so appreciative of my own opinions that I do not fear deceiving myself: for which reason I have not failed to communicate my ideas to learned and sensible men, so that by examining this matter better they might enlighten me where I might have, by ill fate, wrongly supposed. But I can say that I have found everyone in agreement with my conceived opinion. Among others, the Father Abbot Girolamo Tiraboschi <note>Tiraboschi (1731–1794) was a Jesuit scholar and a monumental figure in Italian literary history.</note>, most worthy librarian of His Serene Highness the Duke of Modena, well known for his *History of Italian Literature* <note>original: "Storia della letteratura italiana"</note>, to whom, at the suggestion of the most illustrious Father Abbot Saverio Bettinelli, I communicated my discovery to receive his sentiment; on the date of April 19th of this year, 1775, he wrote to me thus: "*Until now I have not had the opportunity to examine the state of Italian theatrical poetry of the 15th century, since in the history of it I have not yet reached this subject. It seems to me nonetheless that the title of tragedy is not unsuited to the* Orpheus. *It is certainly not a tragedy by Racine or Corneille; but yet it has some idea of tragedy; and it has much more right to that name than the poem of Dante has to that of comedy.*" And on another date, the first day of May: "*That then the* Orpheus *of Poliziano is not only the first Italian drama divided into acts, but absolutely the first among those written in our language, I would not fear to affirm, at least until another is produced that is certainly older. Alamanni, the author of the comedy of Saint Mary Magdalene, lived certainly later than Poliziano, as you will be able to see from what Count Mazzuchelli says of him. All the representations of the* Passion of Christ <note>original: "Passione di Cristo"</note> *and other similar ones that are cited, hardly deserve the name of either drama or poetry. The* Floriana *I do not even know what it is; but I do not see how it can be proven older than the* Orpheus. *No...*"

> *...know if it can be stated with certainty that this was com-*
> *posed in 1472; but certainly it cannot be deferred much further*

It was truly necessary to clarify all these matters for the greater glory of our immortal Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a Florentine humanist and poet under the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> and to illustrate the history of vernacular poetry; and it shall remain concluded, until some other more surprising discovery is made, that our poet was the first restorer, or perhaps the instigator, of the Italian theater. Nor, as witness to this truth, will it be unwelcome to men of letters to see the *Orpheus* <note>original: "Orfeo"</note> reproduced in this new form. I say to men of letters; for the common people, and those who content themselves with a simple and superficial scientific smattering, or those others who, never rising to examine the genius and nature of antiquity, remain so nailed to the modern that they cannot be torn away from it in any way—I do not believe them capable of judging this composition. 

I am of the opinion that such people occasionally hear high praise for the perfect <term>tragedies</term> <note>Dramatic works with a serious tone and a somber theme, typically involving a great person's downfall.</note> and <term>comedies</term> <note>Dramatic works intended to be humorous or to have a happy ending.</note> of our <term>cinquecentisti</term> <note>A term for the 16th-century (the 1500s) Italian writers and artists, known for their strict adherence to Classical rules.</note>, only because they know they have always been held in the highest esteem; otherwise, if they did not fear being hissed at, they would say what they truly feel: namely, that those works are insipid and of little value. They are so prejudiced by certain modern dramas that do nothing but throw dust in the eyes. In the same way, if they ever take this tragedy into their hands, I am certain it will produce in them nausea and annoyance; for they will not know how to first form an idea of the time in which it was composed—a time, that is, still largely unrefined—nor will they know how to judge its too-lovely simplicity, being themselves accustomed to admiring the complications and the marvelous stage-machines <note>elaborate mechanical devices used for stage effects, which were popular in the Baroque era but absent in earlier, simpler drama.</note> that never pleased the Greeks, the Latins, or the good Italians. 

To these people, therefore, I do not gift this tragedy; but rather to those few who, having until now loved the *Orpheus* despite its defects out of the great respect due to its author, will be better prepared to do so in the future, seeing it restored to its true integrity and correct reading. To such people I give it, who, while prizing to the highest degree a painting by Titian or Correggio <note>High Renaissance masters known for their technical perfection.</note>, are also grateful for the imperfect drawings of Cimabue <note>A 13th-century painter considered the "father" of Italian painting, whose work is more primitive but historically vital.</note>. These readers, paying attention to the difference of the centuries, the variety of customs, and the dissimilarity of temperaments, and adapting their intellect to them, will discover in this work the beauty that a clouded and prejudiced eye will never be able to see; and those defects that are there by fatal necessity, they will know to attribute to the age of an author for whom, if fate had been...

->PREFACE<-

...[had fate] been less contrary, taking him away so early in life, we would perhaps have his works corrected by his own hand.¹

Perhaps some would have preferred that, following this discovery of mine, I had devoted myself to gathering all those vernacular <note>The "vernacular" refers to works written in Italian rather than Latin, which was the standard for scholarly writing at the time.</note> works of Poliziano that are found, in order to share a complete collection of his things with the public. I will not say that such an undertaking, had I ever wished it, would not have been easy for me to carry out; knowing well which repositories <note>Refers to private libraries or archives where manuscripts were kept.</note> I should turn to in order to make a collection of such things, nor lacking friends who would have helped me. And indeed, I once had such a thought; but, reflecting later that I could not weave upon the other poems that work entirely my own which I have framed around the *Orpheus*, I resolved to leave such an undertaking to others, contenting myself with having provided for such a collection—should one be made—the complete and perfect *Orpheus*, which from now on can very well be printed without the accompaniment of these Observations of mine.

I will add finally that this work of mine was born from my leisure hours of some years ago. By the year 1769, I had composed it using only the information from the Reggio manuscript <note>original: "codice reggiano"; a manuscript found in the city of Reggio Emilia.</note>; and, Giuseppe Braglia, who then presided over the presses in Mantua, having offered to print it for me, I gave it to him: but I have since thanked God that nothing came of it. Later, with the manuscript of Mr. Vitali and other information acquired from time to time, I improved it: and, since I saw that Comino, the printer in Padua, had such great concern for the vernacular works of Poliziano—having printed them as many as three times with his usual accuracy—I offered it to him without any interest <note>That is, without seeking financial profit.</note>. He accepted it willingly; and on the date of July 7, 1770, he wrote to me:

> « *I have received in due time your most favored letter of the 17th past, with the precious manuscript of Poliziano’s Orpheus, most eruditely illustrated by Your Reverend Fatherhood. Be certain that here, having been examined by a most learned person, it has received infinite applause.* »

From then on, I never thought about this business again; and while I kept my studies turned toward other things, these papers lay forgotten in the trunk. But Father Luigi Tuschini of Ravenna, a reader in theology and a most singular friend of mine, aware of this neglect of mine, has thus roused me and has so greatly made it a matter of conscience for me to defraud the public for so long of my discovery,

# ORPHEUS
## A TRAGEDY.
---

->Silence. Listen. There was once a shepherd<-
->Son of Apollo, named Aristaeus.<-
->He loved with such unbridled passion<-
->Eurydice, who was the wife of Orpheus,<-
->That following her one day out of love<-
->He was the cause of her bitter and cruel fate;<-
->For, as she fled near the waters,<-
->A serpent bit her, and dead she lay.<-

---

V. 1. — *Silence. Listen*. Formulas used by the Latin comic playwrights <note>Poliziano models his opening on ancient Roman theater to give the play a classical feel.</note>: Terence in various prologues: "Give your attention, and with silence pay heed... Give your attention, be present with a fair mind and in silence." <note>original Latin: "Date operam, et cum silentio animum attendite ...... Date operam, adeste æquo animo cum silentio."</note> — *There was* (Ital: *E' fu*). Variant *For he was* (Ital: *Che' l fu*): Vitali Manuscript (A). — v. 2. Variant *Son of Apollo, named Aristaeus*: Vitali Manuscript (A). — v. 3. Variant *With unbridled passion*: Reggiano Manuscript (A). — v. 5. Variant *And following her*: Reggiano Manuscript (A). — v. 7. *Her* (Ital: *Lei*), used in the <term>subjective case|The grammatical case used for the subject of a sentence, such as "she" rather than "her."</term> for *she* (*ella*). See the works of Bartoli and Boccaccio (N). * Bartoli (*The Wrong and Right of the "It Cannot Be Done"*, XLII) provides the following examples of *her* (*lei*) used this way by Boccaccio in the *Ameto*: "She (*Lei*) was named Catola, .... She (*Lei*) made it clear to me, .... Even Medea could not defend herself (*lei*) from it." But above all others, he continues, the one who clearly used *lei* in the subjective case is Fazio in the *Dittamondo* Book II, Chapter XIX: "Wherefore she (*lei*), out of spite and disdain, rushed at him...." To which I add another from our greatest poet <note>A reference to Dante Alighieri, the author of the Divine Comedy.</note>: "....she (*lei*) who spins day and night had not yet drawn the distaff for him" *Purgatorio* XXI. **"Her" for "she"** was used by our ancestors just as it was by the Provençal poets <note>Troubadours from Southern France who heavily influenced early Italian literature.</note>, who wrote in the first case *ela, elha, ella, lei, leys, lieys*. Raimbaut de Vaqueiras: "For this forbids me, from which she gave me abundance, she (*leys*) who is gay, courtly, and noble-speaking." (Because this forbids me, from which she gave me abundance, she who is gay, courtly, and noble-speaking.) Much the same is found in Nannucci in his *Observations on the Pronoun "Lei"*, Corfu, 1841. Even a poet of the 17th century, as regular as any who ever lived, Chiabrera, did not shun *lei* in the subjective case: "...there blooms at every hour a loving pomp, where she (*lei*) rests."

The accompanying scholarly commentary defends the poet's use of specific Italian pronouns by citing classical Latin precedents and famous Italian authors like Dante and Boccaccio.</summary>

->Orpheus, by singing, rescued her from hell;<-
->But he could not keep the command he was given:<-
->And the one who gave it took her back once more.<-

->Out of disdain, he never wished to love another woman,<-

->Now let everyone pay close attention to all the acts,<-
->Of which there are five: and this is the prologue.<- <note>The "argument" or "argomento" was a traditional summary provided at the start of a play to help the audience follow the plot.</note>

v. 10. *To keep the command*: to observe, to maintain. Dante, *Purgatory*, XXVI: "...we did not keep human law." <note>original Italian: "non servammo umana legge."</note> Ariosto, XXI: "to keep his faith in full." <note>original Italian: "per servar sua fede a pieno."</note> — v. 11. The two Manuscripts <note>The editor refers to these as "Codici," meaning hand-copied volumes of the play.</note> which I have utilized both read: *And the one who gave it, took her back again.* To avoid the flawed and unusual repetition of the same word in the rhyme, I have seen fit to correct it to this form (A). <note>Rhyming a word with itself was often considered a technical error in Italian poetry unless the meanings were different.</note> — v. 13. *Wished* (Ital: *Volse*) for *volle* has been used by several good Tuscan authors (N). * Dante, *Hell*, II: "....I came to you just as she wished." <note>original Italian: "venni a te così com' ella volse."</note> And it remains alive in the speech of the Tuscan people. — v. 15. *Now let everyone, etc.* Even assuming that Poliziano had Mercury deliver this prologue, why then include that *Shepherd*—or rather, a *Slavic* shepherd <note>A "pastore schiavone" refers to a shepherd from the Dalmatian coast, a common stock character in early Renaissance drama.</note> according to the Chigi Manuscript—who interrupts the one delivering the prologue to say:

"Pay attention, company; a good omen; Why does Mercury come from heaven to earth?" <note>original Italian: "State attenti, brigata ; buono augurio ; Perchè di ciel in terra vien Mercurio ?"</note> Mercury would have been perfectly well recognized by the audience from obvious signs <note>Such as his winged sandals or caduceus.</note>, without this shepherd—who clutters the scene for so little reason—having to come and tell us it was him. And furthermore, how can it be that Mercury's arrival is credited as a *good omen*, when he is supposed to have announced a tragic event? Come now, such inconsistencies do not align with the noble genius of Poliziano. He therefore could not have written it as it has been read until now; rather, it must be said that the argument or prologue of *Orpheus* was composed by him as it is read in the Reggiano Manuscript, which is free from the many defects that have until now defiled this piece of ancient poetry (A).

<summary>This page concludes the play's prologue, summarizing Orpheus's failed rescue of Eurydice and his eventual death, followed by a scholarly argument favoring the Reggiano Manuscript's cleaner structure over versions featuring an unnecessary shepherd character.</summary>

My Aristaeus, if you do not soon try

<margin>44</margin>
Mopsus, you speak these things to the dead;
So do not scatter your words with me,

<margin>47</margin>
Aristaeus loves, and does not wish to stop loving,
Nor does he seek to be cured of such sweet pains: <gloss>noglie</gloss> <note>The word "noglie" is an archaic or dialectal variation of "doglie" (pains/sorrows).</note>

---

<margin>v. 33.</note> * Petrarch: "All the day I weep; and then at night, when / Wretched mortals take their rest, / I find myself in tears, and my ills redouble." <note>original: "Tutto il dì piango; e poi la notte, quando Prendon riposo i miseri mortali, Trovomi in pianto, e raddoppiarsi i mali."</note> Concerning the loss of appetite, the character *Cosa innamorata* also speaks pleasantly in *The Tancia*, III, 2: "Love has put me into such a great state of worry, / That I have lost the taste for it and the labor: / I am brought to the point that I swallow no morsel, / Except when I have the desire to eat." — <margin>v. 35.</margin> * *face* (torch), here meaning fire or ardor; Petrarch, speaking of Laura's speech, says it is "full of sweet torches." — <margin>v. 38.</margin> Variant *it is not indeed* <note>original: "non è già"</note>: Manuscript Vitali (A). — <margin>v. 41.</margin> All three codices read *its harsh* <note>original: "sue dure"</note> (A). — <margin>v. 44.</margin> * *speak these things to the dead*: as if to say, you speak to the deaf, you speak to the wind, you speak to the desert. I do not recall other examples of this phrase. — <margin>v. 46.</margin> Petrarch: "But the wind carried away the words" <note>original: "Ma il vento ne portava le parole"</note> (N). * Statius: "The windy storms snatched away his useless words." <note>original Latin: "Irrita ventosæ rapiebant verba procellæ." Statius was a Roman poet of the 1st century AD, highly regarded by Renaissance humanists.</note> — <margin>v. 48.</margin> *noglie*. It may seem to others that I should have embraced the Cominian edition here, which has *doglie* (pains) instead of *noglie*, a word truly barbarous and impure. But since it does not seem improbable to me that Poliziano <note>referred to here as N.A.</note> may have written *noglie*, I did not wish to depart from the reading found in the manuscripts. Lodovico Dolce dared to change many words in Poliziano's *Stanzas*; for which he is rebuked by Mencken and Zeno. I do not wish to do as he did. I find ancient examples of the word *zoglia* instead of *gioia* (joy) and *noglie* in place of *noia* (annoyance/sorrow). See the *Letters* of Friar Guittone. <note>Guittone d'Arezzo was a 13th-century Italian poet whose complex, sometimes obscure style was a precursor to Dante.</note>

## MOPSUS.

The pleasant murmuring is not so great <margin>84</margin>
Of the fresh waters that plunge from a rock,
Nor when a gentle breeze blows
Among the tops of the pines and they rustle;
As your rhymes are delightful,
Your rhymes that echo everywhere:
If she hears them, she will come like a puppy. <note>The Italian *cucciola* implies a young, docile dog that is easily led.</note>
But here is Thyrsis sliding down the mountain.

## ARISTAEUS.

What of the calf? Have you found it? <margin>92</margin>

---

"Carry some part [of my words], O winds, to the ears of the gods;" <note>original: "Partem aliquam, venti, divûm referatis ad aures;" from Virgil's Eclogues.</note> and **Ovid**: "The breeze, not envious, brought your charming prayers to me" <note>original: "Detulit aura preces ad me non invida blandas"</note> (**N**). — **line 79.** Variant: *tell how much*: **Ms. V. (A)**. — **line 80.** In the **Reggio Manuscript** it seems one should read *beg her*: but we adhere in this reading to the **Chisian Manuscript**. Noting that this verse is missing in the **Vatican Manuscript (A)**. — **lines 81-82.** Common among our lyric poets. But strange in **Petrarch**: "I melt at the sound of the words, just as if I were a man of ice in the sun." <note>original: "mi struggo al suon delle parole, Pur com’ io fossi un uom di ghiaccio al sole."</note> — **lines 84-85.** **Ovid, Fasti IV**: "of water leaping down from on high;" <note>original: "ex alto desilientis aquae;"</note> and **Homer**: "cold water ran down from a high stone." And **Theocritus**: "Sweeter, O shepherd, is your song than that sounding water there, which distills from up high from that rock" <note>original: "Più soave, o pastore, il tuo canto che quella sonante acqua là, che di su alto da quel masso distilla"</note> (**N**). — **lines 86-87.** **Moschus**: "Where, when much wind blows, the pine sings" <note>original: "Dove, quando spira molto vento, il pino canta"</note> (**N**). **And Theocritus**: "Such a sweet whistling also, O goatherd, that pine there near the springs resounds." And both these and the above verses of **Theocritus** were in the mind of **Virgil**: "For neither does the whistle of the coming South Wind delight me so much, nor the shores struck by the wave, as the rivers that run down through the rocky valleys" <note>original: "Nam neque me tantum venientis sibilus Austri Nec percussa iuvant fluctu tam litora, quam quae Saxosas inter decurrunt flumina valles"</note> **Eclogue V**. — **line 87.** *Rustle* [rombano]. All the texts read *trumpet* [trombano] here: I wished to change it; and following the **Bazzini** edition I was pleased to write *rombano*, as a word more suited to signify that murmur or whistle emitted by the tops of the pines when shaken by the wind; which does not seem so great to me that it could be compared to a trumpeting (**A**). — **line 88.** *Delightful* [solazzevole]. In the first centuries of the language, the ending in *e* for the plural of third-declension feminine adjectives is not rare. **Dante, Paradise, I**: ".... All natures inclined" <note>original: "accline Tutte nature"</note> and **Canto XV**, of the blessed souls, "were concordant in silence" <note>original: "a tacer fur concorde."</note> And examples abound even outside of rhyme and in prose. — **line 90.** *like a puppy*, docile as a *little dog*. *Cucciolo* is said of a dog not yet finished growing. — **line 92.** *Hallo*: *hailo*, you have it. See the **Tuscan grammarians** (**N**).

->THYRSIS.<-

Yes, I have it. I wish its head were cut off,
for it nearly disemboweled me.
It ran at me to butt me with its head:
Yet I eventually guided it back to the herd:
but I can well tell you that its belly is full.

Now I would very much like to hear the reason
why you were so long in returning.

->THYRSIS.<-

<margin>100</margin> I stayed to gaze upon a noble maiden
who goes gathering flowers around the mountain:
nor do I believe I shall ever see another so beautiful,
more graceful in her actions or more lovely of brow:
she sings so sweetly and speaks so sweetly,
that she would turn a river back toward its source:
she has a face of snow and roses, and a head of gold,
and dark eyes and a white dress.

->ARISTAEUS.<-

<margin>108</margin> Stay here, Mopsus; for I wish to follow her;
because she is the one of whom I spoke to you.

->MOPSUS.<-

Beware, Aristaeus, that too great a daring
does not lead you into some wretched place.

->ARISTAEUS.<-

Either I must die this day,
or prove how much power my fate shall have.

**Line 98.** Our two manuscripts clearly say in this verse *Or io vorrebbe la cagion udire* <note>original: "Now I would [incorrect verb form] the reason hear"</note>: and this reading being undoubtedly false, I chose to correct it (A). — **line 106.** **Petrarch**: "The head of fine gold, and warm snow the face;" elsewhere: "She who has snow for a face, gold for hair" <note>original: "La testa or fine, e calda neve il volto" and "Quella che ha neve il volto, oro i capelli"</note> (N). <note>Poliziano frequently uses these "Petrarchan" descriptions—gold hair and snowy skin—which were the standard for beauty in Renaissance poetry.</note> — **line 111.** *Lato* <note>Side/Place</note>. Here simply used for *part* or *place*; like its plural in **Dante**, *Paradiso*, XXIX. ".... this truth is written in many places [lati]," and as the Tuscan people still use it.

<header>SECOND ACT.</header>
<note>The original heading is in Latin: "ACTVS SECVNDVS."</note>

Stay, Mopsus, near this fountain;
For I wish to go seek her beyond that mountain.

### MOPSUS.
<margin>116</margin>
O Thyrsis, and what do you think now of your master?
<note>original: "sire" – here meaning lord or king.</note>

v. 129. Let it be noted that this verse is missing in Manuscript V. (A). — v. 130. Variation: *I am not wolf or bear*: Ms. Vit. (A). **V. 148.** Vitaliani Manuscript: *Wherefore the harm of—* **pitiless** (A). — **v. 149.** Vitaliani Manuscript: *To the weeping I invite you* (A). — **v. 153.** <note>The editor considers this an "exaggeration of the Petrarchan exaggeration"</note> from the poem: "River that often grows from my weeping" <note>original Italian: "Fiume che spesso del mio pianger cresci"</note>. — **v. 155.** **Darkness.** All the texts have this: but it seems to us that *Darkness* <note>original Italian: "Oscurità"</note> is the true reading (Note from the Silvestri edition). — **v. 159-162.** Imitated from the poet Moschus <note>A Greek bucolic poet from the 2nd century BCE</note> in his *Epitaph for Bion*: "Moan for me mournfully, O hills, O Dorian wave; and, O rivers, lament the lovely Bion: now, O plants, weep for me, and, O woods, now deplore: now turn purple, O roses, from mourning, now, O anemones." And from Bion <note>Another Greek poet famous for his "Lament for Adonis"</note>: "All the mountains say, and the oaks, 'Alas for Adonis'; and the rivers bewail the sorrows of Venus; and the springs weep for Adonis on the mountains" (N). — **v. 166-167.** Catullus <note>Roman poet</note>: "like a flower on the furthest meadow, after it has been touched by the passing plow" <note>original Latin: "veluti prati ultimi flos, praetereunte postquam tactus aratro est"</note>. Virgil: "Like a flower pressed down by a maiden's thumb, whether of soft violet or drooping hyacinth" <note>original Latin: "Qualem virginea depressum pollice florem Seu mollis violae seu languentis hyacinthi"</note>; elsewhere: "Just as when a purple flower, cut by the plow, languishes as it dies" <note>original Latin: "Purpureus veluti cum flos succisus aratro Languescit moriens"</note>; thus translated by the poet Ariosto: "As a purple flower dies languishing, which the plowshare leaves cut as it passes." ->MNESILLUS.<-
See how sorrowfully
That poor wretch departs

->ORPHEUS.<-
Now let us weep, O disconsolate lyre;
For the usual song no longer suits us:
Let us weep while the heavens turn on their poles,
And let Philomela <note>In Greek mythology, Philomela was transformed into a nightingale; her name is often used poetically to refer to the bird and its mournful song.</note> yield to our weeping.
O heaven, O earth, O sea, O dire fate!

---
<margin>V. 209-216.</margin> The <term>Satyr</term> <note>Mnesillus, a woodland deity characterized by horse or goat-like features</note> is an actor not yet seen appearing in this drama. This is missing in the previous editions: but a third actor on the scene was very necessary here. <term>Orpheus</term>, having just heard the fatal news, must have remained so astonished that, losing all breath, he was not able to open his voice to lament; as happens to anyone to whom painful news is brought. Meanwhile, then, while <term>Orpheus</term>, overwhelmed by bitter sorrow, remains silent, so that the scene does not remain empty and interrupted, the <term>Satyr</term> speaks, marveling and pitying the state of the unhappy <term>Orpheus</term>. He follows in his footsteps and goes spying on his movements to see then if the mountain will be moved by his song, as is fabled of him. <term>Euripides</term> also introduced <term>Satyrs</term> in his *<term>Cyclops</term>*.
<column-break/>
This usage in <term>woodland</term> <note>original: "boscherecce"</note> and <term>pastoral</term> fables was maintained by <term>Giraldi</term>, <term>Tasso</term>, <term>Guarini</term>, and others (A).
<margin>— v. 209-212.</margin> Similar to what the chorus says in <term>Oedipus the King</term> <note>original: "Edipo tiranno"</note>: "Now how she departed, spurred by wild grief, the wife of <term>Oedipus</term>! I fear lest from this silence some evil may prepare" (N). — *The word "sola" (lonely/solitary) recalls the <term>Virgilian</term> line:* "You, sweet spouse, you on the lonely shore with him, you as the day arrived, you as it departed, he sang" <note>original: "Te, dulcis coniux, te solo in litore secum, Te veniente die, te, decedente, cane"</note> from the *<term>Georgics, Book IV</term>*. And *sola* in the sense of <term>hermit-like</term> <note>original: "romito"</note>, <term>uninhabited</term> <note>original: "disabitato"</note>, or <term>deserted</term> <note>original: "deserto"</note>, as the poet <term>Leopardi</term> first noted (Annotations on the <term>Songs</term> <note>original: "Canzoni"</note>, <term>Bologna</term>, 1824), was used among the Italians by <term>Petrarch</term>: "things will be dark and lonely," by <term>Della Casa</term>: "dark and lonely woods," and many others he cites. We add <term>Ariosto</term>, Canto XXVII: "the loneliest shores."

<summary>Orpheus is paralyzed by the news of Eurydice's death, prompting the Satyr Mnesillus to comment on his silent grief before Orpheus begins a formal lament. The scholarly notes explain the dramatic necessity of the Satyr and the poetic tradition of "lonely" landscapes in classical and Italian literature.</summary>

-> **ORPHEUS** sings with mournful words; **PLUTO** and **PROSERPINA**, as well as **EURYDICE** and **TISIPHONE** <note>One of the three Furies, whose name means "avenging murder." <margin>241</margin>
Pity, pity for the wretched lover,
May pity seize you, O spirits of hell:
Love alone has guided me down here.
I have flown down here upon his wings.

Let this wretched man pass,
Who has heaven and all the elements as enemies,
And comes to obtain mercy or death.
Therefore, open the iron gates for me.

And does he make the dead people weep with him?
<margin>260</margin>
Neither does Sisyphus <note>A king punished in the underworld by being forced to roll a massive boulder up a hill, only for it to roll back down every time he nears the top.</note> press the stone

<margin>269</margin>
Dear husband, since for your love
I left the supernal heaven
And was made queen of hell,
<margin>272</margin>

That could soften my heart.
<margin>275</margin>
Now, full of longing, I wait for that voice;

<note>Translator’s Note: The following scholarly commentary discusses whether certain lines belongs to the original author, Poliziano.</note>

...it is read in the stanzas that [Minos] had come to fill [Pluto] with suspicions and to remind him of the past damages suffered by those who, while living, had previously descended down there; it is likely that he would not have been quiet and that indeed he would have called upon all his forces to put himself on the defense. However, reading nothing of this, we can well assert that that octave of Minos was not inserted here by Poliziano. Moreover, it is entirely unlikely that Minos could speak thus: since, if the sweet sound of Orpheus's lyre had moved all the infernal spirits, there is no reason why Minos should be excluded from such emotion, so as to be able to suggest thoughts of jealousy and suspicion to the King of Avernus <note>A name for the underworld, derived from a volcanic crater lake in Italy believed to be an entrance to Hades.</note>. V. 337-340. Verses from Ovid, Elegy XII, *Amores*. <note>original: "Ite triumphales circum mea tempora lauri. Vicimus: in nostro est ecce Corinna sinu. Hæc est præcipuo victoria digna triumpho"</note> — "Go, triumphal laurels, around my brow. We have won: behold, Corinna is in our embrace. This victory is worthy of a special triumph." (N). — v. 338-339. In the Vittorio Manuscript, it reads as follows: *We have conquered: Eurydice’s life is restored to me. This victory is especially worthy of a crown for me* (A). This outburst by Orpheus in Latin verses was discussed in Observation VI. It only remains to observe that in our two manuscripts, this <term>quatrain<gloss>tetrastico</gloss></term>, though somewhat varied, is entirely composed of Poliziano’s own verses, except for the first one. In the printed editions, however, except for the second line, they are all by Ovid, taken from the first, third, and eighth couplets of the twelfth elegy of the second book of the *Amores*. In the very act where we see Orpheus reaching the height of his contentment, having obtained the woman who constituted all his happiness, we also see him fallen into extreme misfortune, losing her through such a slight error. This is the <term>reversal of fortune<gloss>peripezia</gloss></term>, a part so essential to tragedy, in order to arouse that compassion which the tragic poet must aim his art to acquire. This compassion is not regarded merely as a simple end for the poet, as if it were enough for him to draw only tears and sighs from the spectators; rather, it is usually held as a means leading to the purging of souls from vice and igniting them toward virtue through the example demonstrated on the stage. Here, Poliziano intended to teach how much strength is required in a heart that wishes to reach the possession of its happiness; for it must not only conquer external obstacles, but with much more constancy, the internal ones that the passions always oppose to it. The immoderate impatience and the unrestrained affection of Orpheus are what, after so much effort, lose her irreparably. Let whoever listens to this tragedy, therefore, become wise, and know how to restrain themselves when the occasion arises. These are the exalted goals of the tragic poet, not lost sight of by our Poliziano (A). — v. 341-346. Here too we find Virgil followed by our Author: <note>original: "Illa: Quis et me, inquit, miseram, et te perdidit, Orpheu? Quis tantus furor? en iterum crudelia retro Fata vocant, conditque natantia lumina somnus. Jamque vale, feror ingenti circumdata nocte, Invalidasque tibi tendens, heu non"</note> — "She spoke: 'Who has ruined both miserable me and you, Orpheus? What great madness? Behold, the cruel Fates call me back again, and sleep hides my swimming eyes. And now farewell, I am carried off surrounded by vast night, stretching out my weak hands to you—alas, no [longer yours]...'" <note>The quote from Virgil's *Georgics* (Book IV) breaks off here.</note>

---

the matter and come to a conclusion more quickly, the fourteenth octave of the first book of the aforementioned <term>Stanzas<gloss>The 'Stanze per la giostra', a famous unfinished poem by Poliziano celebrating a Medici tournament</gloss></term>, which begins there in a somewhat different but insignificant way: *How wretched is he who changes his will*. Dr. **Buonafede Vitali**, previously mentioned by me, is of the opinion that this stanza is misplaced here with little good judgment, as it is openly contrary to the laws of good discourse. Orpheus, he once told me, should do nothing here but complain of his sad misfortune, without going on to blame all women, from whom he has so far received no insult. I would not know how to oppose such a strong reason, except that in both the manuscripts and the printed editions of *Orfeo*, this stanza is consistently found; and therefore it cannot be denied that it was placed there by **Poliziano**. 

On the other hand, in defense of my author, I will say that, just as a grieving man easily breaks into even unjust complaints, so, by showing us Orpheus subject to a most violent passion—indeed, fought by several passions at once—he could make him say what he should not and would not have said if his reason had not been clouded by the vehement transport of love, anger, and despair. By making him speak so strangely, the <term>Maenad<gloss>A female follower of Bacchus/Dionysus, often depicted in a state of ecstatic frenzy</gloss></term> could then with reason say to her companions: “*He shall not escape death, / Since he despises every single woman.*” 

If Orpheus did not despise women in any other way, he undoubtedly did so by ignoring new marriages, as Virgil—whom **Poliziano** chose to follow in this fable—assures us, for which he then deserved to be torn apart by the Maenads: <note>original: "Nulla Venus nullique animum flexere hymenæi. Solue hyperboreas glacies Tanaimque nivalem Arvaque riphæis nunquam viduata pruinis Lustrabat; raptam Eurydicen atque irrita Ditis Dona quærens. Spretæ Ciconum quo munere matres, Inter sacra deum nocturnique orgia Bacchi, Discerptum latos iuvenem sparsere per agros." — Virgil, Georgics IV, 516-522</note> “*No love, no marriage-songs could bend his soul. Through Northern ice and snowy Tanais and fields never stripped of Rhipaean frosts he wandered, mourning his lost Eurydice and the useless gift of Dis [Pluto]. The Ciconian mothers, feeling slighted by this tribute, amidst the sacred rites of the gods and the nightly orgies of Bacchus, scattered the youth, torn apart, across the wide fields.*”

Also worthy of observation in this chorus is the use of <term>truncated verses<gloss>In Italian poetry, *versi tronchi*; lines that end on a stressed vowel, creating a sharp, rhythmic beat</gloss></term> so often used in the songs of our own century. Poliziano would perhaps have been scrupulous about cutting words in half, as is used today to make *amore* (love) and *ancora* (yet) rhyme together by saying *amor* and *ancor*: however, he only used words that are naturally truncated and end in an accented vowel (**A**). — **v. 410.** It seems that the manuscript reads *ogn' uom* (every man), since it is written *oghom*. (**A**). — **v. 413.** Poliziano never forgets the custom so highly recommended by Aristotle to the tragic poet; by which it is meant not only that the actors must think and act according to the circumstances of the times in which they lived, but also that one must attribute to them the use of those things which served common life back then. What greater absurdity would there be than someone wishing to lead Achilles onto the field armed with a musket and pistols? He therefore gives the Maenads the horn as a drinking vessel, since, as Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae* (The Banquet of the Learned).</note> attests, the ancients indeed had the custom of drinking from horns: *The report is that men of old once drank from the horns of oxen.* <note>original: "Priseos fama est homines cornibus olim bibisse bovum."</note> (**Deipnosophistae, book II.**) This same fact is gathered from Saint Ambrose (**Book on Elias and Fasting, chapter 17**) and from Dempster, in whose work Pindar commemorates those made of silver: *Drinking from silver horns, they grew wanton.* <note>original: "Ex argenteis cornibus bibentes lascivierunt."</note> (**Dempster, Roman Antiquities, book V, pages 528, 530, 531.**) This sort of glass came into use, according to the commentator on Nican—

...[-horne]d, from the depiction of Bacchus as horned; for it was believed to be an act of religious devotion to drink from a vessel that adorned the forehead of that deity. If this is true, one should never have drunk so much from horns as during the festivals sacred to Bacchus: therefore Poliziano very judiciously gave the Maenads <note>Female followers of Bacchus, also known as Bacchants, often depicted in a state of ecstatic frenzy.</note> the horn here; just as he also did for the Satyrs and the Bacchants in his *Stanzas*, saying in stanza 111 of the first book: "*One drinks with a cymbal; others seem to laugh: one uses a horn, and another makes a bowl of their hands*" (A). — **v. 414.** The fact that until now the *bottaccio* <note>A rustic flask or canteen used by peasants.</note> was named in this verse instead of the *cantaro* [kantharos] is the same as making Poliziano jump from very ancient customs to recent ones—that is, from the ancient use of the horn for drinking to that which our peasants make of the flask. This, however, is too massive an absurdity. As foolish as the reading of "flask" is, just as wise and erudite is that of the "kantharos." This word signified two things: a certain kind of ship and a kind of drinking vessel; to which Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Latin writer known for his "Saturnalia," a collection of lore and literary criticism.</note> bears witness: "*We said above that the kantharos is both a type of cup and a type of ship... and as a cup, it is a well-known thing even from Virgil himself, who most appropriately assigns the cup proper to Father Liber [Bacchus] to Silenus*" <note>original Latin: "Cantharus et poculi et navigii genus esse supra diximus... et pro poculo quidem nota res est vel ex ipso Virgilio qui aptissime proprium Liberi patris poculum assignat Sileno."</note> (Saturnalia, book 5, chapter 21.) The passage from Virgil <note>The great Roman poet; the author is citing his Eclogues.</note> to which Macrobius alludes is this: "*The boys saw Silenus lying in sleep, his veins swollen from yesterday's wine, as always. His garlands, having slipped from his head, lay just nearby; and a heavy kantharos hung by its worn handle*" <note>original Latin: "Silenum pueri somno videre iacentem, Inflatum hesterno venas, ut sempre, Iaccho. Serta procul tantum capiti delapsa jacebant; Et gravis attrita pendebat cantharus ansa."</note> (Eclogue 6, verse 14 and following.) Such a vessel, which according to Celio Rodigino <note>A Renaissance scholar of antiquity.</note> (Ancient Lessons, book 24, chapter 27) was made of clay, must have been a large bowl fashioned on the model of the ship with which it shared a name; and Ravisius <note>Johannes Ravisius Textor, a French scholar.</note> thinks this can be deduced from the cited Macrobius: "*The name was taken from the similarity to the ship of the same name; for Macrobius shows the name kantharos to be that of a ship from the testimony of Menander*" <note>original Latin: "Nomen autem sumpsit a similitudine navigii eiusdem nominis; nam cantharum nomen esse navigii ostendit Macrobius ex Menandri testimonio."</note> (Officina, part 2, number 30.) Since the *kantharos* is therefore such an ancient drinking vessel and proper to Silenus—the god of drunkards no less than Bacchus—it was quite appropriately attributed to the drinking Maenads rather than the modern flask (A). — **v. 423.** Here we retain the reading of the printed editions. Our manuscripts read: *You are drunk, or I do not know* (A). — <term>The End</term> <note>original Greek: "Τελος" (Telos).</note>. The end. Thus it is written in Greek characters in both the Reggio or Vitelli manuscripts. Many are

<summary>Father Ireneo Affò begins his scholarly critique of Poliziano’s Orpheus by arguing that the work should be considered a tragedy despite Poliziano's own use of the term "fable." Affò demonstrates that in the Renaissance, "fable" was a generic term applied to both tragedies and comedies.</summary>
<keywords>Ireneo Affò, Poliziano, Orfeo, tragedy, genre terminology, Medea, Euripides, Plautus, literary criticism</keywords>

--- Page 333 ---
<meta>This page continues Father Affò’s argument that Poliziano’s use of the general term "fable" in his letters does not contradict the work’s formal classification as a "tragedy."</meta>

<page-num>164</page-num>
# OBSERVATIONS

He well knew that the first was a perfect tragedy, and the others a comedy. Likewise, he could give to *Orfeo* the title of tragedy; and needing then to discuss it familiarly in a letter, he could call it a *fable* <term>favola: a common Renaissance term for a dramatic plot or play, regardless of genre</term>, so as to use a generic and common word. And the words of Luigi Riccoboni <note>Luigi Riccoboni (1676–1753) was a renowned Italian actor and theater historian whose works were influential in 18th-century dramatic criticism.</note> fit here very appropriately: *He was therefore content to give his piece the general name of Fable, which in his time was given to almost all types of poem:* $^1$ <note>original French: "Il s'est donc contenté de donner à sa pièce le nom général de Favola, qui se donnait de son temps à presque toutes les espèces de poëme."</note> and it is very helpful to me at the same time to see an author who, although *Orfeo* was not known to him except in the manner in which it has been printed until now, nonetheless had enough insight to place it in the catalog of Italian tragedies. Indeed, although *Orfeo* cannot be called an entirely perfect tragedy, it cannot be denied that the subject is tragic and has a disastrous end; nor can it be concealed that it has most beautiful parts, which, if they have been liked until now even when they were corrupted and broken, will much more meet with the approval of men of letters in the future when restored to their native beauty and integrity. We must therefore believe that the title given to *Orfeo* by its author is that of tragedy, as our manuscripts have sufficiently clarified. However, we should not grant to Quadrio <note>Francesco Saverio Quadrio (1695–1756) was a scholar who wrote an extensive history of Italian poetry.</note> that the first dramas published *now with the title of tragedy, now with the title of tragic act* $^2$ are the *Filolauro* of Demone Filostrato or truly the *Filostrato and Panfila* of Antonio of Pistoia; for these and similar indigestible farces, rather than tragedies, were undoubtedly composed after *Orfeo*, as I am of the most constant opinion: but it will be necessary to mark the era of the first origin of Italian tragedy with the *Orfeo* of the most ingenious Poliziano. And because this drama is also mixed with the pastoral, even if one does not wish to call it entirely of that nature, I will leave it to others to see if Agostino Beccari of Ferrara rightly claimed primacy in writing pastoral fables with the one entitled *Sacrifice* which he published in the year 1555. But Beccari had been preceded not only by Poliziano but also by Giambattista Giraldi Cintio, who ten years earlier had released the *Egle*, that is in 1545, titling it a *Satire* <term>satira: here referring to a "satyr play" in the ancient Greek style, involving satyrs and forest deities</term> for the Satyrs he introduced there, but which was a true pastoral fable in essence.

---

1 *History of the Italian Theater, Catalog of Tragedies, page 123.*
2 *History and Reason of Every Poetry, vol. 3, book I, page 58.*

# OBSERVATION II.
## ON THE ARGUMENT.

->[Page 133, lines 1-16.]<-

This is both the argument <note>In a Renaissance context, the "argument" is a brief summary of the plot provided at the beginning of a play.</note> and the prologue together, or rather one of those prologues which reveal the path of the fable. If the printed *Orfeo* ever came under the eye of Castelvetro <note>Lodovico Castelvetro (1505–1571) was an influential literary critic known for his strict interpretations of Aristotle’s Poetics.</note>, he must have been pleased to see this prologue placed in the mouth of Mercury; for he was of the opinion that prologues, through which the series of future events is revealed, could never be spoken by mortal men but must be considered the work of gods, as they are those who extend their vision even over the future. For this reason, he blamed Terence for always having men deliver the prologue; and he greatly praised Plautus for making use of the deities. I, however, keeping in mind that precept of Horace

> *Let no god intervene, unless a knot worthy of such a liberator*
> *should occur*, <note>1</note> <note>original Latin: "Nec Deus intersit, nisi dignus vindice nodus Inciderit." This famous rule from Horace’s Ars Poetica advises playwrights against using a "god from the machine" (deus ex machina) to solve plot points that don't require divine intervention.</note>

will say that it seems to me a very improper thing to bring a god onto the stage without necessity to announce what must happen among mortals. I observe that the prince of tragedians, Euripides, out of nineteen tragedies of his that remain to us, has only five in which the gods deliver the prologue; and these are *Hippolytus*, *Alcestis*, *The Bacchae*, *The Trojan Women*, and *Ion*: but I also reflect that those deities who act in such a manner are also involved and have an interest and a role in the entire fable. In the others, we always see the prologue delivered by men. This being the case, who does not see that the most ingenious Poliziano could not have led Mercury onto the stage to announce the tragic events of Orpheus, since Mercury had nothing to do with the action? Shall we say perhaps that he did not know how to choose the best examples from among the many? Let him say so who wishes; for I, for my part, have too high a conceit of my author: and I am all the more fixed in the thought that he did not have Mercury say this prologue, as the two manuscripts make no mention of it at all. We can be confirmed in the certainty of the opinion he must have held regarding prologues by the one he sent to Comparino to be placed before the *Menaechmi* of Plautus, which is not seen to be placed in the mouth of any god but rather appears recited by a studious youth. Here the printed editions and—

<meta>This page continues Father Ireneo Affò’s scholarly commentary on Poliziano’s Orfeo, specifically examining the manuscript variations of the play's title and the historical debate regarding the division of dramas into acts.</meta>

The Chigi manuscript <note>A significant Vatican manuscript containing works by Poliziano and other humanists.</note> varies the title of the *Orfeo*; for where it had first been called a *fable* <note>original: "favola"; a term used in the Renaissance for a secular dramatic poem</note>, we now see it denominated a *festival* <note>original: "festa"</note>, stating: *Mercury, announcer of the festival*. This new title could not have come from the pen of Poliziano; for "festivals" were not at all of the same nature as this drama of ours, as their principal strength consisted in dances, morescas <note>A stylized sword dance or pageant common in Renaissance courts.</note>, jousts, tournaments, and stage machines; with the poetry serving more as an interlude than anything else. But in the *Orfeo* we have a truly theatrical work, excluding those entertaining representations that were usually performed in the enclosures <note>original: "steccati"; the fenced-off areas used for jousting and public spectacles.</note>: and whereas the poetry that accompanied festivals consisted mostly of some cantata or dialogue between two or three actors—such as, for example, half of the *Tirsi* by Baldassare Castiglione and Cesare Gonzaga—in the *Orfeo* we perceive a true fable, with a tragic beginning and end, represented by various interlocutors, divided into acts, and accompanied by choruses; so much so that it should not be confused with simple festivals.

the writer supports his opinion by citing various ancient editions of Terence and Plautus that do not have such divisions: hence it is unlikely that Poliziano would have distinguished the *Orfeo* in this way. But let us proceed slowly with this critique. Who among those even slightly initiated in the poetic school has not read the precept of Horace, in which he strictly commands that every drama have neither more nor less than five acts?

> *Let a play be neither shorter nor longer than the fifth act,*
> *If it wishes to be requested and, once seen, performed again.* ¹ <note>original: "Neve minor quinto neu sit productior actu / Fabula quæ posci vult et spectata reponi." From Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

To whom are the expositions of Asconius Pedianus <note>A 1st-century Roman grammarian known for his commentaries on Cicero's orations.</note>, a contemporary of Virgil, regarding certain orations of Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> not known? He writes without riddle: *A play, whether tragic or comic, must have five acts.* ² <note>original: "Fabula sive tragica sive comica quinque actus habere debet."</note> How then can it be said that the ancients did not at all know the distinction being challenged? Nor should it be said to me that Acron <note>An ancient commentator on Horace.</note>, an ancient commentator on Horace who lived around the 7th century of the common era, interpreted the indicated verses thus: *That is, let him not speak in the play with more than five characters:* ³ <note>original: "Idest, non loquatur in fabula plus quinque personis."</note> for he certainly erred, as Horace is not speaking of the actors there—having reserved that topic for further down where he later wrote: *Nor should a fourth person strive to speak.* <note>original: "Nec quarta loqui persona laboret." This refers to the classical rule that no more than three speaking actors should be on stage at once.</note> 

Acron undoubtedly used corrupt manuscripts; or, better yet, he was not the author of those commentaries, as Giano Parrasio <note>A famous Italian humanist and philologist.</note> learnedly set out to prove in a letter to Gaetano Thiene. ⁴ Ascensio, Heinrich Glarean, and so many other ancient and modern writers who illustrated the works of Horace did not explain that passage in such a way; for it is so clear that nothing could be more so; and when joined with the authority of Asconius, it reaches the highest degree of evidence. It cannot, therefore, be doubted that the Latins knew the division of acts, which they took to imitate from the Greeks, Euripides having used it consistently even in the *Satire of the Cyclops*, as the learned Quadrio <note>Francesco Saverio Quadrio, an 18th-century historian of poetry.</note> observes. ⁵ I see that Aristophanes, according to the Latin version of his comedies undertaken by Andrea Divo of Koper <note>original: "Andrea Divo Giustinopolitano"; a 16th-century translator of Greek classics into Latin.</note>, divided the *Plutus* into eight acts; which, although it is outside the rule, nonetheless confirms the premise. With what certainty then can one pretend to affirm that Albertino Mussato <note>A 14th-century poet and statesman whose play *Ecerinis* is considered the first secular tragedy since antiquity.</note> could not divide his *Ezzelino* into five acts, I [cannot see...]

I certainly do not see it. It seems clear that such honest men, who were not at all involved in this current debate, would have had no reason to alter a work published solely for the purpose of enriching civil and political history, rather than poetic history. Therefore, since they did not inform us otherwise, we must suppose that the *Ezzelino* <note>Referring to the *Ecerinis* by Albertino Mussato (1315), the first secular tragedy of the Renaissance, which concerns the tyrant Ezzelino III da Romano.</note> was divided into five acts in the manuscripts as well.

As for the ancient copies of Terence and Plautus <note>Two of the most influential Roman comic playwrights.</note>, whether one prefers manuscripts or printed editions, I would like to be well understood by my detractors. It is one thing to say that *Act I* or *Act II* was not always written there; it is quite another to say that they *should* not have been written there. Oh! It would be a fine thing indeed if, because one does not see the quatrains and tercets separated in Petrarch’s original sonnets, or the stanzas in his songs, one wanted to deny that Petrarch ever distributed the sonnet and the song into specific parts or structures! In those copies where such distinction was omitted, it was implied; and the wise knew well where the end of each act fell.

As Italy gradually became "barbaric" <note>A common Enlightenment-era reference to the Middle Ages following the fall of the Roman Empire.</note> and letters declined, that which was previously well understood began to be forgotten. These dramatic poets, being considered harmful by the early Fathers of the Church, were read by few, and through the neglect of booksellers, they were easily corrupted, leaving out even what would sometimes have been most necessary. Thus, it was not that the acts did not exist in Terence and Plautus, but only that they could not be easily distinguished by those who were not well-versed in these matters. 

Aelius Donatus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note>, a very ancient grammarian who was the teacher of Saint Jerome in Rome during the fourth century, assures us of this when, in the argument of Terence's *Andria* which he commented upon, he wrote: *It is difficult to discern the division of acts in Latin plays.* <note>original: "Divisionem actuum in latinis fabulis internoscere difficile est."</note> This is the answer that must be given to these sophists who refuse to settle even in the light of truth. 

But let us descend a little from earliest antiquity to times closer to Poliziano, and see if any seed of these "blessed acts" was still preserved. The most illustrious Abate Girolamo Tiraboschi <note>A famous literary historian (1731–1794).</note>, in his second letter addressed to me (which I indicated in the preface), writes:

> "This library (belonging to the most serene Duke of Modena) does not have very old editions of Terence and Plautus, but it has several handwritten codices; and truly, in most of them, there is no division, yet it does exist in some. Thus, the necessity of dividing dramas into acts was well known long before Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a key Renaissance humanist whose play "Orfeo" is often cited in discussions of dramatic structure.</note> was born. Let us now turn to those times in which he wrote the *Orfeo*. Who does not know how many grammarians lived in those days? I will pass over many, but certainly not Giorgio Merula, who died around the same time as our poet but was much older; he provided commentary on Plautus and properly divided and distinguished the acts as was necessary: a fact anyone can observe in the many reprints we have of those commentaries. 

Yet, a strange thing occurred! When it came time to print those ancient comedies, even those editors who were convinced of the necessity of such division omitted it. This was done out of a certain desire to match the "fidelity" of some manuscript in those noble first editions. I can offer very clear evidence of this practice, having seen in the library of San Francesco in my homeland a magnificent text of Plautus, printed in folio by Uldarico Scinzenzeler in Milan in the year 1490. It lacks commentaries and act divisions, but it contains a letter at the end from Eusebio Scutario of Vercelli addressed to Giorgio Merula. In it, he gives Merula the highest praise for having known how to untangle the acts in the comedies of that poet, stating that if it was previously difficult to distinguish them, it was due to the negligence and ignorance of the booksellers:

> *Through their ignorance, we were hardly able to recognize the acts and the division in certain comedies—a division which the most celebrated grammarians consider of primary importance for knowledge and understanding in this genre, and which is usually accomplished through the prologue, <term>protasis</term> <note>The introductory part of a play.</note>, <term>epitasis</term> <note>The part of a play where the action tightens and the plot develops.</note>, and <term>catastrophe</term> <note>The final resolution or unraveling of the plot.</note>.* <note>original Latin: "Horum inscitia quibusdam in comœdiis actus internoscere divisionemque... vix percipere poteramus."</note>

Likewise, I have seen in our library of the Nunziata in Bologna a beautiful Terence in folio, printed in Treviso by Master Paolo Ferrari on July 5, 1481, with the commentaries of the aforementioned ancient Aelius Donatus. He indicates where the acts should be distinguished, yet the printer still did not separate them in the text. Indeed, there is something notable in this work: the commentator derives the reason for distinguishing act from act from the text of Terence himself. To these words, Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a famous 4th-century grammarian whose commentaries on Terence were essential to Renaissance education.</note> promptly adds: *I please in the first act: he reasonably said 'first,' because there are five acts, which are the parts of the play.* Guidone <note>Likely Guido Juvenalis, a 15th-century French scholar.</note> also explained these words in this way in his commentaries, which I have seen printed with the comedy in Venice in 1508 at the expense of Lazzaro de’ Soardi. And would these, then, be those ancient editions and those unappealable examples mentioned by Father Bianchi in favor of the stiff opinion and the pedantry that he believed could be supported by reason? If Trissino, Rucellai, Giustiniano, and sometimes Torelli—who did not always neglect the division of acts—and even Sperone, and among the moderns the most scrupulous and religious Lazzarini, held such a distinction as nothing and took no notice of it; could they perhaps for this reason annul those poetic laws that custom, authority, and the succession of centuries had already established? These men indeed did not care for the division of acts, but they were still justly reproved by Gregorio Giraldi: *There are five acts of plays among the Latins; although today some observe this little, performing much shorter plays, and especially in Tuscany.* ¹

But, so as not to go on longer than is appropriate regarding something so clear, let it suffice to have proven that both before and during the time of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the celebrated humanist and author of "Orfeo."</note>, dramas were divided into five acts. Since this fact could not have been unknown to him, it must certainly have been put into effect in the *Orfeo*. Such a thing, I repeat, could not have been unknown to him; for he later made mention of acts where he wrote that tragedy had its origin in the poems of Homer: *The same [Homer] is also held as the highest author of tragedy, since indeed the poems of Homer can seem to be nothing else but certain acts and dramas.* ² He therefore divided the *Orfeo* into five acts; and, to provide variety and so that the decoration and music might turn out differently, he made the first act pastoral, the second nymphal, the third heroic, the fourth necromantic <note>Dealing with the underworld or magic.</note>, and the fifth bacchanal <note>A wild, drunken celebration in honor of Bacchus.</note>. It is no obstacle to see the Vitali manuscript lacking such division; first, because it is not the oldest, and so—

## OBSERVATION IV.
### CONCERNING THE FISTULA.

->[Page 137, line 51.]<-

Here we see the *fistula* <note>The panpipes or syrinx.</note> named, where previously the *zampogna* <note>Usually a type of bagpipe or a simple rustic pipe.</note> was indicated. The worst part in the printed editions of *Orfeo* is that once the *zampogna* is mentioned, and another time the *fistula* is indicated: a matter that is not right; for either Mopsus was playing the *zampogna*, and it should have always been called a *zampogna*; or he was blowing into the *fistula*, and it should have always been called a *fistula*; as these two instruments are, in reality, different from one another. The <term>fistula</term> <note>From the Latin for 'pipe', this refers specifically to the set of graduated pipes joined together, known today as Panpipes.</note> is that little organ-like instrument resulting from several pipes of unequal measure and sound joined together; whence Virgil says:

> *I have a pipe composed of seven unequal hemlock stalks.* 1
> <note>original: "Est mihi disparibus septem compacta cicutis Fistula."</note>

->Horns and pipes made from the bark<-
->Of willow or chestnut.<-
