Wherefore, with great discernment, Father Filippo Bonanni distinguished them in his *Harmonic Cabinet*, speaking of the *fistula* at number XXII and the *zampogna* at number XXVII. Now, the true text of Poliziano cannot be the one that has been printed until now, since these two instruments are poorly confused within it; rather, it will be the one that we have discovered, since, by always referring to the *fistula*, one does not run into any impropriety that might do a disservice to the author's erudition.

### OBSERVATION V.

## ON THE CHORUS OF THE DRYADS.

->[Page 143, v. 150-183.]<-

The chorus of the Dryads <note>Wood nymphs in Greek mythology.</note> mentioned by Virgil was executed by him (Poliziano), but with admirable skill; taking pleasure in imitating within it the choral dances of the Greeks. Galen writes that these people, *as often as they circled the altar from the right while singing, called it the strophe; when indeed they returned from the left, the antistrophe; finally, when they stood before the god and performed the rest of the song, they called it the epode.* <gloss>4</gloss> <note>original Latin: "quoties cantando aram a dextra circuibant, strophen vocabant; cum vero redibant a sinistra, antistrophen: demum, cum in cospectu dei consisterent et cantici reliquum peragerent, id epodon dicebant."</note> Because then the dance so much to

[From the] left as much as from the right was of equal time, and the pause

of an equal number of verses arranged in the same order,
and in the epode <note>The epode is the third part of a Greek choral ode, following the strophe and antistrophe.</note> another different rule was held. Poliziano,
most expert in poetic rules, wished to compose this
chorus of various sections, each of which had a strophe,
antistrophe, and epode; with this condition, however, that the strophe was always
the same and served at once as a refrain and a reprise. Therefore the present chorus on the stage must have been sung

sixteen Dryads. Besides all this, one might ask if all the Dryads of the chorus
sang in a jumble or with some order. To this it is said that
Poliziano could not be ignorant of the law prescribed by Aristotle,
that a single actor must hold the principal part of the
chorus: *The leadership of the chorus should belong to only one of the actors.* <note>original Latin: "Chori summam penes unum dumtaxat ex histrionibus esse oportet."</note> <gloss>3</gloss> A single Dryad had to sing and the whole
crowd then repeat the refrain during the pause: a law
which is also seen observed in the final chorus of the Maenads <note>Followers of the god Dionysus, often depicted in a state of ecstatic frenzy.</note>. To
understand even better how choruses were sometimes distributed
by the ancients, we shall observe a letter by Filippo Pigafetta,
who, narrating how in the year 1585 *Oedipus the King* by Sophocles was performed in the Olympic
Theater of Vicenza—translated from the Greek
by Orsatto Giustiniano—says that *the chorus was formed of
fifteen people, seven per side, and their leader in the middle;
which chorus, with pleasant speech and harmony, fulfilled its
office.* <gloss>4</gloss> Meanwhile, Poliziano wished to compose this chorus
of Dryads, insofar as, as Quadrio <note>Francesco Saverio Quadrio (1695–1756), an author of a massive history of poetry.</note> well says, the choruses
must always be represented by those who likely
had been present and interested, or likely
should or could be present and interested in the action.

## OBSERVATION VI.

### REGARDING THE LATIN ODE THAT WAS READ IN THE PRINTED EDITIONS OF THE ORFEO, BY BACCIO UGOLINI, AND THE LATIN VERSES INTERSPERSED WITH THE TUSCAN ONES.

->[Pag. 145, v. 197-200.]<-

The ode which is read in place of this quatrain in the Comino edition and other printings is the following:
->*O [you who have] long played my games, etc.* <note>original Latin: "O meos longum modulata lusus ec." This is the opening line of a Latin ode composed by Poliziano.</note> <gloss>2</gloss><-

In the Latin works of Poliziano printed by Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515), the famous Venetian humanist and printer.</note>, by Episcopius, by Gryphius, and by others, this ode holds the last place among the author's epigrams with this simple title: *In praise of the Mantuan Cardinal* <note>original Latin: "In laudem Cardinalis Mantuani"</note>: nor can it be doubted that it was written in praise of Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga, at whose request the *Orfeo* was also composed. But in the *Orfeo* printed by Benedetti, and later in the other editions up to the last Cominian one, it is preceded by these words: *Orpheus, singing the following Latin verses upon the mountain on his lyra—which, regarding Master Baccio Ugolini, the actor of said character of Orpheus, are in honor of the Mantuan Cardinal—was interrupted by a shepherd announcing the death of Eurydice.* <note>This rubric suggests that the actor playing Orpheus stepped out of character to praise the play's patron before being pulled back into the plot.</note> First, let the Cominian printing be corrected, where *Braccio* is wrongly read instead of *Baccio*; and then let it be observed how it is taken for certain here that Ugolini was in Mantua when the *Orfeo* was first performed; and furthermore, that he was the lead actor in the tragedy: a matter that is certainly not improbable; indeed, it can be supported by the appearance of very good reasoning. In fact, we have it as certain that he was already an intimate associate <note>The Italian "famigliare" refers to a member of a high-ranking official's household or "famiglia."</note> of the aforementioned cardinal, as gathered from a letter by Lodovico Gonzaga, Bishop-elect of Mantua, whom we have cited elsewhere, which is addressed to Ruffino of Gabbioneta, his...

acting as an agent in Rome on the 10th day of January, 1485. Here are his words:
> *When our Baccio Ugolino—to whom we bear singular love for his virtues and merits, and for having been a most affectionate servant of the blessed memory of our most reverend brother and father the Cardinal, and of our entire house, as he remains today—wishes to stay in that house of ours and have an honorable room suitable for his lodging, assign him one without any resistance or delay, and keep him good company, for such is our full intention.* <note>original Italian: "Quando lo Baccio nostro Ugolino... portiamo singular amore... assignategliene una, e fateli buona compagnia..." This letter from the Bishop-elect of Mantua confirms Ugolino's high standing with the Gonzaga family.</note>

It is not contradictory, then, that in 1472 he could have been in Mantua in the company of Cardinal Gonzaga. This confirms the opinion of Mencken <note>Friedrich Otto Mencken (1708–1754), a scholar who wrote about the life of Poliziano.</note> ^1^, who disapproves of the opinion of Clausing, where he claims that Ugolino was a student of Poliziano ^2^. For if Poliziano, at the age of eighteen, found himself in the company of Ugolino in the service of the Cardinal of Mantua, they must have been at the very least of the same age; and even if one wishes to suppose Ugolino was younger, Poliziano was not yet in a position to be the <term>preceptor</term> <note>a teacher or tutor, often in a private household</note> of another, not for lack of knowledge, but for lack of age and authority. This man was truly named Bartolommeo, but was called Baccio according to Florentine custom, as he was born in Florence. We have testimony of this in the letters of the aforementioned Bishop-elect of Mantua, where he is usually named now one way, now the other. Various praises of him can be seen among the letters of Marsilio Ficino, of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, and of our Poliziano, especially in one written to Francesco Pucci, where among his many virtues it is mentioned that he was a most excellent <term>improvvisatore</term> <note>a poet who composes and recites verses extemporaneously, often to musical accompaniment</note>. ^3^ He was very dear to Lorenzo the Magnificent de' Medici, who later employed him in various embassies and honorable offices. Some of his rhymes are found in certain old collections and manuscripts; a sample of them is also found in the collection of Dr. Buonafede Vitali, a name most dear to me. Returning, however, to the subject of the ode, I do not doubt that it was written on the same occasion as the *Orfeo*, nor do I doubt that it was recited in a full assembly before the Cardinal, either by Baccio or by someone else. But I strongly deny that it was made to be spoken by the character of Orpheus on the stage in the middle of the tragedy. I shall never forget what I read in Aristophanes, the Greek comic poet:

> *A poet, for the plays he must create and represent, must have his own character match the theme.* <note>original Latin: "Oportet poetam virum ad fabulas Quas oportet facere et repraesentare, ad has mores habere."</note> ^4^

<term>Period accuracy</term><note>original: "costume." In 18th-century dramatic theory, this refers not just to clothing, but to the "manners and customs" appropriate to a historical period.</note>, a part of dramatic theory that can never be recommended enough, is absolutely necessary. By "period accuracy," we mean that actors on the stage must think, speak, and act as they would have thought, spoken, and acted in the days in which they lived. If an ancient character is made to think, speak, and act in a modern way, the proper order and <term>verisimilitude</term><note>the appearance of being true or real</note> are completely overturned. A well-educated spectator is easily angered if he sees Achilles, instead of carrying a great shield and spear, armed with a pistol and a musket. Likewise, it is far too disagreeable to see a man who lived many centuries ago come to words with one of our own times; for then that intolerable <term>anachronism</term> is committed, which disrupts not only period accuracy but every other sound law of poetics, criticism, and anything else you like—an error most deservedly condemned by a modern Frenchman.<gloss>1 See the *Telemacomania*, or a Critique of Telemachus.</gloss> This is even more worthy of blame if that actor is led to speak of things about which he could not, and should not, have had any idea. 

Now, we are in such a case. If we wish to suppose that the reported ode was placed in the mouth of Orpheus, here we have an ancient man speaking to a modern man, such as Cardinal Francesco was. Here is a man speaking of things that did not yet exist in his time: for he speaks of Virgil, mentions the name of Maecenas, and discusses the Gonzaga family—all things that are recent compared to the time of Orpheus. Finally, he mentions the "red hat" of the Cardinals, which was not given to them until the time of Paul II, the Supreme Pontiff who died a year before this tragedy was composed;<gloss>2 Platina, in the *Life of Paul II*.</gloss> and he mentions the <term>triple crown</term><note>the "triregno," or the papal tiara with three crowns</note> which he wishes for Gonzaga. These are all things of which it cannot be supposed that Orpheus had the slightest idea. 

Therefore, if we wish to believe that Orpheus, brought onto the stage, recited this ode, we cannot help but accuse Poliziano of being reckless and lacking judgment; we would have to lump him in with the dregs of the most abject composers of fables and plays. Among these, I will always remember a certain Augustinian friar (whose name I forget, that book having been kindly stolen from me) who composed a theatrical *Passion of Christ* in <term>ottava rima</term><note>an Italian rhyming stanza form</note>. In it, he induced the blessed Jesus to make a last will and testament, which is read as being notarized by Saint John the Evangelist, with various Latin texts scattered throughout to which he refers—one especially taken from the Athanasian Creed. But no, Poliziano does not deserve to be bundled together with such a breed of poetasters; and he deserves it even less because he is entirely cleared of this stain by our two manuscripts, in which he must be...

He uses a humorous example of a poorly written Passion play to illustrate the absurdity of such historical errors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Father Affò’s argument regarding the textual integrity of Poliziano’s Orfeo. Having previously argued that a Latin ode to Cardinal Gonzaga was an anachronistic insertion, he now proposes theories on how that error entered the printed tradition and defends Poliziano’s use of Latin within an Italian play.</meta>

<header>BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.</header>

...held until now by experts who likely believed that *Orpheus* was written by Poliziano exactly as it has been read until now. He [Poliziano] therefore brought Orpheus onto the stage in the act of beginning a hymn to Hercules, something very much in keeping with the <term>custom</term><note>historical appropriateness or "decorum"</note> of that ancient Thracian. This hymn, if he had been allowed to finish it, would perhaps have been very short, since Poliziano would not have been ignorant of what Pausanias had written about the hymns of Orpheus; since Pausanias, as Patrizi assures us, *writes that he was concise in his hymns and extremely brief.*¹ But how, someone might ask, was that ode inserted into *Orpheus* instead of this <term>quatrain</term><note>original: "tetrastico"; a four-line stanza</note>? I have already indicated the method in the preface. This tragedy was poorly compiled from memory and cobbled together from fragments of the distributed parts or with the help of someone who had acted in its performance. Since they did not have everything in mind, and many things were forgotten—and among others, the present quatrain—it was thought a very fine thing to place that famous ode in Orpheus’s mouth, as it was something born in the very same circumstances in which *Orpheus* appeared. It was easier to substitute this, as it was a better-known work and one the author had not been as protective of as he proved to be with *Orpheus*. But if this theory is not pleasing, here is another at hand that is perhaps more plausible. The manuscript that served as the standard for all printings made so far had probably been damaged by a missing leaf, which should have contained all the previous action of the Dryads and the quatrain. Later copyists, finding this gap and not knowing how to guess what should be there, and remembering only that in this place certain Latin verses sung by Orpheus should fall, shoved the ode in there, as it could very well fill the space of an entire leaf; and thus they believed they had made up for the defect in the manuscript. It now seems necessary to mention something regarding this mixture of Latin and the <term>vernacular</term><note>original: "volgare"; the common Italian language of the time</note>. To some, who look upon it with a more indifferent eye than mine, the mixture seen here will seem improper. I will not say they are entirely wrong; but I urge them to reflect a little on that century, which was not yet fully refined in certain matters—though, reflecting somewhat on this myself, I find a way to excuse our author. I imagine he thought thus: when Orpheus acts throughout the drama, he speaks no less than the others; and his speech, though put into verse by the playwright, must be assumed to be familiar. Here, however, needing to bring Orpheus onto the stage swept up by <term>inspiration</term><note>original: "estro"; the "poetic fury" or creative heat of a performer</note> and in the manner of a poet who is actually singing, it is necessary to have him speak in a way that shows he is...

> Over-illuminating with your brightness

Matteo Visconte da San Canziano held in high esteem this mixture of Latin and the <term>vernacular</term><note>The "volgare," or the everyday Italian language as opposed to scholarly Latin</note> created by Poliziano, and he cited it as his own justification. Read the most ornate compositions of Poliziano, which you will find mixed with both styles. Is it not permitted for me to do what he did?* <note>original: "Ridebis forsan, Gambe diserte, quod latinum miscuerim vulgaribus... An non licet mihi facere quod ille?"</note> This translation was certainly seen in a dream by Argelati; for in his *Library of Translators* he wrote that the translator had said he intended to imitate Poliziano in translating the works of others from Latin into the vernacular—a thing neither said by him, nor ever done by Poliziano.

# OBSERVATION VII.

## ON THE DUPLICITY OF THE SCENE IN ACT IV.

->[Page 148.]<-

The words found in the Reggio text which say, *For indeed this scene uses a double act*, <note>original: "Etenim duplici actu hæc scena utitur"</note> seem to me somewhat strange; and I believe them to be an error by the <term>scribe</term><note>original: "amanuense"; a person who copies manuscripts</note>. I hold that it should read, *For indeed this act uses a double scene*; <note>original: "Etenim duplici actus hic scena utitur"</note> that is to say, that in this act, two different appearances of the scene were represented to the spectator at the same time. The ancient theater did not have just a single street in which the actors were always seen, and where, by means of <term>revolving prisms</term>... <note>original: "versatili"; likely referring to 'periaktoi,' revolving triangular machines used in early theater to change scenery</note>

machinery could make the scene disappear to bring in another, as happens in modern theater. At that time, the spectator, regardless of where they were positioned, had the pleasure of seeing three avenues open to their gaze; one of which represented, for example, a street, another a palace, and the third a prison. This is how Lorenzo Beyerlinck depicts them: *On the right side of the stage, strangers and guests would emerge; on the left was the prison; the center was occupied by the palace. In the middle section, two additional doors were joined;* <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "Dextra scenæ parte peregrini et hospites egrediebantur; in sinistra carcer erat; medium locum regia obtinebat. Mediæ parti duæ præterea portæ adiunctæ erant;"</note> and this was so they could pass conveniently, if necessary, from one place to another. Dempster <gloss>2</gloss> also describes the ancient theater this way: and the drawings of it, which we find in Vitruvius as illustrated by Daniele Barbaro and reproduced by Quadrio and Bianchi, leave us in no doubt of this truth. Hence it is that, when Pliny, <gloss>3</gloss> and with him Alessandro degli Alessandri, <gloss>4</gloss> commemorate that theater which Scaurus built during his <term>aedileship</term><note>An elective office in ancient Rome responsible for maintenance of public buildings and regulation of festivals</note> <unclear>fecerat</unclear> with a **triple scene**, we immediately understand how it was constructed. The famous Palladio wished to raise the celebrated Olympic Theater of Vicenza with equal architecture, the drawing of which we see in Riccoboni, who speaks of it in this manner: *Scholars cannot understand how, in several places in the comedies of Plautus, two actors find themselves on stage together in a rush and say several lines to one another without seeing each other. The Olympic Theater clarifies all of this for us.* <gloss>5</gloss> <note>original: "Les sçavans ne peuvent pas comprendre comment dans several endroits des comédies de Plaute des acteurs se trouvent sur la scène tous les deux avec empressement et qu'il disent several répliques l'un et l'autre sans se voir. Le Théâtre Olympique nous met au fait de tout cela."</note> One of these places in Plautus is certainly the fifth act of the *Asinaria*, where Argyrippus, Demenetus, and Philaenium are seen carousing inside a house, while on the other side one sees Pamphagus with Artemona, Demenetus’s wife, coming down the street to the door of the house and observing what is being done inside; the audience sees both parties acting at the same time; until Artemona, no longer able to suffer the debaucheries of her old husband, rushes inside the house and vents her anger with bitter words. This being established, I say that the theater where the *Orfeo* was performed in Mantua must have been constructed in such a way that, following the prescribed examples, it opened up two scene representations to the audience in this place: one representing the path *Orpheus* took as he approached hell, the other showing hell itself, where Pluto and Proserpine are seen moved by the new song coming from outside. In that century, the wondrous representations and surprising machines—of which we have very vivid descriptions by many writers of the time—were so frequent that one must suppose that in the scene representing Hell, there were arranged in beautiful order, amidst their torments, Sisyphus, Tantalus, Tityus, Ixion, and the <term>Belides</term><note>Also known as the Danaides, the fifty daughters of Danaus condemned to endlessly draw water in perforated vessels</note>. ## OBSERVATION VIII.

### ON THE <term>POLYMETER</term><note>The use of several different poetic meters within a single literary work</note> USED BY THE POET IN THIS TRAGEDY.

->[Page 148 and following, verses 257-268.]<-

Our manuscripts give us this speech, as well as that of Proserpina, in the form of a <term>madrigal</term><note>A complex form of secular vocal music, often with varying line lengths</note>; whereas the printed editions provide it in <term>ottava rima</term><note>A stanza of eight lines with a specific rhyme scheme (ABABABCC), common in Italian heroic poetry</note>. Poliziano could very well have changed the meter in these two passages so that a more pathetic <note>In the historical sense: "evoking deep emotion or pity"</note> musical tone, corresponding to the quality of the speaker, could take place. I know that the most distinguished Abate Serassi did not entirely approve of Poliziano’s decision, having written in his *Annotations to the Rhymes of Baldassarre Castiglione*: *In Poliziano one reads <term>terza rima</term>, <term>canzonette</term>, <term>ballate</term>, and even a <term>Latin ode</term>; if they were not as beautiful, natural, and refined as they are, certainly such a variety of meter in a single composition could not be pleasing.*¹ But it cannot be denied that this tragedy was adapted for music; it is quite clear that no diversity of tones could have been easily put into use if the entire work had been bound in <term>ottava rima</term>. This was especially true back then when music was still simple, and chapel masters had not yet learned how to make a singer warble for a quarter of an hour over a single syllable, nor how to ruin a poet's verses by cutting them in half—

<meta>This page continues Father Affò’s discussion from page 182 regarding the poetic structure of Poliziano’s Orfeo. Having previously introduced the idea of "polymeter," Affò here argues that the variety of verse forms was a deliberate choice to better serve the musicality of the performance, contrasting it with the more rigid standards of his own time.</meta>

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>BY FATHER IRENEO AFFÒ.</header>

carrying them and repeating them in reverse, to make them serve their capricious <term>cantilenas</term><note>Simple, repetitive vocal melodies, often used here in a slightly disparaging sense to describe modern musical compositions</note>. All verses and all meters have their own harmony, requiring their own determined tempo and perhaps even a different tone. But this truth, which musicians today do not wish to understand, was well understood back then, when art took its rules from nature. In those days, the musician served the poet and accompanied the harmonic notes of the poetic language with song. To Poliziano, therefore, as the composer of *Orpheus*, fell the task of finding varied meters, so that the music might turn out more varied and delightful; and this he did most laudably, in my opinion. I do not know, then, by what law one must insist on a drama being written entirely in one meter, when there is no lack of examples in *Euripides*, *Aristophanes*, and others, who clearly approve the practice of ever-pleasing variety. In our own day, <term>blank verse</term><note>original: "lo sciolto", referring to unrhymed hendecasyllables</note> has sufficiently decided the manner of writing tragedies; but when Poliziano was alive, this wise recourse had not yet been thought of: hence he had to stick to what could be judged best under the circumstances of his times, and especially on the occasion of weaving a drama applicable to music.

## OBSERVATION IX.

### ON THE TITLING OF ACT V (BACCHANAL).

->[Page 155.]<-

<margin>
¹ *Commentaries, vol. I, book 4, chapters 14 and 15.*
² *Progymnasmata before his Bacchanalia.*
</margin>
Baruffaldi, a subject very well known to the literary republic, had no knowledge of the title that Poliziano placed at the head of this final portion of *Orpheus*: nonetheless, departing somewhat from Crescimbeni—who had recognized it as <term>dithyrambic</term><note>A passionate, wild style of choral poetry originally dedicated to the god Bacchus</note>¹—he categorized it among the <term>Bacchic</term> or, as we might say, the <term>Bacchanals</term>.² Some before him had not well distinguished dithyrambic poetry from the bacchanal, as he did: however, since the rule he gives is not so rigorous that these types of poetry cannot be confounded in a certain way, I consider it as much dithyrambic as bacchanalian, in order to conform to the doctrine of Poliziano himself, who showed that both types of poetry were one and the same where he wrote: *The Athenians, at the feasts of Father Liber <note>original: "Liberi patris", a Roman name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, which they call Dionysia, and our people*...

*“They called them Bacchanalia or Liberalia, etc.”*<note>original: "Baccanalia seu Liberalia vocitarunt, ec."</note> $^1$ I say that here Poliziano maintains that the <term>dithyramb</term><note>A wild, rhythmic hymn sung in honor of the god Dionysus</note> and the <term>bacchanal</term><note>A festival or song dedicated to Bacchus, the god of wine and ecstasy</note> are the same thing; for he says that the festivals—or rather the poems praising Bacchus—which Plato called *dithyrambs*, $^2$ were called *bacchanals* by our own people. Since he later titled the act in which the wild revels of the <term>Maenads</term><note>Female followers of Bacchus known for their ecstatic dancing and divine possession</note> are represented in honor of Bacchus as a "bacchanal," it appears even more clearly that he took no pains to distinguish between a dithyramb and a bacchanal. Indeed, the title of "bacchanal" which he used to characterize the dances and songs of the Maenads was also used by him to indicate what Plato distinguished by the title of *dithyramb*. 

Let us now repeat the full meaning of the interrupted words already cited from Poliziano, and see what he teaches us: *“The Athenians, during the festivals of Father Liber [Bacchus]—which they called Dionysia and our people called Bacchanalia or Liberalia—employed not only other types of poetry but especially the old comedies in which the vices of men were cured, because they believed this god specifically presided over the purging of the senses.”*<note>original: "Athenienses festis Liberi patris, quæ Dionysia illi, nostri Baccanalia seu Liberalia vocitarunt, cum poësis alia genera, tum in primis veteres comœdias in queis vitia hominum sanarentur, adhibuerunt, quod hunc præcipue deum purgandis præesse sensibus opinabantur."</note> According to our author, the Greeks therefore performed ancient comedies during the festivals of Bacchus; these, being purposely ordained in honor of that deity, would have been dithyrambic in nature. But the same happened with tragedies, which, according to the teaching of <term>Martin del Rio</term><note>A 16th-century Jesuit scholar and theologian known for his work on ancient drama and magic</note>, were in early times partly satiric—that is to say, instructive and corrective of morals—and partly dithyrambic. $^3$ 

Wisely, however, Poliziano, after giving his tragedy its instructive part, was pleased to complete it with the dithyrambic part, thereby earning the glory of being the first to write dithyrambs in the <term>vernacular</term><note>The common spoken language, in this case, Italian, as opposed to Latin</note>. Let us hear, to his honor, what <term>Mencken</term><note>Friedrich Otto Mencken, an 18th-century scholar and biographer of Poliziano</note> writes of it: *“And, so that it may be more certain what progress Poliziano brought to the study of vernacular poetry, Crescimbeni reports in his 'History of Vernacular Poetry' (Book 1, pages 17 and 170, and in the 'Commentary on the History of Vernacular Poetry' volume 1, book 3, chapter 14, page 151) that that genre of song called the dithyramb was first summoned from Greece to Italy by Poliziano, never before having been adapted to Latin or Italian meters. It is established that the nature of the dithyramb is such that there is a certain mixture of all meters within it; license is given in words and actions; the speech is not cohesive, nor is it fashioned according to a rule; but the poet appears as if stirred by a dithyrambic—that is, Bacchic—inspiration. This is the reason why this genre of song is used mostly in Bacchus’s honor, or as you might more correctly observe, regarding all sorts of playful matters and...”*<note>original: "Et, ut certius constet quid incrementi Politianus vernaculæ poetices studiis attulerit... [continues to] ...de rebus quibusque ludicris et"</note>

*...is usually poured forth with jokes.* <note>original: "iocosis, effundi soleat." This sentence fragment concludes a thought from the previous page regarding the lighthearted nature of Bacchic songs.</note> Poliziano was the first to compose such small songs in our native language, even though Benedict Fioretti <note>Latin: Benedictus Florettus</note>—that most diligent corrector of the Italian language at the start of the 17th century—attempted to cast doubt upon this glory of his. Writing under the pseudonym Udeni Nisieli in the third book of his *Poetic Exercises* (*Proginnasmi Poetici*), Fioretti claimed that a certain <term>dithyramb</term><note>A wild, passionate choral hymn, originally Greek, sung in honor of the god Dionysus/Bacchus</note> he presented was the very first of its kind to be born within Italian borders. (See Crescimbeni, in the book cited). However, if Fioretti had been fortunate enough to have known the works that Poliziano had sung so many years earlier, he would have easily understood that the credit for this invention did not belong to him.

The same must be said against Tolomeo Nozzolini <note>Latin: Ptolomæum Nozzolinum</note>, who, being poorly acquainted with Poliziano’s compositions, wrongly attributed the glory of the first dithyrambic composition to Francesco Maria Gualterotti in the Italian poem *The Silkworm* (*Il Verme della Seta*). This error was noted by Giuseppe Bianchini <note>Latin: Josepho Blanchino</note> in the Preface to the booklet *Toast* (*Brindisi*) by Antonio Malatesti and Pietro Salvetti, and by Domenico Maria Manni in the *Commentary on Florentine Inventions*, chapter 45, page 87. For verses of this kind already exist in Poliziano’s play titled *Orpheus* (*Orfeo*).¹

This primacy as a dithyrambic or <term>bacchanalian</term><note>Relating to the festivals of Bacchus; characterized by drunken revelry</note> poet is also granted to Poliziano by Baruffaldi and many other modern scholars. Crescimbeni, however, was not very careful in this regard; for, after having assigned such glory to Poliziano, he then took it away without realizing it. He labeled as a "dithyramb" an anonymous composition he found in the Atanagi Collection, which begins:

->*Passing with thought through a small grove;*<-
<note>original: "Passando con pensier per un boschetto;" a famous opening line of a 14th-century "caccia" or hunting song.</note>

He believed it to have been written long after Poliziano’s time, in which he was mistaken.² This composition was first recovered from the Vatican manuscripts by Basilio Zanchi of Bergamo, who provided it to Girolamo Atanagi,³ by whom it was published in 1566 in the aforementioned Collection.⁴ But twenty-two years later, in 1588, the *History of the Ubaldini Family* appeared in Florence, written by Giambattista di Lorenzo Ubaldini and printed by Sermartelli. In that work, this same poem was presented anew under the name of Ugolino di Azzo Ubaldini, who flourished around the year 1240 and used a very sweet language in his rhymes. Meanwhile, [this book] having come into the hands of Crescim—

Everyone sees, without me saying another word, the infamous vice <note>A historical reference to homosexuality or pederasty, which Affò, as a priest, views with severe moral disapproval.</note> which is proposed here to be followed, for which destroying fire already rained down from heaven upon the filthy Pentapolis <note>The "Pentapolis" refers to the five biblical cities of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed by fire.</note>. First of all, one must investigate whether Poliziano could have written such verses. I hold that he did, because I do not recognize our poet as being too perfect in terms of moral virtues; nor could the reputation that reached Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), a physician and historian known for his biographical sketches.</note> be entirely feigned or malicious, for he depicts him as having that wicked habit which is inculcated in the mentioned verses.<sup>2</sup> However much Vossio, Menckenio, and Serassi <note>Gerardus Vossius, Johann Burkhard Mencke, and Pier Antonio Serassi: prominent scholars and biographers who defended Poliziano’s reputation.</note> may defend him from the stain of being irreligious, that prologue intended to precede Plautus’s *Menaechmi* <note>A famous Roman comedy about mistaken identity.</note>, which he addressed to Comparino, speaks enough of his corrupt heart;<sup>3</sup> therein he ridicules those religious men who zealously reproached those vices in which he delighted.

Furthermore, one must investigate whether he wrote such verses to indulge the taste, as they say, of his patron <term>Maecenas</term><note>A term for a wealthy patron of the arts, named after the Roman advisor to Augustus.</note>; as if, due to the universal corruption of that century, the Cardinal was inclined toward those foul pastimes. Certainly, we have writers who have left us memories of Cardinal Gonzaga <note>Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga (1444–1483), the patron for whom *Orfeo* was originally performed in Mantua.</note> that are not very flattering in matters of conduct: but I will never dare to believe that a Cardinal and Bishop of Mantua, however wayward he might have been, would wish to allow things offensive to piety and modesty to be said upon a public stage raised at his request. Therefore, even if Poliziano had written it so, he must have later ordered its correction; which consisted of changing the first four verses and suppressing the entire stanza, as seen in our two <term>codices</term><note>Handwritten manuscript volumes.</note>. Poliziano must not have been unwilling to make such a change, since he must have realized that by making Orpheus speak in such a manner, he offended the character of that ancient, venerable figure, of whom it was written that he had withdrawn men from a brutal life through his voice, song, and example; as Horace sang:

> The priest and interpreter of the gods, Orpheus,
> deterred the woodland men from slaughter and foul living;
> for this, he was said to tame tigers and raging lions.
> <note>original Latin: "Silvestres homines sacer interpresque deorum / Cædibus et victu fœdo deterruit Orpheus; / Dictus ob hoc lenire tigres rabidosque leones." From Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note>

And that they are his, we are made certain by the spontaneously lyrical intonation, the full, varied, familiar harmony, the elegantly popular, popularly Tuscan form; we are made certain by the memories and repetitions of concepts, phrases, images, hemistichs <term>hemistich: a half-line of verse</term>, and verses, which are in other rhymes universally recognized as Poliziano's; we are made certain by the reproduction of an entire octave that is among the others often reprinted as our author's. ### CONTINUED LOVE POEMS.

Use it gently in song and celebration
To deliver yourself and your servant from pains.
To satisfy a desire seems a righteous thing,
Nor do I see or ever think what holds you back:
You know and you can, yet you lack the will;
<margin>24</margin>You will later be able to grieve for yourself.

If you do not wish to serve me for conscience's sake,
You commit a greater sin if one dies for you.
If you wish to be mindful of your honor,
Choose a wise and honest lover <term>amadore: an archaic form of 'lover,' implying a suitor who is both devoted and respectful.</term>,
Who has the place, time, and patience
And who knows how to preserve your honor.
If you do it out of cowardice <note>original: "viltà"—here meaning a lack of spirit or excessive shyness</note>, now strip yourself of it
<margin>32</margin>And learn to satisfy some desire of yours.

I see your lovely countenance changing:
Your beauty flees like a flower:
You are not the woman you were a short while ago;
Time consumes and destroys your beauty <note>original: "biltà," a poetic variant of "bellezza" (beauty)</note>.
One who does not make some lover happy
In the world is like a flower born in the chill shade <note>original: "all' ugge," a Florentine idiom referring to the cold shadow where plants cannot thrive</note>,
Which stands a long time without bearing fruit:
<margin>40</margin>One who enjoys a season does not suffer through it all.

I have so little grace with Love,
That I do not dare to ask for mercy <note>original: "merzede"—in courtly love poetry, this refers to the lady's favor or pity</note>;
And I am such an unfortunate servant,
That nothing but death is required of me:
I feel such great pain within my heart,

### CONTINUED LOVE POEMS.

That I curse Love and whoever believes in him:
Yet it is worth neither swearing nor cursing,
<margin>45</margin>For despite myself, I am compelled to follow him.

I would like to know what reason requires
To steal the heart from a faithful lover
And feed him only on glances and words
Without pity for his so many pains.
Do not wonder if a man grieves,
For I am not made of jasper or of diamond <note>The poet uses these stones to represent emotional hardness or invulnerability; he is asserting his human fragility.</note>.
If you do not want me to accuse you before the court of Love,
Make me happy, or return my heart to me.

<margin>56</margin>Return my heart to me, false traitress <note>original: "giudea"—literally "Jewess." In the courtly love tradition of this period, this was used as a derogatory metaphor for a woman who is "faithless" or "an infidel" to the laws of Love.</note>,
For a more merciful lady now asks it of me.
And if I do not love you as I was once wont to do,
Love himself commands it of me because of your harshness:
Because of your vain thoughts and your wicked will
Love does not want me to waste my time in vain.
Return the heart to me, which you stole at the start,
<margin>64</margin>For I wish to give it to one who values it more.

Ungrateful woman, if you have stolen my heart,
Do you not know well that it is right to return it?
If you wish to be cleared of your error,
Return my heart to me and grant me some kindness.
Do you not know that it is a shame and a dishonor to you
To keep your servant in such great pain?
Return my heart to me, and do not make me suffer;
<margin>72</margin>For waiting is a thing too hard to bear.

Seize the good time, before it passes away,
Noble girl, the flower of your years:

## CONTINUED LOVE POEMS.

->If you let this sweet time pass you by,<-
->You will be the first to repent it later,<-
->And first your weary eyes will weep:<-
->To repent too late is worth nothing then:<-
->Woe to her who believes she can make amends <note>The poet warns that lost time in youth cannot be recovered later in life.</note>,<-
<margin>80</margin>->When her hair begins to turn white.<-
->What use will so much beauty be to you,<-
->If you do not take delight in it with others?<-
->What fruit will you have from such harshness,<-
->Except to repent in vain? You will feel only spite.<-
->Your noble grace <term>gentilezza</term> <note>In this context, "gentilezza" refers to the combined quality of noble birth, beauty, and refined manners.</note> is not meant to last forever:<-
->You will yet remember what I have told you.<-
->It seems to me your beauty falls like a flower:<-
<margin>88</margin>->Therefore, make your choice like a wise woman.<-

---

**Verse 79.** *make amends*: to repair or recover time lost in youth. --- **Verse 81 and following.** These are repeated with some variations in the *Rispetti* that begin with the line "Since I first saw your graceful face." --- **Verse 87.** *Toio* and *tuoio*, *meo* and *mieio*, *soio* and *suoio*, instead of *tuo* (your), *mio* (my), and *suo* (his/her), belong to the ancient Florentine dialect: hence the shortenings used by Poliziano and other 15th-century poets who were not strict grammarians; *tuo' biltà* (your beauty), *tuo' fede* (your faith), *mie' core* (my heart) or *mie' pena* (my pain), *tuo' colpa* (your fault), etc.; just as even today the common people of Florence say *la to' donna* (your lady), *il me' babbo* (my father) or *la me' mamma* (my mother), *la so' casa* (his/her house), etc. One could multiply the written examples, but it is not necessary. Let this also apply to other passages in these rhymes where the reader will encounter similar colloquialisms <term>idiotismi</term> <note>The editor uses "idiotismi" in the classical sense of "idioms" or "peculiarities of a specific dialect," not as a modern insult.</note>.

---

## II.

### SERENADE
->OR<-
### LETTER IN <term>STRAMBOTTI</term>¹ <note>A "strambotto" is a traditional Italian verse form consisting of a single stanza of eight lines, typically used for courtly or popular love poetry.</note>.

> O lady, triumphant over every other beauty,
> Noble, virtuous, and graceful,
> Listen to the song with which he speaks to you,
> He who loves you above all else;
> Because you are his shining star,
> And day and night he calls your fair name.
> First and foremost, he sends greetings to you,
<margin>8</margin>
> Then a thousand times he commends himself to you.

> And he humbly prays that you deign
> To consider his perfect faith;
> And that some pity may reign in your heart,
> As is required by such beauty.
> He has seen thousands upon thousands of signs
> Of your noble grace <term>gentilezza</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "gentilezza" implied not just kindness, but a nobility of spirit and refined manners.</note>, and every hour he sees more:

*V. 2. Lady [Dama]*, the beloved woman; whom the Latins called *domina* <note>original Latin: "domina," meaning mistress or lady of the house</note>, and the writers of the 14th and 16th centuries called *donna*; it appears in Pulci: "I have fallen in front of the lady, / Whereby I have lost her love..." **Verse 19. Dami.** "In the explanations of Moniglia’s commentary on *The Noble Servant*, it is observed that, just as beloved young women were called *dame* [ladies], they wished to reciprocate such an honor given by their lovers by calling them in return *dami*, that is, their lords and masters, and that afterwards the word *damo* became common among us, but more so in the countryside, and was not used by the ancients." Marrini, notes to *Lecco da Varlungo*. "He won't know who sends it to him. His *damo* is so refined," Lorenzo de' Medici. "Suddenly you become my *damo* and husband," Buonarroti, *Tancia*. "If the leaves on the olives lasted as long as my *dami* last for me," *Tuscan Love Poems*. — **verse 20. to your face [al tuo viso]:** Florentine edition of 1814. — **verse 21. glory loves you [gloria t' ami]**, read the Florentine Manuscripts, Roscoe, and the editors of 14: **longs for [brami]**, which we have restored to the text to avoid the repetition of the rhyme, is from the Chigiano manuscript, followed by Serassi and Silvestri, and from the Manuscript of Mr. G. Vanzolini. — **verse 22. Trifles and nonsense [Frasche e finocchi]**: vanity, appearance, bagatelles. Pandolfini: "to communicate with you nothing but words and trifles." — **verse 23. And he always [Ed ei sempre mai]**, read grammatically by Serassi and Silvestri: but the colloquial use of *him [lui]* as a subject pleased Machiavelli, nor did it displease Giusti: "... servant... who usually treats the master's things as he [lui] has treated everyone else's." — **verse 26. never finds [mai non trova]**, Vanzolini Manuscript. — **verse 29. would find... mercy [troverre'... merzede]**, Vanzolini Manuscript. — **verse 31. Flirts [Zimbella].** Here it does not seem to mean allures or flatters, as it does metaphorically in other cases; but that it represents the actions and ways of a flighty or unstable lover, compared to the bird that serves the purpose of a decoy <note>original: "zimbellare"</note>. — **verse 32.**

We accepted this verse into the text as other codices reported it, as noted by the Florentine editors of 1814. The Laurentian <term>Laur.</term> <note>Referring to the Laurentian Library in Florence, which houses many Medici manuscripts.</note> followed by Roscoe reads "*I' sol per fedeltà esco*" [I alone out of faithfulness go out]; Serassi and Silvestri, while correcting the *lui* [him], print according to the Chigiano <term>Chig.</term> <note>A significant manuscript collection now in the Vatican.</note> in accordance with us: "*Ei sol*" [He alone], etc. The Vanzolini codex has: "*Che sol per fedeltà esce di greggia:*" [Who alone out of faithfulness leaves the flock], which is unclear. The editors of 1814 print: "*Ma fuor che lui ogni altri ti dileggia,*" [But except for him, everyone else mocks you], as it appears in the Riccardiano <term>Ricc.</term>, although in a different hand than the other verses, and despite having *ogn’ uno* [everyone] instead of *ogni altri*. — v. 34-35. *Sanza* [without]; the printed editions, here and elsewhere, always use *senza*. But *sanza* was common among the ancients and the Florentine people, nor has it entirely disappeared from all Tuscan dialects. — v. 37. *Mille, mille* [Thousands, thousands], edition of 1814. — v. 39. We accepted into the text the reading of Serassi and Silvestri derived from the Chigiano codex, which is also that of the Vanzolini codex. The Riccardiano reads: "*E s’ e’ sapesse bene el suo core;*" [And if he well knew his heart]; the Laurentian, followed by Roscoe: "*E se sapessi bene aprire il suo core;*" [And if he knew well how to open his heart]; the editors of 1814 believed they had fixed everything for the best by printing: "*E se sapesse bene aprire il core.*" — v. 42. *del colmo* [at the height], Laurentian and Riccardiano codices. — v. 43-44. Theocritus, Idyll 25: "And beautiful is the form of youth, but it lives for a brief time." (Editors of 1814.) <note>Theocritus was a Greek poet known for pastoral poetry.</note> — v. 51-52. Theocritus, in the cited Idyll: "And the rose is beautiful, and time decays it." Ausonius: "This rose, which but a moment ago glowed with all the fire of its tresses, now pale, is forsaken by its fallen petals. She marvels at the swift plunder of fleeing time, and that roses wither even as they are born." <note>original: "Hæc, modo quæ toto rutilaverat igne comarum, Pallida collapsis deseritur foliis. (1814 Edition.) An epigram from Burman’s *Latin Anthology*: <note>original: "Dic, quid agis, formosa Venus..."</note> "Say, what are you doing, beautiful Venus, if you do not know how to return a lover's favor? All beauty perishes while time wastes away. Violets wither after the dew; the rose loses its scent; lilies melt away after the spring, their whiteness gone. Fear these examples, I pray: always return your lover's favor:..." Serafino Aquilano, in his *Strambotti*: "Look, lady, how time flies and everything runs to its end: in a short while every violet turns dark, the roses fall and only the thorns remain.... Therefore know your happy time..." — v. 53. *So in the Florentine Codices* and that of Vanzolini. The printed editions read *mai non fassi* [is never done]. — v. 55. *To seize time by the forelock* means to enjoy it: Horace's *carpe diem* [seize the day]. Similarly, we have *to hold fortune by the forelock* to mean having it favorable or supportive. *Forelock* refers to the hair that sits above the forehead and is longer than the rest. Iacopo Soldani, in his satire against philosophers, gives this name of "lock" to the hair of Fortune: "To grab the fluttering forelock of her who flees and then is waited for in vain." (1814 Edition.) — v. 57. <term>IN TRA DUE</term> [In between/Undecided]. A phrase also used by the Greeks: Callimachus, Book I: <note>original: "εν δοιῆ μάλα θυμός"</note> "the heart is in great doubt"; which Salvini translates as "the heart is in two." (1814 Edition.) Petrarch: "To abandon me was often *in tra due* [in the balance]." Matteo Villani also used it as a noun: "Remaining in this *in tra due* [state of indecision]." — v. 58. *if he sleeps or if he is awake*, Florentine Editions of 1814. — v. 60. *for the rest*, in the printed editions. Perhaps it is a phrase similar to *fare resto* which means to terminate or finish; or *a far del resto* which, as a metaphor taken from gambling, means to risk everything. It seems it should be understood as "finish it once and for all." — v. 63. *imbocca* [puts in the mouth], Riccardiano codex and Florentine editions of 1814. *questa ciriegia abbocca* [bite into this cherry]: it seems that figuratively it must mean: put your hand to this work, begin the enterprise. — v. 65-66. *Feed him with nonsense* <note>original: "pasci di frasche"</note>. See above, verse 22. Galateo: "noble souls who do not feed on nonsense and appearances." *vesciche* [bubbles], idle chatter. *To feed on wind* means to give talk, to entertain with vain things (Florentine Editions of 1814). • Following these lines—

...to the errant ones and all those little tyrants who would restrict the language within the limits of their own presumptuous ignorance, here is a most authoritative and most Florentine example of *means* (*mezzo*) in the meaning of *mode, expedient, decision* etc. — line 88. Monti, in the *Proposta*, interprets *to keep in the shade* as *to keep in idleness.* — lines 89-90. Lorenzo de' Medici in his burlesque confession: "I remember still other sins: That by following the words of friars, many sweet pleasures have I already left behind: Of this again I make a confession" — line 93. Petrarch: "That we are all stained with one pitch." (Florentine editions of the 14th century.) Proverbially, it means to have the same defects. — line 94. *sung* (*contato*), according to the editions, except Roscoe. — *zara to whoever it hits.* A proverb that means *to whoever it falls, it is their loss.* Pataffio: "*Zara* to whoever it hits: I have emptied the purse." (Florentine editions of the 14th century.) Buti, in his Commentary on *Purgatorio* VI: "this game is called *zara* because of the forbidden points on three dice, from seven downwards and from fourteen upwards: therefore when they see those points, the players say *zara*." — lines 95-96. A proverbial way to signify that the matter is not as grave as people are led to believe. In a Carnival Song (*Canto carnescialesco*), it is expressed with more novelty: "And then whoever sees the devil for real, sees him with fewer horns and less black." — line 97. *And He did not give you*, the editions. — lines 101-102. *Do not believe*, Riccardi manuscript and editions. *Because of being another's*, that is, even though you belong to another. Certain verses by Serafino Aquilano echo this octave: "Nature has given you some grace, that you may triumph in it and hold it dear: Therefore harvest the grape that is ripe, and do not be stingy with yourself toward yourself." — line 103. *is enough*, Vanzetti manuscript.

It is also called "breaking the ford," and it means to open the road or the path in any difficult juncture. Ovid advises the lover *cera vadum tentet* <note>original: "cera vadum tentet"; Latin meaning "let him test the ford with wax," referring to sending a first message on a wax tablet.</note>. — line 115. *your lover will then have you*: Vanz. codex. — line 117. *straccio* [rag], figuratively means *nothing*, *not a bit*, especially with the verbs *to do* and *to know*. ## III.<sup>1</sup>

### Alas, my lady, why do you grow angry?

*To look through a viewing-tube* <note>original Latin: "dioptram prospicere." A dioptra was an ancient surveying instrument; here it suggests looking closely or precisely.</note>. *Malmantile* III, 50:
"But she who can find the hair in the egg <note>An idiom meaning to be extremely shrewd or to find a tiny detail that reveals a larger truth.</note> perceives that these are all inventions." Giusti, *The Sorcery*: "...a certain Vicar was already warned of it, famous for finding the hair in the egg." — line 124. *Meaning* <note>original: "construtto"</note>, here, refers to the sentiment, the true conclusion. — line 125. *a bit of favor*, Riccardiano and Vanzetti manuscripts. — line 127. *Go with God*, a formula of greeting and departure that the ancients used as readily as we use *goodbye* today. — line 128. A popular Tuscan serenade ends: "Listen to what he says and what he wants: To a good listener, few words. Listen to what he says and what he sends: To the good listener he commends himself."

1 These were published by the editor of this edition in the first issue of the literary journal *The Poliziano*, preceded by the following words: "I have copied these ten stanzas from a paper manuscript in folio, number 2723 of the Riccardiano collection, written in the final years of the 15th century; they are found on page 43 verso, before and after others that are known by everyone to be by Poliziano. They are headed with the initials *L. M.* <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>. But neither Roscoe nor anyone else who searched the writings of Lorenzo de' Medici, nor the Florentine editors of 1825 who could easily see so many manuscripts of the Medici, found that these were ever attributed to him. Furthermore; the Riccardiano manuscript is generous in crediting the Medici with things not his; it gives him the song *This showing of anger on the outside*, which is certainly by Poliziano both by the authority of other manuscripts and by the similarity of style; it gives him two other songs, *He who knows not how paradise is made*, and *Blessed be the day and the hour and the moment*, composed for Ippolita Leoncina of Prato, who is not known to have been courted or sung of by the Magnificent <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, but certainly by Master Angelo <note>Poliziano</note>; and indeed, under the name of Angelo Poliziano, they were later published from a manuscript in the Florentine seminary by the academic Rigoli in his *Essay of unpublished rhymes from the 14th to the 18th century* (Florence, Ronchi, 1825). All this together made me suspect that those stanzas were by Poliziano; especially since I did not find the effective and harsh manner, the rugged and jagged form of the Magnificent; rather, I felt they were full, flowing, and uninhibited, and Poliziano’s rosy ease (sometimes popular in tone but never crudely or barbarously unrefined) shone within them. And the suspicion became certainty..."

¹ From the Riccardian Codex 2723. We believe these stanzas should be inserted among the <term>Continued Love Verses (Rispetti continuati)<span>A series of stanzas linked by a single theme, rather than standalone poems.</span></term>. The Florentine edition of 1814, followed by all subsequent ones, mixed them (pages 78-86) with others that are evidently <term>Isolated Love Verses (Rispetti spicciolati)<span>Single, standalone eight-line stanzas not part of a larger narrative or thematic sequence.</span></term>. But the octet *When I began for you* is the beginning of another composition that we will report later: the other has no connection at all with the subject of these eight, which is a lament on the occasion of departure from the beloved lady; therefore, we reserved it for the *Isolated Love Verses*.

### V.<gloss>1</gloss>

Since I spend the whole day in weeping and sighs,
At evening at least I might rest a little,
And stay for just one hour with a dry face,
Not feeling the heat of the wicked fire,
Which has so consumed and destroyed my heart
That neither time nor place is of any use to me now.
But I ask every grace from Love in vain:
I am ill by day, and then worse by night. <margin>5</margin>
Rejoice, cruel lady, since by loving you have
Led me to a miserable state;
Triumph now over the pains you give me,
Over the grief that destroys me little by little;
Take glory and delight in my woes;
Feed your eyes well on my great fire:
When your soul is sated with my suffering,
Perhaps you will feel pity for such torment. <margin>10</margin>
Mercy now, for I consume myself and burn,
Waiting for some comfort for my ill;
For if by my misfortune it is late in coming,

---

1 These octaves <term>Ottave: Eight-line stanzas, the standard form for Italian narrative and lyric poetry.</term>, which were first published by the Florentine editors of 1814, are found in sequence both in the Laurentian codex <note>A manuscript from the Laurentian Library in Florence, founded by the Medici family.</note> 44 and in the Riccardian codex 2723: except that in the Laurentian, before the last two, two others are interspersed (*I have heard your harsh lament* and *I bless every benign star*) which do not link with the preceding ones. But both Florentine codices have them, and we reproduce them faithfully. Nothing is easier than that the author, treating a similar subject to serve the requests and amusements of his young friends without any literary intent, made use of what was already done another time.

# VII.¹

## LOVER.

The sweet accents of the song I hear
Double the vigor of my weeping:
And every celebration for one who is not content,
For one who is without hope in their love,
Is like a doubling of their lament:
And I feed my heart only on tears.
But only one hope comforts me;
That my heart would still love you so, even if you were dead.

## LADY.

I have heard your cruel lament,
And I see well how much love compels you:
And if I was ever cruel to you, I repent of it,

¹ The four <term>octaves<gloss>stanzas of eight lines with a specific rhyme scheme</gloss></term> above—which in the Florentine editions of 1514 and 1522 and the Milanese of 1525 are the beginning of an unformed and discordant collection to which the name *Stanzas* was attached—are, in the Riccardian Codex 2723 <note>A codex is a handwritten manuscript in book form.</note> (for those who know how to look closely), separated from the others that follow them in the printed versions by a different handwriting and the cessation of the numbering. Also, one who knows how to look will note that in said manuscript, beside the two middle octaves (the 2nd and 3rd), a **D** is marked in the margin, which seems to us to signify **DONNA** [LADY]. The editors of the 1514 edition also suspected this; in a note to the 2nd octave they remarked: *It seems the beloved responds*, and in another at the 4th: *The lover resumes*. Mr. Vanzolini’s manuscript contains the two intermediate stanzas, and both carry the heading **GOSTANZINA** (which is the name of the woman introduced in this <term>tenzone<gloss>a lyric poem in the form of a debate or competition between two poets or characters</gloss></term> of love). With such clues, and with the help of a beautiful variation from the Laurentian Codex 44 in the last verse of the first stanza, we believed we should arrange these four octaves in the form of a dialogue: and that the second octave is a response to the first is also shown to us by the fact that the rhymes of the first are taken up again in the second.

These recall two lines of a sonnet by Petrarch: "I have given you my heart, but it does not please you / To look so low with your haughty mind." <note>original: "V'aggio donato il cor, ma a voi non piace Mirar sì basso con la mente altiera."</note> And there is a popular Tuscan <term>stornello<gloss>a short, often improvised folk poem or song</gloss></term> that says: "Violets in bunches: You asked me for my heart, I gave it to you: Now that you have it, you mistreat it." <note>original: "Viole a mazzi: Mi chiedesti il mio core, io te lo detti: Ora che tu l' ha' avuto, lo strapazzi."</note> — line 3. The <term>codex<gloss>handwritten manuscript book</gloss></term> and the printed editions read *That burning desire* <note>original: "Quello ardente disir"</note>. Our correction <note>changing "Quello" to "Nello"</note> is very simple and evident. — line 4. *Love through her beauty* <note>original: "Amor per sua beltà"</note>, the codex and the Florentine edition of 1814. We accepted Silvestri’s correction. — line 7. The Silvestri edition corrects [the line to], *And the greatest fault that my heart ever holds* <note>original: "E il maggior fallo che il mio cor mai tene"</note>. There was no need for it. — line 12. *yearns* <note>original: "bramma"</note>, in the printed editions: that is, instead of an assonance—which would not be the first in Poliziano's rhymes—it is a license of pronunciation not at all Tuscan. — line 19. I have accepted the correction proposed by Maggi and included in the Silvestri edition: the Codex and the prints read *And that ever I was* <note>original: "E che mai fussi"</note>. The Florentine editors of 1814, by not putting a period or other mark of punctuation at the end of this line, and thereby linking its sense to the following one, make the meaning, it seems to me, extremely obscure and uncertain; the meaning emerges clearly from Silvestri's punctuation which I have adopted. —

The manuscript lacks *gran* <note>great</note>, which is found in the printed editions. — v. 30. *altro servo* <note>another servant</note> is the reading in the manuscript and the Florentine edition of 1514. And here we accepted the correction by Maggi and the Silvestri edition: the manuscript and the Florentine editions read *Sol di* <note>Only with</note>. — v. 36. The manuscript reads: *Vien che tu non sai che cosa sia amore* <note>It comes that you do not know what love is</note>. The Florentine editions of 1514 thought to correct this by reading: *Vien perchè tu non sai che cosa è amore* <note>It comes because you do not know what love is</note>; and they were followed by all subsequent printings. My correction <note>changing "Vien" to "Ben"</note>, while restoring the meaning—which in the printed versions is at the very least highly uncertain—is perhaps less arbitrary. It is very easy for a copyist to mistake *ben* for *vien*: furthermore, anyone with experience in manuscripts of ancient rhymes knows how often personal pronouns are overabundant to the detriment of the verse's meter. — v. 37. Maggi corrected this, and Silvestri printed *Ma quando ferirà* <note>But when it will strike</note>. If not inappropriate, this emendation seems too bold to me. — v. 40. *di miei pianti* <note>of my weepings</note>: the manuscript and the Florentine edition of 1514. — v. 42. *Per conservare* <note>To preserve</note>, the manuscript and the Florentine edition: here Maggi and Silvestri’s correction (*contentare* <note>to satisfy</note>) is required by logic. — v. 43. *a questa a quella* <note>at this at that</note>, the manuscript.

**Verse 47.** *it will be a virtuous thing*, the printed editions. — **v. 52.** The missing verse in the manuscript <note>original: *cod.*</note> and the 1814 Florentine edition is the same as verse 54: which was certainly transcribed here by error by the copyist, as this is not its proper place. — **v. 53.** *you will realize*, the printed editions. — **v. 55.** *Beauty that*, the manuscript. Maggi, in the cited *Appendix*, believes that in verse 54, "is left behind" <note>original: *si lascia*</note> should surely be replaced by "is wept for" <note>original: *si piange*</note>, and that regarding the lost verse, one would perhaps not be far from the truth by supplying it with the one we place here: "How do you not think of the sweet time now, / That your green season passes in vain? / Through tears and sighs and uttering laments / It no longer returns nor turns green again. / Late you will realize your error, / Since in the end one weeps for the time that is lost" etc. Silvestri accepted the correction "is wept for" in his edition. — **v. 58.** *Exit from the*, the printed editions. — **v. 61.** This "Ah" is added in the printed versions: it is missing in the manuscript, and with it the meter of the verse is lacking. — **v. 62.** The manuscript reads "is presented" <note>original: *s' appresenta*</note>: and the Florentine editors of 1814, who at other times had laid hands where it was not necessary, in order to preserve this erroneous reading, read (followed by all other editions): "Ah, do you not see, Love, in my eyes / That my soul and sad heart present themselves?" And the sense? Our correction seems most reasonable to us and supported by the verse that follows. — **v. 63.** *and yet it must be* <note>original: *eppur convien che sia*</note> is the reading in the manuscript and the 1814 Florentine edition. I have accepted Maggi's correction, which also passed into the Silvestri edition.

**Verse 66.** The 1814 Florentine editions do not place any punctuation mark at the end of this verse. — **v. 67.** Maggi, for the honor of fidelity <note>original: *onore della fedeltà*; referring to keeping the poet's intended meaning</note>, would like *is despised* <note>original: *si spreza*</note> to be changed to *is prized* <note>original: *s’ appreza*</note>; and Silvestri puts the advice into effect. There is no need for it, if one looks at the following verse. — **v. 69. and ... your hardness.** It is not read otherwise than this in the codex <note>The "codex" refers to the original handwritten manuscript.</note>. It is evident that after the conjunction a preposition is missing, and the Florentine editors chose to read *within* <note>original: *entro*</note>: and all the printed versions have followed them. Would *and because of your hardness* <note>original: *e per la tua dureza*</note> not have been better? — **v. 73. I was hoping** <note>original: *Io isperavo*</note>, the codex and the Florentine edition. As it corresponds to the rest of the stanza in which the things hoped for are indicated with the future tense, we accepted the correction of Maggi and the 1822 Florentine editors, which was adopted in the Silvestri edition. However, Maggi and the others read, *I wish to hope that* <note>original: *Io sperar vo’ che*</note>: but that *that*, besides being arbitrary, is useless to the syntax, because it is repeated at **v. 75**; and it is useless to prosody <term>prosody: the patterns of rhythm and sound used in poetry</term>, because the syllable that one wants to provide with it to complete the meter of the verse is already represented in the codex by the euphonic *i* <note>original: *i efelustico*; an extra vowel added to the start of a word for better sound</note> of *isperavo*. After this, the printed versions read in this same verse *when you have* <note>original: *u’ arai*</note>. — **v. 76. you will repent**, the prints. — **v. 78.** We adopted Silvestri’s punctuation. The Florentine editors put a semicolon at the end of the verse after *then* <note>original: *poi*</note>. But a suspicion arises in me, that perhaps this verse contains a strange transposition, partly excused by the haste with which the poet wrote if not also by the fervor with which he improvised; and that in short, it should be ordered and understood thus: .... *you will think, since I have loved you so long, that you did a great wrong in tormenting me.*

**Verse 84. *i' m' abbia*** [I might have] is from the printed editions. The **codex reads *per questo abbia* [through this have].** — **v. 85. We accepted the correction by Maggi which passed into the Silvestri edition.** The codex and the Florentine editions read *non ho altro disire* [I have no other desire]. — **v. 86. *diace* [lies]. Maggi, as one who wrote for the *Proposta* <note>The *Proposta* was a 19th-century philological journal focused on the Italian language.</note>, naturally corrected it to *giace*: and the Milanese editor printed *giace*. And truly, why would a Lombard have shown mercy to this coarse expression of the Tuscan commoners? But the people of our countryside still say *diacere* and *diacente* [to lie/lying]. And the exchange of the *g* for the *d* is so natural that in non-plebeian rhymes of the 13th and 14th centuries—namely in a song by Pucciandone Martelli and in the ballad on the defeat of Montecatini—one reads *redina* for *regina* [queen].** — **v. 89. We accepted Maggi’s correction, also adopted by Silvestri:** the codex and the Florentine editions read *Se non ti veggo ancor* [If I do not see you yet]. — **v. 98. *D' amare e* [To love and], the printed editions.** — **v. 99. We adopted Silvestri’s emendation:** the codex and the Florentine editions read *Ma per la* [But for the]. — **v. 106. *il mio misero* [my miserable], the printed editions.**

This place in the codex <term>codex (codice): a manuscript book, as opposed to a printed one</term> is among the *Scattered Love Verses* <note>original: "Rispetti spicciolati"</note>: and it helps us to correct one reading with the other. I read it thus with the Florentine edition of 1822: that of [15]12 has *And you know what life for its love allows me*: the manuscript, *And you know that the life for its love, etc.* Silvestri went too far in correcting: *And only that it may live for your love it consents*. Yet this is the only reading from which some meaning can be drawn. — v. 19. *Would not be for me*, the manuscript.

If there is anything I should say in rhyme,
It is not I who speaks, but only he,
Who holds you, lady, in such high esteem,
That he calls all faces his own mirrors.
Awake, lady foremost among ladies:
Here is the servant placed in another's power;
For if indeed I am a servant to that servant,
Now he begins, and hear my words.
If ever a great thing came to my mind
Speaking through object or through figure,
I pray Apollo <note>The Greek and Roman god of music and poetry.</note> that the speech may be as solemn
As can be, with order and measure.
Like a bird that has clipped feathers,
Which wishes to fly as nature allows it,
So am I; and every humble wit
Is nonetheless some help to my design.

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Therefore it would be necessary, lady, to find
A loftier style and the virtue that distinguishes it.

V. 33. *Now it is from the stanzas* <note>The term "stanzas" here refers to previous printed editions of the poem.</note> — v. 38 *they had to, the stanzas.* — v. 41. *By day I think, the stanzas.* — v. 43. *And then, the stanzas.* — v. 44. The Florentine editions of 1814 and 1822 read with the manuscript: *That the sea dries up in the Alps among the woods* <note>original: "tra’ boschi"</note>. Regarding this, the Critic—in that philological farce by Vincenzo Monti <note>A prominent Italian poet and scholar (1754–1828).</note> titled *The Poets of the First Centuries of the Italian Language* (*Proposal*, vol. III, p. 11)—shouted: "Good God! To rhyme 'woods' (*boschi*) with 'touches' (*tocchi*) and 'eyes' (*occhi*), and not know how to read *That the sea dries up or overflows into the Alps* (*trabocchi*), to indicate that your (the Critic speaks to Poliziano) amorous pains will never end by using the hypothesis of two impossible things: the sea drying up and its overflowing onto the peaks of the Alps!" Monti’s correction passed into the text of the 1825 Milanese edition, and we too have accepted it—not merely for the sake of the rhyme, for this would not be the first half-rhyme <term>assonanza: a rhyme where only the vowel sounds match, common in early Italian poetry</term> that Poliziano made use of. — v. 46. *your beautiful [plural], the stanzas.* — v. 49-52. <meta>This page continues from a blank or damaged folio (page 229) in the collection of Angelo Poliziano’s poetry. We are now entering a section containing a famous "echo poem," a genre where the last syllables of a line are repeated to create a new meaning, personified as the nymph Echo answering the god Pan.</meta>

# PAN AND ECHO.

## I.

->**What are you doing, Echo, while I call you? — I love.**<-
->**Do you love two, or only one alone? — One alone.**<-
->**And I love you alone and no others — I love others.**<- <note>In the original Italian, the echo *Altri amo* (I love others) contradicts Pan's preceding claim that he loves no one else.</note>
->**Then you do not love one alone? — One alone.**<-
->**This is telling me: I do not love you — I do not love you.**<-
->**The one you love, do you love him alone? — Alone.**<-
->**Who has taken you away from my love? — Love.**<-
->**What does he do, the one you love? — Ah, he dies!**<- <note>The Italian word for love, *amore*, is cleverly split by the echo into *Ah more!*, meaning "Ah, he dies!"</note>

---

<margin>Notes on the text and its sources</margin>

This poem is found in the Riccardian manuscripts 2723 and 771, and in the Laurentian 44 (shelf 40), categorized among the <term>Rispetti spicciolati<span>Short, independent Italian folk-style poems, often regarding themes of love.</span></term> It is also found in all the early printed editions of the *Stanzas* and the *Orfeo*, placed immediately after the latter, but with the heading "A most ingenious stanza by the aforementioned author on this subject." We have adopted the title from the very rare Bergamo edition prepared by Rossi.

**Verse 1:** Some of the old printings, such as the Cominian editions and the Florentine editions of 1814, read: *Che fai tu, Eco, mentr’ io ti chiamo? — Amo:* which causes the line to lose a syllable. The Riccardian manuscripts and some printings read *Ecco* instead of *Eco*, as is also seen in the *Stanzas*.
**Verse 2:** *duo* is found in Riccardian 771, some old printings, and the Comino and Silvestri editions; *dua* is used in the Florentine editions of 1814.
**Verse 3:** *Et io te sol* appears in some old printings; *E io te solo* in the Comino and Silvestri; *Ed io te solo* in the Florentine editors of 1814.
**Verse 7:** *t' ha levato* is found in Riccardian 771 and the printed editions.

Poliziano imitated this ingenious composition from an ancient example by the Greek poet Gaurada, whom he cites in chapter XXII of the first century of his <term>Miscellanea<span>A collection of Poliziano's scholarly philological and critical essays.</span></term> There, he also defines these "echoes" as <note>original: "versiculi quidam sic facti, ut in extremis responsitationes ex persona ponantur Echûs, sententiam explentes et morem tuentes illius ultima regerendi."</note> "certain little verses made in such a way that at the ends, responses are placed in the persona of Echo, completing the sense and maintaining the custom of repeating the final sounds." He adds, "We ourselves have composed some such verses in the vernacular, which are now celebrated by musicians and praised through the musical settings of <term>Henricus<span>Refers to Heinrich Isaac (c. 1450–1517), a famous Flemish composer at the Medici court.</span></term>, and which we also sent nearly ten years ago to Piero..." <note>The text cuts off here, but likely refers to Piero de' Medici.</note>

<summary>This page features a clever "echo poem" by Angelo Poliziano, where Pan's questions are answered by the nymph Echo. The scholarly notes document the poem's manuscript history and Poliziano's own classical inspiration and musical collaborations.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Pan and Echo, Echo poetry, Italian Renaissance literature, Heinrich Isaac, Rispetti spicciolati, classical imitation, Medici court</keywords>

<margin>A vertical strip of text on the right side of the original page is faded or missing, affecting several words which have been reconstructed here for clarity.</margin>

"...we gave <note>original Latin: "Contareno veneto patritio non inelegantis ingenii viro mire tum desideranti nonnullisque aliis literarum studiosis dedimus."</note> to Contareno, a Venetian patrician and a man of no small talent who greatly desired it, as well as to several other students of literature." With this, Poliziano claims the glory of being the first to transport these types of ingenious trifles into Italian poetry. He was quickly imitated by Serafino Aquilano, and by many others after the first half of the 16th century, as the love for clever wordplay grew; neither Tasso nor Guarini disdained these "echoes."

### FOR MADONNA
# IPPOLITA LEONCINA
->FROM PRATO.<-

## II.

> Love makes me proclaim and command,
> Beautiful and gentle ladies who are here,
> That whichever of you has captured a heart
> Should return it or give an exchange this day:
> If not, he will issue an excommunication.
> This is a heart that was lost only yesterday;
> And it was seen, when it descended here,
> That one of you enticed it with her song.

Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — verses 1-8. This theme of the losing and stealing of the heart is also sung in the ballad by Lorenzo de’ Medici that begins "Beautiful ladies, I have searched for a long time for my heart etc." and in another by N. <note>likely "N." refers to an anonymous or undetermined author in the collection</note> "Ladies, once again my heart is lost." — verses 7-8. The metaphor is taken from <term>hunting at the decoy-net<span>original: "caccia al paretaio"; a traditional method of catching small birds using nets and a decoy bird to lure them in.</span></term>.

---

## III.

> He who wishes to see the power of nature
> Should come to see this graceful face
> Of Ippolita, who steals the heart with her eyes;
> Let him contemplate her speech, contemplate her smile.
> When Ippolita laughs, modest and pure,
> It seems as if paradise is flung wide open.

->The angels, at her song, without delay,<-
