**Riccardian Codex 2723.** This and six other **Rispetti**; *They used to with their song...*; *For a thousand times well found...*; *She for certain is...*; *My eyes fell down...*; *Pity, lady, for God’s sake...*; *I would already have a bear*; distributed by us under the numbers IV, VI, X, XV, XXV, LIV; in the Riccardian codex they appear in sequence, and are distinguished by a later hand with the title **By L. de' Med.** <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note>. For this reason, the Florentine editors of 1814 omitted them from their printing. Furthermore, both this one and the five following, along with others, were first published by Serassi from the Chigi codex in the community edition of 1765; then by Rigoli, who believed them to be unpublished, from a modern copy in the *Essay of Rhymes by various good authors*, Florence, 1825. — **Verses 1-2.** Recalls the Petrarchan lines:
> « He who wishes to see all that nature
> And heaven can produce among us, let him come to gaze upon her. »
<note>original Italian: "Chi vuol veder quantunque può natura / E 'l ciel tra noi, venga a mirar costei."</note>
— **Verse 7. Dimoro**, used for the sake of the rhyme instead of *dimora* <note>delay, hesitation, or stay</note> (Rigoli). An ancient word, which is also used by Dante:
> « My leader asked without delay »
<note>original Italian: "Dimandò 'l duca mio senza dimoro"</note>
*Inferno XXII.* — **Verse 8. From heaven**, Cominiano edition, Rigoli.

->I descended; and now I pay the penalty,<-
->For I find myself trapped like a thrush.<- <note>The original Italian "impaniato" refers to being caught with birdlime, a sticky substance used by hunters to trap small birds.</note>

**Riccardian Codex 2723 and Mouke Lucchese: Comino, Florentine editions of 1814, Rigoli.** — **Verse 4.** <term>BASILISK</term><note>original: "BABALISCHIO"</note>: a basilisk, a species of poisonous serpent also called a "regulus" <note>Latin for "little king," referring to the crown-like crest on the serpent's head</note> (Rigoli). <term>DEAF ASP</term><note>original: "ASPIDO SORDO"</note>: a species of poisonous serpent. The ancients believed that to avoid hearing an incantation, the asp would press one ear to the ground and plug the other with its tail. Hence our proverb: "to act like the deaf asp," meaning to plug one's ears to avoid listening. Petrarch wrote: ".... found pity deaf as an asp" (1814 Edition). — **Verse 5. I DESCENDED**: taking the simile from birds that descend into nets (1814 Edition). Variation: *and now* in the printed versions. — **Verse 6.** "Your loving eyes found me there, / And caught me like a thrush in a snare." (Tuscan folk songs). — **Verse 7.** *flees*, Mouke codex, Rigoli. — **Verse 8.** *and then*, Mouke codex and printed editions.

### VIII.

->No longer a drop remains for me to sing:<-
->Love gnaws at me as rust gnaws iron.<-
->Let her sing, for she expounds it well,<-
->She who seems a nightingale emerging from its down.<-
->She is the doe, and I am a snail:<-
->She is the falcon, and I am a tortoise.<-
->I cannot find the end of the thread in the skein:<-
->Therefore, you unravel it, for I would make a mess.<-

**Riccardian Codex 2723 and Mouke Lucchese: Comino, Florentine editions of 1814, Rigoli.** — **Verse 1.** *remained* <note>original: "rimasto"</note>, 1814 Florentine editions; *of singing* <note>original: "di cantar"</note>, Mouke codex. — <term>A drop</term><note>original: "Più gocciola"</note>. Perhaps more *breath*, *strength*, or *wind* (Rigoli). "Gocciola" (drop), used metaphorically in both written language and some Italian dialects, signifies *nothing* or *not at all*. — **Verse 2.** The Riccardian codex, the Mouke, and the 1814 Florentine editions read, with an obvious error, *the wife gnaws* <note>original: "la moglie rode"</note>. — **Verse 3.** *if she* <note>original: "se la"</note>, Mouke codex; *explains it* <note>original: "dinocciola"</note>, Comino and Rigoli. Rigoli noted: <term>Dinocciolare</term> is missing from the Dictionary; it perhaps means *to smooth out*, *to explain*, or *to declare*. — **Verse 4.** *the nightingale* <note>original: "l’ usignol"</note>, 1814 Florentine editions; *a nightingale*, the other printed editions. — <term>Downy fuzz</term><note>original: "Caluggine"</note>: that first plumage that birds begin to grow in the nest (1814 Florentine editions). — **Verses 6–7.** *She the... She the...*, Mouke codex. — **Verses 7–8.** Metaphorically: I do not know how to continue the song, I do not know how to begin, or how to extract myself from it; I am tangled. Therefore (addressing another singer or improviser, or perhaps the girl herself who is singing), you go ahead and unravel it, for I would only make people laugh.

# BEAUTY.

## X.

->She is certainly the most beautiful thing<-
->That the sun ever saw in all the world;<-
->Joyful, lovely, noble, sweet, charming,<-
->Full of roses, full of violets,<-
->Courteous, wise, virtuous and graceful,<-
->Benign in appearance, in action, and in words.<-
->Thus she outshines all beautiful women,<-
->As the light of the sun does all the stars.<-

<note>Riccardian Codex 2723: Comino, Rigoli. See the note to <term>Rispetto</term> III. — Verse 2. *saw the sun* <note>original: "vedesse sole"</note>, Riccardian codex. — Verse 5. *and graceful* <note>original: "e graziosa"</note>: the "and" <note>original: "e"</note> which is missing in the Riccardian and in the printed editions is provided to us by the Vanzolini codex. — Verse 7. OUTSHINES. *Spegne-re*, meaning to obscure or extinguish (Rigoli). Bonagiunta Urbiciani <note>A 13th-century Lucchese poet</note>: "... her face / Which quenches every other face and makes them vanish." — Verse 7-8. Petrarch: "With her beautiful face she usually does to others / What the sun does to the lesser stars."</note>

## XI.

->She has deprived heaven of every beauty<-
->And taken the treasures of all paradise,<-
->She has deprived the sun of light and clarity<-
->And placed it in her own splendid face,<-
->From the world she has taken every nobility<-
->Every gesture and beautiful manner and sweet laughter.<-
->Love has given her the gaze and the speech<-
->To make her the most beautiful of all.<-

<note>Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition of 1814. — Verse 1-5. Giusto de' Conti <note>A 15th-century Roman poet known for his collection "La Bella Mano"</note>, song 2: "And heaven of every beauty / Was deprived and of splendor / Since the time she was nourished in swaddling clothes" and further below "In her eyes the sun hid itself." A Tuscan <term>rispetto</term>: "Beautiful lady, who has taken the beauties from the sun, / You have made a new paradise on earth; / And you have taken the splendor from the moon, / From the angels of the..."</note>

## XV.

> My eyes dropped down, sad and aching,
> When I saw the sun rise on high <note>A poetic metaphor comparing the lady's arrival or gaze to the rising sun.</note>:
> My dead tongue froze between my teeth
> And could not form its words:
> All my senses were taken from me
> By her who kills and heals me when she wills:

> — Go forward a little and touch her hand. —

## XVI.

> This girl is so happy and <term>restless</term>,
> That staying by her side, I crumble away.
> Whatever she says or does touches my soul:
> Every act, every sign of hers I <term>treasure</term>.
> I am all on fire, and my heart moans:
> I would like just a <term>tiny crumb</term> of her grace.
> I have played so much like a fish in heat,
> That you have dipped me, Love, even into the pitch <note>A metaphor for being trapped or stuck in the "darkness" or "burning" of passion.</note>.

Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition of 1814, Rigoli. — Verse 1. <term>Frugola</term>, the feminine form of *frugolo*, used to describe someone who is constantly in motion like a child: here perhaps meaning *lively* (Rigoli). — Verse 2. *staying by her* <note>original: "starle"</note>, the printed editions. — Verse 3. *Whatever she* <note>original: "Ciò ch'ella"</note>, the printed editions: .. *touches the uvula* <note>original: "rintocca l' ugola"</note>, Florentine editions of 1814; which declared this meant *it pleases extremely*. —

Verse 4. <term>Aggruzolo</term>. *Aggruzzolare* is missing from the Dictionary: perhaps from *gruzzolo*, a gathering of money or anything else: hence *aggruzzolare* meaning to gather together or hoard (Rigoli). — Verse 6. <term>Scamuzzolo</term>. A tiny part of anything, much like a *minuzzolo* or crumb (Florentine Editions 1814). — Verse 7. *like the fish* <note>original: "come il pesce"</note>.

### XVII.

> O singular beauty who to my eyes
> Showed paradise in a single moment,
> And you are the source of that noble blood <note>The commentator notes this phrase is difficult to interpret; it may refer to the lady's lineage or the "vital spirits" of the poet's own blood being stirred.</note>

Of this and the following verse, we would not wish to assert a legitimate reading, nor would we know how to guess the interpretation. — verse 6. Thus the printed editions; the manuscript reads: *If not upon death while being divided from you.***

### XVIII.

> The first day that I ever saw you,

> If you go, I go; I stay, if you stay;

> I am content, if you have joy;
> And if you have pain, I am sorrowful for it;
> If you weep, I weep; and if you laugh, I laugh.
> And this, Love <term>Cupid</term> commands of me.

**Riccardian Codex 2723 : Florentine edition 1814. — Verses 1-2. *From the first day that I gazed upon you, the printed editions say*; and they place a comma at the end of the second verse. We believe there is no need to change the *the* <note>original: "il"</note> of the first verse into a *from* <note>original: "dal"</note> and make a single sentence of seven verses; provided that the *And* of the second verse is taken as intensive, explaining: The first day that I saw you, I *also* resolved, I *indeed* resolved, to love you faithfully. — verse 3. *If you go, lady, I go; I stay if you stay, the printed editions say.* The manuscript actually has *If you go I go, and I stay if you stay.* Knowing a little of <term>ancient prosody</term><note>The study of the rhythm and sounds of poetry.</note>, one sees the uselessness of the addition, *lady.* The same may be said of verse 4 where the printed editions read *And what you do you.* — verse 7. ### XIX.

->Whether I go, or stay, or in whatever state I may be,<-
->I ever and always think of you, noble lord;<-
->And I have you always in my imagination,<-
->Such that a painter could not do it better;<-
->And it seems to me that I speak with you all the while<-
->And recount to you in part my sorrow,<-
->Saying to you — I am doing poorly, as you see;<-
->And you do not care for it and do not believe me.<-

Riccardian Codex 2723 : Florentine edition 1814. — **Verse 2.** *noble lord*, see *Continuous Rispetti III*; verse 12 — **Verses 3-4.** Iacopo da Lentino <note>A 13th-century poet of the Sicilian School, often credited with inventing the sonnet.</note>: "As a man who holds his mind / On another example and paints / A similar painting, / Thus, beautiful one, I do: / Inside my heart / I carry your image." Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the influential Italian humanist and poet.</note>: "It seems to me that I have within it (the heart) / One who always paints my lady / and speaks of her."

### XX.

->A longing desire that torments my heart<-
->Makes me come to you presumptuously.<-
->The hour that I do not see you is as if I feel<-
->A bitter grief that makes me die:<-
->And my soul only finds itself content<-
->Where your eyes are destined to appear.<-
->In this desire I will always remain strong,<-
->As long as my life lasts, and unto death.<-

Riccardian Codex 2723 : Florentine edition 1814. — **Verse 3.** *it is like what one feels* <note>original: "è al par chi senta"</note>, Florentine edition 1814: *it is as if I feel* <note>original: "è al par ch' i' senta"</note>, Florentine edition 1822. Maggi in the cited *Appendix* proposed that it should be read as *it seems that I feel* <note>original: "el par ch' i' senta"</note>, and Silvestri in his 1825 edition printed *and yet I feel* <note>original: "e' pur ch' i' senta"</note>. The Riccardian manuscript reads clearly as we have printed it: and it seems that it can be explained: When I do not see you it is as if I felt, it is the same as if I feel, such grief as to die from it. The *it seems that I feel* of the critic and the Milanese editor appears rather cold to us. — **verse 8.** <margin>Until my life closes upon death</margin> In the margin of the Riccardian manuscript this verse is written in a different hand: *Until my life closes upon death*, which is also reported with the title of a variant reading in the Moukian manuscript of Lucca.

## XXI.

> A loving gaze, a sweet smile
> Make me for a time feel joyful and content:
> But if at times, disdainful in your face
> I see you, my heart remains sad and discontent.
> Thus now I am in life and now killed,
> Just as I see a change happen in you:
> And in these two opposites the heart is uncertain
> Which is greater: the pleasure or the pain.

Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition 1814. (Livorno, Masi, 1813, vol. I, p. 261-266).
Published with other stanzas of the Noble Author <note>original: "N. A."</note> first from the Riccardian by G. Poggiali in *Series of Language Texts* <note>original: "Serie dei testi di-lingua"</note>. — Verse 1. In a Tuscan folk <term>rispetto</term>: "A sweet smile, a loving gaze." — verse 8. *the pleasure*, in the stanzas.

## XXII.

> Graceful eyes and a gracious gaze
> Which were the first that made me fall in love;
> Serene eyes from which issued that dart
> Which pierced the heart and for which no shield availed;
> Eyes, cause of the fire in which I always burn,
> ~~Without~~ <note>The word "Senza" (Without) is struck through in the original manuscript or working copy.</note> which living is not dear to me;
> To you I come to ask if ever
> I ought to hope for mercy from so many woes.

Riccardian Codex 2723 : Poggiali : Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. *Graceful eyes*, Riccardian: *Graceful eyes, gracious gaze*, Silvestri edition. I have accepted Poggiali's reading — verse 2. *fusti* <note>An archaic Italian form of "foste" (you were), commonly found in early lyric poetry.</note>, in the stanzas. — verse 5. *in which always*, Silvestri.

> Eyes that without a tongue speak to me

> And without hands hold me in sorrow,
> And without feet guide me to death
> Joyfully hoping and blind through love;

### XXIV.

> O comfort of mine who I beheld
> And peace and rest of my sad heart,
> O solemn remedy for my woes,
> O exquisite <note>original: "pellegrino" — in Renaissance poetry, this often means "rare," "singular," or "strikingly beautiful" rather than "wandering."</note> and graceful face;
> O you who always make me sigh,
> Because I can never cease calling upon you;
> Pity for God's sake, pity, pity; for I die,
> If you do not help me, O my dear treasure.

Riccardian Codex 2723 : Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 3. *solemn*: very great (Florentine Edition 1814). — Verse 6. The "you" <note>original: "te"</note> which is present in all the printed stanzas is missing in the codex.

### XXV.

> Pity, lady, for God's sake! ah, no more war,
> No more war, for God's sake! for I surrender to you.
> I am almost dead, I lie on the ground:
> I call myself defeated, and no longer defend myself.
> Bind me, and in whatever prison you wish, lock me;
> For I will be a greater glory to you while living.
> If you fear that I might flee; make a knot
> From your braid, and bind me in your own way.

Riccardian Codex 2723 : Comino, Rigoli. See note to <term>Rispetto</term> III. — Verse 1. *ah* <note>original: "deh"</note>, is missing in the Riccardian. — Verse 1-2. Also found in a popular serenade: "Where is she who shuts herself in and locks / And within her walls makes herself strong?... I am determined to wage war on her.... Surrender, my love - I have surrendered.." — Verse 3. *I lie* <note>original: "io iacio"</note>, Riccardian. — Verse 6. *I will make you* <note>original: "ti farò"</note>, Rigoli. — Verse 8. *braid* <note>original: "treccia"</note>, Rigoli.

### XXVI.

> Water, neighbors! for in my heart I burn.
> Come, help it, for God's sake.

## XXVII.

> Ah, do not be prideful for your beauty,
> Lady; for a brief time steals it from you:
> The blonde braid will turn grey
> That adorns the figure of your beautiful face.
> While the flower is in its loveliness,
> Gather it; for beauty lasts but a little while.
> Fresh is the rose in the morning, and by evening
> She has lost her haughty beauty.

---

## XXVIII.

> While the sun shines in your eyes,
> Spend the time that has deceived many,
> Before the fresh lilies and violets
> Fall from your garden without being gathered.
> And he who grieves too late for his fault
> Well may he lament among the other fools.

### XXX.

> What cruelty it would be if I loved you
> And faithfully gave you my heart,
> And you, lady, sought my death
> And gave me hate in exchange for love,
> I wish that sometimes you would think on it;
> And you would see if you are in error.
> Do you not see that you offend justice,
> If you return hate for faithful love?

From the manuscript of Mr. Vanzolini, where it stands among other *Rispetti* by Poliziano.

### XXXII.

->I must seem like a <term>strange fish</term><note>original: "nuovo pesce"; an idiom for someone who is simple or easily deceived, much like "fresh meat" or a "newbie."</note> to you<-

1. **Strange fish.** "One is called this who is simple and easily <unclear>i</unclear>ndeceived; the metaphor is drawn from <unclear>fi</unclear>sh that we call *fry*... that is, born in the year which <unclear>ar</unclear>e [small], which are little fish and easily caught." • V. # THE FLIGHT.

## XXXIV.

->I do not know for what reason it may be, lady,<-
->Or if it is indeed misfortune or my own defect,<-
->That when I pass by, lady, on the road,<-
->That you flee before my sight<-
->And do not wish for me to see you as before.<-
->If you held me in contempt for some other reason<-
->And that I am not truly worthy of this love,<-
->If you do not wish to tell me, give me a sign.<-

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Riccardian Codex 2723 : Florentine edition of 1814.** In the codex, it is transcribed again further on, with some variety in the second reading; of which we make use for the correction. — **Verses 1-2.** *I would like to know for what reason it is, If it is through my misfortune and my defect*, second reading. — **Verse 4.** *you flee before*, the prints and the codex in the first reading. We adopted the second reading in the text. The second *that* [che] seems superfluous: but it is the function of such <term>pleonasms</term><note>The use of more words than are necessary to convey meaning, often for emphasis or clarity.</note> to prevent the relationship between two propositions joined by a particle from being forgotten, when another secondary proposition intervenes between them. There are beautiful and effective examples of this in Boccaccio and Dante: thus, *Inferno* XXVI, 23: | "So that, if a lucky star or a better fate / Has given me the good, [that] I do not begrudge it to myself." <note>original: "Sì che, se stella buona o miglior sorte / M' ha dato 'l ben, ch' io stesso nol m' invidi." The editor points out that the second "che" (that) serves to reconnect the reader to the beginning of the thought after the interruption of "if a lucky star..."</note> — **Verses 6-7.** We have accepted the second reading in the text: the first is *Or if you held me in suspicion for some other reason / And if I were not truly worthy of your love*. — **Verse 8.** *If you do not wish to tell me*, second reading. |

## HOPE.

### XXXVII.

> I do not dare to lift my eyes high,
> Lady, to gaze upon your beauty;
> For I am not worthy of loving such a lady
> Nor of being a servant to such high beauty.
> But if you would deign to look down a little
> And do injury to your greatness,
> You would see this servant so faithful
> That perhaps you would be less cruel to him.

### XXXIX.

### XL.

> I am the unfortunate little ship
> On the high sea amidst the dark and angry waves,
> Between the shoals and the rocks, poor little thing,
> Battered by the winds and by fortune,
> Without mast or rudder; nor do I see a star,
> And heaven gathers its strength against me:
> Yet the path is shown to me by such a pilot,
> That I hope to arrive safely in port.

### XLI.

May pity take hold of you for my afflicted heart,
Pity; if any pity is still kept within you:
May the fact that I have been your lover move you
From the day when your age was still "in the grass" <note>An idiom meaning in early youth or "green."</note>.
Now that I see every flower opening on the tree,
And already the fruit that loses its bitterness,
I wait to gather the fruit of that beautiful tree,
Unless your cruelty wishes to take it from me.

---

<margin>
**Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition of 1814.** — **Verse 2.** We accept the punctuation of the Silvestri edition and the Florentine edition of 1822: the Florentine editions of 1814 make *Pity* the object of *move you*. — **Verse 3.** *having been there* <note>original: "l' esservi stato"</note>, Florentine editions. — **Verse 4. In the grass.** She was still young and fresh (Florentine editions of 1814).
</margin>

### XLII.

After so much waiting, will the hour ever come,
Will the day so much desired ever come?
For if it must ever come, it would be time
It came before I were buried.
Will my service, not yet acknowledged,
Be the reason that I die in despair?
And will my lament find no pity?
Or will love at last make me content?

---

<margin>
**Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition of 1814.** — **Verse 7.** *will find* <note>original: "troverà"</note>, the printed editions. The question marks added by us to verses 6, 7 and 8 seem required by the sense, which in the other printed editions that lack them is unclear and not without contradiction.
</margin>

### XLIII.

To these many sighs that dwell in the heart
Love will perhaps soon put an end;
For, if I see clearly, they are becoming merciful
Toward me—those divine lights,
The eyes that still give me hope
That I shall gather the flower in the midst of so many thorns.

## XLIV.

->Content I remain in fire like a phoenix,<-
->And like a swan I sing while dying;<-
->For I hope to become happy,<-
->Once I have suffered pain and martyrdom.<-
->Love, you shall see how much it is not permitted<-
->To be cruel to my faithful service;<-
->For, once my pure faith is known,<-
->I hope that you will have some mercy on me.<-

<margin>Riccardian Codex 2723: Poggiali, *Serie ec.* Florentine edition 1814. — "I shall sing in Phrygian rhythms like some swan of Cayster" <note>Cayster is a river in Lydia, modern-day Turkey, famous in ancient poetry for its many swans.</note> — Anacreon. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, "Already dying, the swan sings its funeral songs" <note>original Latin: "Carmina jam moriens canit exequilia cycnus."</note>. This bird, sacred to Apollo, foreseeing the moment of its death, according to what the ancients wrote for us, sends forth a most sweet song. The swans of our day seem to have changed their nature. Delille in his *Gardens*, Book III, said: "The swan to whom error lent lovely songs" <note>original French: "Le cygne à qui l'erreur prêta des chants aimables."</note> (Florentine editions 1814.) — Verse 8. *would have* <note>original: "avria"</note>, the codex: *mercy*, the printed editions. This Rispetto is also found among the <term>Strambotti</term><note>A "strambotto" is a similar short poetic form, often satirical or amorous, popular in the 15th century.</note> of Aquilano: where at verse 6 one reads **TO my LOYAL service**; at 7 **And, having known**. </margin>

## XLVI.

<margin>Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 4. *the last hour*, the printed editions. We accepted the addition of the article from the recent editors. Furthermore, *utimo* for *ultimo* [last] is a common <term>iotism</term><note>A phonetic change where a vowel or consonant shifts toward an "i" sound or is dropped in specific clusters, typical of certain dialects.</note> in Florentine writings of the <term>Quattrocento</term><note>The 1400s, or the 15th century.</note> and is still alive in the speech of the Tuscan people. Verses 5-6. A popular Rispetto: "And after death my spirits will come to seek you where you are."</margin>
Nor could death make me not love you:
For, once my spirit had departed,
It would be necessary, my Lady, that I remain with you
Until your own final hour should come,
And then in the next world,
My shadow would still follow yours forever.
This was given to me by heaven as my fate,
That I should be yours in life and after death.

---

## XLVII.

<margin>Laurentian Codex 44: Florentine edition 14. It was first published by Serassi in the Cominiana edition, then also by Rigoli in the cited *Essay*.</margin>
Do me as much spite as you know how,
Give me as much pain and torment as you wish,
Laugh at my suffering and my woes,
Ruin my every plan and every joy,
Show yourself my enemy as you do,
Keep me always in suspicion, trouble, and hardship;
Yet heaven can never bring it about
That I do not honor and love you with true devotion.

# THE REWARD OF CONSTANCY.

## LIII.

Among all your other virtues, Love,
This one is read clearly and plainly:
He who always does honor to the world,
She <note>Referring to the "virtue" of Love.</note> teaches to love, even if he were dead,
Nor should one who is too constant to his lord
Be wrongly banished from his court.
You who sing my sorrowful verses,
Know that this is the reward of lovers.

Riccardian Codex 2723: Florentine edition 1844. — Verse 1. *virtues* <note>original: "virtudi"</note>, the printed editions. — verses 2-6. To derive a sense from this octave, which is very corrupt in both the codex and the printed editions, we have adopted the corrections put forward by Vincenzo Monti <note>Vincenzo Monti (1754–1828) was a prominent Italian poet and scholar known for his work on linguistic purity and classical translations.</note> in his *Farce of the Poets*, interval IV, scene I. [*Proposal*, volume III, part II], and also adopted in the Silvestri edition. In the codex and in the Florentine printing of 1814, verse 2 reads *This* <note>original: "Questo"</note>; at verse 4, *to love nor say that he is dead* <note>original: "amar nè dir ch’ è morto"</note>; at verse 5, *And that* <note>original: "E che"</note>; at verse 6, *Was of* <note>original: "Fu di"</note>. Here is the explanation provided by Monti in the cited passage: "Love, among your other virtuous laws, this one is observed as being clearly and plainly dictated: it teaches us to love the lover who honors the world with his works, rather than wishing that through the cruelty of his lady he be led to die, or that he be wrongly banished from the court of his lord for having been too constant." — Verse 4. In the <unclear>Monke Inech.</unclear> codex it reads thus: *And the sign of love gave he is dead* <note>original: "E l’ insegna d’ amor ne diede è morto"</note>, with the last four words underlined; in the margin is written: "Perhaps: *of which he is dead* <note>original: "di che si è morto"</note>." Let others see if they can draw a construction from it; to me it seems impossible. — verses 7-8. It appears that Love is responding: unless one understands that the poet is addressing the singer of his *rispetto*.

---

# REPROACHES.

## LIV.

I would have already moved a she-bear to pity;
And yet you remain hard against my many complaints.
What will you have done, once in the grave
You see your faithful servant buried?
Behold the life, behold the flesh and the bones!
What do you want to do with me, cruel woman?

"Jew" <note>original: "giudeo"</note> used to mean "unbeliever" (Messer Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia (c. 1270–1336), a famous jurist and poet of the "Dolce Stil Novo" school.</note>, regarding the eyes of his lady: "O you who are toward me so Jewish / That you do not believe my words without proof"), and for one who is obstinate or fierce (Cecco Angiolieri <note>A Sienese poet known for his humorous, often biting and rebellious sonnets.</note>: "Alas, how is her heart so Jewish!" It is so true that literature, and poetry in particular, is more than a mirror; it is a reservoir—both pure and impure—of noble and honorable aspirations, as well as the superstitions and the biased, savage hatreds of the times to which it belongs. — v. 2. *dare* <note>to give</note>, the manuscript; with an evident error. — v. 8. *ad una* <note>together/at once</note>, the printed editions.

# LAMENTS AND PRAYERS.

## LVII.

> I have the greater pain, though I stay quiet,
> Than he who throws his words into the wind:
> So that the grief grows no more, I stay mild,
> Because it avails me little if I complain.
> To avoid revealing that which I hold secret,
> Sometimes I laugh, though not because I am happy;
> For he who reveals his secret troubles
> Does not diminish the grief but increases the harm.

Riccardian Codex 2723; Florentine edition 14. This is also among the Rispetti of Aquilano <note>Serafino de' Ciminelli (1466–1500), known as Serafino Aquilano, a hugely popular poet-musician of the Renaissance.</note> with these variations: at verse 1 **STAYS QUIET**. At 3 **AND TO NOT GROW GRIEF**, at 5 **I HAVE IN SECRET**, at 7 **HIS SECRET troubles**.

## LVIII.

> There was never in the world a more unfortunate
> Lover, or one more sad and discontent than I;
> For I bear with patience the sin
> That another has committed to my detriment.
> There is one here who thinks to become blessed
> By keeping me in infernal torment,
> Not knowing well how strongly it displeases God,
> He who is the cause of another's death.

Riccardian Codex 2723; Florentine edition 14. — V. 3. *patience* <note>original: "pazienza"</note>, thus in the codex and the printed editions. I suspect it should be read as *penitence* <note>original: "penitenza"</note>. — According to P. Fanfani <note>Pietro Fanfani (1815–1879), a noted Italian philologist and lexicographer.</note> [*Philological Research*, 1847, III, p. 40] it means *suffering, pain* in this verse and in the penultimate verse of Canto X of the *Purgatorio*: "And he who had the most patience in his gestures / Weeping seemed to say: I can do no more." <note>A reference to Dante’s *Divine Comedy*, where souls are bowed under heavy weights in the Terrace of Pride.</note>

### LIX.

**Every lady takes pity on me**
**And every wild beast that hears my lament:**
**I have already moved these stones to pity**
**Upon which I now rest my unhappy body.**
**And there was never anyone who loved a woman**
**Who stood as I do in the rain and the wind:**
**In you alone, lady, my tears cannot**
**Break your sweet and light sleep.**

**Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Poggiali, *Series etc.*: Florentine edition, 1814.**

### LX.

**If your heart shows no pity now**
**To these eyes that have no more tears;**
**May death be pitying of my prayers and my woes,**
**And pull me from my distress.**
**And though I believe that you will take much pleasure**
**From my torment and my loss,**
**Let it not be so, however, that it is said that wrongly**
**I was killed by you only for loving you.**

<meta>This page continues the presentation of Angelo Poliziano's "rispetti" (short lyric poems), specifically concluding the notes for poem LXI and providing the full text for poems LXII and LXIII. > While I weep singing of my torments;
> Rather you hide your loving face:
> Return to my eyes the lights <note>The word "lumi" (lights) is a poetic synonym for "eyes."</note> that you have taken from them.

<term>Riccardian Manuscript 2723</term>: <term>Florentine edition, 1814</term>. — Verse 8. Thus the <term>manuscript</term>; *my* <note>original: "miei"</note>, the <term>Florentine editions</term>. Maggi, in the cited *Appendix*, observed: "The arrangement of the words, certainly disrupted by the copyists, makes this verse harsh. Furthermore, to say *return to the eyes the lights* is the same as if one had said *return to the eyes the eyes*; since *lights* in the plural is a synonym for *eyes* among poets. One should, however, correct it to *light* <note>original: "lume"</note>, meaning *the sight*: and Poliziano himself further ahead, in stanza 9, [\* in this <term>edition</term> <term>rispetto</term> LXIII], points us toward this correction, saying: *Weep, eyes, since Love has taken from us the sweet sight of our Lady*. And the above-noted verse must surely stand like this: *Return to my eyes the light that you have taken from them.*" We do not see this necessity, and we are not displeased by the phrase *returning the eyes to the eyes*. But the reading proposed by Maggi passed into the Silvestri <term>edition</term>.

> So that it may defend itself from death.

> **Weep until she is moved to pity:**
> **And if she has no pity, pray to Love**
> **Not to put me to any longer trial.**
> **But that he return my heart to me**
> **Or that he remove such cruelty from her,**
> **And that he be finally content and sated**
> **To see such cruel torment of mine.**

<term>Riccardian MS 2723</term>: <term>Florentine edition</term> 1814. — Verse 2. In the <term>Silvestri edition</term> it is corrected grammatically: *Weep until she moves to pity* <note>original: "finch' ella a pietà si muova"</note>. We, who do not want despotisms even in grammar, leave it as the <term>manuscript</term> reads <note>The editor defends the original manuscript's phrasing against later "corrections" that aimed to make the poetry follow strict rules of grammar.</note>.

> **I shall complain of you before Love,**
> **Telling how you cause me to die : :**

### LXVII.

> **Succor me, for God's sake; for time is passing.**
> **See, my lady, cruelty defies me:**
> **Succor my wretched and weary soul**
> **Which trusts in your pity alone:**
> **Succor me; for she allows me to die,**
> **Since she sees me in the world without a guide:**
> **Succor me for God's sake, do not be slow;**
> **For a single glance of yours can keep me alive.**

<term>Riccardian Manuscript 2723</term>: <term>Florentine edition</term> 1814. — Verse 2. It seems he makes a subtle abstraction between "my lady" and her "cruelty" which he complains of: an abstraction of which examples abound in the ancient poets. Thus <term>Cavalcanti</term> <note>Guido Cavalcanti was a 13th-century Florentine poet and friend of Dante Alighieri</note>: "If mercy were a friend to my desires, / And its movement were from the heart / Of this beautiful lady..."; and <term>Dante</term>: "It behooves me to call upon my enemy, / My lady Pity <note>original: "Madonna la pietà"</note> that she may defend me." — Verse 8. How does he reconcile this masculine word *slow* <note>original: "tardo"</note> with the feminine *Lady* <note>original: "Madonna"</note>? Let the grammarians see if it could be held as *used* in the manner of an adverb. One could suppose that the poet addressed himself to Love <note>The personified god Cupid/Amor</note>: and then in verse 2 one would need to read, *lady and cruelty*, or, ironically, *lady cruelty*; just as Dante said *My lady Pity*.

> **See my sorrowful and wasted body:**
> **For, if your mercy does not help it now,**

### LXXI.

->Before I drive myself to despair,<-
->I would like to know your ultimate wish;<-
->And, if I do not see mercy reigning in you,<-
->Death at the end will then be no sorrow to me.<-
->Tell me, my lady, what I must do<-
->To ensure that death does not grieve me;<-
->Deign to give answer to my prayers.<-
->A gracious smile costs little.<-

<note>
Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 2. *ultimate* <note>original: "ultima"</note>, the printed editions. — verse 3. *that death be a sorrow to me* <note>original: "che morte mi sia doglia"</note>, the Florentine editions of 1814. Maggi, in the cited Appendix, wrote: "Since *sorrow* <note>original: "doglia"</note> in the second verse [of the final quatrain, i.e., line 4] is a noun, it must be a verb in the fourth [line 6]," and proposed the correction *To ensure that death does not so grieve me* <note>original: "A non voler che morte si mi doglia"</note>: this correction was adopted in the Silvestri edition. The reading of the manuscript gave us light for the true correction, which has *To ensure that death is not a sorrow to me*: where it is evident that *is* <note>original: "sia"</note> is a redundant error caused by the memory of verse 4. — verse 8. We accepted the correction by Maggi adopted in the Silvestri edition: the manuscript and the Florentine editors of 1814 read *Of a gracious smile that costs little*.
</note>

## WAITING FOR THE TIME.

### LXXII.

->The night is long for one who cannot sleep,<-
->But yet is short for one who lies content:<-
->If the day is great for one who lives in sighs,<-
->It quickly passes for one who possesses it in peace:<-
->It is true that hope and desire<-
->Many times turn out to be false for each of them;<-
->But, when the waiting finally reaches its end,<-
->The true good never arrives too late.<-

<note>
Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 2. *one who in contentment* <note>original: "chi in contento"</note>, the printed editions. — verse 3. *The day is... in suffering* <note>original: "Lo giorno è... in martire"</note>, the printed editions. — verse 5. In truth, the manuscript has *their desire* <note>original: "loro desire"</note>: it seemed better to us to follow the printed editions.
</note>

### LXXIII.

<margin>Riccardian Manuscript 2723; Florentine edition 1814. — Verses 1-2. Horace, *Odes* II, 9: "Not always do the rains flow from the clouds upon the bristling fields, nor do uneven storms constantly disturb the Caspian Sea" <note>original: "Non semper imbres nubibus hispidos Manant in agros, aut mare Caspium Vexant inæquales procellæ Usque."</note>. — This <term>rispetto</term> is also found among the <term>Strambotti</term> <note>A "strambotto" is a poetic form nearly identical to the "rispetto," characterized by its eight-line structure.</note> of Serafino Aquilano, with the small difference that in verse 4 he reads **That** *reveals on earth*, etc., and in verse 8, **That** *he who conquers himself* **is well worthy**.</margin>
A heavy storm does not always last at sea,
Nor does a thick mist always darken the sun:
The cold snow remains but a short time in the heat,
And then reveals roses and violets on the earth:
I know that every Saint awaits their feast day,
And that time is accustomed to change everything:
Therefore, it is a wise thought to wait for the right time,
And he who conquers himself is truly worthy of an empire.

---

### LXXIV.

<margin>Riccardian Manuscript 2723; Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. *thorn, the st.* — verse 8. The manuscript reads *That not that harms* <note>original: "Che non che nuoce"</note>. I have accepted the correction by Maggi in the cited Appendix: a correction that passed into the text of the Silvestri edition of 1825. This <term>rispetto</term> is also among the <term>Strambotti</term> of Aquilano; except that in verse 3 he reads *placed in*, in verse 4 **Sometimes**, in verse 7 **Will be health**, and in verse 8 **That everything** *that harms has also virtue*.</margin>
Every sharp and poisonous thorn
Is seen at some time to have bloomed:
Cruel poison placed in medicine
Often brings a man back from death to life:
And the fire that burns and ruins everything
Often heals a mortal wound:
So I hope my suffering may be my salvation,
For that which harms has also some virtue.

## FULFILLED VOWS.

### LXXVI.

I thank you, Love, for every torment
That I suffered and for so many of my woes,
And I am among lovers the most content
That ever existed, even in a thousand years;
Since my ship, driven by a good wind,
Reaches the port, relief from so many harms.
Guide the sail, Love; so that the wind may push,
While the sea still flatters all around.

<margin>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. (Florentine editions 1814.) — Verse 6. *sees the port*, according to the printed editions.</margin>

### LXXX.

->I sowed the field, and another reaps it;<-
->I have spent my labor in vain:<-
->Another has the birds, and I set the net;<-
->Only the feather has remained in my hand:<-
->Another is in the water, and I die of thirst:<-

Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. *and another*, the printed editions. — v. 3. *and I*, the printed editions. — v. 4. *Only... has remained*, the printed editions. — v. 5 and 6. *and I*, the printed editions. — v. 7. *priete* instead of *pietre* [stones], by metathesis <note>Metathesis is the transposition of sounds or letters in a word; here "pietre" becomes "priete" to fit the rhyme or local dialect.</note> (Florentine editions 14). The hyperbole is bold, but not as much as that of Dante, who, speaking of a sudden amorous trembling that came upon him, says: "And because of the intoxication of the great trembling, the stones seem to cry out: die, die" <note>original: "E per la ebrietà del gran tremore Le pietre par che gridin : muoia, muoia." — from Dante's Vita Nuova.</note>. — v. 8. *and another*, the printed editions. — This *Rispetto* is then found repeated in the manuscript with some variations. It is provided below.

### LXXXI.

->I sowed the field, another reaps it;<-
->And I have spent my labor in vain:<-
->Another is in the water, and I die of thirst:<-
->Another has ascended, and I remained on the plain:<-
->Another has caught, and I set the nets,<-
->And only the feather has remained in my hand.<-
->Fortune wrongly makes her wishes glad;<-
->For I burn for you, and you do not help me.<-

Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. *and another*, the printed editions. — v. 2-3. *and*, the printed editions. — v. 4. The Silvestri edition reads with Maggi *and I remained on the plain*. — v. 5. *and I*, Silvestri. This verse is a reminiscence of Petrarch's "And he sets such a net that catches nothing" <note>original: "E la rete tal tende che non piglia."</note>. — v. 6. **THE FEATHER HAS REMAINED TO ME**. Here the participle does not agree with the noun, remaining almost indeclinable <note>In standard Italian, the past participle "rimasto" (remained) would usually change to "rimasta" to match the feminine noun "piuma" (feather). The editor notes this as a rare grammatical exception.</note>: as rarely happens when it is joined with the verb *to be*. Petrarch, Song I: "...feeling... until then struck by his arrow, it had not passed beyond my garment" <note>original: "sentendo... Infin allor percossa di suo strale Non essermi passato oltre la gonna"</note> and Boccaccio, *Decameron*, Day IV, Novel VI: "Nor because of that has anything in the world happened to me, more or less" <note>original: "Nè perciò cosa del mondo più nè meno me n' è intervenuto."</note>. — *remained*, Silvestri.

## LXXXII.

The lovely garden that I tended so much
Another holds, and reaps the fruit:
And the prize that I took and earned
Another has wrongly deprived me of entirely:
And I feed myself on tears and sorrows and woes,
Because he who has the power wishes me thus destroyed:
And I have lost both my time and my labor,
And I am at the mercy of my enemy.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. *cultivated* <note>original: "cultivai"</note>, the printed editions.</note>

---

## LXXXIII.

From the fine field that I plowed with such sweat
Another has taken the harvest while still green:
From the vine that I placed upon the holy tree <note>In traditional Italian viticulture, vines were often "married" to trees (like elms or poplars) for support; "alber santo" likely refers to this practice or a specific consecrated tree.</note>
Another has harvested the bitter grapes:
And the fruit that I gather is grief and weeping
Which the ungrateful earth saves for the cultivator.
Now my heart wastes away and gnaws with rage:
Another has the fruit and enjoys my hardship.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. *The fine field* <note>original: "El bel campo"</note>, the manuscript. I accept the reading of the printed editions. — *wastes away and the heart gnaws itself* <note>original: "strugge e'l cor si rode"</note>, the printed editions among the <term>Rispetti</term> of Aquilano <note>Serafino dell'Aquila (1466–1500), a renowned poet-improviser whose work often overlapped with Poliziano's.</note> with variations: at verse 1. THE GOOD FIELD WHICH, at 2 Another HAS HARVESTED IT FULLY, at 3 THE VINE that I ALREADY PLACED ON THE TREE, at 4 has HARVESTED, at 5 THE fruit, at 7 and 8 THUS PASSING MY LIFE IT GNAWS, THAT ANOTHER UNWORTHY ENJOYS MY HARDSHIPS.</note>

# DESPAIR.

## LXXXIV.

My Lady, my pain would be sweet,
Sweet the weeping, the sighs, sweet the torment,
If I were certain that this chain
Would one day break to make me content.

<summary>This page concludes the "Scattered Rispetti" focused on the betrayal of labor and love, then introduces a new section on "Despair." The poems use agricultural metaphors—gardens, fields, and vineyards—to express the bitterness of unrequited or stolen affection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the collection of "Scattered Rispetti," likely attributed to Lorenzo de' Medici or his circle. Following the themes of the previous page—where the lover lamented a "stolen harvest"—these poems (LXXXV through LXXXVII) shift toward a more somber tone. Here, the poet contemplates death as the only escape from the "chains" of a cruel and unyielding love.</meta>

<page-num>263</page-num>
<header>SCATTERED <term>RISPETTI</term> <note>Short, eight-line poems in <term>ottava rima</term>, a common form for Renaissance lyric poetry.</note>.</header>

> But because the body can hardly sustain itself
> And your beautiful eyes do not change,
> Death will one day loosen this chain
> And put an end to my sad fate.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Poggiali, *Series etc.*: **this chain.** — *Verse* 4. **You loosened** <note>original: "Scioglieste"</note>, Silv. Florentine edition 1814. — *Verse* 3. The manuscript reads: **of** — *Verse* 6. *And the beautiful* <note>original: "E be'"</note>, Florentine edition 1814; *and the beautiful* <note>original: "e i bei"</note>, Silv.</note>

### LXXXV.

> If even your heart is not yet sated
> By seeing so much of my cruel torment,
> I pray that death gives me enough time
> That I may satisfy your desire.
> And, if that is not enough, for my further agony
> Let me die, and let my dust be given to the wind:
> For dying would be a greater sweetness to me
> To please you, lady, than living.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — *Verse* 3. **gives me** <note>original: "mi dia"</note>, the printed editions.</note>

### LXXXVI.

> Oh me! For too much love leads to death
> The heart without hope of help.
> Death will loosen the amorous chain,
> Death will take the hard bit from the heart.
> Yet I do not know if the pain will cease
> When I have run into the arms of death.
> Nor would this be against my will
> If for loving you I remained always in sorrow.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — *Verse* 1. **Alas** <note>original: "Ohimè"</note>, the printed editions.</note>

### LXXXVII.

> I would not have believed such cruelty
> Could reign in so noble a face:
> But now I clearly realize it, and I see how
> Vain is the hope for which I wait.

### LXXXVIII.

> How can my heart ever rejoice?
> If I possessed as much as heaven possesses,
> Only for the pain it has in remembering
> How much good is seen or evil is seen,
> It stands in danger of perishing:
> Unless heaven already by grace provides for me
> That fortune would now grant me
> That, having lost so great a good, death were given to me.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. — Verse 1. We accept the <term>punctuation</term> <note>original: "interpunzione"</note> of the Florentine edition of 1814: the Florentine edition of 1822 and that of Silvestri 1825 place a comma at the end of the first verse and the question mark at the end of the second. — Verses 2-5. "From the second to the fifth verse," Maggi notes in the cited *Appendix*, "there is such a <term>distortion</term> <note>original: "stravolgimento," referring to a confused or convoluted grammatical structure</note> that it cannot be healed even by probable <term>conjecture</term> <note>original: "congettura," a scholar's educated guess to fix a broken text</note>. It was however the editor's duty to note it." At Verse 3 in the Silvestri edition it is noted: "This and the two following verses are truly enigmatic. *Standing in danger of perishing* <note>original: "Pericoloso sta per pericolarsi"</note> seems to be a common idiom, which essentially resolves into saying *it is dangerous*. The passage is found, as it is printed, in the Riccardian manuscript from which the Florentine editors drew these stanzas." We note that at Verse 4 in the manuscript it reads **now evil** <note>original: "or mal"</note> instead of **or evil** <note>original: "o mal"</note> which the printed editions have. — Verse 6. Thus the Florentine editors of 1814: the manuscript is erroneous and redundant. — Verses 7-8. **would grant... would give** <note>original: "concedesse . . . desse"</note>, the printed editions.</note>

### LXXXIX.

> See, lovers, to what extreme fate
> I am reduced only for loving a woman,
> For I feel death already near to my heart
> Nor can I remedy such great harm.

### XC.

> Alas for me, alas! Oh me! what must I do
> In this life without any comfort?
> Must I always weep in this world
> And never leave this horrible port?
> Oh deaf death, do not delay any longer:
> Help my prayers, do not do me wrong.
> For no other refuge is required of me,
> Since for me there is neither pity nor faith.

Dal codice del signor Vanzolini; ov' è fra altri Rispetti del Poliziano.
<margin>From the manuscript of Mr. Vanzolini; where it is found among other <term>Rispetti</term> by Poliziano.</margin>

### XCI.

> Weep, sorrowful eyes, and the heart with you
> Let it weep for its freedom which Love has taken from it:
> Weep for the sweet and beautiful time since
> Love has turned our joy into weeping:
> Weep for the charms and the snares of his
> By which I find myself captured and she is free:
> Weep, sorrowful eyes, until the end
> That death may dry your bitter weeping.

<note>Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Poggiali, *Series etc.* Florentine edition 1814: Magliabechiano Manuscript 735. — Verse 2. **it has** <note>original: "l' ha"</note>, Riccardian manuscript and the Florentine edition of 1814. — Verse 6. **she set free** <note>original: "ella disciolta"</note>, Silvestri edition. We accepted the reading of the Magliabechiano. The Florentine editors of 1814 read with the Riccardian, and **her set free** <note>original: "lei disciolta"</note>. — Verse 7-8. The Magliabechiano: **Weep, oh afflicted eyes, my pain so much, so that pity may find your weeping.** <note>original: "Piangete, o occhi affritti, el mio duol tanto, Acciö che pietà truovi el vostro pianto."</note> — It is also among the <term>Strambotti</term> <note>A short Italian poetic form similar to the rispetto, usually humorous or amorous.</note> of Aquilano <note>Serafino dell'Aquila (1466–1500), a famous poet and musician known for his improvisational style.</note> with these variations: at verse 4 **LOVE YOUR FORTUNE**, at 6 **AND SHE FREE**: verses 7 and 8 agree with the Magliabechiano, except that they read **MY EVIL** and find **PITY OUR**.</note>

### XCII.

> I want to die, if death wishes to take me,
> Since my desire can find no place.
> It is better to die than always with pain
> To go on wasting away like wax in the fire.
> She who could help me does not aid me;
> Rather, she takes my torments as a game.
> Therefore I ask for death as my rescue,
> Since I see myself going from bad to worse.

*Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814.* — Verse 3. "Here there is no rhyme but simple assonance." In the notes of the 1814 Florentine edition, the verse by Petrarch is reported as a variant of the fourth verse: *Like snow in the sun, like wax in the fire* <note>original: "Come al sol neve, come cera al foco"</note>: therefore the author of the *Proposta* <note>that is, the author of the appendix to volume III, part II of the *Proposta*, a famous philological work by Vincenzo Monti</note>, holding this reading as firm, emends by conjecture: " *It is better to die than always to dissolve the heart / Like snow in the sun, etc.* " (Note from the Silvestri edition). The truth is that the 1814 Florentine editors report that verse by Petrarch not as a variant, but for comparison to Poliziano's verse. But the emendation could have been sought in the <term>Strambotti</term> <note>A form of Italian poetry similar to the rispetto, often satirical or amorous</note> of Aquilano, among which this one is included, and where in verses 3-4 one reads: *It is better TO LAY THE WEARY FLESH IN THE EARTH THAN TO GO...* <note>original: "Meglio è LA STANCA CARNE IN TERRA PORRE CHE GIR..."</note>

## THOUGHTS AND IMAGES OF DEATH.

### XCIII.

> When you see these eyes of mine closed
> By Love who at every hour spurs me to the end,
> All breathless from confused thoughts
> You will say — For me this soul abandons itself; —
> And, if you have someone to accuse you of your sin,
> You will find no one who pardons you for it:
> Thus you will go weeping in every direction,
> Grieving for my death and your sin.

*Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814.* — Verse 2. *From death that sometimes, the printed editions.* — **TO THE END**. Understand as the end of life. — Verse 4. The Florentine editors of 1814 note: "At verses 2, 4, and 6, corrections are found in the margin of the manuscript, but in such a miserable state that even the most expert people, consulted by us to decipher the sense, declared themselves unable to succeed. After this, we have taken a very small liberty...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Poliziano’s "Scattered Rispetti," focusing on manuscript variations and corrections made by later editors such as Maggi and Silvestri. <header>SCATTERED <term>RISPETTI</term> <note>Short, popular lyric poems, usually consisting of eight lines.</note>.</header>

and not at all useless to read *he abandons himself* <note>original: "s’ab- bandona"</note> in place of *abandoned* <note>original: "sbandonata"</note> as it is written. » The corrections, which date well after the time of Poliziano, are intended to remove the rhyme in *ona* and change the second-person indicative *pardon* <note>original: "perdona"</note> to the subjunctive, as it did not seem to be in good agreement. — verse 8.

Maggi, in the cited *Appendix*, put forward the correction *your sin* <note>original: "il tuo peccato"</note>, which Silvestri later accepted in his edition. There is no need for it, provided that one understands: *grieving for my death and your sin*, that is, for my death *which is your sin*.

### XCVI.

->— *May he rest in peace!* <note>original Latin: "Requiescat in pace!"</note> placed in peace<-

### XCVII.

Riccardian Manuscript 2723: Florentine edition 1814. Verse 2. *Over the* <note>original: "Sopra il"</note>, the printed editions <note>original: "le st." abbreviation for "le stampe"</note>. — *v. 6. ->Where your beautiful face once appeared for a moment,<-
->Where your sweet words were heard,<-
->It seemed that paradise was there;<-
->Where you were, it seemed the sun was.<-
->Alas! gazing fixedly at your appearance,<-
->Your face is not as it used to be.<-
->Where has your dear beauty fled?<-
->Woe to him who learns at his own expense.<-

->One was bursting from the bud yet;<-
->Some were a bit withered and some were new.<-
->Love then said to me: — Go, pick those<-
->That you see most in bloom upon the thorn. —<-

->When the rose spreads every leaf of its own,<-
->When it is most beautiful, when it is most pleasing;<-
->Then it is good to put into garlands,<-

Riccardian manuscript. — v. 17. **Which one** [Quale]
Poggiali, Vanzelli: **from the bud** [dalla boccia], Laurentian.
— **BURSTING** [SCOPPIAVA]: this is properly
the *carpere* <note>original Latin: "carpere" meaning to pluck or seize</note> of the Latins. **BUD** [BOCCIA]: the bud
of a flower; which in Tuscany they
call the more delicate roses "boccie" [buds]
more gracefully.
What Poliziano said in one [verse],
Ariosto said in two, but
following him: "As a rose that peeks
then out of the bud and with the
new sun grows" *Orlando Furioso*, X, 11. —
**Which ones were** [Quale erano], Magliabechian: *Which were* [Qual eran]
*which were new*, Vanzelli. —
**Withered** [Passe] <note>A term for flowers or fruit starting to dry out or "pass" their peak.</note>
Is said of plants that suffer from
excessive heat ("The herbs for the
withered [heat]" Boccaccio, *Am.*), and also
of fruits when they have passed [passato]
the point of their flourishing
by reason of maturity; and there-
fore rather than "suffering" I would believe it
to be a shortened form of *passare* [to pass]. —
**Then Love said to me**, Vanzelli: *pick* [còi],
same meaning. *Cô'*, *cogli* [pick] (Florentine editions 14)
). **That you see more in bloom**, Vanzelli:
Riccardian. — v. 22. *as much as ... so much*
Vanzelli. — v. 23. *to put it in*
*garlands*, Vanzelli. — v. 24. *Before that*
*it goes there*, Vanzelli. — v. 25. *while*
*it is in bloom*, Vanzelli. — v. 26. *let us*
*pluck* [cogliàn], same meaning. But it is a Florentine habit
to end in **-ano** the first per-
sons plural of the present indicative
and subjunctive. We have examples in
rhyme and prose, very frequent in the *Carnival*
*Songs* and in the *Comedies* of the six-
teenth century; not rare in the fourteenth-century writers.
Translation of Guido Delle Colonne: "We
have [abbiàno] given them so many harmful
terms..." Boccaccio *Nymphal*: "... we have [abbiàno]
To go each from here very far away."
— "Let us pluck [Cogliam] the roses in the adorned morning"
Tasso, *Jerusalem Delivered* XVI, 15 (Florentine editions
14). And Lorenzo de' Medici: "Pick the
rose, o nymph, while it is time."
And see also the last tercets of the cha-
pter by that same Lorenzo, *The moon in*
*the midst of the lesser stars*, which have
much similarity both with the present
ballad and with stanza 78 of the first book of the
*Joust*. But the concept and the form
of these verses is much older.
I choose from certain epigrams of the late
Latinity that are in the *Latin Anthology*
of Burmann: "O what roses I
saw come forth in the morning! They were
being born still, nor was the age equal
for all... While one lifts its head
and while another unfolds its knot [bud],
while for this one the virginal shame is thinned
from its garment [the petals emerge],
lest they perish, pick the roses in the mor-
ning..." <note>original Latin: "O quales ego mane rosas procedere vidi! Nascebantur adhuc, neque erat par omnibus ætas... Dum levat una caput dumque explicat altera nodum, Huic dum virgineus pudor extenuatur amictu, Ne pereant, lege mane rosas." This is a famous theme from the poem "De rosis nascentibus" attributed to Ausonius.</note>

# BALLADS.

### IV.<gloss>1</gloss>

I found myself one day all alone
<margin>2</margin>In a beautiful meadow to take delight.
I do not believe there is a meadow in the world
Where the herbs have such lovely scents.
But when I had entered a way into the green,
I found myself among a thousand lovely flowers
White and crimson and of a thousand colors;
<margin>8</margin>Among which I heard a little bird singing.
->I found myself one day. . .<-
Its song was so sweet and beautiful,
That it made the whole world fall in love.
I drew near very softly to see it:
I saw that its head and wings were of gold:
Every other feather seemed like ruby;
<margin>14</margin>But its beak was of crystal, and its neck and breast.
->I found myself one day. . .<-
I wanted to catch it, it pleased me so much:
But soon it rose into the air in flight,
And returned to the nest where it was born:
I have set myself to follow it all alone.

| ...quickly the maiden grows old; and "The roses came at last. Oh, the spirit of lovely spring! They perish today, unless they are gathered in the morning." <note>original Latin: "cito virgo senescit... Pereunt hodie, nisi mane leguntur." These lines are from a poem traditionally attributed to Ausonius or Virgil, emphasizing the brevity of beauty.</note> <br><br> <gloss>1</gloss> **This was published for the first time** by Poggiali in the cited *Ecclesiastical Series*, I. 268, from the Riccardian manuscript 2723, collated with the Chigiano manuscript where it is said to be "composed at Prato;" <note>Prato is a city in Tuscany where Poliziano spent time.</note> it was then reprinted in the Florentine edition of 14. ### V.<gloss>1</gloss>

Now take this! Love has really played a trick on me, <note>The phrase "accoccare" refers to fixing an arrow to a bow-string, but idiomatically means to strike someone or play a trick.</note>
That I have been led to fall in love in Prato! <margin>2</margin>
I am in love with a young girl
Who is seen sometimes at the jubilees; <note>Religious festivals or years of remission from sins.</note>
So that neither art nor prayers are worth anything with her.

---

V. 19. **crederrei ... ad un**, Riccardiano and Strozzi manuscripts. — v. 20. **se lo potessi**, printed editions. — v. 22. **Ma da po' che cantar**, Poggiali. — v. 23. **WEB (RAGNA)**. "There are other nets called *ragne* (spider-webs), very thin so that they are barely seen in the air, with which many birds are caught; they are stretched upright in the air, tied to two poles in places where birds are accustomed to pass." (Crescenzi X, 19). — **WALL-NET (PARETE)**. A net that is spread over a clearing of the bird-trapping site, with which bird-catchers catch birds by covering them (Florentine Editions, 1814). — v. 25. **per che pur**, Poggiali. — v. 26. **E questo**, Magliabechiano manuscript and printed editions.

<gloss>1</gloss> This was first published by Poggiali in the cited series, page 267, from the Riccardiano manuscript 2723: Poggiali himself affirms that it is also in the Chigiano manuscript, where it is stated that this ballad was composed in Prato. It is also in the Magliabechiano 103 4 [class VII] and in the manuscript belonging to Mr. Vanzolini, where it has this title: **Song by Angelo Poliziano against love.**

V. 1. **Toi**, take: used as an interjection, like saying: Now see, Look at that, Listen, etc. **Lasca, Jealousy III, 11** "Take: he even blusters." **To "accoccare" it to someone** means to do them harm or play a trick: there is a proverb that says "One laughs in your face who strikes you from behind." <note>original: "Tal ti ride in bocca Che dietro te l' accocca."</note> — v. 2. **Ch' io sia condotto a innamorarmi**, the printed editions. — v. 4. The Florentine editions of [18]14 followed by all later editions printed **Who is seen to rejoice** [giubbilar], and noted "Some manuscripts read **Who is seen sometimes at the jubilee** [giubbileo]." We, instead of that nonsensical **to rejoice**, accepted the reading of the Magliabechiano and Vanzolini manuscripts: **at the jubilees** [giubilei]. The Riccardiano manuscript reads **at the jubilee**.

# BALLADS.

Lady, may it ever please you:
<margin>25</margin> Thus one freezes and burns at all hours.
But, if at times you showed some pity
In your eyes, oh divine star,
You would make even stones burn with love:
Pity makes a lady beautiful,
Pity is that from which love is born and dies.

---

*Verse 12. May it ever, lady, vanz.: ever that, Lucca manuscript. — v. 13. freezes, vanz.: and burns, Lucca manuscript and the printed editions, except the Florentine editions of 14. — v. 14. pity, Magliabechiano manuscript. — v. 15. oh living star, copy by Salvini and printed editions. — v. 16. you would make, Magliabechiano: the stones, Laurentian manuscript: the stones, vanz.: you would make love go, Florentine editions of 14, certainly due to a typographical error; for all the manuscripts have "burn," including the Trivulziani ones cited by the author of the Appendix to the "Proposta," where the correction was first put forward. — v. 17. Pity, vanz. — v. 18. Pity, vanz.: Pity, the printed editions, except Poggiali.*

In the cited Moukian manuscript <note>original: "cod. moukiano"; a specific manuscript collection held in Lucca.</note> of the Lucchese library there are some dance songs, which take up the rhymes of others by Poliziano and contrast them in their concepts. Among these is the following, which is like a <term>palinodia</term> <note>A "palinodia" or palinode is a poem in which the poet retracts a view or sentiment expressed in a former poem.</note> of the one printed in the text and which, in the judgment of Mr. Bongi, “could very well be by Poliziano himself:” although from the greater number of stanzas of which the recantation is composed, we would not wish to conclude with Mr. Bongi that the one already printed, to which the unpublished one responds, is “incomplete and maimed.” Nothing is missing in its concept or its flow: and the sententious emphasis of the last two verses shows the conclusion. And, what matters more, the manuscripts agree in giving it to us as we ourselves have recently printed it. Here, meanwhile, is the recantation from the Lucca manuscript:

->This appearing happy at all hours<-
I do not know if it quite pleases me,
Because I find no peace
In those glances and in what appears on the outside.

But, if you care for me, as you show,
Give me a true sign of it.
What is the value to me of seeing you without anything else?
I do not usually harbor disdain,
But this alone is not enough for one who burns and dies.

I thus burn and die, everyone sees it;
So great is my fire;
Though my pure faith is greater,
Which has no place in this,
Because it does not reign where the heart does not burn.

Unite the heart with your tongue;
Because it is a great defect
To carry written on your brow
That which is not then in the breast,
And to keep a man between hope and fear.

Eyes, face, sighs, and words
Give you witness enough
Of my heart, where I burn, where it pains me
And will always pain me,
Until you change or I find another love.

Little song of love, do not depart,
For you would not be accepted
By my lady where my life dwells:
Elsewhere you might go;
But I seek and crave no other lord.

---

## VII.¹

I thank you, Love,
For every pain and torment,
And I am content now with every sorrow.
I am content with all I have ever suffered,
<margin>5</margin>Lord, in your fair kingdom;
Since by your grace, without my merit,
You have given me such a great pledge,
Since you have made me worthy
Of such a blessed smile,
<margin>10</margin>That has carried my heart into paradise.
->I thank you, Love.<-
Into paradise they have carried my heart,
Those beautiful laughing eyes,
Where I saw you, Love, staying hidden
With your burning flames.
Oh lovely, shining eyes
That have stolen my heart from me,
<margin>17</margin>From whence do you draw such sweet power? <note>original: "valore"; in this context, it refers to the efficacy or divine power inherent in the lady's gaze.</note>
->I thank you, Love.<-
I was already in doubt of my life: <note>The phrase "in forse" suggests the poet was at a point of existential crisis or near death from despair before being "saved" by the lady's appearance.</note>
My Lady in a white dress
With a loving smile came to my aid,
Joyful, beautiful, and noble: <note>original: "onesta"; in Renaissance poetry, this signifies a blend of outward beauty and inward virtue or modesty.</note>
Her head was adorned <note>literally: "painted" (dipinta), meaning crowned or decorated.</note>
With roses and violets,
<margin>24</margin>Eyes that surpass the sun in splendor.
->I thank you, Love.<-

---

First published by Sergio di Chigi in the Comino edition of 1765, as a set song <term>canzonetta intonata</term> <note>A "canzonetta intonata" refers to a poem specifically composed to be set to a particular melody or performed with music.</note>; then in the Florentine edition of 1814 from manuscript 23. It is also in the manuscript of Mr. Li without any heading. — v. 6. *your grace* [tuo' merzè], Vanzetti: *your gra-* [tua mer-]. — v. 7. *You have giv-* [M' ha' da-]. — v. 17. *such sweet splendor*, Vanzetti. — v. 19. *But woman* [Ma donna], Vanzetti. — v. 21. *and noble* [ed onesta], recent editions. — v. 24. *The eyes that*. This is the direct object governed by the verb *had* [avea] in verse 22 <note>Meaning the Lady "had her head adorned... and [had] eyes that surpass the sun."</note>. Giuseppe Maggi, in the cited Appendix, emended this, citing the authority of the <term>Trivulziani</term> manuscripts <note>A famous collection of manuscripts originally belonging to the Trivulzio family of Milan.</note>, to *The eyes the sun surpassed* [Gli occhi il sole avanzan]: and the emendation was adopted in the Silvestri edition. — *surpass* [avanzon], Riccardian manuscript.

# BALLADS.

## VIII.¹

He who knows not what paradise is like,
Let him gaze fixedly into my Ippolita's eyes.
From Ippolita's eyes descends
Girt in flames a little angel of love,
Who ignites cold breasts like tinder
And with such sweetness melts the heart
That he keeps saying even as he dies,
<margin>8</margin> — Happy am I, for I am in paradise. —
He who knows not...
From Ippolita's eyes moves
A power <term>virtù</term> <note>In this context, "virtù" refers to a miraculous or celestial power emanating from the beloved's eyes, a common theme in Renaissance love poetry.</note> that flows with such fierceness
<margin>12</margin> That I liken it to Jove’s lightning bolt,
And it breaks iron and shatters diamond:
But the wound has in itself such sweetness
That he who feels it is truly in paradise.
He who knows not...
From the eyes of the beautiful Leoncina <note>A play on her surname, Leoncini; "Leoncina" means "Little Lioness."</note>

---

<note>¹ This is cited by Poggiali in the *Ecclesiastical Series*, I, 270, as existing under the name of N. A. in the Chigian codex; and it was published by Rigoli from a modern copy in the *Essay of Rhymes etc.*, with this title: *Ballad made for Ippolita Leoncina, by Angelo Poliziano*. It is found in the Riccardian codex 2723 among the ballads of N. A., but attributed without any reason to Lorenzo de' Medici with a note [L. M.] in a hand that seems later than the time of the manuscript: and it is found, with the heading *Song by Ang. Poliziano*, in Mr. Vanzolini's codex. —
Line 4. ANGIOLEL: here (and again in XIII, line 36) this is the same as *Angioletto* <note>Little Angel</note>. It is not used as much as its feminine form, *Angiolella*, by the ancient Tuscan writers. To Master Angelo [Poliziano], born in Montepulciano, this word must have sounded in his ears from the dialect of Umbria where it is still alive today. It is also alive in the folk songs of the Marche region: and two men from Pesaro gave it literary life in our days, Perticari and Mamiani. In the sixteenth century, it was not disliked by Varchi: *Rhymes*, 261. — line 5. *That the* <note>original: "Che i"</note>, Rigoli. — line 7. *saying while* <note>original: "dicendo mentre"</note>, Rigoli. But *in mentre* [meanwhile/while] is frequent in Tuscan usage: and it pleased Boccaccio: "while he saw him" <note>original: "in mentre che 'l vedeo"</note> in *Nymph of Fiesole*; and the most refined Firenzuola: "While I was thus waiting in suspense" <note>original: "In mentre che io così sospeso aspettava"</note> in *The Golden Ass*. — lines 15-16. More sensually, Tasso wrote: "And a happy ray seems / To burn in your beautiful eyes, / From whence peace and sweetness and joy flake down." <note>original: "E pare un lieto raggio Arder ne' bei vostr' occhi, Onde pace e dolcezza e gioia fiocchi."</note> But the mystic lover of Beatrice [Dante] wrote: "And from her rays so much fear rains down upon my heart that it makes me tremble." <note>original: "E da' suoi raggi sopra 'l mio cor piove Tanta paura che mi fa tremare."</note> Montemagno wrote: "A rain of roses from the beautiful face..." <note>original: "Pioggia di rose dal bel viso"</note></note>

*showers [piove]*—From this... And note the verb *to rain* or *to shower* which was very pleasing as a metaphor to the ancient poets, especially to Cavalcanti <note>Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255–1300) was a major Florentine poet and friend of Dante; he frequently used meteorological metaphors for the effects of love.</note>: "It seems that into my heart showers / A sweet love; ..." <note>
Line 11. *kills me [m' ancide]*, Florentine editions of 1494. — line 12. In the Riccardiano manuscript, above the word *pure* [only/yet] is written in another hand *pains [pene]*. — line 13. *than a sun [ch' un sole]*, the printed editions. <term>Petrarch</term> <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the influential Italian poet and scholar.</note> "A woman much more beautiful than the sun" (Florentine editions of 1494). — line 16. *They fill me with pleasure [Di piacer m' empion]*, 15th-century Ballads and *Canzone a ballo* of 1562 and 1568, Molinari and Silvestri: *the mind [le mente]*, Magliabechiano manuscript. — line 17. *immediately [immantanente]*, 15th-century Ballads and Molinari: *immediately [immantinente]*, 1494 Florentine editions and Silvestri. — line 18. *sky clears [cielo si serena]*, 15th-century Ballads: *sky becomes clear [cielo s' asserena]*, 1494 Florentine editions. — line 19. *This my beautiful [Questa mia bella]*, Molinari and Silvestri: *siren [serena]*, 15th-century Ballads, *Canzone a ballo* of 1562 and 1568. — line 20. *with her [con suo']*, 15th-century Ballads and *Canzone a ballo* of 1562 and 1568: *with her [con suoi]*, Molinari. — line 21. *the flesh [le carne]*. 15th-century Ballads. — line 25. *Why renew [Perchè rinnuo]*, 15th-century Ballads and *Canzone a ballo* of 1562 and 1568, to the detriment of the meter. lines 27-28. The ancients believed that the asp would burst by means of incantations <term>Virgil</term>, *Eclogues* VIII. <note>original: "Frigidus in pr. cantando rumpitur anguis"</note> "In the meadows, the cold snake is burst apart by singing;" and <term>Ovid</term> in the *Metamorphoses* book VII: <note>original: "Vipera rumpo et verbis et carmine fauce"</note> "I burst the viper's throat both by words and by song." Concerning this belief of the ancients, <term>Pliny</term>, *Natural History* XXVIII, 2: <note>original: "Non pauci et serpentes ipsos recantari credunt: hunc unum esse illis intellectum contrahique Marsorum cantu et in nocturna quiete."</note> "Not a few believe that even serpents themselves are charmed back; that this is their only sense, and that they are drawn together by the singing of the Marsi <note>The Marsi were an ancient Italic people renowned for their supposed magical powers over snakes.</note> and in the quiet of night." (Florentine editions). Regarding the deafness attributed to asps, see *Rispetti spicciati* V, line 4.
</note>

**line 24.** *With his own*, **15th-century Ballads** and **Dance Songs 1562 and 68, Mol. and Silv.** — **line 25.** *there concealed*, **Florentine editions of 1494.** — **lines 25-28. Lure** <term>zimbello: a decoy bird</term> is called "that bird which is tied by one foot to the side of a grove of nets or other places where one stretches to catch birds, which, by pulling that small cord tied to its foot, is made to flutter to incite other birds to swoop down" (**Minelli**, annotations to *Malmantile*, stanza 76, canto VII.) Here then it must mean roughly: Continue to signal and call out, for the moment of being heard will surely come at last. — **lines 30-31.** This is said with allusion to the account in Genesis, that the raven sent by Noah out of the ark to take a sign of how the weather was turning never returned. The figurative phrase "Waiting for the raven" is frequent among Tuscan writers, especially the ancient ones, said of one who waits in vain. "They were waiting for the raven; for, the more they waited for their friend, the further he distanced himself" **Sacchetti**, novella 154. — **line 31.** *When I have*, **15th-century Ballads**, **Dance Songs 1562 and 68, Mol.** — **line 32.** ***am an ant***, **Magliabechiano MS, Florentine editions of 1494, Mol. and Silv.** — **Rowan-tree ant.** The ants that stay in the trunks and stumps of old trees, and, when struck, come out; except, however, those that live in rowan trees. From this arose the proverb *to act like the ant or the great ant of the rowan tree*, which is equivalent to *playing deaf*. "Those who stand firm in the thicket are called rowan-tree ants." **Varchi, Ercolano** (**Florentine Editions 1814**). **Lasca, Sonnets**: "Simon, you are a rowan-tree ant who never crawls out in such a hurry." **Sacrif., Commentary** of the **Intronati**: "You are rowan-tree ants, who do not come out for any knocking." — **line 33.** *be blind*, **Magliabechiano MS and 15th-century Ballads.** — **lines 35-36. Shade** <term>bacìo: a shady site</term>. Name of a site or slope facing north or sheltered from the sun: the opposite of *solatio* (sunny). **Dictionary of the Crusca.** These two verses allegorically come to signify: He will not want the affection you bear me to remain without its consequences; this flower of love will finally produce its fruit.
