## XIII.<gloss>1</gloss>

->Welcome, May<-
->And the wild banner:<-

---

14. *O that I might die here*, Songbooks a, b, and 68, Molini and Silvestri editions. — v. 15. *Before*, Magliabechiano manuscript and Florentine editions of 1514 and 1522. — *I consume myself*, Songbooks a and b of 1562 and Molini and Silvestri editions. — v. 17. **Spirit.** It is difficult to define these "spirits" which have various movements and functions in the psychology of our ancestors, such as at the end of the 13th century, and in the works of Dante and Cavalcanti. <note>In medieval physiology, "spirits" (spiritelli) were thought to be subtle vapors that carried sensory information and emotions through the body.</note> The latter, due to the distance of his beloved, also said:

> "Full of every anguish in a place of fear / The spirit of the sorrowful heart lies." <note>original: "Pien d' ogni angoscia in loco di paura / Lo spirto del cor dolente giace." Guido Cavalcanti was a close friend of Dante and a leading poet of the "Sweet New Style."</note>

Perhaps these **spirits** and **little spirits** are nothing other than personifications of the immaterial part of sensation and emotion. — v. 19. *O my heart*, 15th-century manuscript: *O me heart*, Songbooks of 1562 and 1568 and Molini: *sad and sorrowful* standard. — v. 20. *Shall we see her again? how* standard, etc., except for the Florentine editions of 1514 and 1522. It is found in the Vanzoliniano manuscript with this heading: *Song by Angelo Poliziano for May:* which was meant to be sung by women upon the entry of the jousters into the field, who, as the women crowned them, jousted for their love. It is also found in the *Little Ballads* etc. of the 15th century under the name of *Master Angelo Poliziano*; as well as among other anonymous works in the *Songs for Dancing* of 1562 and 1568. Indeed, the Florentine editors of 1814 note that in a copy of the 1568 edition used by the Crusca Academy, *this ballad is attributed to the Anonymous Author, and before it one finds written in an ancient hand,* **Angelo Poliziano.** <note>The Accademia della Crusca is the premier institution for the study of the Italian language.</note> Despite this, in some modern printings, it is attributed to Lorenzo de' Medici.

V. 2. **Wild banner.** It is the *maio* (*maggio* or "May" in our days), that is, that branch of laurel or another plant which in certain parts of Tuscany is still attached on the first day of May before the doors or windows of girls by young lovers.

My heart was once so gentle,
That at a mere signal it used to fly back;
Because I fed it with a desire for love:
But a lady lured it away with her singing;
<margin>5</margin>Yet afterwards she went on tormenting it so,

This heart of mine took the highest delight
In always being among you, graceful ladies:
However, young maidens, I am suspicious of you,
Though I have no doubt regarding your mothers;
But you are accustomed to being thieves of hearts,
From as much as I have heard of it, my girls.
<margin>14</margin>->Ladies, once again...<-

<margin>Line 17. *non posso*, Florentine editions of 1494. —</margin> **AVALE.** An adverb of time signifying *now*, *at present*. Lorenzo de' Medici, *Nencia*, XIV: "I have brought you a bunch of spurge-laurel / With berries that I gathered just now, just now <note>original: "avale avale"</note>." — **Line 18. *And I too*, received text.**

Lorenzo de' Medici, *Carnival Song*: "The envious and the gossips / Hold the good of others in contempt: / Then they vent themselves by speaking ill, / These gossips that you see." — **Line 9. *they dress it up*, *Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68* and the received text. — **DRESS IT UP WITHOUT SALT,** they pull it down <note>disparage it</note> without any regard or consideration, and, perhaps, even without foundation. — **Line 10. KEEP YOU... IN THE PORCH.** *To keep in the porch* <note>original: "tenere a loggia"</note> means properly to keep someone waiting or in a state of discomfort, as in that passage by Berni (*Orlando Innamorato*, XIX): "This man has kept me in the porch for three days, / And he is but one man and not even a giant." But according to Varchi (*Ercolano* 54) it also means to deceive someone; that is, to mock them; as is clearly understood in this verse by Poliziano and in that of Cecchi (*The Dowry*, I, 1): ".... Certain loiterers who sneer in your face / And then keep you in the porch <note>mock you behind your back</note>."

-> BALLADS. <-

> They are all melons of Chioggia,
> Of one skin and one flavor.
> It is true . .
> These are certain fine candles
> Who have more wind than a ball:
> Full of bows and signs <note>original: "segeri" — a disputed term likely referring to grand gestures or festive signs.</note>
> They stay in caterpillar and in butterfly,
> With the shoulder-band <note>original: "benduccio"</note> upon the shoulder,
> Always with hair-tuft and puffed chest,
> Always with arms [crossed] and facing each other,

**12. Like the melons of Chioggia / of one skin and of one [flavor]** is a proverbial saying used to describe a similarity and conformity of habits (Florentine Editions of 1494). Other pleasant variations: "The cicada and I are just alike, / Like the melons from Chioggia, / Of one skin and one leaf." **Line 13. Fine candles.** <note>original: "Be' ceri"</note> "A fine candle... such a clumsy puppet, the vainglory of an affected person. This saying comes from the custom of offering candles to be carried in churches or sanctuaries with beautiful paintings and gold, and with ribbons, flowers, and similar things; which are carried upright and with every care so that they are well observed and not ruined." Biscioni, on *Malmantile*, canto I, stanza 81. — Ariosto, *The Casket* <note>original: "Cassaria"</note> I, 5: "...more wind than a ball." — Maggi, in the cited Appendix, proposed in a long discourse the reading of this verse as **and of bows of Sir Geri** <note>original: "e d' inchini de ser Geri"</note>; this correction passed into the Silvestri edition so modified that it read **segeri**. We have kept what the manuscripts and editions carry (except those of the *Songs for Dancing* etc.) and whether it <unclear>came</unclear> by typographic error to <unclear>be read as</unclear> *i segeri*; understanding **segeri** as festive signs or, as one would <unclear>properly</unclear> say today, **slovenly** <note>original: "sciamannati"</note>. We do not enter into the etymology of <unclear>this name</unclear>, content to <unclear>bring forward</unclear> a passage from Machiavelli (*Mandragola*, prologue) which suffices to interpret Poliziano's verse: "He values no person, even though they make signs <note>original: "segeri"</note> and greetings that could carry a better cloak than his." Because in this passage of Machiavelli, one must clearly read **to the signs** <note>original: "a' segeri"</note> with the old editions and not **to the signs** <note>original: "a' segieri"</note> with the more recent ones. After *segeri*, the Mulini, Silvestri, and 1834 Florentine editions place a colon. — **Line 16. Caterpillar** <note>original: "Bruco"</note> was said of a man who is in poor condition or badly dressed; and **Butterfly** <note>original: "Farfalla"</note>, of a man of little brain, fickle, and light. But this form **to stay in caterpillar and in butterfly** is somewhat new and obscure: unless it means that they are miserable and at the same time vain; or rather, that they have their thoughts here and there, the metaphor being drawn from the various stages of development of certain insects. — **Line 17. Shoulder-band.** <note>original: "Benduccio"</note> Properly a small strip of linen cloth that is kept attached to the shoulder or belt of children (Florentine Editions of 1494).

And it is printed in the *Small Ballads of the 15th Century* under the heading of **POLIZIANO. M. A. Poliziano and in the Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68.**

**Line 1. we are <note>original: "siam"</note>, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68 and later standard editions: because to you, Vanzolini manuscript: because you, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68 and Florentine editions 14. — BECAUSE.** Although (Florentine editions 14). — **"Siàn" for "siamo" (we are); and further down "Conosciàn" for "conosciamo" (we know): see the note to Ballad III, line 26.** — **line 2. lady, Riccardiano manuscript. — SIMPLETONS <note>original: "balocchi"</note>. Dullards, who let themselves be trifled with, or kept at bay with empty words.** — **line 3. we know, standard editions. — YOU HOODWINK US <note>original: "c'infinocchi"</note>.** <note>The term "infinocchiare" (to fennel someone) comes from the old practice of using fennel to mask the taste of poor-quality wine. In this context, it means to deceive or trick.</note> "When someone wants to show another that they recognize the things they are being made to believe are lies and trifles, they say: You are hoodwinking me, or Don't think you can hoodwink me." Varchi, *Ercolano*. — **line 4. And of all, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68, Molinari, Florentine editions 22, Silvestri. — YOU WANT THE MOCKERY <note>original: "vuoi la baia"</note>.**

* When someone tries to persuade us of what we do not want to believe, to get them away and remove that annoyance from our ears, we tend to say: "You want the prank or the mockery" <note>original: "Tu vuoi la baia o la berta"</note> etc. — Varchi, *Ercolano*. — line 5. *that I was the* <note>original: "essere io il"</note>, Vanzolini edition. — <term>Cucco</term>. A childish word (like "mama’s boy," Latin *matris deliciæ* <note>original Latin: "mother's delights"</note>). <gloss>To be the "cucco" means to be the favorite</gloss> (Florentine Editions 14).
* "Esdram pretended that this was his favorite." <note>original: "cucco"</note> — *Ciriffo Calvaneo* III. 99. — line 6. *that in joy* <note>original: "che in gongon"</note>, 15th-century Ballads, *Songs for Dancing* 1562 and 68, Molinari: *I held you* <note>original: "io ti tenni"</note>, the standard editions. — <term>GONGOLO</term>. From *gongolare*, which is "to rejoice excessively, completely moved by internal joy: whence saying to one, as is customary, in some happiness: You 'gongoli' [rejoice], nothing more can be said." Thus an unpublished commentary on the *Pataffio* cited by Biscioni in the notes to *Malmantile*, VII, 100. According to the Deputies to the *Decameron*, annotation LXXXV, it is a word "that seems made from sound: and there are those who believe it is taken from a certain murmur, more than a voice, of hens: which would be according to the nature of such invented words from known and domestic things, from which the language has also derived *schiamazzare* [to squawk] and *galloria* [exultation]." In the ancient texts of the *Decameron* it is written *gogolare*. — line 7. <term>RISTUCCO</term> [Nauseated]. *Stuccare* and *Ristuccare*; to nauseate, or to sate to the point of nausea (Florentine Editions 14): just as too-fatty foods and prolix speeches with little or no conclusion do. Minucci, Notes to *Malmantile*, VII, 45. — line 8. <term>ATTUCCI</term> [Little acts]. Diminutive of *atti* [acts], in the sense of *lezii* [affectations] (Florentine Editions 14). — line 9. *recovered* <note>original: "rinvienni"</note>, Riccardiano codex: *soon I returned* <note>original: "presto rivenni"</note>, *Songs* 1562 and 68, Florentine editions 14 and 22; *soon I recovered* <note>original: "presto rinvienni"</note>, Molinari and Silvestri. — line 10. <term>HEALTHY AS A ROACH</term> <note>original: "SAN COM' UNA LASCA"</note>. Of entire and perfect health. Juvenal: "more healthy than a fish" <note>original Latin: "pisce sanior"</note> (Florentine Editions 14). — line 11. Taken from bird-hunting with birdlime. And it seems to mean: <gloss>I too know how to mock those who think they are mocking me.</gloss> — lines 13-15. Taken from hunting with a <term>paretaio</term> <note>An enclosure or net system used by bird-catchers.</note>. See Ballad X, lines 26-28. — line 15. *at a finch* <note>original: "a un firinguello"</note>, Vanzolini: *at a* <note>original: "ad un"</note>, Florentine editions 14 and 22, Silvestri. — line 16. *now* <note>original: "ormai"</note>, *Songs for Dancing* 1562 and 68 and later editions — line 17. *other coquettes* <note>original: "altri civetti"</note>, *Songs for Dancing* 1562 and 68 and editions.

Even more than anyone, you are an **owl**. <note>In this context, the owl represents someone who is the butt of a joke or a figure of ridicule because of their clumsy movements.</note>
Go on, go shove yourself into a **tuff**. <note>A type of volcanic rock or soil where owls were known to nest.</note>
Be quiet; and see that it does not show.
->We are not yet. . .<-
All these new **fish**
Have a bit of the **little mocker**; <note>A "dileggino" is someone who playfully flirts or mocks without being sincere in their affection.</note>
And yet they pray that I overturn
The **corner-ear** of the little bag: <note>Refers to the "pellicini"—the protruding corners of a sack. To "overturn the pellicino" means to spill everything one knows or to speak without restraint.</note>
But, if I shake it just a little,
So much stuff would come out of it,
That everyone would then notice it;
And it is better that it does not show.
->We are not yet. . .<-
It is this way, lady, to speak clearly:
You gaze longingly at everyone,
Without making any **distinction**
Whether he is white or green or brown:
You would do better to take just one

later editions. — **COQUETTE** <note>original: "CIVETTI"</note>. *To coquette*; to perform acts of vanity and levity, imitating the movements that an owl makes with its head to allure other birds (Florentine Editions 14). — **line 18. YOU ARE AN OWL**. You are the scorn, the joke (Florentine Editions 14); just as the owl, due to its clumsy movements, is the object of scorn for other birds.— **line 19. TUFF**. A type of arid and solid ground (Florentine Editions 14), chosen by owls for nesting and living.— **line 22. LITTLE MOCKER** <note>original: "DILEGGINO"</note>. One who mocks; who takes pleasure in acting like a lover but is not one (Florentine Editions 14). *Tancia*, III, 2: "But since when have you loved her? You were already considered a little mocker." — **line 23**. *they pray that I overturn, Vanzolini edition.* — **lines 23-24**. *To overturn or empty the corner-ear of the bag* and similar phrases, means to say everything one knows to others without respect or restraint (Florentine Editions 14.) <margin>*</margin> **Corner-ears** <note>original: "Pellicini"</note> are those four things, almost like donkey ears, that are sewn onto the top of bales, two on each side, so that they can be better gripped and more easily handled: this is also often done at the bottom of sacks. And therefore one says not only *to empty and shake the sack*, but also *the corner-ears of the sack*, into which grains of wheat or other things the sack is full of often enter and become trapped. » Varchi; *Ercolano*. *Matteo Franco*, sonnet: "I will take the sack by the corner-ears and shake the seams and the bottom so much, that I know a world of dust will come out of it." — **line 28**. *it is better*, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 68 and posthumous editions. — **line 29**. *woman, Riccardiana manuscript.* — **line 31. DISTINCTION** <note>original: "DIVARO"</note> for difference <note>original: "divario"</note>. The ancients used to remove the *i* from certain words: thus *varo* for *vario* [various/different] used by Dante (Florentine Editions 14), — **line 32**. *white, green, Vanzolini edition.*

# XX.¹

->Let everyone sing, for I shall sing,<-
->Dondol dondol dondolò.<- <margin>2</margin> <note>A rhythmic, nonsensical refrain typical of Renaissance dance songs, similar to "tra-la-la."</note>
->I am already fed up with promises,<-
->Make it so that the barrel is finally tapped.<- <note>A metaphor for moving from talk to action or reaching a conclusion.</note>
->You keep me amused with distractions<-
->With hands full of crickets.<- <note>In Italian lore, "having a head full of crickets" means being full of whims or empty fantasies. Having "hands full of crickets" implies holding nothing of substance.</note>

->This eel still slips away.<-

<margin>V. 34. *I am good, Florentine editions.* — v. 35. *to say, Riccardian manuscript.*</margin>
¹ This is cited by Poggiali in his *Series, etc.*, as existing among others by the "Anonymous Author" in the Chigi codex; it is also in Mr. Vanzolini's codex with this heading: *Song by Angelo* **Poliziano** *to the lady, that she should perform deeds and not demonstrations*. It is also in print in the *Ballatette* of the 15th century under the heading of *Master Angelo Poliziano*, and in the *Dance Songs* of 1562 and 1568.

Line 2. *Dondolo, dondolo, dondolò*; the printed editions use this with an insult to the meter of the verse. — line 4. **Tapped**. *To tap* <note>original: "Spillare"</note> is to draw wine from the barrel through the tap: here it is a metaphor, but without the obscene double meaning that the Florentine editors and the compilers of the Tramater Dictionary would suggest: it means, "Make it so that we come to some conclusion." — line 5. *at the amusement, Vanzolini manuscript.* — **Amusement** <note>original: "Badalucco"</note>. *A pastime, pleasant entertainment, or hobby.* (Florentine Editions 14.) Here *to keep at amusement* is the same as *to keep at bay* or to stall someone. — line 6. *With the hands full of, Dance Songs* 1562 and 68: *With the hands full of*, Florentine editions 14 and 22. — **Full of crickets**. That is, empty. "Crickets" <note>original: "grilli"</note> is a metaphorical term for fantasies and whims without consistency. — lines 7-8. **Billi Billi**. The *Crusca Dictionary*, which cites these two current lines under this entry (always attributing them to Lorenzo de' Medici and reading in the eighth line "yet **it slips** away," which is not in any text I have seen), explains **Billi Billi** as endearments, caresses, and the like. I, at least in this passage, by deduction from the context and from a passage in the *Morgante* [by Luigi Pulci], XXII, 101 ["Astolfo replied: so many sweet nothings (billi billi), why don't you tell me that Gan has deceived her?"], would understand it as *chatter, idle talk, or speeches without effect*. Line 8 means: one never comes to the point: the conclusion escapes, just as an eel slips out of the hands of one who tries to hold it. — lines 9-10. **Firefly, Firefly** <note>original: "Lucciola, Lucciola"</note> etc. These are the words of a...

->“Come to me,”—to what end for me?<-
->Still busy, still drilling<- <note>original: "buchero." A term for boring a small hole into a barrel to taste the wine.</note>
->To have a sample of the wine.<-
->When I am all thrilled with delight,<- <note>original: "solluchero." A rustic term meaning to be deeply moved or physically titillated by joy.</note>
->It is Saint Anthony of May.<- <note>An idiomatic expression likely referring to a festival or a specific time of year when expectations are frustrated or things are out of season.</note>
->You lead me through the village<-
->By the nose like a buffalo;<- <note>Equivalent to the English "leading by the nose," like an ox or buffalo being guided by a ring.</note>
->You lead me even with fife<-
->And drum: no more now, no.<-
->We have played peek-a-boo so much,<- <note>original: "cu cu."</note>
->That someone is already mocking us:<-
->And, if the game lasts longer,<-

---

...a children's ditty, when, on those beautiful June evenings when the air is all shimmering with those little creatures <note>fireflies</note>, they run about holding out hats and caps to catch them, and sing as an enticement: *Firefly, firefly, come to me; I will give you the King's bread,* etc. Look at how far kings and loaves of bread manage to tuck themselves! — **vv. 11-12.** Follows the metaphor of **v. 4.** — **Drilling.** <term>Buchero</term>: Understand this as the boring and tapping used to make the barrel flow. — **v. 13.** **I am thrilled with delight.** <term>Mi solluchero</term>: I am moved, I am softened: a word from the countryside (Florentine Editions 14). — **v. 15.** *through the village*, Dance Songs 1562 and 68. — **v. 16.** **By the**, Ballads of the 15th century: *By the [el]*, Dance Songs 1562 and 68: *by the [il]*, recent editions: *like a buffalo*, Vanzolini manuscript. These two verses mean: You lead me around and guide me with deceptions and promises to do what I would not want, and you make me a ridiculous spectacle to the people. Ambra, *The Basket* <note>original: "Cofaria"</note> IV, 15: "They have spun me around like a spinning wheel, and led me by the nose like a buffalo." — **v. 17-18.** **Fife** <note>original: "zuffolo"</note>, as with the word **buffalo** <note>original: "buffolo"</note> in the verse above, Dance Songs 1562 and 63, Florentine editions 14 and 22. And these place a semicolon at the end of the verse. — **You lead me.... with fife and drum.** Taken perhaps from the jugglers and others of that sort who lead strange beasts through fairs and markets, and to the sound of fife and drum make them dance and gather people to see them. — **v. 19.** *we have played peek-a-boo* <note>original: "abbiam fatto a cu cu"</note>, Dance Songs 1562 and 68 and recent editions. **We have played peek-a-boo.** Buonnarroti, *The Tancia* III, 11: "...Tanc. I'm staying: What are you looking at? Cecc. I’m looking to see if Preto is playing peek-a-boo nearby." Where Salvini notes: "That is, he is acting like the little owl, rising and lowering himself and opening his eyes wide; from the cry of the owl." And the Tramater dictionary explains this passage of Poliziano in this way. However, I would believe that it refers to a certain children's game, where one or some hide themselves, others go looking for them, and those hidden stick their heads out a little bit saying *cuckoo* and then immediately pull back, as if inciting and mocking the seekers at the same time. And such is *playing at cuckoo*; a term which is not imitative of the owl, as one reads in some Dictionaries, but of the cuckoo bird.

The translator argues that the phrase "cu cu" refers to a children's game of hide-and-seek rather than the movements of an owl.</summary>

<note><sup>1</sup> This is cited by Poggiali in the *Series*, etc., as existing under the name of N. ### XXI.<sup>1</sup>

->I am, lady, the little pig<-
->Who wags his tail constantly<-
->All day long and never knots it:<- <note>A metaphor for persistent but ultimately fruitless or incomplete effort.</note>
->But you shall be the little donkey.<-
->For the little donkey seems to know his tail<-
->Only when he no longer has it:<-
->If some fly then happens to bite him,<-
->He makes a great lament over it.<-
->This bird will fall into the trap.<- <note>original: "impanierà." Literally "to be caught in birdlime," a sticky substance used to trap birds.</note>

**V. 22. <term>CUCCUVEGGIA</term> : <term>Decoy-owl</term> [Civetta].** You will see what a fine little owl you will make! **<term>Civetta</term>** is also the name for "a type of game, where the person in the middle cannot be struck when they touch the ground with their hand; and so, now rising, now ducking, they strike now one, now the other [of the players], and these in turn strive with blows to knock the hat or cap off their head, which is the goal of the game." **Tramater Dictionary.** — **v. 23. <term>CAMPEGGIA</term>.** To be in agreement. It is also said of colors, when they are distributed in such a way that they stand out gracefully from one another. **(Florentine Editions 14.)**

**V. 1. <term>I am, lady</term> [son, donna], Riccardiano ms.** Just as the animal named by the poet, despite always wagging its tail, never succeeds in knotting it, so the poet, though working to achieve the aim of his intentions, does not succeed. — **v. 4. <term>the donkey</term> [l’asino], Riccardiano ms.** — **v. 6. <term>the donkey</term> [l’asin], Riccardiano and Laurentian mss... <term>when he does not</term> [quand’ e’ non], 15th-century Ballads.** — **v. 8. <term>then makes</term> [allor fa], Riccardiano ms.** With this comparison of the **<term>little donkey</term>**, which is certainly not gallant, it is meant to tell the lady that she will only recognize the value of her "good" [her lover] when she is deprived of it and can no longer have it. Thus in the ***Morgante*** [by Luigi Pulci] XXII, 118, Astolfo, reproaching Charlemagne for driving away Orlando and putting all his trust in the traitor Ganelon, says to him: "And you act, as the saying goes, like the little donkey, who always seems to know his tail only when he doesn't have it, and the flies are eating him." — **v. 9. <term>WILL FALL INTO THE TRAP</term> [IMPANIERÀ].** Intransitive. Meaning: This bird, which now mocks the decoy-owl, will nevertheless in the end fall into the lime-traps; he will remain caught in the birdlime.

**V. 11. THE FIG AT THE TOP.** The fig that is at the summit of the tree. — **v. 12.** *oncino* <note>hook</note>, in modern editions. — **v. 13.** *none scorgi* <note>do not perceive</note>, Laurentian manuscript and 15th-century *Ballatette*. — **v. 14.** *un mie' par* <note>a peer of mine</note>, Vanzolini manuscript; *par fra ciotoli* <note>a peer among pebbles</note>, Riccardiano manuscript; and after the word *fra* <note>among</note> is written in another hand, *di sopra, giù* <note>above, below</note>. — **v. 15.** *le mani* <note>the hands</note>, *Canzoni a ballo* of 1562 and 1568 and later editions. — **v. 16.** *caggi più ciambottoli* <note>fall more tumbles</note>, Florentine editions of 1514 and 1522. — **<term>CIMBOTTOLI</term>.** Falls: the blows one takes on the ground when falling. Varchi, in *L'Ercolano*: "falling, he makes a tumble, or rather a *cimbottolo*." — **v. 17.** *andiam là pe' viottoli* <note>let us go there through the paths</note>, read by Silvestri on the authority of the Bergamo edition edited by Serassi. — **LET US TAKE TO THE PATHS** <note>original: "Dianla pe' viottoli"</note> means, *let us set out through the paths, let us go through the paths*: and it is a figurative construction similar to *darla* or *darsela a gambe* <note>to take to one's legs/to bolt</note>. — **v. 18.** *di qualche dama* <note>of some lady</note>, *Canzoni a ballo* 1562 and 1568 and later editions. — **v. 19-20.** Metaphorically: There is another woman, and a beautiful one, who seeks to draw me to herself. — **v. 20.** *Ch' ancor ei* <note>Who also he</note>, Silvestri. — **v. 21.** The metaphor of the innkeeper continues. — **v. 21.** *i' non vo' bere* <note>I do not want to drink</note>, Laurentian and Riccardiano manuscripts. — **v. 22. <term>METADELLA</term>.** A measure which, when used for liquids, holds half of a jug: in Tuscany it is more commonly called a *mezzetta*. — **v. 23. <term>BIONDELLA</term>.** We read in a *Dictionary of Natural Sciences*, Florence, Batelli, 1832, vol. III, page 533: "**Biondella**. In Tuscany, this is the common name for the *gentiana centaurium* <note>Common Centaury</note> or *erytraea centaurium*; so called according to Dalechamps because it was used to make hair blonde <note>original: "biondi"</note>. Also indicated by this name are the *daphne gnidium* <note>flax-leaved daphne</note> and the *reseda luteola* <note>dyer's rocket</note>, which are capable of producing a yellow dye." Redi notes: "The lesser centaury..., because when cooked in lye it makes the hair blonde, we in Tuscany call *biondella*."

V. 25. *drento* <note>inside</note>, Riccardiano manuscript. — v. 28. **To make a little pot of little pots** <note>original: "Fare pentolinio de' pentolini"</note> is explained by the *Dictionary* as "To live meagerly, to fall into misery." In this passage by Poliziano and in the one from the *Carnival Songs* cited in the *Dictionary* — "But those [women] who waste [time], as many do, must later make little pots" — it seems it should be understood as: "They will have to repent," or "They will have to live lacking what they could have had." — v. 29. **OPEN MOUTHS.** Here used affectedly for "mouth." — v. 30. **TRICK.** <note>original: "CILECCA."</note> A mockery made to others by pretending to give them something and then not giving it. Regarding the proverb *to play the trick*, Varchi writes in *The Ercolano*: "When one shows a desire to give something to someone and perform some significant benefit for them, and then does not do it, one is said to have played the trick on them; which is also called a *natta* <note>a lump or trick</note>, and sometimes a *vescica* <note>bladder/trifle</note> or *giarda* <note>mockery</note>." (Florentine Editions, 14). — v. 31. **YOU OWL ME.** <note>original: "MI GUFI."</note> You mock me. To hunt like an owl: Plautus <note>a Roman comic playwright</note>: "To laugh with white teeth" <note>original Latin: "Albis dentibus irridere," meaning to mock openly</note>. — **FÁMI** for *mi fai* <note>you do/make to me</note>. Certain words, when they are not whole, as Bartoli observes, but truncated, lose the last vowel in the affix. Thus we have in Dante *levàmi*, *vedràmi*, which mean *mi levai* <note>I rose</note> etc.: in Passavanti *dati*, *hai*, for *ti dài* <note>you give yourself</note>, *l'hai* <note>you have it</note>: and in Boccaccio *vuotù*, *fàmi*, for *vuoi tu* <note>do you want</note>, *mi fai* <note>you make me</note>. **To make mouths** <note>original: "Far bocchi"</note>, to purse the lips toward someone as a sign of contempt, in the manner of a monkey (Florentine Editions, 14). — v. 32. **There is one [female]**, Laurentian manuscript: *there is one [male]*, Riccardiano manuscript. — **TO FEED BY BEAK** <note>original: "IMBECCARE"</note>, properly to put food into the beaks of birds that do not know how to peck for themselves (Florentine Editions, 14). — v. 34. **SUCKS THEIR FINGERS AFTERWARD.** This is the same as the more common *To lick one's fingers*; said of anything that is very pleasing, even metaphorically. — v. 36. **LIKE A LITTLE SPARROW.** In reference to amorous endearments. Plautus, *The Ass-Dealer*, III. 3: "Call me your little sparrow" <note>original Latin: "Dic me tuum passerculum"</note>. — v. 37. Here it means, it seems to you that you are fortunate and very content.

<note>Commentary at the bottom of the page in two columns.</note>

**V. 27. I shout at her**, Magliabechiano and 14th-century Ballads: **I call to her**, other versions: **go and lie down**, 14th-century Florentine editions. — **v. 29-30.** One says **"He holds his soul with his teeth"** of someone who is so worn out in flesh and strength that it seems the soul would exhale if he did not restrain it by clenching his teeth. But the old woman of the ballad cannot even do this, because she has not even one tooth to serve as *medicine*—that is, as a remedy against the exhaling of her soul. — **v. 30. has none**, Silvestri. — **v. 31. Shining ones.** Eyes: so called in slang (14th-century Florentine editions). — **v. 32.** What would be unpleasant and difficult to say clearly is hidden with a metaphor. Similarly, Ariosto in the prologue of *The Cassaria* says: "the eyes that turn their scarlet linings outward." — **v. 33. Divine virtue.** A pun: wine. — **v. 34. drips on her**, Silvestri. — **v. 36. Woodcock.** A well-known bird with a long beak and feathers similar to a partridge: also called a *beccaccia* (14th-century Florentine editions). **v. 40. a spiderweb**, Riccardiano manuscript, 14th-century Florentine editions, and Silvestri. — **v. 42. Belly.** <term>Peccia</term>: stomach or paunch (14th-century Florentine editions): "although (Minucci notes in the annotations to *Malmantile*, VI, 101), of the part from the stomach to the pubic bone, *peccia* seems closer to the stomach, and *pancia* closer to the pubic bone." — Those who have the stomach for it can see a similar example of this ballad in another commonly attributed to Lorenzo de' Medici, but which is by Bernardo Giambullari, beginning "This doting old woman," found in the collections of *Short Ballads and Songs for Dancing* we have often cited.

### XXIV.<note>This ballad is attributed to Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned scholar and poet in the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>

->I want to tell you indeed<-
->(Oh, listen, my ladies)<-
->Of certain great follies of yours:<-
->But let it be worth your pardon.<-
->If you were more discreet<-
->Regarding the matter of love,<-
->You would be much happier<-
->While still saving your honor.<-
->One should not keep a lover<-
->Forever in the pillory:<- <note><term>Pillory</term> (original: *gogna*): A wooden framework used for public punishment; here Poliziano uses it as a metaphor for the emotional torment or "shackles" a lady imposes on a suitor.</note>
->For the poor wretch at last must<-
->Reveal his pains.<-
->I want to tell you indeed. . .<- <note>Indicates the repetition of the opening refrain.</note>
->When he sees that you seal up<-
->Even your ears, he cries out loudly;<- <note><term>Seal up the ears</term> (original: *impeci gli orecchi*): To coat with pitch, an idiom for stubbornly refusing to listen or pretending to be deaf.</note>
->For one cannot hide chickpeas<- <note><term>Hide chickpeas</term> (original: *coprire e ceci*): A Tuscan idiom meaning one cannot hide the truth or keep a secret, just as a bag of chickpeas is lumpy and noisy.</note>

<note>The following is a philological commentary on the poem above, explaining the nuances of the Tuscan dialect and comparing various historical editions.</note>

I know how to cast one's eyes around with curiosity and vanity and with feminine allurements: in the same way that Luigi Pulci in the *Morgante*, XXIV, 41, used the phrase *to play the coquette* <note>original: <term>far la civetta</term>, literally "to act like the little owl," referring to the jerky, attractive head movements the bird makes</note>: "Did I not see you speak with Bianciardino / In the garden and here and there playing the coquette?" Both manners of speaking are very lively in Tuscan usage. — **v. 63. SHE STRIKES ME.** <note>original: <term>Mi saetta</term>, literally "she arrows me"</note> Nowadays one would say, with less efficacy and a bit of barbarism, *she hits me* or *she makes an impression on me*. — **v. 67.** *go, stay*, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 1568 and Molini edition. — **v. 69.** *fingers, eyelashes*, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 1568 and modern editions. — **v. 70. IN A FLIRTATIOUS WAY.** <note>original: <term>Alla smanziera</term></note> From *smanziere*, one eager to make love or a gallant <note>original: <term>drudo</term></note> (Florentine Editions 14). Modern printings have a comma or a semicolon at the end of this verse, and read together with the ancient ones *Make* <note>original: <term>Fare</term></note> at the beginning of the following verse, after which they place a full stop. — **v. 71. KIND FACE.** <note>original: <term>Buona cera</term></note> A good countenance. *Cera* for *face* <note>original: <term>volto</term></note> was used by the ancients even in high style, and it is very common in familiar Tuscan speech. — **v. 72. BET.** <note>original: <term>Posta</term></note> Occasion or opportunity: or better perhaps, the sum of money that players agree shall be at stake for each round in a game; used here metaphorically. And *to refuse* <note>original: <term>disdire</term></note> is to decline or say no, whatever certain of our linguistic masters might say. — **v. 76.** *Wherever* <note>original: <term>Dove</term></note>, Riccardian manuscript. — **v. 78. TO PLAY TRICKS.** <note>original: <term>Far natte</term></note> According to Varchi, in the *Ercolano*, it is the same as *playing a prank* <note>original: <term>far le cilecche</term></note>. *Natta* means a joke or a trick; metaphorically it refers to a type of tumor <note>original: a sebaceous cyst</note>, similar to how one uses the word *cyst* <note>original: <term>vescica</term>, literally "bladder" or "blister"</note> in the same sense of a "swelling" lie or deception. *Ciriffo Calvaneo* III, 79: "...let no one watch that he does not make a joke or a trick <note>original: <term>natta</term></note>." — **v. 80.** *Always have*, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 1568 and modern editions.

**V. 81. *know... message*, Laurentian manuscript.** — **v. 84: *flee either the dandies*, Laurentian manuscript.** — **v. 86. *with their*: the printed editions.** And this verse essentially means: Have nothing to do with them. — **v. 87. *there*, the printed editions.** — **v. 88. the manuscripts read *They have*:** we believed we should follow all the printed editions which read *They have of them* <note>original: <term>N' hanno</term></note>, meaning of the ladies, of beloveds. The Florentine editors of 1814 cite a verse by Berni in *Orlando Innamorato*: "Every Christian will have a hundred of them per shoelace." Baldovini in *Cecco*: "For you want four suitors for every pocket." — **v. 89. *The donkey of the*, Laurentian and Riccardian manuscripts.** To act like the potter's donkey (or donkey-like) is said of one who stops to chatter with anyone he finds; because the potter's donkey stops at every door. *Dictionary of the Crusca*. But here it is applied specifically to the dandies who set themselves to ogling and flirting with every woman: which is even clearer in this example from G. M. Cecchi's *The Page*: "...And this other one / Who isn't content with twenty women? / The potter’s donkey: although this / Is a vice of the nation." — **v. 93. *at a*, Florentine editions of 1814 and 1822 and Silvestri.** — **v. 95. *As I see*, the printed editions.** — **v. 96. MUSTY.** <note>original: <term>Muffaticci</term></note> Musty, metaphorically, of a bad disposition (Florentine editions of 1814). — **v. 97. *rogues*, Ballate of the 15th Century, Songs for Dancing 1562 and 1568, Molini. Neither *gnaffo* nor *ignaffo* are currently recorded in the Dictionaries: where however we have *gnaffa*: which according to Alberti means a rogue, according to Amati, one with a flattened nose; but for Cesari it means a prostitute: in which sense it is truly used also by Varchi in *The Mother-in-Law*, act 1, scene 4, line 2.** — **NUMBSKULLS: men of coarse and obtuse intellect, called so from the large head of this fish <note>original: <term>ghiozzi</term>, a type of goby fish</note> (Florentine editions of 1814).**

<margin>Between line 116 and 117: » and « "The mind will be fit to be captured then, when it is most joyful, just as a crop will flourish in rich soil; while hearts rejoice and are not constrained by shame, they lie open: then Venus enters with her smooth art." <note>original Latin: "Mens erit apta capi tunc quum lætissima rerum Ut seges in pingui luxuriabit humo; Pectora dum gaudent nec sunt adstricta pudore, Ipsa patent: blanda tum subit arte Venus." # BALLADS.

->If you should say—"There are so many<-
->That I do not know what to do,"—<-
->I could teach you:<-
->But I do not wish to say it.<- <margin>10</margin>
->When there are so many suitors<-
<note>original: <term>manzieri</term>, an archaic term for lovers or seekers of "manze" (sweethearts).</note>
->Who walk upright and with puffed-out chests,<-
<note>original: <term>in persona vanno e in petto</term>, an idiom meaning to walk with a proud, upright, or boastful posture.</note>
->Who today are not where they were yesterday—<-

---

**v. 7.** *you said*, Florentine editions of 1814. Regarding this verse, **Maggi** in the cited *Appendix* observes: "All the verses must be octosyllables <note>A verse line of eight syllables, common in Italian poetry</note>; but in octosyllabic verses the accent must fall on the third syllable: therefore: **Se diceste, e’ sono tanti.**" And this correction was passed into the Silvestri edition. But the truth is that in the sung poetry of the ancients, as in the folk poetry of all times, there is great liberty in the arrangement of accents, which are determined more by the inflection of the voice in song than by a fixed rule of prosody. While reading, make a brief pause on the third syllable, *di*, and glide lightly over the fifth, *si-e’*; and you will feel the full harmony of the octosyllable. — **v. 10.** *But I do not wish to however*, Maggi and Silvestri, here and at **v. 18.** But even here there was no need for repairs; consider that the ancients were not accustomed to eliding monosyllables, and if one pauses on the third syllable, *no ’l*, gliding very lightly over the fourth, *vo’* — **v. 11.** *so many suitors*, the stanzas. — **SUITORS**: here I would understand it, strictly according to the etymology, as seekers or followers of *manze* or *amanze*, lovers. — **v. 12.** *they have you in person*, Florentine editions of 1814. Upon which reading Poliziano himself is introduced to speak in the Farce *The Poets* which is in the *Proposta*: "Are you familiar with the phrase *To stand* or *To go in chest and in person* <note>original: <term>Stare o Andare in petto e in persona</term></note> for *To walk* or *To stand upright of body*, and it is usually said of those who go about chest-out and live the fine life. I made use of this expression in the Ballad *My ladies, etc.*; and in the second stanza, speaking of the dandies, I said: **When there are so many suitors who walk upright and chest out etc.** Now this Tuscan phrase has not been understood at all by my Tuscan illustrator. He has substituted the verb **to walk** with the verb **to have**, and has read *v'hanno* <note>they have you</note> instead of **vanno** <note>they go/walk</note>." Thus, in the persona of Poliziano, writes **Vincenzo Monti**. But it should be noted that more commonly one reads and says *To go upon the person* (**Sigoli**, *Travels*, "How well they walk upon their person"), and that of *to go in chest* there are truly no other examples than this one by Poliziano: there is, however, the phrase *To stand in chest and in person* meaning *To stand firm and immobile in a place*: thus Firenzuola, pleasantly, in the dispute over letters with Trissino: "It seems to me that without doing a thing in the world he [the letter *k*] stands in the middle of the alphabet in chest and in person to laugh at those etc." — **v. 13.** *Today not*, Florentine editions of 1814. And from such a false reading proceeded the uncertainty in the understanding of this stanza: wherefore **Maggi** proposed changing the **And** that begins the following verse into **Since** (and this was done in the Silvestri edition) and to place a period at the end of verse 14.

->And they have you by the forelock;<-

->And know how to manage the situation<-
->And appear wild to them.<-

---

**v. 14. THEY HAVE YOU BY THE FORELOCK.** This is not entirely clear; unless it is meant to signify, **They hold you at their mercy or in their power.** For this expression, Dictionaries provide examples only in figurative senses, such as *To have the lion, or fortune, or time by the forelock*. — **v. 15. One must then steer clear, Florentine editions of 1814.** Maggi, in the previously cited *Appendix*, proposed reading *It is necessary* <note>original: <term>Uopo è</term></note> instead of *One must* <note>original: <term>Bisogna</term></note>, and *clear* <note>original: <term>netto</term></note> as the last word of the verse: however, he asserts that the Trivulziano manuscript reads, with a better lesson, *play clean* <note>original: <term>giucar netto</term></note>. The Riccardiano manuscript also reads *netto*. We did not accept the first correction; and we find it better to read **Bigna**, a shortening used by the Florentine common folk for the third person indicative of *to need* <note>original: <term>bisognare</term></note>, of which examples are found in the middle-class writers of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and which is still alive in the speech of the Florentine countryside. See the Comedies of **Fagiuoli** <note>Giovanni Battista Fagiuoli (1660–1742), a Florentine poet and playwright known for using local dialect.</note>. — **v. 19. VAIN FLIRTS.** Metaphorically, a **Civettone** is a false lover who courts women more out of vanity and the desire to brag about it than out of love (Florentine editions of 1814). — **v. 20. HAVE IT, that is, the brain.** **To have the brain above the cap** means **To proceed recklessly and with little sense** (Florentine editions of 1814). This phrasing is not recorded in Dictionaries as Poliziano uses it, *To have it above the cap*. — **21. They gaze at the, Florentine editions of 1814.** Maggi proposed, and Silvestri corrected in his edition: *Gazing at the*. Here it must mean: They look toward the air, swaggering and reckless. — **v. 22. Where their madness carries them (Florentine editions of 1814).** Maggi proposed and Silvestri corrected in his edition: *They go where the fool throws*. — **v. 24-25. THEY RAISE, that is, they lift.** Here the Florentine editors of 1814 had the "skill" to read in the manuscript, *That it is in the actors (!!!) then a laugh*. The good Maggi was scandalized by this, and by mere conjecture proposed to emend it: *And they make stories and laughter out of it, such that I could never say it*. — **v. 27. One must give them the shovel,** Riccardiano manuscript and Florentine editions of 1814.

### XXVII.<sup>1</sup>

Here we accepted the correction by Maggi, which was adopted in the Silvestri edition: such transpositions of words to the detriment of the verse's meter were not infrequent liberties taken by ancient copyists. — **To give the shovel** <note>original: <term>Dar di pala</term></note>: to drive them away, to sweep them out: or, as one would say today, **to take up the broom** <note>original: <term>pigliar la granata</term></note>. — v. 28. **Send them to the general**. I would not know how to explain it, except by taking it as a variant of the phrase **To deal in generalities** <note>original: <term>Spacciare pel generale</term></note> (equivalent to the other still-living phrase, **To stay on generalities** <note>original: <term>Stare su le generali</term></note>) interpreted thus by Varchi in the *Ercolano*: "It is said of those who, when asked or requested for something, answer finally without wanting too much to restrict themselves and come, as they say, to the point <note>original: <term>a' ferri</term>, literally "to the irons."</note>." — v. 32. **To have one**, Silvestri edition. — v. 33. **But leave for me your other suitors**, the manuscript and the Florentine editions of 1814: **But leave your other suitors**, Florentine editions of 1822. We accepted Maggi's correction adopted in the Silvestri edition.

<sup>1</sup> This Ballad is found in a small book of poems by various authors where the *Mantellaccio* <note>A satirical 15th-century Florentine poem.</note> appears, and it is attributed to Poliziano (Florentine Editions of 1814). It is also in the *Little Ballads etc. of the 15th Century* and in the *Songs for Dancing of 1562 and 1568*, noted in both printings with a 'P' at the beginning.

v. 4. **With whom etc.** In courtly language <note>original: <term>lingua aulica</term>, the refined language of the nobility.</note> one should say **With whom** <note>original: <term>Con che</term> or <term>con cui</term></note>. But the Tuscan people never, or rarely, use the signs and prepositions that grammar requires for the declination of the pronoun **that** <note>original: <term>che</term></note>, which is used by these people as indeclinable and absolute. And of this use, most classical and noble examples abound. Boccaccio, *Decameron* X, 8: "In which thing perhaps I would not be so liberal, if wives were found as rude or with that difficulty **that** <note>Meaning: "with which."</note> friends are found," and in the Introduction: "it seems to me I see the shadows of those who have passed away and not with those faces **that** <note>Meaning: "with which."</note> I was accustomed to:" in both of which passages, grammatically, one should have said **With which** <note>original: <term>Con che</term></note>. And many other examples of this use of **that** <note>original: <term>che</term></note> in different positions could be brought from Boccaccio and Petrarch.

v. 7. *avrei* <note>original: I would have</note>, Florentine editions of '14 and recent prints. — v. 11. *Ora i’* <note>original: Now I</note>, Ballads for dancing 1562 and '68, and recent prints: *ch’ egli è* <note>original: that he is</note>, Florentine editions of '14 and recent prints. — v. 13 and following. Maggi proposed reading *Full I find it*: and the correction passed into the Silvestri edition. We accepted, removing the redundancy of the "it" <note>original: <term>la</term></note>, the reading from the 15th-century Little Ballads: *I find it is full*. **FULL OF DREAMS.** Empty, with nothing. Thus *to live on dreams* and *to eat dreams* is said of one who has nothing to live on or eat. — v. 22. *finding himself awakened* <note>original: <term>isvegliato</term></note>, 15th-century Ballad, where *isvegliato* is certainly a typographical error instead of *isvogliato* <note>original: listless/unwilling</note>: *finding him awake*, Ballads for dancing 1562 and '68, Florentine editions of '14 and recent prints.

### XXVIII.¹

There is no more beautiful game
Nor one that pleases everyone more
Than being two and appearing as one:
<margin>4</margin> Let whoever does not believe it try it a little.
   Whoever does not know how to do it,
   Let them come to me so I may teach them.
   It is not necessary to use
   Much wit to learn it;
   Provided it comes from nature,
   As it comes to the little donkey
   Who is never so small
<margin>12</margin>   That he does not know how to do it a little.
I once saw a woman who was there
At first not very skilled,
And then by the second evening
She became a fine mistress of it.
Upon a broom plant stem

Your youth will not always be green,
As it is now.
A long time has already passed
Since I made myself your servant:
Now I see myself abandoned
Without ever having committed a fault:
Oh, have pity on me, my lord, <note>In the tradition of courtly love, the beloved is often addressed with titles of nobility or mastery, regardless of the gender of the recipient.</note>
Because of your great beauty.

I was indeed once among the chosen
In the highest and most worthy state;
Now I find myself among the neglected,
A wretched, unfortunate soul.
Love is certainly too ungrateful,
Giving to you such great beauty.

Do not wish without cause
To thus completely abandon me:
You have no reason, however,
To wish to leave me so:
Arise now to console me
By removing such hardness from your heart.

Nothing is so deceptive
As the time of youth:
Therefore, grant peace now
To your servant who is so humble.
Bitterness does not usually reign
In a noble heart <note>The "noble heart" (original: *cor gentile*) is a central theme in medieval and Renaissance Italian poetry, suggesting that true nobility is found in the capacity to love and show mercy rather than in social rank.</note>
Such as yours.

It is a quirk of the Tuscan language to transform certain nouns into the feminine that are masculine in the common language. Malispini and Villani use *cimiera* for *cimiero* <note>the crest of a helmet</note>. And Pulci in the *Beca*, stanza VIII, uses *pifferina* <note>a feminine diminutive of 'piffero,' a fife or small flute</note>. ## [APOCRYPHAL.]

### XXXV.

"O lovely mountain girls and shepherdesses,
From whence do you come so graceful and fair?" —
— "We come from the mountain heights near a little grove:
A tiny little hut is our dwelling,
With father and mother in a small bed <note>This likely refers to a humble, single-room dwelling where the family shared a living and sleeping space.</note>,
Where nature has always nourished us:
We return in the evening from the flowery meadow,
Where we have grazed our little sheep." —
— "What is the land where you were born?
For such beautiful fruit <note>A poetic metaphor for the young women themselves.</note> shines above all others.
You seem to me like creatures of love,
So much do your faces glow:
Neither gold nor silver shines upon you;
And though poorly dressed, you look like little angels.
Your beauties may well complain,
Since you show them only between valley and mountains;
For there is no land of such great heights <note>Referring to great cities or noble courts.</note>
Where you would not be worthy and honored.
Now tell me if you are content
To stay in the mountains so poor." —
— "Each of us is more content
To follow the herd to the pasture,
Than each of you [city women] is
To go dancing within your walls:

<meta>This page continues the philological discussion of the ballad introduced on page 346, debating whether the poem belongs to the Renaissance humanist Angelo Poliziano or the earlier 14th-century poet Franco Sacchetti.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>
<header>BALLADS.</header>

->We seek neither wealth nor further fortune,<-
->Save for beautiful flowers, and let us make little garlands.<- <margin>26</margin>

---

<margin>V. 26. little garlands <note>original: "ghirlandelle"</note>, Florentine editions 24.</margin> This ballad is not found in any of the manuscripts known to me that contain the rhymes of <term>Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant scholar and poet in the court of Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, nor even in the collection of 15th-century <term>Ballads</term>. It is, however, found in the two collections of *Songs for Dancing* by <term>Sermartelli</term> (1562 and 1568) and in another by <term>Simbeni</term> (1614), though not under Poliziano's name; indeed, the Simbeni edition attributes it to the <term>Magnifico</term> <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note>, and in the Sermartelli printings, it appears among those without an author's name. It is found, however, in the <term>codices</term> <note>handwritten manuscript books</note> that contain the rhymes of <term>Franco Sacchetti</term> <note>A famous Florentine writer (c. 1332–1400) known for his "Trecentonovelle"</note> and under his name; and it is given to Franco Sacchetti in several collections of *Ancient Rhymes*. In the manuscripts and printings that attribute it to Sacchetti, it has many <term>variant readings</term> <note>different versions of the text</note> and one extra stanza. Despite this, since the last century, it was attributed to Poliziano in some collections (for example, in the *Ancient Lyric Poets*, volume VI of the *Italian Parnassus* collected by <term>Rubbi</term>); and it is attributed to him by all modern editions of his poems, beginning with the Milanese edition of the *Italian Classics* (1808). One might believe that Poliziano had reworked it for use in some masquerade or festival of his time, and that from this arose the rumor attributing it to Poliziano. One might believe this, I say, if the <term>reading</term> <note>specific version of the text</note> assigned to Master <term>Angiolo</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano</note> were not more irregular and corrupt than the one bearing the name of the ancient storyteller and poet. I believe it belongs to the latter, both because of the authority of the manuscripts and because of the similarity it has to other pastoral ballads by Franco, and for its greater simplicity and ingenuity of style compared to Poliziano's verses. Perhaps this ballad by Franco remained for a long time in the mouths of the people; hence certain flaws and errors we recognize in the second version. It was therefore admitted, with other songs that are evidently popular—and which bear the scars of that popularity—into the Sermartelli collections. Finding it there, so graceful and pure in comparison to others that are somewhat crude or artificial, led those who did not know Sacchetti's rhymes to attribute it to the most graceful and pure poet of the 15th century. In any case, I place below the version assigned to Sacchetti by the manuscripts and many printings, following the Lucca edition of the *Rhymes of Master Franco Sacchetti*, published by Franchi and Maionchi, 1853. The editors wisely note: "This most graceful composition is also read among the *Songs for Dancing* by various authors, 1562, 1568 editions, etc., but with many variations. It was often attributed to Poliziano and to <term>Lorenzo de' Medici</term> and printed as their work, with manifest error and a worse reading. A <term>spiritual parody</term> <note>a religious version of a secular song, often using the same melody</note> of it is found in the *Book of Lauds* by various authors, and begins: *O lovely virgins of Jesus, where do you go so graceful and fair?* <note>original: "O vaghe di Giesù o verginelle, Dove n' andate si leggiadr' e belle?"</note> See the <term>Bonardo</term> edition on page 52."

> O lovely mountain shepherdesses,
> From whence do you come so graceful and fair?
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What is the land where you were born,
> Which brings forth such beautiful fruit more than others?
> You seem to me like creatures of love,
> So much does your face shine with beauty!
> Neither gold nor silver shines upon you,
> And poorly dressed you seem like little angels.

We stay in the mountains near a little grove:
A poor little hut is our dwelling:
With father and mother in a small bed
We return in the evening from the flowered meadow,
Where nature has always nourished us,

## I.¹

->I am constrained, since Love desires it,<-

<note>original Italian: "Io son constretto, poi che vuole Amore / Che vince e sforza tutto l' universo". This is the opening of a famous poem whose authorship is the subject of the following scholarly commentary.</note>

<warning>The left edge of the page is cropped, resulting in the loss of several characters at the beginning of each line in the left-hand column. Missing text has been reconstructed where possible for clarity.</warning>

This song was first [published] among a few other things of the [author] after the *Stanzas* and the *Orfeo* [by the house] of the Bazaleri in Bologna [around 1494], and then in Venice in 1506 [by Melchior]re Sessa and Pietro di Ravani. [Stagnino] of Monferrato later [faithfully] reproduced the edition; and then it came without further [doubt] among the *Rhymes* of Our Author <note>Poliziano</note> given [by the] Florentine [publishers] of 1814 and their [successors]. And already Father Affò, who [included i]t in the Bazaleri edition, [showed] he did not doubt the au[thorship] of it, when, in the last [disputati]on on the *Orfeo*—omitted in [this] edition because it is now [considered out of] date—he [drew the] argument from verses 124-141 that Poliziano was not of such a wretched and [base] [condi]tion as Varillas [claimed]. <note>Antoine Varillas (1624–1696) was a historian often criticized for inaccuracies regarding the status and character of Renaissance figures.</note> Certainly those verses do not [refer] to the person of the [author]. And that sign which gives [glory to his] fatherland should be understood [as the insig]nia of the Medici: "to profess [to be] a spirited dispenser of [the gifts of] fortune is to speak as a prince, never as a poet." This last observation is by Maggi, in the previously cited *Appendix* to volume III, part II, of the *Proposta*. This Maggi, admitting that **BY THE STYLE** the song could be believed to be *by Poliziano*, recognizing in it expressions that **STRONGLY** **RECALL** those read in the *Stanzas for the Joust*, was led to conjecture "either that Poliziano had written it in the name of the magnificent Giuliano, brother of Lorenzo, or that it was the work of Giuliano himself." Too rapid, to tell the truth, is the transition from one conjecture to the other. It was later found in a manuscript of the Marquis Trivulzio under the name of Giuliano de' Medici the Younger: and under this name, and with two other songs of his, it was printed by Silvestri at the end of the *Poems* of Poliziano. But I would not wish to run too quickly toward gifting the song *I am constrained* to the Duke of Nemours. <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1479–1516), son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, was the Duke of Nemours.</note> It is true that he is one of the speakers in Bembo’s *Prose* <term>Prose della volgar lingua|A foundational 1525 work on the Italian language</term> and in Castiglione's *The Courtier*; it is also true that he had a reputation in his day as a good rhymer. But the songs—

### To narrate with humble verse
### The great joy that abounds in my heart. <note>These lines are from the poem under discussion.</note>

***

...the songs and known sonnets by him, found in the collection on the death of Serafino Aquilano, in Crescimbeni, in the *Poligrafo* [Year IV], in Roscoe’s *Life of Leo X*, and in Silvestri’s appendix, are too common and too inferior to this most elegant, soft, and colorful song for them and this one to be considered the children of a single father. Furthermore, while the same Giuliano was alive and well—he who claimed to be a poet and, as a powerful lord, could command respect even in poetry—would such a beautiful thing have been printed among the works of another author without him or his friends reclaiming it for the *most magnificent* poet? 

In any case, Maggi and the author (perhaps Maggi himself) of the *Notice* placed before the three songs that follow Poliziano’s poems under the name of Giuliano de’ Medici in the Silvestrian edition, are inclined to believe the song in question belongs to the Giuliano killed by Bandini <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478), brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent, was assassinated during the Pazzi Conspiracy by Francesco de' Pazzi and Bernardo Bandini dei Baroncelli.</note> rather than to Giuliano, Duke of Nemours. They are driven to this by "knowing from the *Commentary on the Pazzi Conspiracy* that this Giuliano also wrote verses: <note>original Latin: "scripsit nonnulla carmina mire gravia et sententiarum plena"</note> *he wrote several poems that were wonderfully grave and full of wise sentiments*; and even more by the assertion there that he was <note>original Latin: "magni roboris et virtutis"</note> *of great strength and virtue*; which matches what the song says: *As robust as experience suggests.*" 

Regarding the poetic talent of the elder Giuliano, apart from the testimony of Master Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano</note>, no monuments remain to give us a sample: and the present song, with its very soft style and tender emotions, would not exactly correspond to the praise of being *wonderfully grave and full of wise sentiments*. And if the song were truly his, how is it that we have no other samples from such a graceful poet—who would rank among the most elegant of the time, surpassing even his brother Lorenzo in elegance and equaling Poliziano—when we have samples not only from the younger Giuliano and Piero, but even from Cosimo the Elder? 

I believe, therefore, that Angelo Poliziano composed this song in the name and service of the young lord with whom he shared the closest intimacy. And this would not be the first time that Poliziano lent his verses to Giuliano de’ Medici: for among the Latin epigrams of Poliziano, there is one addressed to *Simonetta* <note>Simonetta Vespucci, the famed beauty of the Florentine Renaissance and alleged muse of Botticelli and the Medici.</note>, where it is noted: <note>original Latin: "Julii est sententia a me versibus inclusa"</note> *"The thought is Giuliano’s, enclosed in verses by me."* And who knows if the song is addressed to that very Simonetta, later sung of so gracefully in the *Joust*? Furthermore, those praises that the lover so liberally gives himself—of nobility, wealth, beauty, and vigor—seem more appropriate if written by a third party: for praising oneself so crudely to the face of one's beloved is permitted only to Polyphemus the Cyclops in pastoral poetry. Finally, since these verses so closely resemble the best of Master Angelo in their elegance, softness, and color; until I am shown something from either Giuliano that can even remotely be compared to them; I shall continue to consider them the work of Poliziano.

***

V. 1. *constrained since*. Modern editions.
— v. 2. "This lord who forces all the world." Petrarch, *Triumph of Love* III. <note>A reference to Love personified as a powerful conqueror.</note>

<margin>12</margin>Of his timid tongue, does not love.

<margin>20</margin>With that host which is the enemy of love.

**Verse 13.** • "Give audience together to my grieving final words" <note>original: "Date udïenza insieme Alle dolenti mie parole estreme"</note> Petrarch, song 27. (Florentine Editions, 1814). — **v. 15.** Truly Crescimbeni reads *Mostra* <note>Shows</note>. — **v. 16:** "Crowned with oriental gems" <note>original: "Di gemme orïentali incoronata"</note> Petrarch (Florentine Editions, 1814) — **v. 17-18.** "When the horns of the moon had met with its orb full" <note>original: "Cornua cum lunæ pleno simul orbe coissent"</note> Ovid (Florentine Editions, 1814). — **v. 19. GREAT FOUNTAIN** : here used for the sea. I do not recall ancient examples: but on the authority of Poliziano, Cesarotti used this figure in the translation of Ossian’s *Berrathon*: "Like the moon that descends into the great fountain," and Foscolo in the fragments of Alcaeus: "...the island swimming through the Icarian fountain" — **v. 26.** *of mine*, Florentine editions of 1814 and 1822 and Silvestri. But that the grass feeds on weeping—on tears—is logical; on the eyes, no. Here the *from* [da] makes one feel the derivation of the unspoken moisture upon which the grass and flowers were feeding.

Verse 99. **Mene : me**. A <term>Tuscan idiom</term> <note>a regional speech pattern specific to Tuscany</note> used by writers in the early centuries who added an *e* or the syllable *ve* to *me* and other such monosyllables, saying *mee* or *meve* for *me*. From the 1400s onward, they more commonly added *ne*. However, examples of this exist as far back as the 1200s: Iacopone da Todi wrote: "Christ invites us to himself [sene], / And says: Come to me [mene]." — v. 109-112. To make sense of this stanza, we believed we must read *Ch' è a* (What is there), placing the question mark at the end of the sentence. The 1858 Florentine edition reads *Che a dir* (That to say), without a question mark. — v. 114. Understand the subject "faith" as belonging to the verbs "consumes" and "undoes." — v. 115. We felt it necessary to change the reading of the 1858 Florentine edition, which was "Alas, foolish to whom," into "Alas! foolish is he who."

<note>The following are editorial notes from the 1858 Florentine edition.</note>

...than others. Instead of *rappator* (thief/snatcher) one should probably read *zappator* (hoer/peasant): and *tracano* or *tarcano* is perhaps no different from *tarchiano*, which in Tuscan usage is said of peasants and means "coarse" or "boorish." *Caterchio* would be a corruption of *terchio*, an antiquated word with the same meaning; according to Bianchini, *Lucchese Vocabulary*, cited by Pietro Fanfani in the *Vocabulary of Tuscan Usage*. And *marca terra*? perhaps *land of the Marches* or *from the Marches*? <note>The Marches are a region of central Italy, historically seen as a frontier area.</note> Or should it be read as *marca o terra*, understanding *marca* as a possession, territory, or district? (see Ducange.) — verse 215. FOR. Here it means, "Although." — verse 224. THEMSELVES (*Sè stessi*) for *himself* (*sè stesso*); here and in verse 230 in the rhyme. It appears that this ending in *-i* was used especially when *stesso* (self) referred to a person; just as in the same case one continued to use *egli, quegli, questi* instead of *ello, quello, questo*. Dante, *Inferno* IX, 28: "Thus spoke the master: and he himself <note>original: "egli stessi"</note> turned me." Lorenzo de’ Medici, *Ballades*: "I do not complain of you nor of myself <note>original: "me stessi"</note>." But Dante (*Paradiso* V, 133) also refers it to the sun: "Just as the sun, which hides itself <note>original: "egli stessi"</note> because of too much light." — verse 226. CARRY (*Portar*). To endure: as above, at verse 128, *porto* (I carry/endure). Iacopone da Todi: "To you it was not fearful to carry <note>endure</note> pain for me." — verse 231. Thus the manuscript has it. (Note from the 1858 Florentine edition.) Perhaps in verse 229 one should read *Volse* (He wished).

The Florentine editors of 1814 first published it among the *Rhymes* of **N. However, it was already in print in the *Collection of all the Triumphs, Chariots, Masquerades and Carnival Songs etc.*, edited by **A. F. Grazzini**, Florence, **1558**, and in another edition by Canon **Bracci**, dated Cosmopoli <note>A pseudonym for Livorno</note> **1750**: and it appeared there with the title *Triumph of the Goddess Minerva*, under the name of **M. Agnolo Divizio da Bibbiena**. To whom we gladly return it, also because it has no similarity to Poliziano's style, and because the ugly Magliabechiano manuscript that attributes it to **N. A.** seems to us to have little authority.

# VI.¹
## ON THE DEATH OF THE MAGNIFICENT LORENZO DE’ MEDICI.
### I.

> Death, to take away the richest treasure
> That was under the heavens, haughtily uprooted

---

**Verse 18.** The Magliabechiano manuscript and the **1814** Florentine edition read, *Che desiam è tante lune*: but the verse must be a **hendecasyllable** <term>endecasillabo</term> <note>A line of poetry consisting of eleven syllables, the standard meter of Italian high poetry.</note>, which is why Maggi, in the oft-cited Appendix, proposed the emendation, *Che tutti desiammo, è tante lune*. Already the Molinari edition and the **1822** Florentine edition had corrected it, but outside the rhyme scheme, as *Che desiam, è tante lune e tante*. The Silvestri edition did better: *Che desiammo, è tante e tante lune*. The two collections by C. Carn., which at verse 16 read *la fortuna* [fortune], here nonsensically have: *Che desiavi tanto e tanto : l’una.* We accept the Silvestri emendation, without however changing the word *desiam* [we desire]. — **v. 19.** *L’onorato*, C. Carn. **1558** and **1750**. — **v. 21.** *Ch’ avrai*, ibid.

**¹** This and the following chapter and the triplet in the style of an epitaph were published by the Florentine editors of **1814** from the Riccardian manuscript **2599**, which is highly incorrect (where Giovanni Mazzuoli, known as "Lo Stradino" <note>A colorful 16th-century Florentine book collector and eccentric known for his vernacular manuscripts.</note>, collected several compositions regarding the House of Medici), and were later reproduced by Molinari [**1819**] and others; until Silvestri excluded them from his edition [**1825**] with this **warning:** "I have rejected the two chapters on the death of Lorenzo de' Medici inserted in editions prior to mine, because, in the judgment of the learned, they are so wretched and reviled that it would do a great injustice to Poliziano to hold them as his own: and a Trivulzian manuscript assigns them to Giuliano, the son of Lorenzo de' Medici." We also do not believe these verses to be the work of Poliziano, but we cannot concede that they are the handiwork of Giuliano, Lorenzo's son. The reader will clearly sense that it is a follower and a favorite of the House of Medici speaking, and not a son or brother. Furthermore, when Lorenzo died in **1492**, Giuliano was only thirteen years old. Be that as it may, in reproducing them, if for no other reason than as a historical document, we have compared them against the Riccardian manuscript; we have made use of a few corrections from the Molinari edition; and we have ventured some of our own. Are physicians not permitted to perform experiments on "a worthless subject"? <note>original: "in anima vili." A Latin legal and medical maxim suggesting it is better to experiment on something of little value before risking something precious.</note>

The editor argues that while the verses are likely not by Poliziano, they remain valuable historical documents of the Medici circle.</summary>

The phrasing of this sentence responds better to the two lines by Virgil [*Eclogue I*] from which it is imitated: <note>original: "Ante leves ergo pascentur in æthere cervi, Et freta destituent nudos in litore pisces."</note> "First, therefore, shall light stags graze in the air, and the seas leave the fish naked on the shore." 
— v. 33. **THE WOODS AND MOUNTAINS.** Implied: *shall be, or it will be believed they moved behind, etc.* 
— v. 40. From here until the end of verse 50, the various sentences depend on **First everyone will believe** from verse 37. 
— **AT THE GOLDEN FLEECE.** That is, in the enterprise of the Golden Fleece. 
— v. 49. **Your virtue** <note>original: "Sua virtù"</note>, the manuscript and the 1814 Florentine edition. 
— v. 52. **even the** <note>original: "in sino il"</note>, instead of **COMMON PAGANS**: the common people of paganism, or the pagans. As is not uncommon in our thirteenth and fourteenth-century writers and in the Provençal poets, the preposition of the second case [the genitive "of"] is omitted here: Guittone [d'Arezzo], *Letters*: "Lady mother [of] God;" <note>original: "Madonna madre deo"</note> and "day [of] judgment" <note>original: "die giudicio"</note> is common among the ancients for *the day of judgment.* 
— v. 56-57. Alludes to the Camel- <note>The note likely intended "Camelopardo," the archaic term for a giraffe.</note>

**OF THESE:** meaning those of Lorenzo. — **THE BEAUTIFUL CHOIR OF NYMPHS:** The choir of the — v. 61. **And the sea,** etc. Certain accidental phenomena were said to have foretold the death of the Magnificent <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, just as they once foretold that of Caesar. A lightning bolt fell, two days [before his death], upon the dome of Santa Maria del Fiore <note>The main cathedral of Florence.</note>; for three nights in a row, streaks of fire were seen in the sky, starting from Fiesole and moving toward San Lorenzo, where the Medici family tombs are located. —

**POLIZIANO.** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist scholar and close friend of Lorenzo.</note>

v. 67. **FLOWS BY.** <note>original: "ALLUVIA"</note> The Tuscan versifier, with this ugly verb—the creation of which no one will envy him—intended to say what the Latin poets signified in similar cases with the word *adluit* <note>meaning "washes against" or "flows near."</note>. A massive rainstorm disturbed the entry into Rome on March 22, 1492, of Giovanni de' Medici, Lorenzo's son, who, having been honored with the cardinal's purple, was coming to take his place in the consistory. Lorenzo died on April 8, 1492. — v. 78. **RELATIVE:** common father, *father of the fatherland*. <note>original: "padre della patria"</note>

# VARIOUS RHYMES.

[To be] but a smoke of a vainglory,
  Snow in the sun; already so much proclaimed
  That it has filled every poem and history.
Truly this stubborn human living,
  Without valuing who is upright or who rules,
  Always placed death at everyone’s side.
O protector of your holy law,
  Medici <note>The poet uses the Latinate "Medice."</note> born in stone <note>A wordplay on his father's name, Piero, which means "Peter" or "Stone."</note>, upon you indeed rains

Neither for so many great deeds and long merits
  Do you care any longer; but, as if you were lowly
  Among so many fames of times past,
Only, if ever you were merciful and humble
  When you were on earth, in heaven you give yourself comfort,
  O lover of your noble people.
Your burning desire you had brought to port,
  Having made from the sacred council <note>The College of Cardinals.</note>

  Illustrious heir and true successor
  To the virtues of that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious and civil laws.</note>;

That under the reckless lordship of Piero, the Catos and Fabricius and Brutus would have wanted to return to life is I know not whether more stupid or nauseating adulation by this wretched versifier: but, as if by design, when he was writing such nonsense, Filippo Strozzi was already born—who in his final years was to seem and boast himself a Cato in respect to Cosimo—and around that time Francesco Ferrucci was being born, who was in part the Fabricius and entirely the Decius of the glorious republic, daughter of Rome; and later he was to be born <note>referring to Lorenzino de' Medici</note> "who with a strong arm dealt the first Duke of Florence his death." — v. 36. *E Caton*, the printed editions. — v. 37. *In cupo lato*, the printed editions: the manuscript is not very clear: we have believed the current emendation to be reasonable. — v. 39. The verses toward the end of the stanzas carry a period and no other punctuation—or only a comma—at the end of the following verse. — v. 41. **APPEARS** <note>original: "PARE"</note>: following verse 37, it means: she reveals herself. 51. **And nor Lavinia**, manuscript reading for: **Turnus, Pallas**, as found in the printed editions. — v. 53-4. This is roughly what Ariosto sang in very different verses: 
> "Augustus was not so holy nor so merciful as the trumpet of Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> sounds; his having good taste pardons him for his wicked proscription;" <note>Referring to the idea that Augustus’s crimes were forgiven by history because he patronized great poets like Virgil.</note>

and this is what happened to most of the Medici. — v. 55. Dante, *Purgatorio* I, regarding Cato: 
> "...death in Utica was not bitter to you for her [liberty's] sake." 

— v. 62. **VALERIUS THE SUPERLATIVE**: that is, Valerius Maximus. Admire this new invention <note>The commentator is praising the poet's clever nickname for the historian.</note>. The sentence structure seems to be this: As for Rome, only Titus the Paduan, Justin, and Valerius Maximus preserve immortal her noble throng, that is, the great number of her glorious sons.

<summary>This page concludes a poetic argument that military and political greatness (represented by Scipio, Caesar, and Cato) only achieves immortality through the work of great writers and historians (like Virgil, Cicero, and Livy). It specifically links this classical tradition to the Medici family's patronage of the arts.</summary>
