V. 82. *immortal idea*, the editions. By this "idea" it seems we should understand literature in general, or rather the glory and virtue of studies and erudition. As we can see, this worthy versifier believed he was preaching *for his own benefit* <note>original: "pro domo sua."</note> and fighting *for his altars and hearths* <note>original: "pro aris et focis," meaning for his home and livelihood.</note>; but he had as much to do with poetry and Poliziano as his Valerius of the *superlative* had to do with history and Livy. — 85. *human dead* <note>original: "uman morto"</note>, the editions. Reading, as I do, strictly according to the manuscript, *dead*, we find in the preceding word the substantivized adjective *human* <note>original: "umano"</note> for *human being*, the plural of which, *the humans* <note>original: "gli umani"</note>, is rejected by purists as being of French usage. Like Latin, they ought to say: the example of our versifier, who nonetheless may have some authority in the language, should be added as a more striking example to the two from the *Morgante Maggiore* <note>An epic poem by Luigi Pulci (1432–1484).</note>, which Mamiani—guilty of "injured purism" for having written *the humans*—brought to his own defense in the preface to the *Poesies*, Florence, 1857. — v. 88-93. <header>VARIOUS RHYMES.</header>

### III.¹

->**Cruel death that came into this body!**<-
->**For after he died, the world went upside down:**<-
->**While he lived, he kept everything in peace.**<- <margin>3</margin>

---

<margin>⁴</margin> This <term>epitaph</term> <note>A short text honoring a deceased person, often intended for a tombstone.</note> appears to have been written some years after the death of the <term>Magnificent</term> <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and a massive patron of Renaissance culture.</note>, when the harmony among the Italian lords had dissolved, and the "barbarian ruin" <note>A common historical reference to the foreign invasions of Italy, specifically the French invasion of 1494.</note> loomed over the beautiful country. He did not see it, just as <term>Angelo Poliziano</term> <note>A brilliant humanist scholar and poet close to Lorenzo.</note>—who died nearly two months before the entry of <term>Charles VIII</term> into <term>Florence</term>—did not see the expulsion of <term>Piero de' Medici</term>. And here, after five years of study, more than once interrupted by the trembling expectation and the tumult of marvelous events—not the least of which was the expulsion from Florence of the foreign lordship that succeeded the Medici—finally lifting my hand from these poor illustrations today, May 31, 1863, not without a feeling akin to grief, I take my leave of you, O glorious father of the most glorious Renaissance.

->THE END.<-

<summary>This page presents a concluding three-line epitaph for Lorenzo de' Medici, emphasizing how his death led to the end of peace in Italy. The editor provides a poignant closing note dated 1863, reflecting on the historical parallels between the 1490s and his own era.</summary>
<keywords>Lorenzo the Magnificent, Angelo Poliziano, Charles VIII, Florence, Italian Wars, Renaissance, 1863, epitaph, Piero de' Medici</keywords>

<meta>This page contains a portion of a poem written in terza rima (a three-line stanza form) from the "Miscellaneous Rhymes" section of the collection. # MISCELLANEOUS RHYMES.

It would be, if he did not have the pen with him,
<margin>66</margin>Compared to the sea, a tiny stream.
You, Greece, if Homer were not with you,
Achilles would not only be unnamed
<margin>69</margin>But never even known as a Greek.
And the barbarian Hannibal would not have gone
To lose his eye upon the cold Apennines,
<margin>72</margin>Nor would he have been so victorious at Cannae,
If he had believed that in a single morning
He would lose both life and name, when he took
<margin>75</margin>The ring to his mouth and the serpentine poison. <note>Hannibal is said to have committed suicide by drinking poison hidden in a ring to avoid capture by the Romans.</note>
And he who conquered so much land,
I mean Alexander, would have exerted in vain
<margin>78</margin>So great an effort for such great deeds.
Therefore your good father <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent," who was Poliziano’s patron.</note> loved his Poliziano,
Because he knew that he
<margin>81</margin>Held the pen in hand for him alone.
Love you also this immortal idea,
Glorious virtue, the light of day
<margin>84</margin>In Latin, Greek, Arabic, and Chaldean. <note>Refers to the four major languages of ancient scholarship.</note>
It can raise every dead human from the urn
Forever, and recall our Tuscany
<margin>87</margin>From the lowly and nocturnal people.
All of you, work with your virtue

---

V. 82. *immortale idea* [immortal idea], the editions. By this "idea" it seems one should understand literature in general, or the glory and virtue of studies and erudition. As one can see, the worthy versifier believed he was preaching <term>pro domo sua<gloss>for his own benefit</gloss></term> and fighting <term>pro aris et focis<gloss>for altars and hearths; for his very existence</gloss></term>: but he had as much to do with poetry and Poliziano as his *Valerio of the superlative* had to do with history and Livy. — 85. *uman morto* [human dead], the editions. Reading strictly according to the manuscript, as I do, *morto*, we find in the preceding word the substantivized adjective *umano* [human] used for "human being," the plural of which, *gli umani* [the humans], is rejected by purists as being of French usage. They should have said "Latin": the example of our versifier, who nonetheless may have some authority in language, should be added as a more striking instance than the two from the *Morgante Maggiore* <note>A famous 15th-century heroic-comic poem by Luigi Pulci.</note> which Mamiani—guilty of "lese-purism" for having written *gli umani*—brought to his own defense in the preface to the *Poems*, Florence, 1857. — v. 88-93. He addresses all the sons of Lorenzo together or the entire...

The commentary discusses linguistic debates regarding "purism" in the Italian language.</summary>
<keywords>Poliziano, Homer, Hannibal, Alexander the Great, Lorenzo de' Medici, Italian Purism, Mamiani, Morgante Maggiore, Terza Rima, literary immortality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the poem in terza rima addressed to a member of the Medici family. # MISCELLANEOUS RHYMES.

So excellent and vast, that material is never 
<margin>90</margin>lacking for us; the heavens show you such light!
O divine lineage, unconquered and free,
destined for great deeds, fame, and trials,
<margin>93</margin>weary of life sooner than of doing good! <note>The Medici family. Line 93 references a magnificent verse by Petrarch concerning Camillus: "Weary of life sooner than of doing good." (original Latin: *Di vita prima che di ben far lasso*)</note>
Trophies, colossi, temples in Rome to Jove,
aqueducts, columns, amphitheaters,
<margin>96</margin>and pools and baths never seen elsewhere,
and effigies, statues, and theaters
have not been able to preserve, in the end,
<margin>99</margin>the ancient fame of the old fathers.
All things high, immortal, and divine,
whatever was ever made upon the seven hills <note>The seven hills of Rome, representing the height of Roman civilization.</note>,
<margin>102</margin>yet is turned into ash and ruins.
But those whom the Muses exalt at their springs
flourish forever, budding and green;
<margin>105</margin>while ports, scepters, purple robes, arches, and bridges fail. <note>Line 105: "E MANCA" means they fail or come to an end. Other versions say "Ne mancan" (nor do they lack).</note>
See: your laurel always turns green again
upon the mountain where you may yet ascend:
<margin>108</margin>for whoever believes otherwise wastes time.
I could inflame you with a thousand examples;
but, because I called you a burning <term>pyrope</term> <note>original: *piropo*; a fiery red gemstone, often identified as a carbuncle or garnet, symbolizing intense brilliance or passion.</note>,
<margin>111</margin>I know that you still burn to spend your coin. <note>Line 111: The panegyric concludes with a reference to the "conio" (coin/minting stamp).</note>
These people hoped for nothing else
from you. Show, then, such ardor
<margin>114</margin>to surpass your relative in fame.
Earth, sea, and heaven grant you favor.

---

<summary>This page concludes a poetic tribute to a member of the Medici family, arguing that while the physical monuments of ancient Rome have crumbled into ruin, the glory bestowed by literature and the Muses is immortal. The poet encourages his patron to surpass the fame of his ancestors through virtuous deeds and the support of the arts.</summary>

<keywords>Medici family, immortality of poetry, Roman ruins, Muses, Petrarch, Camillus, pyrope, laurel, patronage</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the collection of miscellaneous rhymes. This final page provides a three-line epitaph for Lorenzo the Magnificent and the editor's concluding remarks from 1863.</meta>

# MISCELLANEOUS RHYMES.

### III.¹

->**Cruel death that came into this body!**<-
->**For after he died, the world turned upside down:**<-
->**While he lived, he held all things in peace.** <margin>3</margin><-

---

<margin>*</margin> This epitaph appears to have been written some years after the death of the Magnificent <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), known as "the Magnificent," was a statesman and patron of the arts who maintained a delicate balance of power in Italy.</note>, when the harmony among the Italian lords had dissolved, and the "barbarian ruin" <note>A reference to the foreign invasions of Italy, specifically by the French and Spanish, which began shortly after Lorenzo's death.</note> hung over the beautiful country. Angelo Poliziano <note>A renowned humanist scholar and poet close to Lorenzo.</note> did not see it, just as he did not see the expulsion of Piero de' Medici; he died nearly two months before the entry of Charles VIII into Florence. And here, after five years of studies—more than once interrupted by fearful expectations and the tumult of marvelous events, not the least of which was the expulsion from Florence of the foreign lordship that succeeded the Medici—finally lifting my hand from these poor illustrations, today, May 31, 1863, not without a feeling akin to sorrow, I take my leave of you, O glorious father of the most glorious Renaissance.

->THE END.<-

<summary>This concluding page features a poignant three-line epitaph for Lorenzo de' Medici, lamenting the chaos that engulfed Italy after his death, followed by the editor's personal sign-off in 1863.</note>
<keywords>Lorenzo the Magnificent, Angelo Poliziano, Charles VIII, Florence, Italian Wars, Medici family, Renaissance, 1863</keywords>
